H₂SO₄ at 0 °C to 25 °C, often with acetone as co‑solvent.

Hydration of trifluoroacetaldehyde to its gem‑diol; water adds across the carbonyl to give 2,2,2‑trifluoro‑1,1‑ethanediol; the equilibrium lies toward the diol in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst or special conditions are required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of a para‑bromo‑nitro aromatic with sulfide ion; purpose is to install a thiol group. The bromide is displaced by S^2‑ (from Na2S) to give 4‑nitrothiophenol. Typical conditions: Na2S (often hydrated) in polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, heated to 80‑120 °C under inert atmosphere; sodium bromide formed as by‑product.

Double‑replacement/precipitation (acid‑base) reaction; cadmium acetate reacts with ammonium hydroxide to produce cadmium hydroxide precipitate and soluble ammonium acetate; the transformation involves exchange of the cadmium and ammonium ions and precipitation of Cd(OH)₂; performed in aqueous solution, typically at ambient temperature, with careful control of NH₄OH concentration to avoid dissolution of the precipitate.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of benzene with 4‑hydroxybenzoyl chloride using aluminum chloride; forms 4‑hydroxybenzophenone (a diaryl ketone) and HCl; performed anhydrous at 0‑25 °C in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide under nitrogen.

Acid–base neutralization forming the calcium salt of L‑aspartic acid. Purpose is to produce calcium L‑aspartate, a soluble calcium source. Key transformation is proton transfer from the carboxyl groups of L‑aspartic acid to the hydroxide, yielding water and the calcium chelate. Typical conditions: aqueous suspension of Ca(OH)₂ mixed with L‑aspartic acid at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (≈40 °C) with stirring until dissolution; no catalyst needed.

Acid anhydride synthesis by reacting 2,2‑dimethylpropanoic acid with acetic anhydride; yields pivalic (2,2‑dimethylpropanoic) anhydride and acetic acid; typically refluxed in an inert solvent (toluene or dichloromethane) with removal of the generated acetic acid; no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic iodination of5‑chloro‑8‑hydroxyquinoline with N‑iodosuccinimide; replaces a hydrogen on the quinoline ring to give clioquinol and succinimide; usually carried out at temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile.

O‑Methylation of catechol to veratrole using methyl triflate as the methyl donor and pyridine as base; produces two equivalents of pyridinium triflate as by‑product; conducted under anhydrous conditions in dichloromethane or dichloroethane, typically 0 °C to rt.

Hydrolysis (carbonate decomposition) of methyl propan‑2‑2‑yl carbonate with water; purpose is to cleave the carbonate to simple alcohols and carbon dioxide. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl, releasing methanol, isopropanol and CO₂. Conducted at ambient to mild heating (25–60 °C) in aqueous medium; can be acid‑ or base‑catalyzed (e.g., 0.1 M HCl or NaOH) to speed the reaction. No special solvent required beyond water.

Acid‑catalyzed ring‑opening hydration of tetrahydrofuran with water in the presence of p‑toluenesulfonic acid, affording 1,4‑butanediol; performed by refluxing the THF/water mixture with catalytic TsOH, often in bulk or in a biphasic system at elevated temperature.

Radical benzylic bromination of propylbenzene using bromine (or Br₂ with a radical initiator such as peroxide or UV light) to give 1‑bromopropylbenzene; carried out in an inert, non‑polar solvent like carbon tetrachloride or benzene at ambient temperature under photochemical or peroxide initiation.

Acid–base neutralization; liberates free benzidine from its dihydrochloride salt. Aqueous sodium hydroxide (2 equiv) deprotonates the benzidine·2HCl, forming benzidine, water and NaCl. Typically carried out at ambient temperature in water; no catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (fluorination) reaction; dimethylchlorosilane (Me₂SiClH) reacts with anhydrous hydrogen fluoride, substituting the chlorine atom for fluorine to give dimethylfluorosilane (Me₂SiFH) and hydrogen chloride gas. Usually carried out at 0–25 °C in excess HF as both reagent and solvent, using PTFE‑lined equipment; no additional catalyst.

Alkaline hydrolysis using sodium carbonate; the carbonate acts as a mild base to hydrolyze the P–F and P‑O‑isopropyl bonds, yielding sodium methylphosphonate, isopropanol, NaF, and releases CO₂ from carbonate neutralization; performed in aqueous Na₂CO₃ solution (≈0.5 M) at 40–80 °C; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl chloride by pyrrolidine to give N‑benzylpyrrolidine. The amine attacks the benzylic carbon, displacing chloride as HCl. Conducted in an anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acitrile, DMF) often with excess pyrrolidine or a base to trap HCl; reflux or room‑temperature conditions are common.

Reductive dimerization of nitrobenzene to azoxybenzene. Sodium dithionite reduces nitrobenzene under basic aqueous conditions (NaOH) to the azoxy linkage (Ph‑N=N(O)‑Ph). Reaction is performed at moderate temperature (0‑25 °C) in water; no metal catalyst is needed.

Jones oxidation; primary benzylic alcohol oxidized to the corresponding carboxylic acid (4‑dimethylaminobenzoic acid). Chromic acid (CrO₃/H₂SO₄) in acetone oxidizes the –CH₂OH group, producing water and Cr₂O₃ as the reduced chromium product. Usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature, under stirring, with aqueous acetone as solvent.

Jones oxidation (strong oxidation); oxidizes adamantan-1-ol to adamantane-1-carboxylic acid; uses chromium(VI) oxide in sulfuric acid (CrO₃/H₂SO₄) in aqueous acetone; reaction carried out at 0–25 °C with stirring; yields chromium(III) sulfate and water as by‑products.

Halogen exchange / reagent generation; PCl₅ reacts with trimethylsilanol to give trimethylsilyl chloride, POCl₃ and HCl. The reaction proceeds via substitution of the silanol OH by chlorine, forming TMSCl and phosphoryl chloride. Conducted anhydrously under inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to reflux in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., dichloromethane); no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed O‑methylation (transesterification) of quercetin using dimethyl carbonate under microwave heating. K₂CO₃ detonates phenolic OH groups, and dimethyl carbonate transfers methyl groups, yielding 5‑hydroxy‑3,7,3',4‑tetramethoxyflavone with CO₂ and methanol as byproducts. Typical conditions: sealed microwave vessel, 120‑150 °C, dimethyl carbonate as solvent, K₂CO₃ (1‑2 equiv). No metal catalyst needed.

Thermal decomposition (dehydration) of manganese(II) hydroxide to manganese(II) oxide; purpose is to obtain the oxide by loss of water; key transformation Mn(OH)2 → MnO + H2O; typically performed by heating the solid at 300‑400 °C in the absence of air; no solvent, often under inert atmosphere.

Hydrolysis (neutral or mild acid) of acephate. The N‑acetyl amide bond is cleaved, releasing acetic acid and generating O,S‑dimethyl phosphoramidothioate (the deacetylated metabolite). Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient or slightly elevated temperature (20–60 °C); water is the solvent, no special catalyst required.

A double‑displacement/precipitation reaction between sodium hydroxide and lead(II) metavanadate; purpose is to convert insoluble lead(II) hydroxide into a precipitate while forming soluble sodium metavanadate; key transformation NaOH + Pb(VO3)2 → NaVO3 (in solution) + Pb(OH)2 (solid); carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, no special catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of the aromatic ring of toluene to give methylcyclohexane; purpose is to fully saturate the benzene ring; key transformation C6H5CH3 + 3 H2 → C6H11CH3; typically performed under high H2 pressure3–5 MPa) at 120–180 °C using a metal catalyst such as PtO2, Pd/C, or Raney nickel; reaction is run in an inert organic solvent (e.g., ethanol, cyclohexane) or neat.

Acid‑base metathesis of methanol with sodium carbonate to generate sodium methoxide, carbon dioxide and water; purpose is to produce the alkoxide reagent; key transformation 2 CH3OH + Na2CO3 → 2 NaOCH3 + CO2 + H2O; carried out by refluxing methanol with solid Na2CO3; methanol acts as both reactant and solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Solid‑state double decomposition between calcium oxide and ammonium chloride releasing ammonia gas; purpose is to generate gaseous NH3 and form calcium chloride; key transformation CaO + 2 NH4Cl → CaCl2 + 2 NH3↑ + H2O; performed by heating the mixture (typically 200–300 °C); no solvent, reaction proceeds in the gas phase; inert atmosphere not required.

Type: Oxidative cleavage of an alkene (acidic, cold KMnO₄). Purpose: convert the C=C bond into carboxylic acids and CO₂. Key transformation: cleavage of but‑3‑enoic acid to give propanedioic acid (malonic acid), carbon dioxide, MnO₂ precipitate, and water. Typical conditions: dilute KMnO₄ in aqueous H₂SO₄, temperature 0‑5 °C, short reaction time; MnO₂ removed by filtration.

Nucleophilic substitution of a secondary alkyl iodide with ammonia form a primary amine; 2‑iodohept reacts with excess NH₃ (gaseous or in anhydrous ethanol/ammonia solution) to give 2‑heptylamine and HI; typically heated at 80‑120 °C in a sealed tube or pressure vessel, with the HI neutralized by a base (e.g., NaOH) if desired.

Grignard addition of methylmagnesium bromide to ethyl octanoate, yielding a tertiary alcohol (2‑methyl‑2‑nonanol) and ethanol as by‑product; purpose is to synthesize a branched tertiary alcohol from an ester; key transformation CH3MgBr + CH3CH2COOCH2CH3 → (CH3)2C(OH)C9H19 + CH3CH2OH; performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, under nitrogen or argon; excess Grignard reagent is often used; no external catalyst is required.

Direct synthesis (combination) redox reaction; elemental sodium reduces bromine to form sodium bromide; carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere, often at low temperature to moderate the exothermicity, no solvent or catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 4‑bromophenol; the hydroxyl group directs nitration to the ortho position, giving 4‑bromo‑2‑nitrophenol and water. Performed with concentrated HNO3 (often with H2SO4 as a catalyst) at 0–5 °C, then warmed; reaction medium is a mixture of nitric and sulfuric acids.

[2+2] Cycloaddition of a perfluoroalkyne with elemental sulfur – Hexafluoro‑2‑butyne reacts with sulfur (often S₈) under thermal or photochemical activation (120–150 °C) in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or toluene. The process forms the four‑membered heterocycle 3,4‑bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,2‑dithiete via a cycloaddition that inserts two sulfur atoms across the C≡C bond. No additional catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation of magnesium sulfate with sodium carbonate; Mg²⁺ exchanges anions to form insoluble MgCO₃ while Na⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ yielding Na₂SO₄ in solution. Performed in water, typically at ambient or slightly elevated temperature to enhance precipitation; no catalyst is used.

General type: deprotonation (acid‑base) of a terminal alkyne with an organolithium base to generate a lithium acetylide. Purpose: prepare a nucleophilic acetylide for subsequent carbon‑carbon bond formation. Key transformation: n‑butyllithium abstracts the acetylenic proton of trimethylsilylacetylene, forming butane and lithium trimethylsilylacetylide. Typical conditions: dry, aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether, temperature from –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

General type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) methylation using a sulfonium salt. Purpose: O‑methylation of phenoxide to give anisole while producing dimethyl sulfide as a benign by‑product. Key transformation: phenoxide oxygen attacks a methyl group of trimethylsulfonium tetrafluoroborate, breaking the S‑C bond, yielding dimethyl sulfide and anisole; the tetrafluoroborate anion pairs with Na⁺ to form NaBF₄. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or DMF), mild heating (40–80 °C), often under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

General type: halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution) on a triazine ring. Purpose: replace the three chlorine atoms of cyanuric chloride with bromine to afford 2,4,6‑tribromo‑1,3,5‑triazine. Key transformation: each Cl on the triazine is displaced by Br⁻ from sodium bromide, producing three equivalents of NaCl and the tribromo product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF, reflux or elevated temperature, excess NaBr; no catalyst required.

General type: oxidative conversion of a primary allylic alcohol to an α,β‑unsaturated carboxylic acid (chromic‑ oxidation). Purpose: synthesize but‑2‑enoic acid from but‑2‑en‑1‑ol. Key transformation: the primary alcohol is oxidized first to the aldehyde and then further to the carboxylic acid under acidic dichromate conditions, while the C=C double bond remains intact. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄, Na₂Cr₂O₇ (or K₂Cr₂O₇) as oxidant, heating to 80–120 °C, often with reflux; no additional catalyst.

General type: base‑mediated neutralization/hydrolysis of an ammonium nitrate salt. Purpose: liberate free 2‑aminoethanol from its azanium nitrate salt. Key transformation: OH⁻ deprotonates the protonated amine, yielding water and the free amine; nitrate pairs with Na⁺ to give NaNO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring; no special catalyst needed.

General type: double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Purpose: exchange anions to precipitate insoluble lead chromate, often for isolation or analytical detection. Key transformation: Pb²⁺ combines with CrO₄²⁻ to form yellow PbCrO₄ solid, while Na⁺ pairs with SO₄²⁻ to remain in solution as Na₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, room temperature, vigorous stirring; product filtered; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution/dehydration of chloromethanol with hydrogen chloride to afford dichloromethane. The hydroxyl group is protonated, water departs to give a chloromethyl carbocation that is captured by chloride ion, yielding CH₂Cl₂. Typically performed by refluxing chloromethanol in excess gaseous or aqueous HCl at 50‑80 °C; the acid itself serves as the catalyst.

Acid–base salt formation; aqueous neutralization of ammonia with carbon dioxide and water yields ammonium bicarbonate; typically performed by bubbling CO₂ into a cold aqueous NH₃ solution at 0‑20 °C; no catalyst required; water acts as solvent.

Acylation (esterification) of an alcohol with acetyl chloride in the presence of pyridine; purpose is to protect or modify the hydroxyl as an acetate ester. Ethyl 4‑hydroxybutanoate reacts with acetyl chloride to give ethyl 4‑acetoxybutanoate and HCl, which is scavenged by pyridine to form pyridinium chloride. The reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform under inert atmosphere; pyridine serves both as base and solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); chlorine electrophilically attacks meta‑cresol to give 3‑methyl‑4‑chlorophenol and HCl; carried out in aqueous or mildly acidic medium at 0‑30 °C to limit poly‑chlorination; chlorine gas is the reagent; no additional catalyst.

Oxidative synthesis of persulfuric acid; concentrated H₂SO₄ reacts with H₂O₂ to form peroxydisulfuric acid (H₂S₂O₈) and water; conducted at low temperature (0‑5 °C) in excess sulfuric acid; no separate solvent or catalyst beyond the acid; careful temperature control is essential.

Acid–base precipitation reaction where calcium bicarbonate reacts with oxalic acid to give calcium oxalate solid, carbon dioxide and water; performed in water, often with cooling to enhance precipitation, no catalyst needed.

Halogenation of alcohol with phosphorusabromide; PBr₅ reacts with methanol to produce methyl bromide, hydrogen bromide, and phosphorus oxybromide (POBr₃); performed under anhydrous conditions, often in a dry inert solvent such as CH₂Cl₂, at 0‑25 °C; inert atmosphere may be used; no catalyst.

Hydrolysis/decomposition of dianilinomercury; water attacks the Hg–N bonds of dianilinomercury, liberating aniline and precipitating mercury(II) oxide; usually carried out by stirring the solid in refluxing water (80‑100 °C) or aqueous base; no catalyst required.

Redox oxidation of Fe(II) by chlorine; Cl₂ oxidizes FeCl₂ to FeCl₃ while being reduced to chloride ion; performed in aqueous (often acidic) solution at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; no additional catalyst.
Redox reaction; purpose to oxidize Cr(II) to Cr(III); Cl2 acts as oxidizing agent, converting Cr²+ to Cr³+; reaction in aqueous solution under acidic conditions; no additional catalyst required.

Carbothermic reduction of scandium oxide with carbon to yield scandium metal and carbon monoxide; conducted at very high temperatures (≈1500‑2000 °C) in a furnace under inert or reducing atmosphere; carbon acts as reductant, no additional catalyst.

Acid-base reaction; neutralization of phosphoric acid with ammonium carbonate; carbonate protonation releases CO2, producing diammonium hydrogen phosphate; aqueous solution, typically at ambient temperatures; water as solvent.

Esterification (acylation); synthesis of amyl acetate (ester) via nucleophilic attack by amyl alcohol on acetic anhydride; mild heating, often catalyzed by acid (e.g., H2SO4); acetic acid or inert solvents used.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage) of octan‑2‑yl benzoate; water attacks the carbonyl carbon, producing benzoic acid and 2‑octanol. Conducted by refluxing the ester in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1–2 M HCl) or with aqueous base followed by acid work‑up. The reaction proceeds to completion over several hours, and the products are separated by extraction.
Double displacement (precipitation); AgNO3 and SnBr4 exchange ions forming insoluble AgBr; aqueous medium drives reaction due to AgBr low solubility; no catalyst required.
Oxidation of alcohol to carboxylic acid; H2O2 oxidizes 4-hydroxybenzyl alcohol to 4-hydroxybenzoic acid in presence of acetic acid; typically acidic conditions and heat; catalytic systems may vary.

Oxidation of 4‑hydroxy‑2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine to the nitroxide using m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (mCPBA); carried out in CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to rt; yields 4‑hydroxy‑2,2,6,6‑tetramethylpiperidine‑1‑oxyl and m‑chlorobenzoic acid; analogous peracid oxidation of a secondary amine to a nitroxide radical.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2) with a strong amide nucleophile. Purpose: convert the alkyl chloride into a primary amine. Key transformation: Cl is displaced by NH₂⁻ from sodium amide, followed by protonation to give cyclopentylamine. Typical conditions: NaNH₂ dissolved in liquid ammonia, low temperature (−33 °C to 0 °C), inert atmosphere.

Pd‑catalyzed oxidative acetate transfer (acetoxylation) of 2‑phenylethanol with vinyl acetate; the alcohol is esterified to 2‑phenylethyl acetate while vinyl acetate is reduced to acetaldehyde; typical conditions include Pd(OAc)₂ (5 mol %), a base (e.g., triethylamine), toluene or dioxane as solvent, 80‑120 °C under inert atmosphere

C‑alkylation of diethyl malonate (active‑methylene alkylation) with allyl bromide via SN2 to give diethyl 2‑allylmalonate; performed in dry polar aprotic solvent (DMF, MeCN) with potassium carbonate or the potassium diethyl malonate salt, heated to reflux (≈60‑80 °C).

Enzymatic methyl transfer; S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine donates a methyl group to the C‑6 position of 5‑methylbenzimidazole yielding 5,6‑dimethylbenzimidazole and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine; conducted in aqueous buffer (pH 7‑8) at physiological temperature (30‑37 °C) with the appropriate methyltransferase enzyme.

Double‑displacement metathesis/precipitation; barium perchlorate exchanges anions with lithium sulfate to form insoluble BaSO₄ (precipitates) and soluble LiClO; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Mitsunobu esterification; triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate activate salicylic acid, allowing coupling with phenol to produce phenyl salicylate, with triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazine dicarboxylate as by‑products; standard conditions use THF or dioxane, 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere.

Metal‑acid reaction; magnesium metal reacts with octanoic acid to form magnesium octanoate and liberate hydrogen gas. Typically carried out by heating the acid with excess Mg (neat or in a non‑protic solvent such as THF) under reflux.

Decarboxylation; removal of the carboxyl group from ferrocenecarboxylic acid to regenerate ferrocene. Thermal decarboxylation is typically carried out by heating the ferrocene‑1‑carboxylic acid under an inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen) at 180–250 °C, sometimes in a high‑boiling solvent like diphenyl ether or in the melt. No external catalyst is essential, although copper salts can be used to promote the process. Carbon dioxide is liberated as the sole gaseous by‑product.

Acidic tin(II) chloride reduction of a nitro group; SnCl₂ in concentrated HCl reduces 3,5‑dimethyl‑1‑nitrobenzene to 3,5‑dimethylaniline, producing water and oxidizing SnCl₂ to SnCl₄. Conducted by refluxing the substrate in aqueous HCl with excess SnCl₂.

Oxidative dissolution (redox) of manganese arsenide with nitric acid; HNO₃ oxidizes Mn to Mn³⁺/Mn²⁺ forming soluble manganese nitrate, and oxidizes As to arsenic acid (H₃AsO₄). Conducted by refluxing MnAs in concentrated HNO₃ (≈70 %) at 80‑120 °C until complete dissolution; aqueous medium, no extra catalyst.

Esterification of 4‑methylphenol with acetyl chloride; a nucleophilic acyl substitution forming 4‑methylphenyl acetate and HCl. Typically run in an aprotic solvent (CH2Cl2 or CHCl3) at 0 °C to rt with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the released HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; converts N‑butylacetamide into acetic acid and butylamine by cleavage of the C–N bond; water adds across the amide carbonyl under strongly acidic conditions (e.g., 6 M HCl) at reflux (≈100 °C) for several hours; aqueous or aqueous/alcoholic solvent; no special catalyst other than the acid.

Aminolysis of an ester; methylamine attacks methyl pivalate, displacing methanol and giving N‑methyl pivalamide. Usually performed reflux in a solvent like toluene or benzene with excess amine to drive the equilibrium toward product.

Direct fluorination of niobium nitride; a route to niobium pentafluoride (NbF₅). Passing F₂ gas over NbN at elevated temperature (300–500 °C) converts the nitride to NbF₅ while nitrogen gas is liberated. Conducted in a fluorination reactor with corrosion‑resistant materials; no catalyst needed.

Redox/metathesis reaction; reduces Cu(II) to insoluble Cu(I) iodide and oxidizes iodide to elemental iodine; CuCl2 aqueous solution is mixed with excess KI at room temperature, often in water; the CuI precipitates as a white solid, I2 dissolves giving a brown color, KCl remains in solution; no catalyst required.

Esterification (carbamate formation); carbamic acid reacts with methanol, eliminating water to afford methyl carbamate. Performed under mild acid catalysis (e.g., HCl or p‑TsOH) with continuous removal of water (azeotropic distillation) to shift the equilibrium.

Jones oxidation of a primary allylic alcohol; chromic acid (CrO₃/H₂SO₄) oxidizes 3,7‑dimethyloct‑6‑en‑1‑ol to the corresponding carboxylic acid, yielding water as a by‑product. Carried out in acetone at 0 °C to room temperature.

Intramolecular oxidative cyclization of o‑allyl phenol to benzofuran. CAN generates a phenoxy radical that adds to the pendant allyl double bond, forming a new C–O bond and closing the furan ring with loss of a small fragment (often as formaldehyde). Reaction is carried out in MeCN/H₂O (≈1 : 1) at 0‑25 °C; CAN is the stoichiometric oxidant and acid.

Double displacement (metesis) reaction in aqueous solution; used to exchange anions and precipitate the less soluble praseodymium fluoride while forming soluble potassium nitrate; typically carried out by dissolving the salts in water, stirring at ambient temperature, and filtering the precipitate.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution forming a carbonate; phenol acts as nucleophile toward a carbonyl bromide (COBr₂) to generate diphenyl carbonate with release of HBr; performed under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, often with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HBr.

Transesterification/decarboxylative esterification;ionic acid reacts with dimethyl carbonate to give methyl propionate and methanol while carbon dioxide is liberated; catalyzed by a base (e.g., NaOMe or K₂CO₃) or a metal alkoxide, heated at 150–200 °C in a sealed reactor or under reflux in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or polar aprotic media.

SN2 alkylation of a carboxylate (nucleophilic substitution) where the propionate anion displaces chloride of phenethyl chloride to afford 2‑phenylethyl propionate and potassium chloride; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at elevated temperature (80–120 °C) with stoichiometric potassium propionate and often a phase‑transfer catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes ethyl bromoacetate to give the sodium salt of bromoacetate and ethanol; performed in aqueous NaOH solution, typically heated under reflux; the product mixture is acidified to isolate the free acid if desired.

Condensation amidation; formic acid reacts with isopropylamine to form N‑isopropylformamide with elimination of water; usually driven by removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) or by employing a dehydrating agent; carried out under reflux in a solvent such as toluene or xylene, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid or using coupling reagents for higher yields.

Metal reduction / preparation of a nickel boride catalyst. Sodium borohydride reduces NiCl2, producing Ni2B (nickel boride) as a fine black solid, hydrogen gas and NaCl as by‑products. Typically carried out in anhydrous alcoholic solvent (e.g., ethanol or THF) under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to rt; the evolution of H2 is observed and the Ni‑B precipitate is filtered and washed.

Base‑promoted nitrile hydrolysis (acid–base conversion). Aqueous NaOH hydrolyses the three cyano groups of tris(2‑cyanoethyl)phosphine to the corresponding carboxylates, yielding tris(2‑carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP) and ammonia, with NaCl formed from the original HCl salts. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; after completion the mixture may be acidified to isolate the free phosphine as its sodium salt or as the free acid.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of formic anhydride with ammonia; yields formamide and formic acid. Typically run in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen; no catalyst required.

Selective oxidation of a secondary alcohol (Dess‑Martin oxidation). Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidises the 6‑hydroxy group of codeine to a keto group, converting codeine into hydrocodone. The reaction is performed in an aprotic, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; the by‑products are the reduced iodine(V) reagent (iodobenzoic acid) and traces of water.

Salt neutralisation / free‑base liberation. Cystamine dihydrochloride is treated with two equivalents of NaOH, which deprotonates the ammonium centres, releasing free cystamine (NH2CH2CH2)2S2, water and sodium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution at rt with stirring; the free diamine can be extracted into an organic solvent or isolated after lyophilisation.

Hydrolysis of cyclopentanecarbonyl chloride; general type = acid‑chloride hydrolysis (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose = obtain the free carboxylic acid; key transformation = Cl is replaced by OH, generating cyclopentanecarboxylic acid and HCl; typical conditions = aqueous work‑up at 0 °C → room temperature, often with a slight excess of water; common solvents/catalysts = reaction can be run in a biphasic system (e.g., CH₂Cl₂/water) and a base such as NaHCO₃ or pyridine is used to neutralize the liberated HCl.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification for synthesis of di‑tert‑butyl dicarbonate (Boc₂O). Purpose: preparation of a carbamate protecting reagent. Key transformation: tert‑butanol reacts with dimethyl carbonate, exchanging methyl carbonate groups for tert‑butoxy groups to give Boc₂O and methanol (5 t‑BuOH + 6 DMC → 3 Boc₂O + 8 MeOH). Typical conditions: reflux (80‑120 °C) with removal of methanol to drive equilibrium, catalytic base such as KOtBu, Na₂CO₃ or DMAP. Often performed neat or in a high‑boiling solvent (toluene).

Redox oxidation of iodide (iodine generation). In acetic acid solution, sodium iodide is oxidised by sodium periodate to molecular iodine while the periodate is reduced to sodium iodate;etic acid is converted to sodium acetate and water is formed. Typically performed at rt in a mixture of AcOH/H2O, the reaction provides a convenient in‑situ source of I2 for subsequent iodination reactions.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); purpose is to introduce an acetyl group onto benzene to form acetophenone; acetyl chloride is activated by the Lewis acid BF3·OEt2, generating an acylium ion that attacks benzene, producing acetophenone and HCl; carried out under anhydrous conditions in an inert atmosphere, using benzene (or another non‑coordinating solvent) as solvent, at 0 °C to ambient temperature; BF3·OEt2 is the catalyst.

Double displacement (acid–base) reaction; sulfate from sulfuric acid exchanges with acetate on copper(II) to produce copper(II) sulfate and acetic acid; conducted in aqueous medium, usually with mild heating to aid solubility; no catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium dihydrogen phosphate; upon heating (≈200‑300 °C) the solid breaks down to releaseous NH₃ and H₂O while forming solid P₂O₅ (phosphorus pentoxide). No solvent; carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere or open furnace.

Carbothermal reduction‑halogenation of lutetium(III) oxide; solid Lu₂O₃ is mixed with elemental iodine and carbon and heated strongly (≈900‑1100 °C) in a sealed tube or inert furnace. Carbon reduces the oxide to LuI₃ while itself is oxidized to CO gas. No liquid solvent; often performed under argon or vacuum.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl bromide with aqueous ammonia; 2‑bromo‑6‑methylheptane reacts with excess NH₃ (often in water/ethanol) at 0‑50 °C to give 2‑amino‑6‑methylheptane and HBr (present as NH₄Br). Reaction proceeds best in polar protic solvent; temperature kept low to suppress elimination.

Oxidation of a methyl group on an aromatic ring; 2,4‑dinitrotoluene is treated with chromic acid (generated from Na₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄) under reflux (≈80‑100 °C). The benzylic CH₃ is oxidized to a carboxyl group, yielding 2,4‑dinitrobenzoic acid and water. Acidic aqueous medium is typical; the reaction is a strong oxidizing (chromic‑acid) oxidation.

Photocatalytic oxidative hydroxylation; pyrene dissolved or suspended in water with TiO₂ (anatase) is irradiated with UV light (λ < 385 nm). Photo‑generated holes produce •OH radicals that hydroxylate pyrene to 1‑hydroxypyrene, while coupling of •OH gives H₂O₂ as a by‑product. Conditions: aqueous TiO₂ slurry, ambient temperature, continuous UV illumination, often oxygen‑saturated.

Oxidative enzymatic deamination/decarboxylation of L‑tyrosine; purpose is catabolism of the amino acid to a phenylacetaldehyde. Key transformation: removal of the α‑amino group as NH3, decarboxylation to CO2 and oxidation of the side‑chain to 4‑hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde with formation of H2O2. Typical conditions: aqueous buffer, molecular oxygen, enzyme (e.g., tyrosine oxidase/monoamine oxidase) at physiological pH and temperature; no external solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑base reaction with strong acid; treatment of disodium hexanedioate with concentrated H2SO4 protonates the carboxylate groups to afford adipic acid, while sodium ions combine with sulfate to form Na2SO4. Performed in a mixture of water and conc. H2SO4, often with gentle heating to drive off water and improve conversion.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑vinylpyridine to give 2‑ethylpyridine. The C=C double bond is reduced by H₂ in the presence of a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Pt, Raney Ni) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–80 °C, atmospheric pressure; reaction proceeds under mild pressure.

Acid–base/metathesis reaction of nitrosyl chloride with ammonium hydroxide; NOCl hydrolyzes in the presence of NH₄OH to give NH₄Cl and NH₄NO₂. Conducted in aqueous solution at ≤ 0 °C to prevent thermal decomposition of the nitrite. No special catalyst required.

Reaction type: acid‑mediated dehydration (conversion of amidoxime to amidine). Purpose: synthesize acetamidine hydrochloride from acetamidoxime. Key transformation: the N‑O bond of the amidoxime is removed; SOCl₂ acts as a chlorinating/dehydrating agent, releasing HCl and SO₂ and forming the C=N amidine functionality. Typical conditions: stir the amidoxime hydrochloride with excess thionyl chloride under anhydrous conditions, often inloromethane or chloroform, at 0 °C to reflux; pyridine or a tertiary amine may be added to trap HCl. Common solvents/catalysts: inert organic solvent (CH₂Cl₂, THF); no additional catalyst needed.

Reaction type: acid leaching/solid‑liquid digestion of fluorapatite. Purpose: industrial production of phosphoric acid and hydrofluoric acid while generating gypsum as a solid by‑product. Key transformation: Ca₅(PO₄)₃F reacts with H₂SO₄, phosphate groups are converted to H₃PO₄, fluoride is liberated as HF, and calcium is precipitated as CaSO₄. Typical conditions: mix fluorapatite with excess conc. H₂SO₄ and heat to 200–250 °C in a sealed or vented reactor; reaction proceeds in the melt, no separate solvent. Common reagents: concentrated (≈98 %) sulfuric acid; reaction often performed under nitrogen to prevent oxidation.

Nitrosation of a secondary amine. Purpose: formation of the nitrosamine N‑nitrosopyrrolidine. Key transformation: nitrous acidgenerated in situ from NaNO₂/HCl) reacts with pyrrolidine to give N‑nitrosopyrrolidine + H₂O. Typical conditions: cold (0‑5 °C) aqueous acidic medium, often in water/acetone mixture. No catalyst required.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed transesterification. Purpose: exchange ethyl ester groups for methyl groups, yielding the dimethyl ester and ethanol as a by‑product. Key transformation: the carbonyl oxygen of diethyl 2‑methylpropanedioate is protonated by H₂SO₄, facilitating nucleophilic attack by methanol; ethoxy groups are displaced as ethanol, and the ester is converted to the methyl analogue. Typical conditions: excess methanol, catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄ (1–5 %), reflux (≈65 °C) for several hours; removal of ethanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the reaction forward. Common solvent: methanol itself serves as both solvent and reactant; inert atmosphere is optional.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenolytic dealkylation). Purpose: removal of a propyl substituent from propylbenzene to regenerate benzene and produce propane. Key transformation: a metal catalyst cleaves the C(sp²)–C(sp³) bond under hydrogen, adding hydrogen to both fragments; the propyl group is reduced to propane, while the aromatic ring regains aromaticity as benzene. Typical conditions: high‑pressure H₂ (30–50 atm), temperature 200–300 °C, using a supported metal catalyst such as Pt/C, Pd/C, or Raney Ni; reaction performed in a liquid hydrocarbon solvent (.g., cyclohexane) or under solvent‑free conditions in a flow reactor. No additional reagents required.

Reaction type: metathesis/halogen‑exchange organometallic synthesis (formation of tetraaryltin). Purpose: preparation of tetraphenyltin, a useful organotin reagent. Key transformation: each phenyl group from phenyl‑lithium replaces a chloride on SnCl₄, producing LiCl and the tetra‑phenyl‑tin product. Typical conditions: low temperature (−78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere, using dry ethereal solvents such as THF or diethyl ether; phenyl‑lithium is added slowly to a solution of SnCl₄ to control exotherm. Common solvents/catalysts: anhydrous THF or Et₂O; no additional catalyst is required.

Halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution) of POCl3 with KF to replace one chloride by fluoride, yielding POCl2F and KCl. Used to prepare phosphoryl dichloride fluoride. Usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone or DMF at reflux temperature; solid KF is added to a solution of POCl3 under inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) of 3‑bromopyruvic acid by sulfide ion from Na2S, converting the α‑bromo carbon to a thiol group and forming mercaptopyruvic acid with NaBr as by‑product. Typically performed in aqueous or aqueous‑ethanol medium, mildly heated (40‑60 °C) and neutral to slightly basic pH to keep sulfide nucleophilic.

Grignard addition to an imine (Schiff‑base) followed by aqueous work‑up. Purpose: synthesis of N,N‑dimethyl‑1‑phenylethylamine. Key transformation: methylmagnesium bromide adds to the C=N bond of N‑[(E)‑benzylideneamino]‑N‑methylmethanamine, forming a magnesiated intermediate; protonation yields the tertiary amine and MgBrClitates. Conditions: anhydrous ether or THF, 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar). Quench with dilute NH₄Cl. No additional catalyst.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) in aqueous solution where AgNO₃ reacts with CsIO₃ to form soluble CsNO₃ and sparingly soluble AgIO₃, which precipitates. Typically carried out at room temperature in water; the mixture is filtered to isolate the AgIO₃ solid.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose: prepare 2,5‑dichlorobenzoyl chloride for further acylation or coupling reactions. Key transformation: the carbonyl oxygen is replaced by chlorine, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: add thionyl chloride (1.2–1.5 equiv) to the acid in dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to rt; often a base such as pyridine or triethylamine is added to scavenge HCl; the reaction is usually performed under anhydrous conditions with inert atmosphere.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 4‑chlorobenzyl chloride by the nitrogen of 2‑imidazoline, forming the antihistamine antazoline and releasing HCl. Reaction is usually performed in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or isopropanol) with a mild base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to scavenge HCl, heated under reflux for several hours.

Acid‑base/complexation reaction of ammonium bifluoride with silica (SiO₂) yielding water, ammonium fluoride and ammonium hexafluorosilicate ((NH₄)₂SiF₆). Conducted in aqueous solution, often with heating (80‑100 °C) to promote dissolution of SiO and formation of the fluorosilicate complex.

Reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; NaBH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of 2‑ethylhexanal, converting the C=O into a C‑OH group and generating 2‑ethylhexanol, while the borohydride is oxidized to sodium borate. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature in protic solvents such as methanol, ethanol, or a methanol‑THF mixture; reaction proceeds under inert atmosphere and is quenched with water or dilute acid.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an ester; water attacks the carbonyl carbon of nonyl acetate, cleaving the C–O bond to give acetic acid and 1‑nonanol. In acidic hydrolysis, dilute HCl (or H₂SO₄) is used at reflux (≈80 °C) in aqueous ethanol; in basic hydrolysis (saponification), NaOH or KOH in water/ethanol at reflux followed by acid work‑up yields the same products.

DCC‑mediated amide coupling (peptide‑bond formation). Purpose: preparation of Tolibut (an anilide). Key transformation: dicyclohexylcarbodiimide activates the carboxyl group of 4‑amino‑3‑methylbenzoic acid, allowing nucleophilic attack by 4‑methylaniline to form the amide; dicyclohexylurea is liberated as by‑product. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or DMF, 0 °C then rt, under nitrogen. No metal catalyst.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution with acetate; purpose is to convert a primary alkyl bromide into the corresponding acetate ester, a protected alcohol or fragrance precursor. Acetate ion (CH₃COO⁻) attacks the carbon bearing Br, displacing Br⁻ and forming 3‑methylbutyl acetate and KBr. Common conditions: polar aprotic solvent (acetone or DMF), potassium acetate in excess, reflux or ambient temperature; often performed under dry conditions to avoid hydrolysis. No catalyst needed.

Intramolecular dehydration of a dicarboxylic acid to a cyclic anhydride; heating 2,2,3,3‑tetramethylsuccinic acid in the presence of a strong dehydrating agent (e.g., acetic anhydride, P₂O₅, or POCl₃) removes water and closes the five‑membered ring to give tetramethylsuccinic anhydride. Conditions generally involve reflux in dry pyridine or toluene at 120–150 °C, with removal of generated acid by azeotropic distillation.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) of 3‑ethyl phenyl acetate; NaOH attacks the carbonyl to give 3‑ethyl phenoxide, which after acid work‑up yields 3‑ethyl phenol and sodium acetate stays in solution. Conditions: aqueous NaOH, 60‑100 °C, reflux; followed by acidification (e.g., with HCl) to free the phenol.

Type: Metal‑hydride reductive dehalogenation. Purpose: Replace halogen atoms with hydrogen to afford the saturated alkane. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbon bearing Br and Cl, reducing both C–X bonds to C–H, yielding propane, LiBr, LiCl, and Al(OH)₃ as by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), reflux, under nitrogen or argon. No catalyst required.

Simple acid–base neutralization to form an inorganic salt; gaseous or aqueous NH₃ reacts with hexafluorophosphoric acid (HPF₆) to produce ammonium hexafluorophosphate (NH₄PF₆). The reaction is carried out in water at 0–25 °C to avoid hydrolysis of the PF₆⁻ anion; the salt precipitates upon cooling and can be filtered and dried.

High‑temperature reduction of a rare‑earth oxide by hydrogen; Ho₂O₃ is exposed to flowing H₂ gas at temperatures above ~1500 °C in a quartz or alumina tube furnace. Hydrogen reduces the oxide to metallic holmium, producing water vapor as the only by‑product. The process is conducted under an inert carrier gas (Ar) to control the hydrogen partial pressure and prevent oxidation of the metal product.

Reaction type: salt formation/oxidation (preparation of solid oxidizer). Purpose: synthesize sodium perborate as an oxidizing agent. Key transformation: hydrogen peroxide adds to sodium metaborate forming the perborate complex (NaBO3·nH2O). Typical conditions: aqueous sodium metaborate solution, addition of H2O2 at 0–40 °C, pH neutral to slightly basic, followed by crystallization. Common solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Acid‑base double‑displacement precipitation; aqueous sodium hydroxide neutralizes magnesium dihydrogen phosphate, forming insoluble Mg(OH)₂ (precipitate) and soluble sodium dihydrogen phosphate, typically at ambient temperature in water.

Reaction type: zinc/ammonium chloride reduction (Béchamp reduction) of an aromatic nitro group. Purpose: convert 2,3‑dichloronitrobenzene to 2,3‑dichloroaniline. Key transformations: nitro group is reduced to an amino group; zinc is oxidized to ZnCl2; ammonium chloride supplies protons, generating NH3 and H2O as by‑products. Typical conditions: reflux mixture of substrate, excess zinc dust and solid NH4Cl in aqueous ethanol or water, 60–100 °C. Common solvents: ethanol/water; no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization with evolution of CO2. Purpose: generate monosodium arsenate salt. Key transformations: arsenic acid transfers a proton to bicarbonate, producing carbon dioxide, water and NaH2AsO4. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring. Common solvent: water; no catalyst.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization (metal acetate formation). Purpose: prepare bismuth acetate. Key transformations: bismuth hydroxide reacts with acetic acid, releasing water and forming bismuth acetate (Bi(OAc)3). Typical conditions: reflux in excess glacial acetic acid or in acetic acid as solvent. Common solvent: glacial acetic acid; no catalyst.

Type: Acid–base neutralization / salt metathesis of a thiolate. Purpose: protonate sodium methanethiolate to release methanethiol. Key transformation: CH3S–Na+ abstracts a proton from HCl, forming CH3SH and NaCl. Typical conditions: dilute aqueous or mixed aqueous/organic medium, addition of HCl at 0 °C to ambient temperature, vigorous stirring; product extracted into an organic layer.

Acid‑base neutralization leading to precipitation; employed to obtain cadmium phosphate. Cd(OH)₂ neutralizes phosphoric acid, substituting OH⁻ for PO₄³⁻ to give Cd₃(PO₄)₂ (insoluble) and water. Carried out in water, often with stirring and mild heating; the phosphate precipitates out, allowing isolation by filtration; no catalyst needed.

Reaction type: acyl chloride esterification using pyridine as base. Purpose: acetylate 4‑methoxybenzyl alcohol to afford its acetate protecting group. Key transformations: acetyl chloride reacts with the alcohol to give 4‑methoxybenzyl acetate and pyridinium chloride. Typical conditions: anhydrous dichloromethane (or THF) at 0 °C then room temperature under inert atmosphere. Catalyst/base: pyridine (stoichiometric). No additional catalyst.

Swern oxidation; converts the secondary alcohol 1-(2-methoxyphenyl)ethanol to the corresponding ketone 2‑methoxyacetophenone. Key transformation: oxidation of –CH(OH)– to –C(=O)– using oxalyl chloride to activate DMSO, followed by addition of triethylamine to neutralize HCl. Typical conditions: oxalyl chloride (1.0 equiv) and DMSO (2.0 equiv) in dry dichloromethane at –78 °C, then substrate addition, then triethylamine (3.0 equiv) at –78 °C to 0 °C. Solvent: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂; inert atmosphere advisable.

Acid‑base neutralization and salt metathesis. Potassium carbonate reacts with the hydrobromide salt of ethylamine, liberating free ethylamine base while carbonic acid decomposes to CO2 and H2O; potassium ions combine with bromide to give KBr. Typically performed in aqueous solution with gentle heating to drive off CO2.

Methylation (O‑methylation) of morphine using diazomethane. The phenolic hydroxyl of morphine is methylated to form codeine, with nitrogen gas released as by‑product. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dry diethyl ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is usually done under an inert atmosphere to avoid diazomethane decomposition.

Double displacement reaction; forms iron(II) carbonate precipitate; carbonate ion from sodium carbonate displaces acetate; aqueous environment at room temperature; sodium carbonate acts as a weak base.

Reaction type: Double displacement/precipitation. Purpose: Preparation of magnesium hydroxide or strontium sulfate. Key transformation: Ion exchange forms strontium sulfate and magnesium hydroxide precipitates. Conditions: Ambient conditions. Solvent: Water. Catalyst: None required.

Acid‑salt metathesis (double displacement). Concentrated sulfuric acid protonates the phosphateion of nickel(II) phosphate, releasing phosphoric acid and forming soluble nickel(II) sulfate in the aqueous phase. Carried out in water, often with heating to enhance dissolution and complete conversion.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to the corresponding acyl chloride using thionyl chloride; nicotinic acid → nicotinoyl chloride; by‑products SO2 and HCl gas evolve; performed under anhydrous conditions, typically in dry dichloromethane or chloroform, with reflux or gentle heating; inert atmosphere may be used.

Halogenation/oxidative substitution of germane. Elemental iodine reacts with GeH4 to replace a hydrogen atom with iodine, yielding hydrogen iodide and iodogermane (GeH3I). The reaction proceeds via radical or electrophilic pathways, typically under UV irradiation or mild heating in an inert gas atmosphere; no solvent is required or a non‑reactive solvent such as dry benzene may be used.

Acid leaching of silicate. Concentrated hydrochloric acid attacks magnesium silicate, breaking the Si–O–Mg linkages to produce silica (SiO2) precipitate, water, and soluble magnesium chloride. Performed in aqueous HCl with reflux heating; the solid SiO is filtered off after cooling.

Double‑replacement precipitation. Thallium(I) nitrate reacts with ammonium carbonate in aqueous solution; thallium carbonate, being poorly soluble, precipitates while ammonium nitrate remains in solution. The reaction is carried out at ambient temperature in water, and the thallium carbonate solid is isolated by filtration.

Thermite redox displacement: aluminium reduces tin(IV) oxide to tin metal while being oxidized to aluminium oxide; performed by mixing Al powder with SnO₂ and heating to high temperature (≈1000 °C) in an inert atmosphere, no solvent required.

Peroxide synthesis (solid‑liquid reaction). Magnesium oxide reacts with hydrogen peroxide solution to form magnesium peroxide and water. Provides a route to solid peroxide storage compounds. Carried out in aqueous H₂O₂ (typically 30 % w/w) at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) to limit peroxide decomposition; no catalyst required.

Diazotization–cyclization: 2‑aminobiphenyl is treated with NaNO₂ and HCl to form a diazonium salt, which undergoes intramolecular electrophilic aromatic substitution with loss of N₂ to give carbazole; carried out in aqueous HCl at 0–5 °C then gently warmed, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed aziridine ring‑opening hydrolysis: 1‑aziridineethanol reacts with water (often with a catalytic amount of HCl or NaOH) to cleave the three‑membered ring, yielding 2‑aminoethanol (ethanolamine); performed at ambient to reflux temperature in aqueous media.

Selective catalytic hydrogenation of an acid chloride to an aldehyde (R‑COCl → R‑CHO). Hydrogen gas over palladium on barium sulfate (a poisoned Pd catalyst) reduces 2‑methylbutyryl chloride to 2‑methylbutanal. Typical conditions: 1 atm H₂, Pd/BaSO₄ in a dry, inert solvent such as ether or THF, at ambient temperature; reaction is stopped before further reduction to the alcohol.

Diazotization followed by hydrolysis (Sandmeyer phenol formation): 2‑aminonaphthalene is converted to the corresponding diazonium salt using NaNO₂/HCl at 0 °C, then warmed in aqueous solution so that the diazonium group is replaced by OH, producing 2‑naphthol, N₂ gas and NaCl; typical conditions are cold acidic medium followed by mild heating.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of a di‑methyl ester to the corresponding dicarboxylic acid (azelaic acid) and methanol. Usually treated with aqueous NaOH (1–2 eq) at reflux, then acidified to pH 1–2 to precipitate azelaic acid. Solvent mixture of water/ethanol or water/THF; no additional catalyst needed.

Fluorination oxidation: elemental fluorine reacts with ruthenium pentafluoride gas to add one more fluorine atom, forming ruthenium hexafluoride (RuF₆); conducted in the gas phase under excess F₂ at elevated temperature (≈150–250 °C) and moderate pressure, no solvent.

Enzymatic/acyl‑transfer reaction where acetyl‑CoA donates its acetyl group to the hydroxyl of L‑serine, forming O‑acetyl‑L‑serine and Coenzyme A; part of biosynthetic pathways for sulfur‑containing amino acids; occurs under physiological pH in aqueous buffer with the enzyme serine acetyltransferase; no synthetic solvents or catalysts required.
Acid‑base neutralization: fluoroacetic acid reacts with aqueous ammonium hydroxide to form ammonium fluoroacetate and water; performed at room temperature in aqueous solution, no catalyst required.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration (condensation) of a β‑amino alcohol with acetyl chloride to form a 2‑phenyloxazoline; the acid chloride acylates the amine, then the pendant hydroxyl attacks the amide carbonyl, closing the five‑membered oxazoline ring and releasing HCl. Typically performed in anhydrous organic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base (e.g., triethylamine) to scavenger the generated HCl.

Type: Wurtz coupling (alkyl‑halide coupling with sodium metal). Purpose: formation of a C‑C bond between two cyclohexyl radicals to give bicyclohexyl. Key transformation: single‑electron transfer from Na to bromocyclohexane generates a cyclohexyl radical, which dimerizes; NaBr is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF), reflux, excess sodium metal, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen).

Solution‑combustion synthesis of barium ferrite nanoparticles using glycine as a fuel together with iron(III) nitrate and barium hydroxide. The redox reaction rapidly oxidizes glycine, producing CO₂, N₂ and H₂O gases while the metal ions form BaFe₁₂₁₉ (barium ferrite) solid. Conducted by dissolving the reagents in water, evaporating to a viscous gel, and heating to ignition temperatures of 200–300 °C in an open crucible; no additional solvents or catalysts are required beyond the nitrate salts.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an aryl bromide (Pd/C) to the corresponding aniline; removes the bromine from 4‑bromo‑2‑methylaniline to give 2‑methylaniline. Used for de‑bromination while preserving the amino group. Typical conditions: H₂ (1–3 atm), 5–10 % Pd on carbon, solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, room temperature to 40 °C.

Acid‑base salt metathesis; purpose is to liberate free tartaric acid from its ammonium‑sodium salt. The strong acid HCl protonates the tartrate anion, yielding tartaric acid while the sodium and ammonium become their chloride salts. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, 0 °C to ambient temperature, dropwise addition of conc. HCl with stirring. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Oxidative side‑chain oxidation; potassium permanganate in alkaline aqueous medium oxidizes the ethyl group of 1‑ethyl‑2‑nitrobenzene to a carboxylic acid, yielding 2‑nitrobenzoic acid, MnO₂ precipitate and water. Reaction run at reflux (80–100 °C) with excess KMnO₄, followed by acid work‑up.

Reaction type: acid–base displacement (salt‑acid metathesis). Purpose: regenerates free sorbic acid from its calcium salt. Key transformation: proton transfer from HCl to the sorbate anion, releasing Ca²⁺ as CaCl₂ and producing sorbic acid (CH₃CH=CH‑CH=CHCO₂H). Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stoichiometric HCl (1 equiv) added to a suspension of calcium sorbate; the mixture is stirred until the salt dissolves and the pH drops to ~1–2. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Dehydration of 2,2,2‑trifluoro‑1,1‑ethanediol to trifluoroacetaldehyde using phosphorus pentoxide as a strong dehydrating agent. P₂O₅ absorbs the two hydroxyl groups as water, generating phosphoric acid and the aldehyde CF₃CHO. The reaction is carried out under anhydrous conditions, typically by gently heating the diol with excess P₂O₅ in a dry, inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen) to avoid moisture.

The reaction is a reduction of a rare earth metal oxide. Type: reduction. Purpose: production of elemental lanthanum. Key transformation: lanthanum sesquioxide (La₂O₃) reduced to metallic La via hydrogen gas acting as a reductant. Conditions: typically requires high temperature (e.g., above 800°C) under a hydrogen atmosphere. No catalyst required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of terbium(III) nitrate to afford terbium(III) oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Upon heating the solid nitrate to 600–800 °C in a furnace, the nitrate ions break down, releasing NO₂ and O₂ gases while the terbium centers oxidize to Tb₂O₃. No solvent is used; the reaction is performed in a dry air or inert gas flow to control oxidation state.

Potassium permanganate oxidation; oxidizes an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding benzoic acid. The aldehyde is treated with an aqueous solution of KMnO₄, typically under slightly alkaline conditions (pH ≈ 8–9) and heated to reflux. The aldehyde carbonyl is converted to a –CO₂H group while the aromatic ring remains intact. Water is the solvent; excess permanganate is reduced to MnO₂ precipitate.

Base‑ind E2 elimination of 2‑chloropropane with sodium amide (NaNH₂) to produce propene, sodium chloride and ammonia. NaNH₂, a strong, non‑nucleophilic base, abstracts a β‑hydrogen while the chloride leaves, forming the C=C bond. The reaction is carried out in liquid ammonia or an aprotic polar solvent such as THF at low temperature (‑30 °C to 0 °C) under an inert atmosphere; ammonia generated as a by‑product may remain dissolved in the solvent.

Transesterification (alcoholysis) – octyl acetate reacts with methanol to exchange the alkoxy groups, producing methyl acetate and octanol. The reaction proceeds via nucleophilic attack of methanol on the carbonyl carbon, followed by departure of octanol. Requires excess methanol and a catalyst (commonly acid such as H₂SO₄ or base such as NaOMe). Conducted at 50–80 °C under reflux; methanol itself serves as both reactant and solvent.

Oxidative cleavage of glycolic acid by sodium periodate (NaIO₄) yielding oxalic acid, water and sodium iodate. Periodate oxidizes the α‑hydroxy acid, breaking the C‑C bond adjacent to the hydroxyl group. Conducted in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C, often buffered to neutral pH, with stoichiometric amounts of NaIO₄; the reaction proceeds without additional catalysts.

Simple metathesis / base‑mediated hydrolysis; sodium hydroxide exchanges its anion with the acetate ligand of methylmercury acetate, producing methylmercury hydroxide and sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; the reaction mixture is usually stirred in water or a water‑organic mixture (e.g., water/ethanol). No special catalyst is required, but care must be taken due to the toxicity ofomercury species.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis: phenyl 2,2‑difluoroacetate is cleaved by water under acidic conditions to give 2,2‑difluoroacetic acid and phenol; reaction is refluxed in aqueous HCl or dilute acid; water serves as solvent and the acid acts as catalyst.

Reductive dehalogenation (metal‑mediated reduction) of 1,2‑dichloroheptane to heptane. Zinc dust acts as the reducing metal, donating electrons that replace the two chlorine atoms with hydrogen from acetic acid, forming zinc chloride as a by‑product. The reaction is usually performed by heating the alkyl dichloride with excess zinc in glacial acetic acid (1–2 M) under reflux for several hours.

Thermal decomposition of an ammonium salt; solid‑phase heating under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) at ca. 300‑400 °C; ammonium pertechnetate decomposes to technetium dioxide (TcO2), nitrogen gas (N2) and water vapor (H2O); no solvent or catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts alkylation) of phenol with isobutylene to give 2‑tert‑butylphenol. The reaction proceeds via protonation of isobutylene to generate a tert‑butyl carbocation which attacks the aromatic ring ortho to the hydroxyl group. Typical conditions employ a strong Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, HCl) or a Lewis acid (AlCl₃, zeolite) at temperatures from 0 °C to 80 °C. The reaction is usually carried out in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon disulfide, and the product is isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (S_NAr) where dimethylamine displaces the fluorine atom of 4‑fluoronitrobenzene, yielding 4‑(dimethylamino)nitrobenzene and HF. The electron‑withdrawing nitro group activates the aromatic ring toward nucleophilic attack. Reactions are typically run in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 80–130 °C. A base (e.g., triethylamine pyridine) is often added to scavenge the HF and to drive the reaction to completion.

Acid–base salt metathesis; purpose is preparation of a non‑coordinating tetrafluoroborate salt. Triethylamine hydrochloride is protonated by HBF4, yielding triethylammonium tetrafluoroborate and liberating HCl. Typically carried out in dry acetonitrile or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Reaction type: ligand‑exchange complexation forming a hexacyanometallate. Purpose: generate the inorganic complex potassium hexacyanochromate(III), often used as a cyanide source or analytical reagent. Key transformation: six cyanide ligands from KCN coordinate to Cr(III) centre, dis chloride ligands; concomitant formation of KCl. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, excess KCN (3–4 eq), ambient temperature or gentle heating (≤50 °C) for 1–2 h; pH kept neutral to mildly basic to prevent precipitation of Cr(OH)₃. Common solvent: water; the resulting K₃[Cr(CN)₆] is isolated by evaporation or crystallisation.

Ligand exchange on an iodine(III) center; trifluoroacetic anhydride reacts with iodosylbenzene to replace the oxo ligand with two trifluoroacetoxy groups, forming bis(trifluoroacetoxy)iodobenzene and liberating one equivalent of trifluoroacetic acid. The transformation is performed in an inert, aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, under an inert atmosphere. No external catalyst is required; the anhydride itself acts as both reagent and activating agent.

Conversion of an alcohol to a chloride using phosphorus oxychloride (Appel‑type chlorination). 3,3,3‑Trifluoro‑1‑propanol reacts with POCl₃ in the presence of a tertiary amine base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to give 3‑chloro‑1,1,1‑trifluoropropane and phosphate by‑products. The reaction is carried out at 0 °C to reflux in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, under nitrogen. The amine neutralizes the generated HCl and facilitates the formation of the alkyl chloride.

Copper‑catalyzed aerobic oxidation of a secondary allylic alcohol to the corresponding ketone. The Cu(II) chloride acts as a redox catalyst, being reduced to Cu(I) while the alcohol is oxidized; molecular oxygenoxidizes Cu(I) to Cu(II). Typical conditions: O2 atmosphere (balloon or flow), 5–10 mol % CuCl₂, often with a nitrogen‑based ligand (e.g., 2,2′‑bipyridine) in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or dichloromethane, temperature 25–80 °C. Purpose: conversion of 1‑octen‑3‑ol into the more oxidized 1‑octen‑3‑one.

SN2 substitution of benzyl bromide with methylamine, analogous to reaction 1 but with a more reactive bromide leaving group; yields N‑methylbenzylamine and hydrogen bromide. Conducted in an aprotic solvent (e.g., MeCN, THF) at 0 °C to rt, often with a stoichiometric base (triethylamine, pyridine) to trap HBr.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); propyl chloride is activated by anhydrous AlCl₃ to generate a propyl carbocation which attacks benzene, producing propylbenzene and HCl. Reaction carried out in a dry, non‑protic solvent (e.g., carbon disulfide, nitrobenzene, or dichloromethane) at 0–50 °C under nitrogen, using stoichiometric AlCl₃ and maintaining anhydrous conditions.

Type: Selective reduction of a Weinreb amide to an aldehyde (DIBAL‑H reduction). Purpose: Produce benzaldehyde from N‑methoxybenzamide. Key transformation: DIBAL‑H adds a hydride to the amide carbonyl, giving a mono‑alkoxide that on acidic quench furnishes benzaldehyde and N‑methoxy‑N‑methylamine. Conditions: −78 °C, dry THF, inert N₂/Ar, then methanol or aqueous work‑up; no additional catalyst.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acid chloride with ammonia to afford a primary amide (butyramide) and HCl. The reaction is usually out in anhydrous conditions with excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, or in a basic solvent (pyridine, triethylamine) that scavenges the liberated HCl. Typical temperature: 0 °C to room temperature to limit side‑reaction (e.g., formation of nitrile). Solvent can be THF, dichloromethane, or pyridine itself. Purpose: synthesis of the amide functional group from a readily available acyl chloride.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of the cyclic enol ether2,5‑dihydrofuran with peracetic acid to give γ‑butyrolactone and acetic acid as by‑product. The peracid inserts an oxygen adjacent to the carbonyl‑like C=O of the oxidized intermediate, expanding the five‑membered ring to a six‑membered lactone. Conditions: 0 °C to rt, dilute solution of peracetic acid in dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) to accelerate the rearrangement. Purpose: conversion of a cyclic ether into a valuable lactone.

Alkali‑metal reduction (metallothermic) of TiCl₄ with sodium; produces titanium metal and sodium chloride; Na reduces Ti⁴⁺ to Ti⁰ while forming NaCl; carried out at elevated temperatures (≈600–800 °C) under inert gas; reaction often done in a sealed vessel to contain volatile Na and TiCl₄ vapors; no solvent.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; purpose is to introduce a nitro group meta to the aldehyde; key transformation is substitution of a hydrogen on the benzene ring by a –NO₂ group yielding 3‑nitrobenzaldehyde and water; performed with concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ (nitrating mixture) at 0–5 °C then 40–60 °C; the acid mixture acts as both solvent and catalyst.

Electrophilic demethylation of the aryl methyl ether in eugenol using boron tribromide afford hydroxychavicol (4‑allyl1,2‑dihydroxybenzene). BBr₃ acts as a strong Lewis acid, forming a complex with the methoxy oxygen and effecting cleavage of the C–O bond to generate the phenolic OH and release MeBr (which is trapped as HBr in the work‑up). Reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in CH₂Cl₂ at –78 °C to 0 °C, then allowed to warm to rt. Typical work‑up includes quenching with methanol or water. Purpose: conversion of a protected phenol into the free catechol derivative.

Aminolysis of an acyl fluoride; ammonia attacks acetyl fluoride to give acetamide and HF; typically conducted in excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃ at 0–25 °C, optionally with a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) to capture HF and drive the reaction to completion.

Protonation (acid‑base salt formation); methylamine (CH3NH2) is dissolved in a polar solvent (e.g., ethanol or water) and treated with hydroiodic acid at 0 °C to ambient temperature, giving the methylammonium iodide salt (CH3NH3I); no catalyst needed.

Prilezhaev epoxidation of the terminal double bond of 1,3‑butadiene with peroxyacetic acid to give 1,2‑epoxybut‑3‑ene (butadiene monoxide) and acetic acid. The peracid transfers an oxygen atom to the alkene in a concerted, stereospecific fashion. Conditions: dilute peroxyacetic acid in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, temperature 0 °C to 25 °C, inert atmosphere to avoid polymerization of the diene. The reaction may be catalyzed by a small amount of acid (e.g., TsOH) to increase the rate. Purpose: preparation of a mono‑epoxide from a simple conjugated diene.

Nucleophilic substitution of cyanogen bromide by methanol to afford methyl cyanate (CH₃OCN) with concomitant formation of HBr. The methanol oxygen attacks the electrophilic carbon of the C≡N‑Br moiety, displacing bromide and generating the O‑alkyl cyanate. The reaction is typically conducted in excess methanol as solvent, often with a weak base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize the generated HBr and drive the reaction to completion. Temperature may be reflux (≈65 °C) or ambient, depending on desired rate. Purpose: synthesis of an alkyl cyanate ester from the highly reactive cyanogen bromide.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a secondary alkyl bromide; purpose is to replace the bromine with a hydroxyl group, giving 3‑hydroxybutan‑2‑one; water attacks the carbon bearing bromine (often via an SN1 mechanism), forming the alcohol and releasing HBr, which is usually neutralized by the aqueous medium; performed in refluxing water or dilute aqueous base, no catalyst required.

Diazonium coupling (triazene formation); used to synthesize 1‑phenyl‑3‑methyltriazene as a protecting group or chromophore. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of methylamine on the electrophilic benzenediazonium cation forming a N‑N‑N triazene and releasing HCl. Typically performed in aqueous medium at 0–5 °C under basic (often NaOH) conditions to keep the amine deprotonated; no external catalyst required.

Direct chlorination of platinum to form platinum(II) chloride; purpose is preparation of PtCl2; key transformation: Pt(s) + 2 Cl2(g) → PtCl2(s); typically performed at 450–550 °C under a flow of chlorine gas; solid‑gas reaction, no solvent; sometimes carried out in sealed quartz tubes to contain chlorine.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) between NaOH and calcium metaborate. Purpose: exchange of cations to obtain soluble sodium metaborate and precipitate calcium hydroxide. Reaction proceeds in water with stoichiometric NaOH, usually at ambient or mildly elevated temperature; stirring ensures complete ion exchange. No catalyst required.

Acidic redox reaction where potassium permanganate oxidizes sodium hypophosphite to sodium phosphate while Mn(VII) is reduced to Mn(II); yields potassium sulfate, manganese sulfate, water; conducted in aqueous sulfuric acid (moderate concentration) at 20–60 °C, KMnO₄ added portionwise, no external catalyst required.

Condensation of an aldehyde with hydroxylamine to give an aldoxime. Butanal and hydroxylamine (often as its hydrochloride) in aqueous or alcoholic medium, buffered to pH 4‑5, afford butyraldoxime. Typical conditions: room temperature to gentle reflux, optional pyridine or mild base to neutralize HCl; no external catalyst required.

Transfer‑hydrogen reductive amination of vanillin to vanillylamine using Pd/C and ammonium formate. Ammonium formate decomposes on Pd/C to generate H2 in situ, which reduces the aldehyde to the corresponding primary amine via an imine intermediate. Typical conditions: Pd/C (10 % w/w), ammonium formate (excess), solvent such as methanol or ethanol, temperature 50–80 °C under nitrogen; reaction produces CO2 and H2O as volatile by‑products.

Acid‑base salt formation (neutralization) between H2SO4 and K2SO4 to give potassium hydrogen sulfate (KHSO4). One proton of sulfuric acid transfers to the sulfate ion, producing two equivalents of the bisulfate salt. Conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to concentrate and crystallize KHSO4; no catalyst needed.
Double displacement reaction. Neutralizes sulfuric acid and converts magnesium trisilicate to silicic acid and magnesium sulfate. Occurs in aqueous conditions.

Type: disproportionation/oxidation-reduction of chlorine in alkaline solution; Purpose: preparation of bleaching agents (sodium hypochlorite); Key transformation: Cl2 reacts with aqueous NaOH to give NaCl, NaOCl and H2O; Typical conditions: cold (0‑25 °C), dilute NaOH, aqueous phase; Common solvent/catalyst: water (no additional catalyst).
Double displacement reaction. Forms mercuric iodide precipitate; commonly carried out in aqueous solution.
Cyclization condensation. Isatoic anhydride reacts with cyclohexanone and propylamine to yield proquazone, involving CO₂ release. Typically requires heat and/or catalytic conditions.
Fischer esterification. Converts 2-chloropropionic acid to methyl ester using methanol under acidic catalysis, often sulfuric acid.
Redox reaction. Sulfur dioxide reduces iodine to hydrogen iodide while being oxidized to sulfuric acid. Proceeds in aqueous solution, often under mild or ambient conditions.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); phenol is converted to ortho‑chlorophenol while releasing HCl. The strongly activating phenoxide directs chlorine to the ortho position. Typical conditions involve generating phenoxide with a base (e.g., NaOH) and adding Cl₂ gas at 0–5 °C to control over‑chlorination; the reaction is often performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent, sometimes with a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ to accelerate the electrophilic attack.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling; phenylboronic acid couples with 1‑bromo‑2‑butene to forge a new C(sp²)–C(sp³) bond, affording (E)‑1‑phenyl‑2‑butene. Potassium carbonate serves as the base, and Pd(OAc)₂ is precatalyst that is reduced in situ to Pd(0). The reaction is usually run under an inert atmosphere at 80–100 °C in a polar aprotic solvent such as dioxane, THF, or DMF, often with a small amount of water to aid boronate activation. By‑products are boric acid, KBr and the(0) catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution of a phenolic OH with chloride (dehydrative chlorination) using thionyl chloride; 3‑chlorophenol is converted into 1,3‑dichlorobenzene with concomitant release of HCl and SO₂ gases. The reaction proceeds via formation of an aryl‑sulfonyl chloride intermediate that collapses to the aryl chloride. Common protocol: reflux the phenol in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine with excess SOCl₂ (often 1.5–2 equiv) at 60–80 °C, using pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Hydrazinolysis of an ester (nucleophilic acyl substitution); methyl nicotinate reacts with hydrazine to afford nicotinic acid hydrazide and methanol. The reaction typically uses excess hydrazine (2–3 equiv) and is conducted under reflux in ethanol or methanol for several hours. Mild heating (∼65 °C) under atmospheric pressure suffices; the by‑product methanol is removed by evaporation after completion.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a potassium salt; orotic acid is deprotonated by potassium hydroxide to give the water‑soluble potassium oxonate salt and water. The procedure uses aqueous KOH (1 equiv to the acidic proton) at ambient temperature or with gentle heating (≤50 °C) to ensure complete dissolution. No special catalysts are required; the reaction is straightforward salt formation.

Salt formation (acid‑base reaction); the primary amine 3,5‑dimethyladamantan‑1‑amine is protonated by hydrochloric acid to produce memantine hydrochloride, a crystalline pharmaceutical salt. Typically the amine is dissolved in anhydrous ethanol or isopropanol, and cold aqueous HCl (or HCl gas) is added at 0–5 °C. The mixture is stirred, then the precipitated salt is filtered, washed with cold solvent, and dried. No additional reagents are needed.

A metal-acid redox reaction where dysprosium metal is oxidized and hydrogen ions are reduced to produce dysprosium(III) sulfate and hydrogen gas. Conducted with heated sulfuric acid, often in aqueous solution. No additional catalysts needed.

Transesterification; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy group of an ester. n-Butanol attacks the carbonyl of isopropyl acetate, displacing isopropanol and forming n‑butyl acetate. Typically acid‑catalyzed (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base‑catalyzed (NaOEt) under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as toluene or benzene; removal of the more volatile alcohol drives the equilibrium.

General type: hydrolytic decomposition (thermal hydrolysis) of a substituted urea. Purpose: breakdown N‑methylurea into its constituent amines and carbon dioxide. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon of N‑methylurea, leading to cleavage of the C–N bonds and release of methylamine, ammonia, and CO₂. Typical conditions: elevated temperature (180–220 °C) in aqueous solution; reaction can be accelerated by acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) catalysis. No special catalyst is required beyond the heat and, optionally, a pH modifier.

Carbothermic reduction; used to produce carbon disulfide from metal sulfide. Tin(II) sulfide is reduced by elemental carbon at high temperature, yielding CS₂ gas and metallic tin. Reaction is carried out in a sealed or flowing inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at 800–1000 °C in a quartz tube or furnace; no solvent required.

Protonolysis (acid‑alkyl exchange) of a metal alkyl; converts trimethylindium to indium trichloride while generating methane gas. Performed in an aprotic, moisture‑free solvent such as THF or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; HCl gas or a solution in ether is added dropwise. No additional catalyst needed.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using thionyl chloride (chlorination); purpose is to activate the pyridine‑4‑carboxylic acid for subsequent coupling reactions; the acid reacts with SOCl₂, replacing the OH with Cl and releasing SO₂ and HCl gases; typically carried out under dry conditions in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to scavenge HCl, at 0 °C to reflux; inert atmosphere is advisable.
Thermal decomposition (calcination); sodium carbonate decomposes on strong heating to give sodium oxide and carbon dioxide; performed in a furnace at ~850 °C; no solvent or catalyst.

Thermal decomposition (pyrolysis) of methyl formate; yields carbon monoxide and methanol. Conducted at elevated temperatures (300–450 °C) in the gas phase or in a sealed reactor; can be enhanced with solid acid catalysts (e.g., zeolites). No solvent; product gases are separated by condensation (methanol) and gas analysis (CO).

Metathesis (double‑replacement) salt exchange to prepare samarium(III) acetate. Aqueous solution of SmCl₃ is mixed with sodium acetate; NaCl precipitates (or remains soluble depending on concentration) and samarium acetate stays in solution. Reaction performed at room temperature or mild heating (≈50 °C) with stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base/complexation reaction forming zinc picolinate. Zinc oxide reacts with picolinic acid upon heating, producing water and the chelated zinc picolinate salt. Typically carried out in refluxing ethanol or water–ethanol mixture at 80–120 °C; excess acid drives completion, and the product is isolated by cooling and filtration. No external catalyst needed.

The reaction is an acylation/cyclization. Purpose: formation of 1,2-benzoxazole via acetic anhydride-mediated cyclization of 5-nitro-2-aminophenol. Key transformation: acetylation of the amine followed by intramolecular condensation to form the oxazole ring. Conditions: typically mild heating, possibly in acetic acid or inert solvent. Anhydrous conditions may apply.

This is an acylation of an amine. Purpose: synthesize N-methylacetamide from methylamine using acetic anhydride. Key transformation: acetyl group transfer to methylamine, with triethylamine acting as a base to neutralize the acetic acid byproduct. Conditions: room temperature in aprotic solvents (e.g., dichloromethane).

This is a solid-state metathesis reaction. Purpose: synthesize silver molybdate (Ag2MoO4) from molybdenum trioxide (MoO3) and silver oxide. Conditions: high-temperature calcination (e.g., 400–600°C); no solvent required.

This is a salt metathesis reaction. Purpose: form ammonium metaborate and regenerate NaOH. Key transformation: exchange of counterions in aqueous solution. Conditions: ambient in water; proceeds without catalysts.

Thermal decomposition of ammonium nitrate into ammonia and nitric acid vapors; employed in the laboratory preparation of nitric acid and in fertilizer processing. Key transformation: cleavage of the N–O bond releasing NH3 and HNO3. Performed by heating solid NH4NO3 to ~170–200 °C under controlled pressure; often in a distillation apparatus, no solvent or catalyst.

This is an aromatic hydroxylation reaction. Purpose: introduce a hydroxyl group at the 6-position of flavone for functionalization. Key transformation: oxidation of C6-hydrogen to a hydroxyl group. Conditions: transition metal catalyst (e.g., Cu, Fe) with oxidants like H2O2 or tert-butyl hydroperoxide in polar solvents (e.g., acetonitrile/water).  
None.
