Zinc dust reacts with acetic acid to generate ZnCl2 and hydrogen equivalents that replace the chlorine, giving 2‑methylbutane. Conducted by refluxing the substrate with excess zinc in glacial acetic acid.

Acid dissolution/halogenation; Ti2O3 reacts with aqueous HCl to give TiCl3 (titanium(III) chloride) and water. Performed at 50–80 °C with stirring in dilute to concentrated HCl solution; reaction proceeds without additional catalyst.

Simple acid‑base double‑displacement (salt metathesis); magnesium acetate reacts with perchloric acid to give acetic acid and magnesium perchlorate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required; the mixture is usually stirred until complete dissolution and then the products are isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to its acid chloride using oxalyl chloride; pivalic acid is activated to pivaloyl chloride while oxalyl chloride decomposes to CO, CO₂ and HCl gases. Conducted under anrous conditions (dry dichloromethane or chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; excess oxalyl chloride is removed by evaporation, and the crude acid chloride is used directly or purified by distillation.

Acid‑base protonolysis of an organozincethylzinc reacts with aqueous HCl to give ZnCl2 and methane. Purpose is to quench the highly pyrophoric reagent and generate CH4. Key transformation: Zn–CH3 bonds are protonated to release CH4, Zn is converted to ZnCl2. Typical conditions: dilute aqueous HCl at 0‑25 °C, vigorous stirring, inert atmosphere recommended. No special solvent beyond water; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative conversion of barbituric acid to violuric acid with concentrated nitric acid; nitric acid oxidizes the barbituric ring, releasing CO₂ and water and forming violuric acid (a red‑colored pyrimidine‑dione). Usually carried out by refluxing barbituric acid in ~70 % HNO₃ at 80–100 °C for several hours; the reaction mixture is then cooled, neutralized, and violuric acid is precipitated or extracted with a suitable organic solvent.

Deprotonation of isopropanol with sodium hydride to afford sodium isopropoxide and H₂; standard method for preparing alkoxides for nucleophilic substitution or elimination; performed in dry aprotic solvents such as THF or DMF under nitrogen or argon, usually at 0 °C to room temperature.

Halide exchange metathesis between sodium iodide and tetraethylammonium brom; reaction swaps anions to afford tetraethylammonium iodide and sodium bromide. Commonly performed in acetone or ethanol where NaI is sparingly soluble, driving precipitation of NaBr; mixture is stirred at room temperature, then filtered to isolate the quaternary ammonium iodide.

Acid‑base neutralization of the disodium salt of glutamic acid with hydrochloric acid; protonation of the two carboxylate groups yields free L‑glutamic acid and sodium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution at 0–25 °C; after adding HCl dropwise to a cooled solution of disodium 2‑aminopentanedioate, the mixture is stirred, and the glutamic acid is isolated by crystallization or pH‑adjusted precipitation.

Acid‑base neutralization and dehydration; solid‑state heating of diphosphoric acid with zinc carbonate decomposes the carbonate to CO₂ and H₂O and yields zinc pyrophosphate (Zn₂P₂O₇); typical conditions: dry heating around 200‑300 °C to drive off gases; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidation of a para‑methoxy‑substituted benzyl alcohol to p‑anisaldehyde with TBHP; generally carried out with a TEMPO/Cu or a vanadium‑based catalyst in a polar aprotic solvent (acetonitrile, dichloromethane) at ambient to mild heating; the benzylic CH₂OH group is oxidized to the aldehyde and TBHP is reduced to tert‑butanol.

Double‑displacement metathesis precipitation; aqueous solutions of magnesium sulfate and barium chloride exchange ions to form insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble magnesium chloride; performed at room temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of phenylboronic acid pinacol ester to phenylboronic acid; reaction type: ester hydrolysis; purpose: liberate the free boronic acid for subsequent reactions; key transformation: water attacks the boronate ester, releasing pinacol and forming the boronic acid; typical conditions: aqueous acidic (e.g., 0.1 M HCl) or basic medium, ambient to mild heating (25‑60 °C); solvent: water or aqueous ethanol.

Acid‑base neutralization; hydrogen cyanide reacts with basic barium oxide (or barium hydroxide) to produce water and barium cyanide (Ba(CN)₂); carried out in aqueous medium at moderate temperature, often by bubbling HCN gas into a Ba(OH)₂ solution; no catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) cyanation; 1‑chloropropane undergoes copper‑catalyzed displacement of chloride by cyanide from CuCN to give n‑propyl cyanide and CuCl; typically refluxed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO; CuCN used stoichiometrically or as a catalyst, no additional catalyst required.

Halide exchange (metathesis) of a metal halide; hydrogen bromide reacts with niobium(V) chloride, releasing HCl gas and substituting bromide for chloride to form niobium(V) bromide (NbBr₅); conducted in the gas phase or sealed tube at 150‑200 °C, often with excess HBr; no solvent or catalyst.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification; methanol attacks the carbonyl of ethyl phenylacetate, displacing ethanol and forming methyl phenylacetate; performed by refluxing excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOCH₃); removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium; methanol acts as both reactant and solvent.

Hydration (addition) of an aldehyde; forms the gem‑diol (methanediol) from formaldehyde in water; equilibrium between formaldehyde and its hydrate; occurs spontaneously in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst or special solvent required.

Diiodomethane + zinc-copper couple → methylene + zinc iodide: Redox reaction. Purpose generates methylene species via reduction of diiodomethane, used for cyclopropanation. Key transformation: Zn acts as a reductant, cleaving C–I bonds to form methylene. Conditions: mild (room temperature), ether solvents. Catalyst: activated zinc-copper couple.

Type: esterification of an acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose: prepare ethyl propiolate; key transformation: ethanol attacks the carbonyl of prop‑2‑ynoyl chloride, displaces chloride and yields the ethyl ester with HCl as by‑product; typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, presence of a non‑nucleophilic base (pyridine, triethylamine) to capture HCl; common solvent: dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride.

Redox oxidation; stannous sulfate (SnSO4) is oxidized to stannic sulfate (Sn(SO4)2) by hydrogen peroxide in the presence of sulfuric acid; carried out in aqueous acidic medium (dilute H2SO4) at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and the acid provides the necessary acidic environment.

Metathesis/reduction–oxidation; sodium sulfide reduces gold(III) chloride to gold(I) sulfide (Au2S) while being oxidized to elemental sulfur; sodium chloride is formed as a by‑product; generally performed in aqueous solution with excess Na2S, heated under reflux; water is the solvent.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis): aqueous sodium arsenite reacts with silver nitrate, precipitating poorly soluble silver arsenite (AgAsO₂) while forming soluble sodium nitrate (NaNO₃). Purpose is to isolate arsenic as an insoluble silver salt; carried out at ambient temperature in water, no catalyst.

Double‑displacement (acid‑base) reaction; neodymium(III) oxalate reacts with perchloric acid to exchange anions, producing oxalic acid and neodymium(III) perchlorate; performed in aqueous solution, usually at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent.

Reductive dehalogenation using zinc dust in aqueous ethanol; purpose is to remove all bromine atoms from a polybromoalkane to give the corresponding saturated alkane; key transformation is replacement of C–Br bonds by C–H via single‑electron transfer from Zn and proton donation from ethanol, forming ZnBr2 as by‑product; typical conditions involve excess Zn dust, reflux in a mixture of ethanol and water, often under an inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst required.

Lewis‑acid catalyzed esterification; succinic anhydride reacts with ethanol in the presence of zinc chloride to form diethyl succinate and water; reflux in anhydrous ethanol with catalytic ZnCl2 (often 5–10 mol %) gives good yields; ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Single‑replacement (acid‑metal) reaction; gallium metal dissolves in aqueous hydrochloric acid, producing gallium(III) chloride (GaCl₃) and liberating hydrogen gas. Conducted in water at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; excess HCl ensures complete conversion, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous double displacement where lead(II) nitrate reacts with sodium carbonate and sodium hydroxide to form insoluble basic lead carbonate (a lead carbonate‑hydroxide precipitate) and soluble sodium nitrate; carried out in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of an arylboronic acid to phenol; phenylboronic acid is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to give phenol and boric acid; the reaction is carried out in aqueous media, often with a mild base (NaOH or K₂CO₃) at 0 °C to rt, and may be accelerated by a catalytic amount of a transition‑metal complex (e.g., Cu²⁺).

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) using an acyl chloride; pyridine acts as a base and nucleophilic catalyst, deprotonating glycidol’s hydroxyl group so it attacks methacryloyl chloride, yielding glycidyl methacrylate ester and pyridinium chloride as by‑product; typically performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; pyridine also serves as acid scavenger.

Grignard addition to nitrile (nucleophilic addition); purpose: synthesize a ketone from a nitrile. Methylmagnesium bromide attacks the carbon of cyclohexanecarbonitrile forming an imine magnesium intermediate; aqueous work‑up hydrolyzes it to cyclohexyl methyl ketone. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux, dry atmosphere; quench with water.

Reaction type: double displacement (metathesis). Purpose: synthesis of iron(III) pyrophosphate. Key transformations: sodium pyrophosphate exchanges anions with iron(III) chloride, precipitating iron(III) pyrophosphate and producing sodium chloride. Conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature; driven by low solubility of iron pyrophosphate. Solvent: water.

Formation of an acid chloride using oxalyl chloride; 3,3‑dimethylbutanoic acid reacts with (COCl)₂ to generate 3,3‑dimethylbutanoyl chloride, with CO, CO₂, and HCl released. Conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in dry dichloromethane; a catalytic amount of DMF is often added to accelerate the reaction.
Solid‑state nitridation of titanium dihydride with nitrogen gas to give titanium nitride and hydrogen gas. Requires high temperature (800‑1200 °C) under flowing N₂; occurs in a furnace, no solvent.

Acid‑base salt exchange (metathesis); stronger formic acid protonates acetate anion of magnesium acetate, producing acetic acid and magnesium formate; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive equilibrium forward; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑metal oxide neutralization; copper(I) oxide reacts with hydrobromic acid to give copper(I) bromide salt and water; conducted in aqueous HBr solution, usually with mild heating to ensure complete dissolution of the oxide; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of HBr to 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene; Markovnikov addition places Br on the more substituted carbon to give 2‑bromo‑2,3‑dimethylbutane. Typically done with gaseous or 48 % aqueous HBr at 0‑25 °C, often in dichloromethane or acetic acid as solvent, no catalyst required.

Gas absorption/acid‑base reaction; sulfur dioxide dissolved in water reacts with sodium hydroxide to form sodium bisulfite (NaHSO3); performed in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature to prevent further oxidation to sulfate; no catalyst needed.

Redox reduction; methylarsonic acid (As V) is reduced by ascorbic acid to monomethylarsonous acid (As III), while ascorbic acid is oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid; carried out in aqueous medium, typically at pH 3–5 and ambient temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Acid-mediated decomposition (acid hydrolysis) of potassium hexafluorosilicate; concentrated H2SO4 protonates the silicate anion, liberating HF gas and SiF4 vapor while forming soluble K2SO4. Typically performed by slowly adding solid K2SiF6 to hot conc. H2SO4, under anhydrous conditions, with the gaseous products collected by condensation or trapping.

Transesterification (ester exchange) between propionic acid and vinyl acetate; the acyl group of vinyl acetate is transferred to propionic acid, yielding vinyl propanoate (vinyl propionate) and acetic acid. Usually catalyzed by a small amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (e.g., NaOMe) in an inert organic solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, with removal of the volatile acetic acid to drive equilibrium.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) neutralization between ammonium hydroxide and tricalcium phosphate; purpose is to produce a soluble ammonium phosphate fertilizer and calcium hydroxide as by‑product. Key transformation: PO₄³⁻ anions exchange cations, forming (NH₄)₃PO₄ (or its hydrated form) in solution while Ca²⁺ combines with OH⁻ to precipitate Ca(OH)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous slurry of Ca₃(PO₄)₂ mixed with dilute NH₄OH at room temperature; vigorous stirring to facilitate ion exchange. The reaction may be conducted under mild heating (30–50 °C) to improve dissolution. No additional catalysts; water is the solvent.

Acid‑carbonate reaction; purpose is to convert insoluble bismuth(III) carbonate into soluble bismuth(III) bromide while evolving carbon dioxide gas. Performed in aqueous solution of hydrobromic acid at room temperature or mild heating; water acts as solvent, no catalyst required.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC): 1,1‑diphenylpropan‑2‑ol is oxidized to 1,1‑diphenylpropan‑2‑one; conducted in dry CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to rt using stoichiometric PCC, sometimes with silica to aid work‑up.

Transesterification / carbonate formation between glycerol and dimethyl carbonate yielding glycerol carbonate and methanol; employed to prepare glycerol carbonate, a valuable solvent and monomer. Glycerol’s primary hydroxyl attacks dimethyl carbonate, displacing methanol and forming a five‑membered cyclic carbonate. Conducted at 80–150 °C, often under solvent‑free conditions or with excess DMC as solvent, using a basic catalyst such as K₂CO₃, Na₂CO₃, Zn(OAc)₂, an ionic liquid, or an organocatalyst (e.g., TBD). Methanol is removed (e.g., reduced pressure) to drive the reaction forward.

Hydrolysis of dimethyl tin dichloride; water attacks the Sn–Cl bonds, producing dimethyl tin oxide (Sn(CH3)2O) and releasing two equivalents of HCl. Typically carried out under reflux in a mixture of water and a miscible organic solvent (e.g., THF) to keep the organotin species dissolved, with the acidic aqueous layer later neutralized or vented to remove HCl gas.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr) of 2,6‑dichloropurine with aqueous ammonia to give 2,6‑diaminopurine; ammonia displaces the two chlorine atoms on the purine ring. Reaction is performed in ethanol/water (1:1) under reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours; excess NH3 drives the substitution to completion, and the product precipitates on cooling.

Double‑replacement/precipitation reaction between ammonium phosphate and calcium nitrate; calcium ions combine with phosphate to form sparingly soluble tricalcium diphosphate, while ammonium nitrate remains in solution. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature or mild heating; the solid Ca3(PO4)2 is filtered off, and the filtrate contains NH4NO3.

Double‑replacement precipitation; aqueous sodium sulfide reacts with gold(I) chloride solution to give insoluble gold(I) sulfide and soluble sodium chloride; carried out at ambient temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst needed.

Oxidative ozonolysis of hept‑2‑ene in the presence of hydrogen peroxide: ozone cleaves the double bond and the peroxide work‑up oxidizes the resulting aldehyde fragments to the corresponding carboxylic acids, producing acetic acid and pentanoic acid. Reaction carried out in a mixture of O₃ and aqueous H₂O₂ (or H₂O₂ in an organic solvent) at low temperature (–78 °C to 0 °C), then allowed to warm for complete oxidation.

Metathesis (hydride transfer) reaction; used to generate the strong reducing agent lithium triethylborohydride (Superhydride) and aluminum trihydride. Triethylborane reacts with LiAlH4 to exchange the ethyl groups for hydride, giving Li+ Et3B– and AlH3. Typically carried out under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) in dry THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with stirring; no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (salt metathesis) reaction; employed to exchange cations and precipitate calcium sulfate while forming soluble ammonium benzoate. Calcium benzoate and ammonium sulfate in aqueous solution swap anions, producing ammonium benzoate (soluble) and calcium sulfate (insoluble). Conducted in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the precipitate is filtered off. No catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification of gallic acid with methanol; purpose: convert the carboxylic acid to its methyl ester (methyl gallate); key transformation: protonated carbonyl of gallic acid is attacked by methanol, water is eliminated and the ester is formed; typical conditions: reflux in methanol with catalytic sulfuric acid (0.1‑1 equiv), removal of water by azeotropic distillation or Dean–Stark; common solvent: methanol itself.

Oxidation of a primary propargylic alcohol to a carboxylic acid (propiolic acid). The transformation converts the –CH2OH group of propargyl alcohol into –COOH while preserving the C≡C triple bond. Commonly performed with strong oxidants such as KMnO4 in acidic medium (H2SO4) under reflux, or with Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4) or TEMPO/NaClO. Reaction carried out at reflux temperature; work‑up isolates prop‑2‑ynoic acid.

Reductive dehalogenation (hydride reduction) of 1,2,3‑tribromopropane to propane using lithium aluminium hydride. LiAlH4 supplies hydride that replaces the three bromine atoms, producing propane and the by‑products aluminium bromide and lithium bromide. Conducted in dry ether or THF under nitrogen, refluxing the mixture for several hours. No additional catalyst; reaction quenched carefully with water or dilute acid.

Hydrolysis reaction; diborane reacts violently with water to yield boric acid (H3BO3) and hydrogen gas (H2). The key transformation is cleavage of B–H bonds and oxidation of boron to the +3 oxidation state while protons are reduced to H2. Typically performed at ambient temperature in aqueous media; no catalyst required, but the reaction is exothermic and must be controlled.

Metal‑halogen exchange to generate an organolithium reagent; lithium metal inserts into the C–I bond of isopropyl iodide forming isopropyl lithium and lithium iodide as a precipitate; typically carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to –78 °C under nitrogen or argon atmosphere.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction of elemental holmium with bromine to form holmium(III) bromide. A classic metal‑halogen synthesis where 2 Ho atoms react with 3 Br2 molecules to give 2 HoBr3. Performed by adding bromine vapor to finely powdered holmium or by heating the elements together in a sealed tube or under a nitrogen atmosphere, typically at 200–400 °C. No solvent or catalyst is required; product is collected as a crystalline solid.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (ester cleavage); ethyl acetate reacts with water to regenerate ethanol and acetic acid; refluxed in dilute aqueous acid (e.g., 5‑10 % H2SO4) or, alternatively, base‑catalyzed saponification; common solvent is a water‑organic mixture (e.g., water/toluene) to improve phase contact.

Cross‑coupling (Wurtz‑type) of an alkyl bromide with a Grignard reagent to form a new C–C bond. Purpose: synthesize a higher‑alkane (hexadecane) from two C8 fragments. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of octylmagnesium bromide on 1‑bromooctane followed by reductive elimination, giving hexadecane and MgBr₂ Typical conditions: transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., CuI or NiCl₂·DME) in an ethereal solvent (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux, then aqueous work‑up to remove magnesium salts.

Carbamate formation via CDI activation; used to convert the phenolic hydroxyl of terbutaline into the tert‑butyl carbamate prodrug bambuterol; the alcohol attacks the carbonyl of carbonyldiimidazole forming an imidazolyl carbonate intermediate, which is displaced by tert‑butylamine to give the carbamate and imidazole as by‑product; typically carried out under anhydrous conditions in DMF or THF at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is required beyond the CDI reagent.

Acid–base precipitation (neutralization) reaction; employed to prepare the orange pigment barium chromate from inexpensive reagents; barium carbonate reacts with chromic acid, the carbonate is protonated to release CO₂ and H₂O while the barium cation pairs with the chromate anion to precipitate BaCrO₄; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid product is filtered and washed.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of HCl to 1,2‑dichloropropene, converting the C=C double bond into a C–Cl bond to give 1,2,3‑trichloropropane; typically carried out at ambient temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, no catalyst required.

Acidification of a chromate salt; used to generate chromic acid in situ and to convert rubidium chromate soluble rubidium chloride; two equivalents of HCl protonate the chromate ion, forming H₂CrO₄ and liberating two equivalents of RbCl; the reaction proceeds in water, often at 0 °C to control exotherm; no special solvent or catalyst is required.

Double displacement/precipitation (acid‑base) reaction; employed to obtain scandium phosphate, often as a precursor for phosphide or oxide materials. Aqueous scandium nitrate is mixed with phosphoric acid, typically at room temperature or with slight heating. ScPO4 (often as a hydrated solid) precipitates, while nitric acid remains in solution. No catalyst; water is the solvent; the solid is isolated by filtration and washing.

Protonolysis of trimethylsilyldiazomethane to liberate diazomethane; a convenient, safer source of diazomethane for methylation reactions; the acidic proton of acetic acid displaces the trimethylsilyl group, producing trimethylsilyl acetate and free diazomethane gas; carried out in anhydrous ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to –10 °C under inert atmosphere; the reaction is typically performed in a sealed or vented system to contain the toxic diazomethane.

Type: Reduction of aldehyde to primary alcohol using NaBH4. Purpose: Convert propionaldehyde into 1‑propanol. Key transformation: Hydride addition to the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide that is protonated to give the alcohol; chlorine‑containing by‑product is none. Typical conditions: NaBH4 (1.1–1.5 equiv) in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol or a MeOH/THF mixture, 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere optional. No additional catalyst required.

Intramolecular dehydration (cyclodehydration) to form an anhydride; thermal conversion of benzene‑1,2,4‑tricarboxylic acid (trimellitic acid) to trimellitic anhydride with loss of one molecule of water; heating the solid acid above 200 °C, often in the melt or in a high‑boiling solvent such as o‑xylene, drives the condensation of two adjacent carboxyl groups; the process may be catalyzed by a small amount of acid or by using acetic anhydride as a dehydrating agent.

Double‑displacement/complexation reaction to form a holmium(III) oxalate complex; three ammonium oxalate molecules coordinate to two Ho³⁺ ions, yielding the tris‑oxalato holmium(III) anion and precipitating six equivalents of ammonium nitrate; performed in aqueous solution with equimolar mixing of the salts, often warmed gently (≈50 °C) to promote complex formation; the solid holmium oxalate complex can be isolated by filtration and washed with cold water.

Ester aminolysisamid); ammonia attacks methyl octanoate giving octanamide and methanol. Typically performed by bubbling excess gaseous NH3 or using aqueous NH3 in the ester, heated under reflux (120‑150 °C). No catalyst needed; polar aprotic solvents (e.g., dimethylformamide) may be used to dissolve the ester and improve contact.

Acid‑base neutralisation; hydrazoic acid (HN₃) protonates ammonia to form ammonium azide (NH₄N₃). Conducted in aqueous solution at low temperature (0‑5 °C) because HN₃ is volatile and shock‑sensitive. No catalyst; the reaction is exothermic and must be stirred gently.

Metal‑acid redox (hydrogen evolution); samarium metal reduces the protons of glacial acetic acid to H₂ while being oxidised to Sm³⁺, forming samarium(III) acetate. Usually carried out under inert atmosphere (N₂) with reflux of glacial acetic acid (≈ 118 °C). Excess acid ensures complete dissolution; no external catalyst required.

Nucleophilic S‑alkylation (SN2) of L‑cysteine thiolate with sodium chloroacetate to give carbocine (S‑carboxymethyl‑L‑cysteine); purpose: synthesis of thioether‑protected cysteine; key transformation: –SH → –S‑CH2‑CO2H; carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑ethanol medium, pH 8‑9 to generate thiolate, typically at 0‑25 °C; sodium chloride formed as by‑product.

Mercuric‑catalysed acetoxylation of acetylene (addition reaction); acetylene adds across the O–H of acetic acid in the presence of HgCl₂ to give vinyl acetate. Industrially performed at 60‑120 °C under acetylene pressure (1‑5 atm) in aqueous/acetic acid mixture with catalytic HgCl₂ (0.1‑1 mol %). The reaction is heterogeneous; the mercury salt acts as a Lewis acid promoter.

Acidic hydrolysis of 2‑methoxypentane; protonation of the ether followed by nucleophilic attack of water gives the corresponding alcohols, 2‑pentanol and methanol. Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ether hydrolysis. Conditions: dilute mineral acid (e.g., 5‑10 % H₂SO₄) with reflux in a water‑containing solvent such as aqueous ethanol or tetrahydrofuran; temperature around 80‑100 °C; no external catalyst beyond the acid.

Acidic ether hydrolysis; protonation of the ether oxygen followed by water attack cleaves 1‑methoxybutane into 1‑butanol and methanol; performed by heating the substrate in aqueous sulfuric acid (concentrated H2SO4, often 60–80 °C) with water as solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization (aqueous). Samarium(III) hydroxide dissolves in hydrochloric acid to afford samarium(III) chloride and water: Sm(OH)3 + 3 HCl → SmCl3 + 3 H2O. Reaction proceeds at ambient temperature in water; stirring sufficient, no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base double displacement; sulfuric acid protonates the selenite ion of zinc selenite, releasing selenous acid (H₂SeO₃) while Zn²⁺ combines with sulfate to give zinc sulfate. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient to modestly elevated temperature (20‑ °C). No catalyst required; stoichiometric amounts of reagents give quantitative conversion.

Direct synthesis (combustion) oxidation; purpose: form thulium oxide (Tm₂O₃) from the metal; 4 Tm + 3 O₂ → 2 Tm₂O₃; requires heating (typically 300–600 °C) in an oxygen atmosphere; solid‑gas reaction, no solvent; no catalyst.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (alkylation). Dimethylamine attacks the electrophilic carbon of ethyl tosylate, displacing the tosylate anion which is protonated to give p‑toluenesulfonic acid, while the amine becomes N,N‑dimethylethylamine. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile or DMF), ambient to moderate temperature; often carried out under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst required.

Precipitation (metathesis) reaction; hydrogen sulfide gas is bubbled through an aqueous solution of PbCl₂, resulting in insoluble lead(II) sulfide precipitate and release of HCl into solution; carried out at ambient temperature, often in mildly acidic medium; common in qualitative analysis of lead ions.

Transesterification (alkoxy exchange). Diethyl terephthalate undergoes exchange of its ethoxy groups with methanol, producing dimethyl terephthalate and liberating ethanol. Catalysed by an acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (e.g., NaOMe) under reflux; removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium forward. Solvent can be the excess alcohol itself or a high‑boiling inert solvent such as toluene.

Redox oxidation–reduction (gas‑solid reaction). Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide while nickel(III) oxide is reduced to nickel(II) oxide, effectively transferring oxygen from Ni2O3 to CO. Requires elevated temperature (300–600 °C) in the gas phase; no solvent or catalyst beyond the solid oxide.

Alcoholysis / transesterification of an ester. Ethanol attacks isoamyl formate, displacing isoamyl alcohol and forming ethyl formate. Typically catalysed by a protonic acid (e.g., sulfuric acid) or a mild base, carried out under reflux in a solvent‑free mixture or in an inert solvent such as toluene; removal of the more volatile product (ethyl formate) shifts equilibrium.

Acid–base reaction of a metal carbonate with hydrofluoric acid. Hydrogen fluoride protonates the carbonate ion, yielding carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO2 and H2O) and forming manganese difluoride as the inorganic salt. Conducted in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature; excess HF ensures complete conversion. No additional catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox (combustion/thermite‑type) reaction; metallic aluminum reduces ammonium perchlorate (NH4ClO4) upon ignition, producing aluminum trichloride (AlCl3), aluminum oxide (Al2O3), nitrogen gas (N2) and water (H2O). Provides large exothermic energy and is employed in composite solid rocket propellants. Conducted as a dry powder mixture, ignited by a spark or flame; no solvent or added catalyst.

Thermal cracking (β‑scission) of isopentane to give 2‑methylpropene and methane; purpose is to produce low‑molecular‑weight alkenes and gases; key C–C bond cleavage yields an alkene and a small alkane; performed at high temperature (≈500‑800 °C) in the gas phase, often under inert atmosphere; can be carried out in a furnace without solvent, occasionally over solid acid catalysts (e.g., silica/alumina or zeolites) to lower the temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification: isopropylparaben is reacted with excess methanol under sulfuric‑acid catalysis to give methylparaben and isopropanol; the reaction is carried out in methanol solvent with 1–5 % H₂SO₄, reflux for 4–8 h, and removal of isopropanol to shift the equilibrium.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange counter‑ions to isolate insoluble barium sulfate. Key transformation: Li2SO4 + BaI2 → BaSO4 (solid) + 2 LiI (in solution). Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration (substitution) of naphthalene; purpose is to introduce a nitro group at the 1‑position. Key transformation: naphthalene reacts with the nitronium ion generated from conc. HNO3/H2SO4 to give 1‑nitronaphthalene and water. Conducted in a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids, temperatures 0–50 °C, sulfuric acid acts as both solvent and catalyst.

Haloform reaction (base‑promoted oxidation) of a methyl ketone; purpose is to cleave acetone to bromoform and a carboxylate. Key transformation: acetone is brominated by NaOBr, then undergoes C‑C bond cleavage giving CHBr3 (bromoform) and NaCH3COO (sodium acetate) plus water. Usually performed in aqueous NaOH with NaOBr generated in situ (e.g., NaBr + NaOCl), temperatures 0 °C to reflux; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Bimolecular elimination (E2); converts 1-iodooctane to 1-octene via deprotonation with potassium tert-butoxide. Proceeds in polar aprotic solvents (e.g., THF) under heating. Sterically hindered base promotes Hofmann elimination.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of a nitrate ester; purpose is to remove one nitrate group from isosorbide dinitrate, yielding the mononitrate and nitrate ion. Key transformation: isosorbide dinitrate reacts with NaOH to give isosorbide mononitrate, NaNO3 and water. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, often at reflux or elevated temperature; water is the solvent, no external catalyst needed.

Acid–base (carbonate decomposition) reaction; purpose is to generate ErF3 and release CO2. Hydrofluoric acid reacts with Er2(CO3)3, protonating the carbonate to evolve CO2 and water, while the erbium cation combines with three fluoride ions to form ErF3. Typically performed in aqueous HF at room temperature to 60 °C with excess HF. Water/HF solution acts as solvent; no catalyst required.

Salt metathesis between potassium cyanate and ammonium carbonate; exchanges cations to give ammonium cyanate and potassium carbonate in aqueous solution; serves as a convenient route to ammonium cyanate, a precursor in the Wöhler synthesis of urea.

Acid‑catalyzed Markovnikov hydration of an alkene; purpose is to convert 3‑ethylpent‑1‑ene into the corresponding secondary alcohol. Key transformation: addition of H2O across the double bond in the presence of H2SO4 gives 3‑ethylpentan‑2‑ol. Performed with concentrated sulfuric acid (often as aqueous H2SO4) at 0–50 °C; the acid serves as both catalyst and proton source.

Acid‑base double displacement (salt formation) reaction; purpose is to generate barium azide and release CO2. Key transformation: BaCO3 reacts with hydrazoic acid (HN3) to form Ba(N3)2, CO2 and H2O. Carried out in aqueous solution, preferably cold (0–5 °C) to limit azide decomposition; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Fischer esterification of a dihydroxy dicarboxylic acid (tartaric acid) with ethanol to afford the diethyl ester; acid catalyst such as sulfuric acid under reflux, excess ethanol serves as solvent and reactant, water is removed to drive the reaction.

Salt metathesis (halide exchange) where silver chloride reacts with tetrabutylammonium bromide to precipitate insoluble AgBr and form tetrabutylammonium chloride; typically carried out in water or a polar aprotic solvent at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Copper(II)-catalyzed aerobic oxidation of phenylglyoxal to phenylglyoxylic acid; molecular oxygen serves as the oxidant, CuCl₂ activates O₂, water is generated; usually performed in aqueous or mixed solvent at mild temperature, no additional reagents.

Redox precipitation (formation of Prussian‑blue type complex); ferricyanide oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ while Fe²⁺ reduces Fe³⁺ in the cyanide ligand, yielding insoluble iron(III) hexacyanoferrate(II) and soluble KCl; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often slightly acidic; no catalyst required; purpose: synthesis of the pigment Prussian blue or analytical Fe precipitation.

Fischer esterification of phenylglycolic acid with cyclopentyl alcohol to give the ester cyclopentolate, eliminating water; acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) and reflux in toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark trap are common conditions.

Oxidation of pyridine to pyridine N‑oxide using in‑situ formed peracetic acid from acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide; reaction done at 0–25 °C in a polar organic solvent such as dichloromethane, no metal catalyst required.

Electrophilic α‑bromination of bromoacetic acid with bromine to afford 2,2‑dibromoacetic acid and HBr; typically performed in an inert solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or glacial AcOH) under cooling (0 °C) to control the exotherm, sometimes initiated by light.

Formation of benzyl chloroformate from benzyl alcohol, phosgene and triethylamine; triethylamine scavenges the HCl generated, producing triethylammonium chloride; carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in dry dichloromethane under nitrogen atmosphere.

Solid‑state oxide synthesis; preparation of strontium tungstate (SrWO₄) as an inorganic pigment or functional material. Mixing stoichiometric WO₃ and SrO powders, grinding to homogeneity, then calcining at 1200–1300 °C in air (often 2–4 h). No solvent; the reaction proceeds via diffusion of ions in the melt or solid lattice, yielding SrWO₄ and releasing heat.

Base‑promoted E2 dehydrohalogenation; conversion of 6‑bromo‑1‑hexene to 1,5‑hexadiene. Sodium ethoxide acts as a strong base in ethanol, abstracting a β‑hydrogen (C‑5) while the C‑6–Br bond leaves, forming the second C=C bond and NaBr. Typical conditions: refluxing EtONa in absolute ethanol (or dry EtOH) for 1–2 h under inert atmosphere; the reaction is homogeneous, no catalyst required.

Double displacement precipitation; ammonium hydroxide provides OH⁻, yielding soluble ammonium fluoride and insoluble iron(II) hydroxide; conducted in aqueous NH₄OH, often with mild heating to aid precipitation; water solvent, no catalyst.

Strong hydride reduction of an ester (LiAlH₄ reduction); the ester is fully reduced to the corresponding primary alcohol (phenethyl alcohol) and the acyl fragment is reduced to ethanol; generally run in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux, with 2–3 equivalents of LiAlH₄; work‑up with aqueous acid.

Salt metathesis (double‑displacement) to exchange counter‑ions of pralidoxime. Aqueous sodium methanesulfonate is mixed with aqueous pralidoxime chloride; the Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ and the mesylate anion pairs with pralidoxime cation, producing sodium chloride (soluble) and pralidoxime mesylate, which can be isolated by crystallisation or precipitation. Room‑temperature stirring in water; no catalyst needed.

N‑alkylation of adenine at the N⁶ position using isopentenyl acetate, yielding N⁶‑isopentenyladenine (ainin) and acetic acid. Purpose: introduce an allylic isopentenyl side chain onto a purine base. Key transformation: deprotonation of the exocyclic amine of adenine, nucleophilic substitution on the allylic acetate (SN2′ or SN1‑like) with concomitant loss of acetate. Typical conditions: adenine is suspended in pyridine (or DMF) with a strong base (NaH, K₂₃) and heated to 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere; the reaction mixture is then worked up to remove acetic acid and isolate the cytokinin.

Borrowed‑hydrogen (hydrogen‑transfer) amination of a secondary alcohol. Iridium‑based catalyst (e.g., IrCl(CO)(PPh₃)₂) together with a base such as KOtBu catalyzes oxidation of isopropanol to acetone, condensation of the resulting carbonyl with ethylamine to give an imine, and subsequent transfer hydrogenation of the imine back to the secondary amine N‑ethyl‑2‑propanamine. Water is the only stoichiometric by‑product. Conditions: 100–120 °C in a high‑boiling solvent (toluene, THF, or the alcohol itself) under inert atmosphere; catalyst loading 1–2 mol %.

Acyl‑substitution condensation forming benzoic anhydride. Sodium benzoate nucleophilically attacks the carbonyl carbon of benzoyl chloride, displacing chloride to give the mixed anhydride intermediate that collapses to the symmetric anhydride while releasing NaCl. Performed in an aprotic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature, often with pyridine acting as both solvent and HCl scavenger. No external catalyst required.

Type: reduction (Bechamp reduction of aromatic nitro to amine). Purpose: convert a nitro group on 3,4-dimethyl nitrobenzene to the corresponding aniline. Key transformation: –NO2 group is reduced to –NH2 while elemental iron is oxidized to FeCl3; water is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: excess iron powder added to aqueous hydrochloric acid (≈3 M), mixture heated under reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours. Common solvent/catalyst: aqueous HCl serves as both solvent and acid; iron acts as the reducing agent; no additional catalyst needed.

Type: partial oxidation (gas‑phase reforming). Purpose: generate synthesis gas (syngas) from methane. Key transformation: CH4 reacts with limited O2 to give CO and H2 (no full combustion to CO2/H2O). Typical conditions: high temperature (800‑1200 °C) in a tubular reactor; often performed at atmospheric or elevated pressure; reaction may be catalyzed or non‑catalytic. Common catalysts (when used): nickel, copper, or rhodium on alumina; otherwise the reaction proceeds thermally without solvent.

Oxidation (redox) of mercurous chloride (Hg2Cl2) by chlorine gas to produce mercuric chloride (HgCl2); performed by bubbling Cl2 through an aqueous suspension of Hg2Cl2, sometimes in the presence of excess chloride ion to stabilize HgCl4²⁻; ambient temperature, no catalyst.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (SN2 amination). Purpose: replace the α‑chloro substituent of α‑chloroacetophenone with an amino group to afford phenacylamine. Key transformation: Cl is displaced by NH2‑ (generated in situ from NaNH2), forming phenacylamine and NaCl. Typical conditions: dry liquid ammonia as solvent, sodium amide (NaNH2) added under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), temperature kept low (‑33 °C) or gently warmed; reaction time 1‑3 h. No additional catalyst; strictly anhydrous conditions required.

Type: metal ion reduction (chemical reduction of Au(III) to Au(0)). Purpose: synthesize elemental gold (often as colloidal particles). Key transformation: AuCl4⁻ is reduced by NaBH4, yielding Au⁰, NaCl, HCl, and sodium metaborate (NaBO2). Typical conditions: aqueous solution of tetrachloroauric acid at room temperature or 0‑5 °C; NaBH4 added dropwise under vigorous stirring; reaction completes within minutes. Common solvent: water (sometimes mixed with ethanol); no external catalyst needed.

Type: acid‑base (hydride–water) reaction. Purpose: generate rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen gas; often used to produce H2 or to quench alkali metal hydrides. Key transformation: RbH reacts with H2O, producing RbOH and H2. Typical conditions: ambient temperature, solid RbH added to water under inert atmosphere to avoid moisture‑sensitive side reactions; reaction proceeds rapidly with bubbling of H2. No solvent beyond the water medium; no catalyst required.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (double SN2) leading to diamine formation. Purpose: synthesize ethylenediamine from 1,2‑dibromoethane using ammonia as nucleophile. Key transformation: each bromide is displaced by NH2‑ from NH3, with the intermediate ethylene diamine formed; ammonium bromide is generated as the by‑product. Typical conditions: excess aqueous or alcoholic ammonia, reflux (≈80‑100 °C) for several hours; sometimes pressure‑sealed vessels are used to retain ammonia. Common solvent: ethanol or water; no metal catalyst required.

Acid‑base exchange (alkoxide‑acid metathesis); used to convert aluminum ethoxide into aluminum acetate while generating ethanol; the alkoxide protonates the carboxylic acid producing the metal carboxylate and an alcohol; typically performed by mixing the reagents neat or in a non‑coordinating solvent (toluene, THF) at ambient temperature to reflux, allowing ethanol to be removed to drive the equilibrium; no catalyst required.

Catalytic dehydrogenation (or dehydro‑elimination) of 2,2‑dimethylbutane to give 2,3‑dimethyl‑1‑butene and molecular hydrogen. Purpose: convert a saturated alkane into a terminal alkene for further functionalization. Key transformation: removal of a β‑hydrogen and a hydrogen from the adjacent carbon, forming a C=C double bond and releasing H₂. Typical conditions: high‑temperature (300–400 °C) flow of the alkane over a metal catalyst (Pt/Al₂O₃, Pd/C, or Cr₂O₃); the reaction is carried out in the gas phase or in a sealed autoclave, sometimes with a hydrogen‑acceptor additive to drive the equilibrium.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitro aromatic compound; converts nitrobenzene to aniline, with water as the only stoichiometric by‑product; hydrogen gas adds across the N=O bonds in the presence of a heterogeneous Pd/C catalyst; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 25–80 °C, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate; catalyst loading ≈5–10 % Pd by weight.

Pictet‑Spengler cyclization (acid‑catalyzed imine formation followed by intramolecular electrophilic aromatic substitution); couples benzaldehyde with 2‑phenylethylamine to give 1‑benzyl‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroisoquinoline; trifluoroacetic acid protonates the aldehyde, promotes imine formation and activates the aromatic ring for cyclization; usually performed in dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature, then warmed to reflux; TFA is used in catalytic amounts (10–20 mol %); no metal catalyst needed.

Reduction (deoxygenation) of 2,6‑dimethylpyridine N‑oxide to the parent pyridine using phosphorus trichloride, producing phosphorus oxychloride as the by‑product. Purpose: regenerate the pyridine ring from its N‑oxide for subsequent synthetic steps. Key transformation: PCl₃ attacks the N‑O bond, forming POCl₃ and releasing the neutral pyridine. Typical conditions: dissolve the N‑oxide in a non‑protic solvent (CH₂Cl₂ or CHCl₃), cool to 0 °C, add PCl₃ dropwise under nitrogen, then stir at room temperature for 1–2 h; the mixture is quenched with ice water and extracted to isolate the pyridine.

Hydrolysis of methyl 2‑hydroxyacetate to regenerate glycolic acid; purpose is the reverse of esterification. Either acid‑catalyzed (dilute HCl, reflux in water) or base‑catalyzed (NaOH, then acid work‑up) water adds across the ester, producing glycolic acid and methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous medium at 80–100 °C; for acid hydrolysis a catalytic amount of H⁺ is used, for base hydrolysis stoichiometric NaOH at room temperature to 60 °C followed by neutralization. Solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Transesterification (alcoholysis) of phenyl methacrylate with ethanol; purpose: synthesis of ethyl methacrylate monomer; key transformation: phenoxy group exchanged for ethoxy, releasing phenol; typical conditions: catalytic amount of strong acid (p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or sodium ethoxide, reflux in anhydrous toluene or xylene, phenol removed by distillation or azeotropic drying; common solvents: toluene, xylene; catalyst: p‑TsOH or NaOEt.

Double‑displacement/precipitation: beryllium fluoride reacts with ammonium hydroxide, forming beryllium hydroxide precipitate and ammonium fluoride in solution; carried out in aqueous ammonium hydroxide at room temperature, solid filtered off.

Williamson ether synthesis (alkylation of a diol) to afford 1,2‑dimethoxyethane (glyme); ethylene glycol is deprotonated (commonly with NaH, K₂CO₃ or Cs₂CO₃) and the resulting alkoxide attacks methyl iodide, displacing iodide; two equivalents of MeI give the dimethyl ether and generate two equivalents of HI; performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to reflux; a base is essential to scavenge the generated HI and drive the reaction to completion.

Nucleophilic epoxide opening (SN2) of cyclohexene oxide with sodium azide; azide attacks the less hindered carbon giving trans‑2‑azidocyclohexanol. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, 0 °C to reflux (≈80 °C), using NaN₃ in excess; the reaction is tolerant of air and moisture.

Claisen [3,3]‑sigmatropic rearrangement of an allyl aryl ether; converts (prop‑2‑en‑1‑yloxy)benzene into the ortho‑allyl phenol (2‑prop‑2‑enylphenol); performed by heating the neat substrate or in a high‑boiling solvent (toluene, xylene) at 200–250 °C for several hours; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of L‑glutamic acid with sodium bicarbonate; the carboxylic acid is deprotonated to give sodium L‑glutamate while CO₂ and H₂O are released. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with gentle stirring; no special catalyst required.

Dehydration of gamma-hydroxybutanoic acid to form gamma-butyrolactone. Type: Intramolecular nucleophilic acyl substitution (lactonization). Purpose: Formation of cyclic esters. Key transformation: Hydroxyl group attacks terminal carbonyl carbon, forming a 5-membered ring lactone. Conditions: Acidic conditions (e.g., H2SO4) with heat. Common solvent: Benzene or toluene to remove water azeotropically.

Halogenolysis/oxidative substitution of a Hg–C bond; chlorine reacts with diethylmercury, cleaving one Hg‑C bond to give ethyl chloride and ethylmercury chloride. Typically carried out at low to moderate temperature in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂), often under light to initiate radical formation; no external catalyst.

Thermal disproportionation of germanium(II) oxide; two GeO units convert to elemental germanium (Ge⁰) and germanium dioxide (GeO₂). Conducted at high temperature (typically > 800 °C) under an inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) to avoid oxidation; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Ligand exchange on a gold(I) sulfide complex; purpose is to replace dimethyl sulfide with a stronger phosphine ligand to obtain chloro(triphenylphosphine)gold(I); the reaction swaps SMe₂ for PPh₃ producing AuCl·PPh₃ and liberating free dimethyl sulfide; typically performed in dry dichloromethane or chloroform under an inert atmosphere at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Thiocarbamoylation of 4‑hydroxybenzylamine with thiocarbonyl diimidazole (TCDI) to afford 4‑hydroxybenzyl isothiocyanate, with concurrent release of two equivalents of imidazole. Reaction is performed in anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, usually under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is required.

Ozonolysis of estragole (4‑methoxy‑allylbenzene); purpose is oxidative cleavage of the terminal alkene to afford 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde and formaldehyde. Ozone adds across the C=C bond forming an ozonide that, after reductive work‑up (e.g., Zn/AcOH or dimethyl sulfide), fragments into the two aldehydes. Typical conditions: O₃ gas bubbled through a solution of estragole in dry dichloromethane or methanol at –78 °C to –40 °C, followed by reductive work‑up at low temperature under inert atmosphere.

NaBH₄ reduction of 1,2‑dipylethanone (a ketone) to the corresponding secondary alcohol, 1,2‑diphenylethanol; the by‑product is sodium borate (NaBO₂). Reaction is carried out in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol, often at 0 °C to room temperature; the hydride donor NaBH₄ acts as the reducing agent without need for a catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution (basic hydrolysis) of 2‑chloro‑3‑methylbutane with aqueous NaOH to afford 3‑methyl‑2‑butanol and NaCl; hydroxide attacks the secondary carbon, usually via an SN1 pathway in protic solvent, sometimes competing with elimination; performed in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux, often using a water/ethanol solvent system.

Type: base‑catalyzed condensation (Friedel‑Crafts‑type cyclization) to form an isocoumarin ring. Purpose: construct the heterocyclic lactone core of isocoumarin from a simple aromatic anhydride and an aldehyde. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the acetaldehyde carbonyl on the carbonyl of phthalic anhydride, followed by intramolecular acylation and loss of water to give the fused lactone. Typical conditions: mixture of phthalic anhydride, acetaldehyde and sodium acetate heated to 120–150 °C, often under solvent‑free or melt conditions; sodium acetate acts as both base and catalyst. Common media: neat or in a high‑boiling polar solvent such as acetic anhydride; no external catalyst required.

Type: Aqueous redox oxidation (halogen‑oxidant). Purpose: Oxidation of selenite (SeO₃²⁻) to selenate (SeO₄²⁻) using chlorine as oxidant, producing hydrochloric acid. Key transformations: Cl₂ reacts with H₂O to give HCl and HOCl HOCl oxidizes Na₂SeO₃ to Na₂SeO₄ while being reduced to Cl. Typical conditions: Room‑temperature aqueous solution, mild stirring, neutral to slightly acidic pH. Solvent: Water; no additional catalyst needed.

Type: Wolff–Kishner reduction (hydrazone‑based deoxygenation of a carbonyl). Purpose: replace the carbonyl oxygen of 3‑hexanone with two hydrogens to afford n‑hexane. Key transformation: condensation of hydrazine with the ketone to give the corresponding hydrazone, followed by base‑induced elimination of nitrogen gas and water to generate the alkane. Typical conditions: excess hydrazine, strong base such as sodium ethoxide, high‑boiling solvent (e.g., ethylene glycol or diethylene glycol) heated to 180–220 °C under an inert atmosphere. Common solvents/catalysts: NaOEt as base; no transition‑metal catalyst needed.

Type: acid–base neutralization (salt formation) accompanied by gas evolution. Purpose: convert the highly reactive chlorosulfonic acid into a more manageable ammonium salt while releasing hydrogen chloride gas. Key transformation: HSO₃Cl + NH₄OH → NH₄HSO₄ + HCl (g). Typical conditions: addition of chilled aqueous or gaseous NH₄OH to chlorosulfonic acid maintained at 0–5 °C to control vigorous exotherm and HCl evolution. Common media: dilute NH₄OH solution; reaction often performed in a fume hood due to HCl release.

Acid‑base neutralization; strong base lithium hydroxide neutralizes hydrochloric acid to afford lithium chloride and water; exothermic reaction carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water solvent, no catalyst.

Type: acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of a primary alcohol to an alkene. Purpose: convert 1‑butanol into the corresponding terminal alkene, 1‑butene. Key transformation: protonation of the hydroxyl group, loss of water to generate a carbocation, followed by β‑hydrogen elimination to form the C=C bond. Typical conditions: excess strong acid such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄, heating to 170–180 °C, often with a Dean‑Stark trap or continuous removal of water to drive the equilibrium. Common solvents: the acid itself serves as both catalyst and reaction medium; sometimes carried out in toluene or cyclohexane as an azeotropic solvent.

Thionation of benzophenone with Lawesson’s reagent to give thiobenzophenone and 2,4,6‑trimethylpyridine (collidine). Purpose: replace the carbonyl oxygen with sulfur. Key transformation: O→S conversion of the ketone, with Lawesson’s reagent acting as the sulfur source, generating collidine as by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in dry toluene, xylene or THF under nitrogen, 1‑2 h. No additional catalyst; Lawesson’s reagent itself.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction between aqueous rubidium selenide and silver nitrate forming insoluble silver selenide precipitate and soluble rubidium nitrate; purpose is isolation of Ag2Se or removal of selenide ions; key transformation is Ag+ reacting with Se2‑ to give Ag2Se solid while Rb+ pairs with NO3‑; carried out by mixing the two aqueous solutions at ambient temperature with stirring, followed by filtration of the precipitate; water is the solvent; no catalyst.

Type: High‑temperature solid‑gas chlorination/oxygen transfer. Purpose: Production of phosgene (COCl₂) and zinc‑group chloride (ZrCl₄) from carbon tetrachloride and zirconium dioxide. Key transformations: CCl₄ donates carbon and chlorine to form COCl₂; ZrO₂ accepts oxygen and is chlorinated to ZrCl₄. Typical conditions: Heated solid mixture (≈400‑600 °C) in a quartz tube under flowing inert gas (N₂ or Ar). No solvent; catalyst not required.

Amide acylation: the primary amine of 2‑(methylamino)acetic acid reacts with acetic anhydride to form the N‑acetylated product 2‑[acetyl(methyl)amino]acetic acid, releasing one equivalent of acetic acid; usually done at rt in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base like pyridine or DMAP.

Peracid epoxidation (Prilezhaev reaction); converts the C=C of acrylic acid to an epoxide (glycidic acid) while reducing peracetic acid to acetic acid; typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetone; no catalyst required, avoid strong bases.

Double‑displacement metathesis/precipitation; exchanges K⁺ and Be²⁺ to form soluble potassium chloride and insoluble beryllium carbonate; carried out in aqueous solution with stirring at ambient temperature, followed by filtration to isolate the precipitate.

Redox oxidation of ferrocyanide by nitric acid; Fe(II) in potassium ferrocyanide is oxidized to Fe(III) in potassium ferricyanide while nitrate is reduced to nitrogen dioxide and water; conducted with cold, concentrated HNO₃ in water, temperature kept below ~30 °C to control gas evolution; no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation): propylamine attacks acetyl chloride, displacing chloride to give propyl acetamide (propylacetamide) and hydrogen chloride. The purpose is to synthesize a secondary amide. Key transformation is conversion of an acyl chloride to an amide with loss of HCl. Commonly carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, using an organic base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to scavenge the HCl. The reaction is usually exothermic and may be performed under nitrogen.

N‑Methylation (alkylation) of melamine using dimethyl sulfate; four N‑H groups of melamine are methylated to give altretamine (tetramethylmelamine) while potassium carbonate neutralizes the resulting hydrogen sulfate to potassium hydrogen sulfate; reaction run in an anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) with K₂CO₃ as base at 0–50 °C under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base salt exchange; hydrochloric acid protonates tetrabutylammonium acetate to form acetic acid and tetrabutylammonium chloride; carried out in water or a water/ethanol mixture at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst needed.

Ester hydrolysis (acid or base catalyzed); purpose is to convert the methyl ester of L‑histidine into the free amino acid; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon of the ester, breaking the C–OCH₃ bond to give L‑histidine and methanol; typical conditions involve aqueous medium at reflux with either a dilute mineral acid (e.g., HCl, pH ≈ 1) or a base (NaOH) followed by neutralisation; common solvent is water or a water‑organic mixture such as water/ethanol.

Osmium‑tetraoxide‑catalyzed syn‑dihydroxylation (Lemieux–Johnson oxidation); purpose is to introduce two vicinal hydroxyl groups at the 9,10‑positions of anthracene; key transformation is cycloaddition of OsO₄ across the central C=C bond forming a cyclic osmate ester, which is then oxidatively cleaved by N‑methylmorpholine N‑oxide (NMO) to release 9,10‑anthracenediol and regenerate OsO₄; typical conditions are catalytic OsO₄ (≈1–5 mol %), stoichiometric NMO, in a mixed solvent such as acetone‑water (1:1) at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction is usually performed under an inert atmosphere and protected from light.
Disproportionation of silicon monoxide; two SiO molecules rearrange upon heating to give Si (solid) and SiO₂ (solid); occurs spontaneously above ~1500 °C; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid–base neutralisation (salt formation); purpose is to convert the acidic thiobarbituric‑acid derivative into its sodium salt (thiopental sodium) for pharmaceutical use; key transformation is deprotonation of two equivalents of 5‑ethyl‑5‑(1‑methylbutyl)‑2‑thiobarbituric acid by sodium carbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and yielding the sodium thiopental salt; typical conditions are aqueous solution at ambient temperature with gentle stirring; the reaction is performed in water or water‑ethanol mixture; the precipitated CO₂ evolves as a gas.

Strong oxidative cleavage of chroman with KMnO4; the cyclic ether is broken to phenol (from the aromatic ring) and acetaldehyde (from the side chain) while MnO2 precipitates; purpose is oxidative fragmentation of the heterocycle; typical conditions: aqueous KMnO4, neutral to alkaline medium, heating to reflux; after reaction the mixture is filtered to remove MnO2 and worked up to isolate products.

Halide displacement (acetate substitution) using silver acetate; purpose is to replace the bromide in propargyl bromide with an acetate group to give propargyl acetate; key transformation is Ag⁺ precipitation of bromide as insoluble AgBr, driving the SN2 attack of acetate on the primary carbon; typical conditions involve stirring the reactants in a dry, aprotic solvent such as acetone or dichloromethane at reflux or at room temperature, protected from light to avoid photodegradation of Ag⁺; the solid AgBr is filtered off after completion.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) acid‑base reaction; purpose is to generate lactic acid and precipitate insoluble calcium oxalate, often used for removal of calcium ions; key transformation is exchange of the calcium cation from calcium lactate with the oxalate anion from oxalic acid, forming calcium oxalate (CaC₂O₄) as a white precipitate and liberating two equivalents of lactic acid; typical conditions are aqueous solution at room temperature or slight warming, with vigorous stirring; the reaction is carried out in water; the solid calcium oxalate is filtered off.

Catalytic hydrogenation; purpose is to fully saturate the aromatic naphthalene ring to give decalin (decalin = decahydronaphthalene). Key transformation is addition of ten hydrogen atoms across the two fused benzene rings, breaking aromaticity. Typical conditions: hydrogen gas at 1–50 atm, temperature 50–150 °C, Pt/C (5–10 wt %) as catalyst, often in an alcoholic solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, or under neat conditions.

Phosphorylation via carbonyldiimidazole activation; purpose is to install a phosphate ester on the phenolic hydroxyl of 4‑hydroxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine to afford psilocybin. The CDI reacts with phosphoric acid to form an activated phosphorimidazolide which transfers the phosphate to the phenol, releasing CO₂ and two equivalents of imidazole. Typical conditions: anhydrous DMF or pyridine, 0 °C to rt, stoichiometric phosphoric acid and CDI (1.1–1.5 eq each), reaction run under nitrogen, purification by aqueous work‑up and chromatography.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitrile; purpose is to reduce trifluoroacetonitrile to the primary amine 2,2,2‑trifluoroethylamine. Key transformation is addition of two hydrogen atoms to the C≡N bond, giving a C–NH₂ group. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 10–50 atm, 25–80 °C, Raney Ni, Pd/C, or Pt/C as catalyst, solvent such as methanol or ethanol; reaction often proceeds to completion within several hours.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone; purpose is to convert diethyl sulfide into diethyl sulfone using peracetic acid as the oxidant. The reaction proceeds via a sulfoxide intermediate that is further oxidized to the sulfone, with each equivalent of peracetic acid delivering an acetyl group that is released as acetic acid. Typical conditions: room temperature to 40 °C, dichloromethane or ethyl acetate as solvent, two equivalents of peracetic acid (often generated in situ from acetic acid/H₂O₂), reaction time 1–4 h, aqueous work‑up removes acetic acid.

Hydrolysis of a silyl ester; purpose is to cleave trimethylsilyl acetate to give acetic acid and trimethylsilanol. Water attacks the silicon‑oxygen bond, displacing the acetate group. Typical conditions: aqueous medium (often mixed with a miscible organic solvent such as THF or MeCN), ambient temperature, optionally mild acid or base catalyst (e.g., 0.1 M HCl or Na₂CO₃) to accelerate the reaction; completion in minutes to an hour.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann‑type N‑aryl coupling; purpose is to form the C–N bond between piperazine and 3‑bromo‑1‑(trifluoromethyl)benzene, yielding 1‑(3‑(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)piperazine. Key transformations: oxidative addition of the aryl bromide to CuI, transmetalation with the deprotonated piperazine (generated by K₂CO₃), and reductive elimination to give the aryl‑amine product and KBr. Typical conditions: CuI (5–10 mol %), K₂CO₃ (2–3 eq), DMF or DMSO as solvent, reflux (≈110 °C) under inert atmosphere for 12–24 h; product isolated by filtration, aqueous work‑up, and chromatography.

High‑temperature solid‑state redox (metallothermic reduction) of vanadium(V) oxide by magnesium metal, producing magnesium oxide and vanadium(II) oxide. The reaction performed in an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at 600–900 °C in a sealed crucible or tube furnace; no solvent is used, and stoichiometric magnesium serves as the reductant.

Acid‑base exchange (salt metathesis); aqueous HCl added to dimethylammonium formate converts the anion to chloride, producing dimethylammonium chloride and freeing formic acid; done in water at 0‑25 °C, no catalyst.

Electrophilic cleavage of a diselenide by chlorine; diphenyl diselenide reacts with Cl₂ gas (or a source of Cl⁺ such as N‑chlorosuccinimide) to break the Se–Se bond and generate phenylselenyl chloride (PhSeCl). The reaction is performed in an inert, non‑protic solvent like carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often using a slight excess of chlorine; the stoichiometry is PhSeSePh + Cl₂ → 2 PhSeCl.

Acid‑catalyzed skeletal isomerization of a branched alkane, converting 3‑ethyl‑4‑methylhexane into the more thermodynamically stable 2,4‑dimethylheptane via carbocation rearrangement. Commonly achieved with solid acid catalysts (e.g., zeolite H‑ZSM‑5 or Al₂O₃) at 150–250 °C under a hydrogen atmosphere to suppress cracking. No solvent is required in the vapor‑phase process.

Redox single‑displacement reaction of aluminum metal with anhydrous hydrogen bromide; aluminum is oxidised to Al³⁺ producing aluminium bromide (often AlBr₃·(solvent) or AlBr₃ gas) while H⁺ is reduced to H₂. Requires anhydrous conditions, often reflux in a dry non‑protic solvent such as dry benzene, toluene or carbon tetrachloride, or performed in a sealed tube; no additional catalyst.

Conversion of a benzoate salt to the corresponding acid chloride using oxalyl chloride; the reaction proceeds via formation of a mixed anhydride, releasing one equivalent each of CO₂ and CO, and generating benzoyl chloride and ammonium chloride. Typically conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge HCl.

Aerobic catalytic oxidation of 2,5‑dimethylfuran to maltol (3‑hydroxy‑2‑methyl‑4‑pyrone). Molecular oxygen serves as the oxidant, and the transformation is facilitated by metal oxide or heterogeneous catalysts (e.g., Au/TiO₂, Cu–Al mixed oxide, or vanadium‑based catalysts) in either aqueous or alcoholic media at 80–150 °C under O₂ pressure (1–5 atm). Water is formed as a by‑product and oxygen gas is released from the peroxide intermediates.

Acid‑base redox reaction of silver(II) oxide (AgO) with sulfuric acid, yielding silver(I) sulfate, water, and molecular oxygen. The process occurs in aqueous H₂SO₄ at ambient temperature or mild heating (≤80 °C); the silver oxide is reduced while the acid supplies protons, and the liberated oxygen evolves as gas. No additional catalyst is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; purpose is to exchange metal cations and isolate nickel(II) hydroxide as a solid precipitate while forming soluble aluminum acetate; key transformation is Ni²⁺ (from nickel acetate) combines with OH⁻ (from aluminum hydroxide) to give Ni(OH)₂ precipitate and Al³⁺ combines with acetate to give Al(OAc)₃ in solution; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Halogen exchange (iodination) reaction in which germanium tetrachloride is treated with hydrogen iodide to replace chloride ligands with iodide, producing germanium tetraiodide and hydrogen chloride; typically carried out in anhydrous liquid HI or HI gas at 100‑200 °C in a sealed tube, no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitroso functional group; purpose is to convert 4‑nitrosalicylic acid to the pharmaceutical intermediate 4‑aminosalicylic acid; key transformation is the addition of H₂ across the N=O bond to give an NH₂ group, with Pd on carbon as the heterogeneous catalyst; usually performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to 50 °C; the Pd/C catalyst is essential, no additional reagents are needed.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC); purpose is to obtain 2‑(pyridin‑2‑yl)acetaldehyde without over‑oxidation to the corresponding acid; key transformation is removal of two hydrogen atoms from the benzylic CH₂OH group to form the carbonyl; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane at room temperature under an inert atmosphere; PCC acts as the oxidant, no extra catalyst is needed.

Fischer esterification of a pyridine‑2‑carboxylic acid. Ethanol reacts with 2‑chloronicotinic acid in the presence of an acid catalyst (concentrated H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, or HCl) to form ethyl 2‑chloro‑3‑pyridinecarboxylate and water. The mixture is refluxed in excess ethanol (often with a Dean–Stark trap) at 78 °C until equilibrium shifts toward ester formation.

Double displacement (ion‑exchange) metathesis reaction; purpose is to swap nitrate and acetate anions between lead(II) nitrate and potassium acetate, yielding lead(II) acetate and potassium nitrate; key transformation is Pb²⁺ pairing with two acetate ions while K⁺ pairs with nitrate ions; carried out in aqueous solution, often at room temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Base‑catalyzed condensation (step‑growth polymerization) of phenol with formaldehyde to form a phenolic resin; purpose is to produce a thermosetting polymer (e.g., Bakelite); key transformations include electrophilic aromatic substitution (methylolation) of phenol by formaldehyde followed by cross‑linking to give methylene‑bridged phenolic units with elimination of water; reaction is conducted in alkaline medium (KOH) in water or methanol at 60–120 °C; the hydroxide ion acts as the catalyst; no additional catalyst is needed.

General type: catalytic cracking (heterogeneous). Purpose: production of a C3 alkene and a C4 alkane from a straight‑chain alkane. Key transformation: C‑C bond cleavage in heptane to afford propene (C3H6) and butane (C4H10). Typical conditions: temperatures 500–750 °C with acidic solid catalysts (e.g., zeolites, alumina). Common solvents/catalysts: solid acid catalysts; reaction conducted in gas phase, no solvent.

Redox (oxidation–reduction) reaction of arsenite with concentrated nitric acid; purpose is to oxidize arsenic(III) to arsenic(V) while reducing nitrate to nitrogen dioxide gas; key transformations: As³⁺ in calcium arsenite is oxidized to H₃AsO₄ (arsenic acid) and nitrate (NO₃⁻) is reduced to NO₂; calcium ions pair with nitrate to give calcium nitrate; typically performed by heating the solid mixture in concentrated HNO₃, often under reflux; concentrated nitric acid acts both as reagent and solvent; no external catalyst is required.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction accompanied by acid‑base gas evolution; purpose is to generate insoluble silver carbonate while converting bicarbonate to carbon dioxide and water; key transformations: Ag⁺ pairs with CO₃²⁻ to precipitate Ag₂CO₃, K⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to give KNO₃, and the bicarbonate ion decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with gentle stirring; water is the solvent and no catalyst is needed.

Hydrolysis of chlorine monofluoride; a non‑redox hydrolytic cleavage where ClF reacts with water to form HF and hypochlorous acid (HOCl). Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction is rapid and exothermic, requiring no special catalyst.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis). Beryllium chloride reacts with phosphoric acid to form insoluble beryllium phosphate precipitate and hydrogen chloride gas. Performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Redox reaction between chromium(II) acetate and potassium permanganate: Cr(II) is oxidized to Cr(III) acetate while permanganate is reduced to insoluble MnO₂ (Mn(IV)), with concomitant formation of potassium acetate and water; usually performed in aqueous solution under neutral to slightly alkaline conditions, with stirring to precipitate MnO₂.

Double displacement/metathesis precipitation; synthesis of gallium sulfide by exchanging sulfide and chloride ions; Na2S reacts with GaCl3 to form insoluble Ga2S3 and NaCl; typically performed in aqueous solution with heating under inert atmosphere; water as solvent, no additional catalyst.

Reductive amination; formation of the secondary amine Furfenorex from phenylacetone and 2-furfurylamine; carbonyl of phenylacetone condenses with the amine then is reduced to give N‑(2‑furyl)‑1‑phenyl‑2‑propanamine; commonly carried out with NaBH3CN or NaBH(OAc)3 in methanol or ethanol at 0‑25 °C, buffered with acetic acid.

Intramolecular acylation/cyclization of anthranilic acid with acetic anhydride to form the lactam oxindole; excess acetic anhydride heated to reflux (120–150 °C) and serves as solvent; acetic acid is generated as by‑product; product is oxindole.

SN2 alkylation of the malonate anion with methyl iodide to afford methyl malonate (methyl propanedioate) and NaI. Typical conditions include a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at room temperature or gentle heating; the reaction proceeds via direct nucleophilic substitution.

Oxidation of trioxorhenium (ReO₃) with hydrogen peroxide to produce perrhenic acid (HReO₄) and water; H₂O₂ serves as the oxidant in a redox process. Typically performed in aqueous solution at room temperature, sometimes with mild acidification; no additional catalyst is required.

Oxidation of primary alcohol to aldehyde using acidic dichromate (Jones oxidation); ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III); reaction performed in aqueous H2SO4 solution at 0‑25 °C; water as solvent, no additional catalyst.

Quaternization (SN2 alkylation) of dimethylbenzylamine with benzyl bromide to give the quaternary ammonium salt bibenzonium bromide; the lone pair on nitrogen attacks the benzylic carbon displacing bromide; usually carried out in refluxing acetonitrile or ethanol, neat or with a polar aprotic solvent; no catalyst required.

O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of resorcinol with methyl iodide under basic conditions to afford 1,3‑dimethoxybenzene; phenoxide ions generated by NaOH attack methyl iodide in an SN2 process; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH or K2CO3 with excess MeI in DMF or acetone at reflux; no additional catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed intramolecular cyclodehydration of bis(2‑hydroxyethyl) sulfide to form 1,4‑oxathiane; phosphoric acid protonates hydroxyl groups, facilitating loss of water and ring closure; carried out by heating the diol with conc. H3PO4 (or other strong acid) at 120‑150 °C; solvent‑free or in toluene; acid acts as catalyst.

Carbonation/precipitation reaction; inorganic carbon capture. CO₂ dissolved in water reacts with calcium silicate (Ca₂SiO₄) to form insoluble calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) precipitate and silica (SiO₂). Typically performed in aqueous slurry at ambient to moderately elevated temperature (20‑80 °C) under atmospheric or mild CO₂ pressure. No catalyst required; common solvents are water or water‑mixed brine; stirring promotes solid–liquid contact.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol; decanoic acid is reduced to decanol with concomitant formation of water. Common methods include LiAlH₄ (3 equiv) in dry THF at reflux, or catalytic hydrogenation (e.g., Raney Ni, H₂, 50–100 atm, 80 °C) or borane‑THF complex; anhydrous conditions and aprotic solvent (THF, ether) are typical.

Hydrolysis of a metal formate (acid‑base reaction). Aluminum formate [(Al(HCOO)₃] reacts with water, liberating three equivalents of formic acid (HCOOH) and precipitating aluminum hydroxide (Al(OH)₃). Conducted in aqueous medium, often at mild heating (30‑60 °C) to drive equilibrium toward products. No catalyst needed; neutral pH conditions favor complete hydrolysis.

Ketalization (acetal formation) of 3-pentanone with ethylene glycol to give a cyclic ketal; purpose is carbonyl protection. Key transformation is condensation of the ketone carbonyl with the diol to form 2,2-diethyl-1,3-dioxolane with loss of water. Typical conditions: catalytic p‑toluenesulfonic acid or BF₃·OEt₂, reflux in toluene or benzene with a Dean–Stark trap (or use molecular sieves) to remove water. Common solvents: toluene, benzene, dichloromethane.

Acid‑base displacement to generate hydrofluoric acid. Sulfuric acid reacts with two equivalents of ammonium fluoride (NH₄F) to produce two equivalents of hydrogen fluoride (HF) and ammonium sulfate ((NH₄)₂SO₄). Performed in dilute aqueous solution, usually at low temperature (0‑25 °C) to minimize HF volatilization. No catalyst; excess acid ensures quantitative HF release.

N‑methylation of indole via strong base (nucleophilic substitution, SN2). Sodium hydride deprotonates the indole N–H, releasing hydrogen gas (H₂) and forming sodium indolide. The resulting anion attacks methyl iodide (MeI) in an SN2 step, yielding 1‑methylindole and sodium iodide (NaI). Typical conditions: anhydrous polar aprotic solvent (DMF, THF, or DMSO), inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), temperature 0 °C to rt. Sodium hydride is the base; no external catalyst required.

Enzymatic dehydration (elimination) of homo‑isocitric acid to homo‑aconitic acid. The reaction removes one molecule of water, creating a double bond within the carbon chain, analogous to the aconitase step in lysine biosynthesis. Catalyzed by the Fe‑S enzyme homo‑aconitase under physiological conditions (pH 7‑8, 25‑37 °C). In vitro, similar dehydration can be achieved with dehydrating agents (e.g., POCl₃, P₂O₅) in dry organic solvent, but the natural pathway relies on the enzyme.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride with sodium cyanide to afford the corresponding nitrile; used to introduce a –C≡N group. Typically carried out in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or DMSO at 50‑100 °C; sodium cyanide is added as a solid or aqueous solution and the inorganic chloride by‑product precipitates.

Acid‑base reaction with bicarbonate (gas‑evolving neutralization); purpose is to liberate methylamine and remove acid as CO₂. Key transformation: HCO₃⁻ reacts with the methylammonium ion, producing CO₂, H₂O and NaBr. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, mild heating to promote CO₂ evolution. Common solvent: water. No catalyst required.

Metathesis/double‑displacement; exchanges chloride for fluoride to give dysprosium trifluoride; DyCl3 + 3 NaF → DyF3 ↓ + 3 NaCl; conducted in water or dilute aqueous solution, usually with slight heating (40–80 °C) to improve solubility and precipitation of the less‑soluble DyF3.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide to vinyl bromide; Markovnikov addition of HBr gives 1,1‑dibromoethane (both bromines on the same carbon). Conducted with HBr gas in an inert solvent (CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂) at room temperature or under reflux; no catalyst is typically required.

Acyl‑chloride mediated esterification (acyl substitution) of tropine to give homatropine. Tropine’s secondary alcohol attacks phenylacetyl chloride, forming the phenylacetyl ester (homatropine) and releasing chloride ion.
