Pyridine acts as a base and nucleophilic catalyst, scavenging HCl and driving the reaction forward. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to rt, under inert atmosphere. No additional catalyst required beyond pyridine.

Nucleophilic substitution (silicon alkylation) where methyl lithium replaces the chloro substituent on 1‑chloro(dimethyl)vinylsilane, producing 1‑trimethyl(vinyl)silane and LiCl. Typically carried out under inert atmosphere in anhydrous THF or diethyl ether at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed to rt; no additional catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis: sodium hydride deprotonates cyclopentanol to give the cyclopentoxide ion, which undergoes SN2 attack on methyl iodide to afford cyclopentyl methyl ether and NaI. Conducted in dry aprotic solvent (THF or DMF) at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen; NaH is the base, no catalyst.

Type: hydrolysis of an acid chloride (nucleophilic acyl substitution); purpose: convert prop‑2‑ynoyl chloride to the corresponding carboxylic acid; key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon, displaces chloride and yields prop‑2‑ynoic acid with release of HCl; typical conditions: aqueous workup at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base such as pyridine to scavenge HCl; common solvent: anhydrous ether or dichloromethane with added water.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution; converts a primary alkyl chloride to an ether; chlorine is displaced by methoxide to give 1‑methoxyoctane and NaCl; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at reflux; no catalyst required, sodium methoxide is the nucleophile.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of methyl bromide by azide ion; prepares methyl azide, a versatile azide precursor for click chemistry. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at 0 °C to reflux; no catalyst required, though a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., TBAB) can be used to improve yield.

Acid‑ neutralization: hydrogen selenide (H2Se) reacts with two equivalents of lithium hydroxide in aqueous solution to form lithium selenide (Li2Se) and water. Performed in water or mixed water/ethanol at ambient temperature; straightforward salt‑formation, no catalyst.

Proton abstraction (base generation): ethyl lithium a proton from diisopropylamine, yielding lithium diisopropylamide (LDA) and ethane gas. Reaction is run at –78 °C in dry THF under nitrogen to avoid side reactions; LDA is used as a strong, non‑nucleophilic base.

Fischer esterification; converts a hydroxy‑carboxylic acid to its methyl ester to protect the acid function; key transformation is condensation of the carboxyl group with methanol forming a methyl ester and water; typically performed with catalytic mineral acid (e.g., H2SO4) under reflux in excess methanol, often with a Dean‑Stark trap or azeotropic removal of water to drive the equilibrium.

Oxidation of benzylic alcohol; MnO2 serves as a stoichiometric oxidant to convert benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde while being reduced to MnO and water; carried out at room temperature to 50 °C in an aprotic organic solvent such as dichloromethane, ether or acetonitrile; solid MnO2 is added in excess, no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (chlorination): chlorine gas electrophilically attacks the activated aromatic ring of 3,5‑dimethylaniline, giving 2‑chloro‑3,5‑dimethylaniline and HCl as by‑product. Usually performed in a dilute acid medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) or with a Lewis‑acid catalyst (FeCl3, AlCl3) in an inert organic solvent (CCl4, CH2Cl2) at 0–25 °C to control regioselectivity and prevent over‑chlorination.

Oxidation of aldehyde to carboxylic acid (Jones oxidation): fluoroacetaldehyde is oxidized by dichromate in sulfuric acid to fluoroacetic acid, while the Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) sulfate and sodium sulfate is formed from the sodium counter‑ion. Conducted in aqueous H2SO4 at 0 °C to reflux, often using a mixture of water and acetone as solvent; the dichromate acts as the oxidant, no additional catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization to form a pharmaceutical salt; the free base naphazoline is converted to its hydrochloride by treatment with aqueous HCl, yielding the more water‑soluble naphazoline hydrochloride; typically performed at room temperature in water or a water–ethanol mixture, often with stirring until dissolution is complete.

Hydrolytic decomposition of peracetic acid; water attacks the peroxy bond, cleaving peracetic acid into acetic acid and hydrogen peroxide; generally carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required, though mild acid or base can accelerate the reaction.

Double displacement reaction; used to precipitate barium sulfate, commonly for qualitative ion analysis; anion exchange between barium bromide and magnesium sulfate in aqueous solution; conducted in water; no catalyst required.

Regioselective oxidative aromatic hydroxylation; the flavone luteolin (5,7,3’,4’-tetrahydroxyflavone) is further hydroxylated at the 5′ position of the B‑ring to give tricetin (5,7,3’,4’,5′‑pentahydroxyflavone); commonly achieved with copper(II) salts and hydrogen peroxide or enzymatic P450 systems; reactions are run in polar solvents (e.g., methanol or aqueous buffer) at 0–40 °C under aerobic conditions.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative acylation (directed C–H functionalization) of thiophene; acetyl chloride serves as the acyl source, oxygen oxidizes Cu(II) to Cu(III) which facilitates the transfer of the acetyl group to the 2‑position of thiophene, affording 2‑acetylthiophene with release of HCl; typical conditions use Cu(OAc)₂ as catalyst in acetic acid or dioxane, O₂ atmosphere, 80–120 °C, and inert stirring.

Acid–base salt formation (SO₂ absorption); sulfur dioxide gas dissolves in aqueous potassium sulfite, forming potassium bisulfite (KHSO₃) via addition of SO₂ to the sulfite ion; performed in water at room temperature, often in a gas‑scrubbing setup; no additional reagents are required.

Hydroboration–oxidation of methyl vinyl ether; diborane adds across the C=C bond of the vinyl ether to give a trialkylborane intermediate, which is subsequently oxidized by hydrogen peroxide in basic (NaOH) aqueous solution to furnish 2‑methoxyethanol (anti‑Markovnikov addition of water); reactions are conducted in an aprotic ether solvent such as THF at 0 °C to 25 °C for the borane step, followed by aqueous NaOH/H₂O₂ oxidation at ambient temperature.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction in aqueous solution; silver permanganate (AgMnO4) reacts with sodium chloride (NaCl) to produce insoluble silver chloride (AgCl) as a white precipitate and soluble sodium permanganate (NaMnO4). Conducted in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous solution; iron(II) ions exchange with ammonium ions to form sparingly soluble iron(II) fluoride precipitate and soluble ammonium nitrate; performed at ambient temperature in water.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (reverse of Fischer esterification). Purpose: regeneration of the allylic alcohol and acetic acid. Key transformation: water attacks the protonated carbonyl of the acetate, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to release acetic acid and the alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous mineral acid (HCl or H₂SO₄), reflux (80–110 °C), often in a mixed solvent such as methanol/water.

Acidic chlorination (halogenation) of isocyanuric acid using calcium hypochlorite; produces trichloroisocyanuric acid, a solid chlorine donor/disinfectant; carried out in aqueous HCl medium, typically 0–25 °C; water as solvent.

Dehydrofluorination (E2 elimination) of a tertiary alkyl fluoride; purpose is to generate the alkene 2‑methylpropene by removal of HF; hydroxide ion abstracts a β‑hydrogen while the fluoride leaves, producing potassium fluoride, water, and the alkene; commonly carried out with aqueous or alcoholic KOH solution at elevated temperature (reflux), often in ethanol or methanol as solvent; strong base and heat drive the elimination.

Metathesis precipitation; hydrofluoric acid reacts with bismuth(III) sulfate to give insoluble bismuth(III) fluoride and aqueous sulfuric acid; conducted in aqueous HF, often at low temperature; water solvent.

Hydrolysis of an imine (Schiff base) to an amine and aldehyde; water cleaves 1-(2-chlorophenyl)-N-phenylmethanimine yielding aniline and 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde; usually performed in aqueous acidic or neutral medium with mild heating (≈50 °C).

Nucleophilic substitution/condensation forming the organophosphate insecticide Phosmet; dimethyl phosphorodithioic acid attacks N‑chloromethylphthalimide, displacing chloride which protonates pyridine to pyridinium chloride; performed in an aprotic organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with pyridine as base, 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of carbon tetrachloride over nickel; hydrogen reduces CCl₄ to chloroform while generating hydrogen chloride; carried out at elevated temperature (200–300 °C) and hydrogen pressure (5–10 atm) in the presence of a nickel catalyst, often in the gas phase or with a non‑reactive solvent.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; cadmium chloride reacts with calcium carbonate to exchange anions, precipitating cadmium carbonate while calcium chloride stays dissolved. Performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst needed; filtration isolates the insoluble CdCO₃.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl bromide by a thiol. Ethanethiol is deprotonated (often with a mild base such as NaH or Et₃N) to generate the ethylthiolate anion, which attacks the carbon bearing the bromide of 4‑bromobutan‑1‑ol, displacing Br⁻ and forming 4‑ethylsulfanyl‑butan‑1‑ol. The by‑product is HBr, which is usually scavenged by the base. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere optional.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt metathesis). Triethylamine acts as a non‑nucleophilic base and abstracts the proton from piperidine·hydrochloride, giving free piperidine base and forming the salt triethylammonium chloride. Often performed in an aprotic organic solvent (CH₂Cl₂, THF) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Phosphorylation (formation of a phosphate ester) via nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus. The phenolic oxygen of p‑nitrophenol attacks the phosphorus of diethyl chlorophosphate, displacing chloride. Pyridine serves both as solvent and base, capturing the released HCl to give pyridinium chloride. Reaction is typically run in dry pyridine or pyridine/CH₂Cl₂ mixture, at 0 °C to room temperature, under anhydrous conditions.

Negishi cross‑coupling (Ni‑catalyzed C(sp²)–C(sp³) bond formation). Phenylzinc bromide transfers the phenyl group to ethyl bromide in the presence of a nickel(II) chloride catalyst (often with a phosphine ligand such as bis‑diphenylphosphinoethane). The result is ethylbenzene. Standard conditions: THF as solvent, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), 50–80 °C, catalyst loading 5–10 mol %.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction in aqueous solution. Ammonium hydroxide exchanges its cation with magnesium octanoate, precipitating insoluble magnesium hydroxide while forming soluble ammonium octanoate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; stirring and slight heating may be used to improve precipitation.

metathesis/acid‑base exchange in aqueous medium. Hydrobromic acid protonates the acetate ligands of copper(II) acetate, liberating acetic acid and substituting bromide for acetate on the metal centre, yielding copper(II) bromide. Usually performed in water or aqueous HBr solution, at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Combustion/oxidation of diphosphane; molecular O2 oxidizes P2H4 to phosphorus pentoxide (P2O5) with concomitant formation of water. Conducted by heating diphosphane in a stream of O2 (often flame or sealed tube at >200 °C); no solvent, reaction is highly exothermic.

Peracid of azobenzene to azoxybenzene; acetic acid and H2O2 generate peracetic acid in situ, which oxidizes the N=N bond of azobenzene to the N‑O‑N (azoxy) functionality, releasing water. Carried out at 0–25 °C in a mixture of glacial acetic acid and water, sometimes with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H2SO4) to promote peracid formation.

Mitsunobu esterification to form butacaine; the primary alcohol of 2‑(diethylamino)ethanol is activated by triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate, allowing nucleophilic attack by p‑butoxybenzoic acid to give the ester (butacaine) and by‑products triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazinedicarboxylate. Conducted at 0 °C to rt in anhydrous THF or dry dichloromethane under nitrogen; reagents are used in stoichiometric amounts, no additional catalyst needed.

Three‑component synthesis of propranolol via epoxide opening; 1‑naphthol reacts with epichlorohydrin under basic conditions (e.g., NaOH) to give a β‑hydroxy ether epoxide, which is then opened by isopropylamine to afford the β‑aryl‑oxy‑propylamine (propranolol). Typical protocol: reflux 1‑naph with epichlorohydrin in aqueous NaOH or ethanol, isolate the epoxide intermediate, then add isopropylamine at 0–25 °C. Solvent: ethanol or water‑ethanol mixture; no metal catalyst required.

Conversion of a dicarboxylic acid to its acid chloride (PCl5 chlorination); phosphorus pentachloride reacts with propane‑1,3‑dicarboxylic acid, replacing the –OH groups of both carboxyl functions with –Cl, yielding propanedioyl dichloride, while generating HCl and POCl3 as gaseous by‑products. Performed in anhydrous chlorinated solvent (e., dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; excess PCl5 is often used to drive completion.

Dehydrogenative coupling (dimerization) of pinacolborane to bis(pinacolato)diborane with release of H₂; used to generate a diboron reagent for borylation chemistry; typically heated (80‑120 °C) in anhydrous aromatic solvent such as toluene or THF in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst (Ir, Rh, Ni) or a strong base (KOtBu).

Acid‑ salt metathesis; cadmium tellurite reacts with aqueous HCl to give soluble cadmium chloride and tellurous acid (H₂TeO₃); performed in water at ambient temperature, often with excess HCl; no special catalyst required.

Aerobic oxidation of 3,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde to protocatechuic acid, with O₂ as oxidant and H₂O₂ formed as by‑product; usually catalyzed by metal ions (Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺) or enzymes in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media at room temperature to ~60 °C; purpose is conversion of an aldehyde to the corresponding dihydxybenzoic acid.
Protonation (acid‑base reaction) of lithium thiocyanate by HCl to give hydrogen thiocyanate (HSCN) and lithium chloride; carried out in aqueous solution, typically at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst needed.

Fischer esterification: acid-catalyzed condensation of carboxylic acids (methacrylic) with phenols; yields phenyl methacrylate and water via protonation of the carbonyl group, alcohol attack, and water elimination; conducted in refluxing solvent (e.g., xylene or toluene) with concentrated H2SO4 catalyst.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed transesterification of n‑butanol with methyl acetate to form butyl acetate and methanol; generally refluxed in a solvent such as toluene or a toluene‑methanol mixture with a catalytic amount of acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (NaOMe, K₂CO₃); removal of methanol drives the equilibrium toward products.

Solution‑phase organometallic decomposition/ligand‑exchange; indium(III) acetate reacts with tris(trimethylsilyl)phosphine to form InP nanocrystals, with hexamethyldisiloxane as by‑product; In(OAc)3 + P(SiMe3)3 → InP + (Me3Si)2O (plus organic residues); performed in high‑boiling non‑coordinating solvents such as octadecene or trioctylphosphine at 200‑300 °C under argon; no additional catalyst required.

Neutralization (acid‑base) of propiolic acid with NaOH to yield sodium propiolate and water; performed in aqueous NaOH at 0‑25 °C; used to generate the sodium salt for further synthetic transformations; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of 2‑iodoethanamine with aqueous ammonia, giving ethylenediamine and ammonium iodide; conducted in excess NH₃(aq) at 40–60 °C, aqueous medium serves as both solvent and nucleophile.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Converts the carboxylic acid of 4‑hydroxybenzoic acid into its sodium salt, increasing water solubility. Key transformation: deprotonation of the acid by bicarbonate, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and generating sodium 4‑hydroxybenzoate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating to evolve CO₂; often performed in water or aqueous ethanol. No catalyst required.

Redox (acid‑metal) reaction; dilute nitric acid oxidizes nickel metal, forming nickel(II) nitrate, nitrogen monoxide gas, and water. Conducted in aqueous dilute HNO₃ (≈3–6 M) at room temperature with stirring. The NO gas is emitted and may be detected by its blue‑green flame. Water is the solvent; no additional catalyst.

Thermal dehydration of thiocarbamic acid to isothiocyanic acid; an elimination reaction where water is expelled. Usually carried out by heating neat thiocarbamic acid at 150‑200 °C under an inert atmosphere; no solvent is required, though a mild acid or base catalyst can be used to promote the dehydration.

Heterocycle formation via cyclocondensation to 5‑amino‑1,3,4‑thiadiazole‑2‑thiol. Purpose: construct a 1,3,4‑thiadiazole ring from a hydrazide precursor. Key transformation: carbon disulfide reacts with the terminal hydrazine carbonyl to give a dithiocarbazate intermediate, which cyclizes with loss of small molecules (e.g., H₂S, water) to afford the thiadiazole ring bearing an amino group and a thione at C‑2. Reaction is usually performed in ethanol or water with a base such as NaOH or K₂CO₃, under reflux for several hours. No transition‑metal catalyst is required.

Redox metal displacement where rubidium metal reduces mercury(II) chloride to elemental mercury while forming rubidium chloride. Conducted in a dry, aprotic solvent such as THF or diethyl ether under an inert atmosphere; rubidium is added gradually at 0 °C to ambient temperature, and the reaction proceeds vigorously.

LAH reduction of 2‑ethoxypropanal (an aldehyde) to 2‑ethoxypropanol ( primary alcohol). Performed in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C then allowed to warm to reflux under nitrogen; excess LiAlH₄ is quenched carefully with water or dilute acid after completion.

Simple acid–base neutralization: hydrochloric acid protonates sodium oxalate to give sodium hydrogen oxalate and sodium chloride. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature by mixing stoichiometric amounts; no additional catalyst or special conditions are required.

Acid digestion of barium phosphate with concentrated nitric acid to produce phosphoric acid and barium nitrate. Reaction is a protonation/solubilization step performed by heating solid barium phosphate in excess hot concentrated HNO₃ (≈68 %) in aqueous medium; the resulting barium nitrate remains soluble while phosphoric acid is liberated.

Halide exchange (metathesis) between silver chloride and tributyl tin bromide; purpose to prepare tributyltin chloride for further organotin chemistry; key transformation is replacement of bromide on tin by chloride with precipitation of insoluble AgBr; typically carried out in an apro solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; AgBr is filtered off.

Staudinger reduction of an organic azide; purpose is to convert a phenethyl azide into the corresponding phenethylamine under mild, non‑hydrogenative conditions; the azide reacts with triphenylphosphine to give an iminophosphorane intermediate, which is hydrolyzed by water to release phenethylamine, triphenylphosphine oxide, and N₂ gas; usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as THF or dichloromethane at 0‑25 °C, with water added after formation of the intermediate; no additional catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); exchange of cations between the dimethylammonium oxalate and barium chloride to precipitate insoluble barium oxalate. Reaction is performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the barium oxalate precipitates and is filtered off, leaving dimethylammonium chloride in the filtrate.

Selective hydrogenation of acetylene to ethylene; used industrially to remove acetylene impurities from ethylene streams. Conducted at 150‑200 °C and 1‑5 atm H2 pressure over a palladium or nickel based catalyst (Pd/Al2O3, Ni‑Zn). Often performed in the gas phase; optional inert carrier gas (e.g., N2) or light liquid solvent (toluene) when operated in slurry.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylation (alkoxycarbonylation) of 1‑bromo‑2‑methylprop‑1‑ene with carbon monoxide and methanol to give methyl methacrylate; industrial route to MMA; key steps are oxidative addition of the vinyl bromide to Pd(0), CO insertion, methanolysis to form the ester and reductive elimination; performed under 30–50 bar CO pressure, 50–80 °C, in methanol or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) with a PdCl₂/phosphine catalyst and a base such as triethylamine.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑nitrofluorene over palladium on carbon to afford 2‑aminofluorene; purpose is reduction of the nitro group to an aniline; key transformation is addition of H₂ to the –NO₂ group yielding –NH₂ with water as by‑product; typically run at 1–5 atm H₂, 25–80 °C, in ethanol or ethyl acetate; Pd/C acts as the catalyst and is removed by filtration.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction). Purpose: Saturate the conjugated diene to afford the fully reduced alkane, hexane. Key transformation: Addition of two equivalents of H₂ across the two C=C bonds, converting CH2=CH‑CH2‑CH2‑CH=CH2 to CH3‑CH2‑CH2‑CH2‑CH2‑CH3. Typical conditions: Expose hexa‑1,5‑diene to H₂ (1–5 atm) in the presence of a heterogeneous catalyst such as 5 % Pd/C, PtO₂ (Adams’ catalyst), or Raney Ni, in an alcohol solvent (ethanol, methanol) or ethyl acetate, at 25–60 °C. Reaction time ranges from 1–4 h depending on catalyst loading.

Electrophilic nitration of uracil with nitric acid to give 5‑nitrouracil; purpose is introduction of a nitro substituent at the C‑5 position of the pyrimidine ring; key transformation is attack of the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) generated in situ on the activated C‑5 carbon; usually performed in dilute HNO₃ or HNO₃/acetic acid at 0–25 °C; water is formed as the only by‑product; no external catalyst required.

Mixed‑acid nitration of 4‑aminoazobenzene using fuming nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid to produce 4‑amino‑4'‑nitroazobenzene; purpose is to install a nitro group para to the azo linkage on the second phenyl ring; key transformation is electrophilic aromatic substitution by the nitronium ion; reaction is carried out at 0 °C to 5 °C initially, then allowed to warm to ambient temperature, in the acid mixture; water is liberated; the strong acids act as both solvent and catalyst.

Markovnikov addition of hydrobromic acid to a terminal alkene (hydrohalogenation). Purpose: install a bromine at the more substituted carbon, yielding 2‑bromo‑2,5‑dimethylhexane. Key transformation: protonation of the double bond to form a secondary carbocation at C‑2, followed by nucleophilic attack by Br⁻. Typical conditions: aqueous or gaseous HBr (1–2 M) in a non‑protic solvent (CH2Cl2, CHCl3), 0 °C to reflux; sometimes a peroxide is omitted to avoid anti‑Markovnikov pathways.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amidation of 8‑methyl‑6‑nonenoic acid with 4‑hydroxy‑3‑methoxybenzylamine using N,N‑diisopropylcarbodiimide (DIC) to afford capsaicin; purpose is synthesis of the natural product via peptide‑coupling chemistry; key transformation is activation of the carboxyl group by DIC to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate, which then reacts with the amine to give the amide bond while releasing N,N‑diisopropylurea; typically performed in dichloromethane or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a catalytic amount of DMAP; no metal catalyst required.
Oxidation; converts uranium dioxide to uranium trioxide, a higher oxidation state oxide. UO2 is heated in flowing O2 at 400‑600 °C (calcination); no solvent or catalyst.

Decomposition of hydrogen peroxide; H₂O₂ breaks down into water and oxygen; reaction is slow at room temperature but accelerated by catalysts such as manganese dioxide, catalase, Fe³⁺, or Cu⁺; often performed in aqueous solution with mild heating; catalyst is essential for practical rates.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution analogous to reaction 2, but using potassium hydroxide; yields 1‑pentanol and potassium bromide; performed in aqueous or alcoholic KOH under reflux (≈80‑100 °C); common solvents are water or ethanol.

Phosphoryl transfer (kinase‑catalyzed phosphorylation); ethanolamine is phosphorylated by ATP in the presence of ethanolamine kinase, yielding phosphoethanolamine and ADP. Typical enzymatic conditions: aqueous buffer (pH 7.5–8.0), Mg²⁺ (1–5 mM) as cofactor, 25–37 °C, and ATP in slight excess (1–2 eq). Reaction often performed in Tris‑HCl or HEPES buffer; no organic solvent needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis of a primary alkyl chloride). Water attacks the carbon bearing chlorine of 1‑chloro‑2‑nitroethane, displacing Cl⁻ to give 2‑nitroethanol and generating HCl. Typically performed in aqueous medium, often warmed or refluxed; polar protic solvents such as water or aqueous ethanol are used. No catalyst required; the reaction serves to convert a nitro‑substituted alkyl chloride into the corresponding nitro‑alcohol.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of methyl iodide with cyanide ion. Tetraethylammonium cyanide supplies CN⁻, which attacks the methyl carbon, producing acetonitrile and tetraethylammonium iodide. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF) at ambient or mild heating. No additional catalyst; purpose is the generation of a nitrile from an alkyl halide.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation; transforms a ketone into an ester using a peracid. Meta‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) reacts with the carbonyl of 1‑phenylhexan‑1‑one in dichloromethane (0 °C to rt) to give phenyl hexanoate and the by‑product m‑chlorobenzoic acid. The peracid acts as the oxidant; no metal catalyst is needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of tridecanal to tridecane, effecting full reduction of the aldehyde to a saturated alkane. Raney nickel activates H₂, delivering two equivalents of hydrogen to the carbonyl carbon and oxygen, which is removed as water. Performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in ethanol or isopropanol at 50–80 °C for 2–6 h.

Transmetalation to prepare a Grignard reagent; sec‑butyl lithium transfers the sec‑butyl group to magnesium bromide, producing sec‑butylmagnesium bromide and lithium bromide; performed in dry THF under nitrogen or argon, often at low temperature (–20 °C to 0 °C) to maintain reagent stability.

Lucas test – SN1 substitution of a tertiary alcohol to a tertiary chloride. ZnCl₂ acts as a Lewis acid to activate tert‑butanol toward nucleophilic attack by chloride from concentrated HCl, yielding tert‑butyl chloride and water. Usually carried out in concentrated aqueous HCl with ZnCl₂ at room temperature or under gentle reflux. The reaction is used to identify tertiary alcohols by rapid chloride formation.

Conversion of an amine to an isothiocyanate via nucleophilic attack on N,N‑dimethylthiocarbamoyl chloride. Aniline attacks the thiocarbonyl carbon, displacing dimethylamine and chloride; the product is phenyl isothiocyanate, with dimethylamine·HCl as a by‑product. Performed in anhydrous dichloromethane or toluene at 0 °C to room temperature, often in the presence of a base such as pyridine to scavenge HCl. Useful for synthesizing aromatic isothiocyanates.

Acid–base/fluorination reaction of a rare‑earth oxide; purpose is to convert basic samarium oxide into the water‑soluble fluoride; key transformation: Sm2O3 + 6 HF → 2 SmF3 + 3 H2O; typical conditions: aqueous HF (≈5–10 M) at ambient temperature or mild reflux (50–80 °C); no catalyst, water is both solvent and product.

Redox single‑displacement reaction. Iron metal reduces nitrosyl chloride; Fe⁰ is oxidized to FeCl₂ while each NOCl is reduced to nitric oxide (NO) and chloride joins the iron. Typically carried out in a dry, inert atmosphere (e.g., nitrogen glovebox) at room temperature or slight heating, with no catalyst. Generates FeCl₂ and NO gas; employed in laboratory preparations of nitric oxide.

Redox metal displacement reaction in acid; zinc metal reduces aqueous protons to hydrogen gas while being oxidized to Zn2+, which pairs with bromide to give ZnBr2; occurs in dilute sulfuric acid solution at room temperature or mild heating; aqueous medium, no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of a disulfide to thiols. Molecular hydrogen cleaves the S–S bond of diisopropyl disulfide in the presence of a transition‑metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Raney Ni) to afford two equivalents of 2‑propanethiol. Conducted under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in a solvent such as ethanol or methanol at room temperature to 50 °C. This reduction is used to obtain thiols from disulfides.

Hydrolysis of lanthanum nitride; purpose is to convert the metal nitride into its oxide and generate ammonia gas; key transformation is LaN + H₂O → La₂O₃ + NH₃ (balanced as 2 LaN + 3 H₂O → La₂O₃ + 2 NH₃); typical conditions involve heating the solid nitride with excess steam or water at elevated temperatures (300‑600 °C); reaction is performed in aqueous medium with no added catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement/metathesis reaction; purpose is to precipitate cobalt(II) hydroxide while forming soluble ammonium carbonate; key transformation is CoCO₃ + 2 NH₄OH → Co(OH)₂ (s) + (NH₄)₂CO₃; carried out at ambient temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed cyanide protonation and sulfate formation; purpose is to liberate hydrogen cyanide gas and produce mercury(II) sulfate; key transformation is Hg(CN)₂ + H₂SO₄ → HgSO₄ + 2 HCN; typically performed with dilute sulfuric acid at low temperature (0‑5 °C) to control HCN evolution; no additional catalyst, reaction conducted in aqueous solution under a fume hood.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a guanidinium salt; purpose is to generate guanidinium dihydrogen phosphate, often used as a buffer or reagent; key transformation is H₃PO₄ + C(NH₂)₂ → [C(NH₂)₃]⁺ + H₂PO₄⁻ (overall guanidinium dihydrogen phosphate); performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Aminolysis (amide formation) of an ester; reaction of methyl 2,2,2‑trichloroacetate with ammonia yields 2,2,2‑trichloroacetamide and methanol; usually conducted neat or in ethanol with excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, heated (reflux) for several hours.

Hydrolysis (cleavage) of a tert‑butyl ester; purpose is to revert the ester back to trifluoroacetic acid and regenerate tert‑butanol. Key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl of the tert‑butyl ester, producing TFA and t‑BuOH; can proceed under acidic, neutral, or basic conditions. Typical conditions: aqueous medium (often dilute NaOH or HCl) with heating (reflux) for several hours. No special catalyst; the reaction is generally straightforward.

Mixed Claisen condensation (base‑catalyzed β‑keto‑ester synthesis); purpose is to form ethyl 4‑methyl‑3‑oxopentanoate and ethanol; key transformation involves deprotonation of methyl isobutyl ketone by NaOEt to give an enolate, which attacks ethyl acetate, yielding the β‑keto ester and ethanol; typical conditions are anhydrous ethanol or THF, sodium ethoxide (1‑2 equiv), reflux under nitrogen; catalyst is sodium ethoxide; solvent is dry ethanol.

Fischer esterification of 2‑aminobenzoic acid with menthol; purpose is to produce menthyl anthranilate, a fragrance ester; key transformation is the condensation of the carboxyl group of anthranilic acid with the hydroxyl of menthol to give menthyl anthranilate + H₂O; carried out by refluxing the reactants in toluene (or xylene) with a catalytic amount of a strong acid such as H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, often using a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water; acid acts as catalyst, solvent is anhydrous aromatic hydrocarbon.

Fermentation/biotransformation of fructose to lactic acid; a homo‑lactic acid bacterial pathway or chemical base‑catalyzed retro‑aldol cleavage converts the six‑carbon ketohexose into two molecules of the three‑carbon α‑hydroxyacid; typically carried out in aqueous medium at 30–37 °C, pH 5‑6, using a starter culture (e.g., Lactobacillus spp.) or, chemically, NaOH at 80‑120 °C with subsequent oxidation of the resulting dihydroxyacetone intermediate.
Metathesis reaction; aqueous NH4NO3 exchanges anions with CrCl3·6H2O, producing NH4Cl, soluble Cr(NO3)3 and water; carried out in water at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Condensation cyclization of formaldehyde with o‑phenylenediamine to give benzimidazole; a nucleophilic attack of the diamine on the carbonyl forms a Schiff base which cyclizes and eliminates water; performed under mild heating (80‑120 °C) in ethanol or acetic acid, often with a catalytic amount of acid to accelerate dehydration.

Salt metathesis forming aluminium selenide; solid‑state double displacement of AlCl₃ with Na₂Se yields Al₂Se₃ and NaCl; carried out under strictly anhydrous conditions in a glovebox or sealed tube, heated to 300‑500 °C to promote diffusion, with inert atmosphere (argon) to prevent oxidation.

SN2 alkylation of dimethylamine with ethyl chloride; primary alkyl halide reacts with a secondary amine to give N,N‑dimethylethylamine and HCl; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as THF or DMF at 0–25 °C, using excess amine or a base (e.g., triethylamine) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Oxidation of 4‑methoxyphenethyl alcohol to 4‑methoxyphenylacetaldehyde using Dess‑Martin periodinane; the periodinane transfers an oxygen atom to the primary alcohol, giving the aldehyde under neutral, mild conditions; typically run in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, with 1.1–1.5 equiv DMP, under nitrogen, and the reaction is quenched with aqueous Na₂S₂O₃.

Oxidation of osmium metal by ozone to produce osmium tetroxide; ozone gas reacts with elemental Os at low temperature, forming the volatile OsO₄ oxide; conducted in a flow of dry O₃ over finely divided Os in a quartz tube at –78 °C to 0 °C, under inert carrier gas (e.g., nitrogen) to avoid over‑oxidation or explosion.

Metallothermic reduction of boron trichloride with sodium; purpose is to obtain elemental boron; the three B–Cl bonds are broken and NaCl forms as the only by‑product; performed under strictly anhydrous, oxygen‑free conditions in a sealed stainless‑steel or quartz tube, heated to 600–800 °C so that sodium is molten and reacts with gaseous BCl3; no solvent; the reaction can be run in a sodium melt or with a supporting inert salt.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrodeoxygenation) of 1‑octanol to octane and water. Purpose: convert a primary alcohol into a hydrocarbon fuel by removing the oxygen. Key transformation: cleavage of the C‑O bond and replacement with C‑H, delivering octane and H₂O. Typical conditions: 50–100 bar H₂, 200–300 °C, solid metal catalyst such as Pd/C, Pt/Al₂O₃, Ni‑Mo on silica; often run neat or in a high‑boiling hydrocarbon solvent.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary alkyl chloride with hydroxide. Hydroxide ion attacks the carbon bearing the chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ and forming 1‑propanol. Usually carried out with aqueous NaOH or NaOH in ethanol/water, heated to reflux (≈60‑80 °C) to drive the reaction; no catalyst is required.

SN2 O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of 5‑hydroxypsoralen with methyl bromide using potassium carbonate. Purpose: install a methoxy group at the 5‑position of psoralen. Key transformation: phenoxide generated by K₂CO₃ attacks CH₃‑Br, forming 5‑methoxypsoralen and KBr/CO₂. Typical conditions: reflux in acetone or DMF, K₂CO₃ (2–3 eq), sometimes catalytic KI, temperature 50–80 °C.

Conversion of pentanoic acid to valeryl chloride using triphosgene. Reaction type: preparation of an acyl chloride from a carboxylic acid via a carbonyl‑chloride reagent. Purpose: generate the acid chloride for subsequent acylation steps. Key transformation: the –COOH group reacts with the reactive carbonyl chloride ofhosgene, releasing CO₂ and HCl and forming R‑C(=O)Cl. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt in dry dichloromethane, with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap HCl; 1 eq triphosgene for every 3 eq acid.

High‑temperature oxidation of cerium silicide with oxygen. Reaction type: combustion/oxidation of a metal silicide. Purpose: convert the intermetallic into its constituent oxides. Key transformation: silicon is oxidized to SiO₂ and cerium to CeO₂ (3 O₂ + CeSi → 2 SiO₂ + CeO₂). Typical conditions: heating in air or O₂ atmosphere at several hundred to >800 °C; solid‑state reaction, no solvent.

Acid‑base neutralization forming copper(II) triforoacetate. Reaction type: salt formation from a metal oxide and a carboxylic acid. Purpose: prepare Cu(CF₃CO₂)₂ as a soluble copper source. Key transformation: CuO reacts with two equivalents of CF₃CO₂H, yielding Cu(CF₃CO₂)₂ and H₂O. Typical conditions: stirring at room temperature or gentle reflux in excess trifluoroacetic acid; the acid can serve as both reagent and solvent (neat).

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration of 3‑ethylpentan‑2‑ol to 3‑ethylpent‑2‑ene. Reaction type E1/E2 elimination (deation). Purpose: synthesize the corresponding internal alkene. Key transformation: removal of water from the secondary alcohol, forming a C=C bond between C‑2 and C‑3. Typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, 80–180 °C, often in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or neat; solid acid catalysts (e.g., Amberlyst‑15) can also be employed.

Type: Carboxylation of a Grignard reagent. Purpose: convert the organomagnesium compound into a carboxylic acid. Key transformation: addition of CO₂ to the C–Mg bond of 4‑fluorobenzylmagnesium chloride forming a magnesium carboxylate, followed by acidic work‑up to afford 4‑fluorophenylacetic acid. Typical conditions: solution of the Grignard in dry ether or THF at 0 °C to –78 °C, CO₂ gas bubbled through, then quench with dilute aqueous NH₄Cl or HCl. No catalyst required.

Redox disproportionation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes lithium peroxide to produce oxygen gas while both form lithium hydroxide. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Halogenation/metathesis (solid‑state redox); chlorine gas oxidizes phosphorus in terbium phosphide to phosphorus trichloride and simultaneously forms terbium chloride. Conducted by heating the solid mixture (≈300‑500 °C) in a sealed tube under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction of chloric acid with silver nitrate yielding soluble silver chlorate and nitric acid; performed in water at ambient temperature; mixture is filtered to separate any insoluble silver salts (though AgClO₃ is soluble) and the resulting nitric acid remains in solution.

Single‑replacement halogen displacement; chlorine displaces iodine from magnesium iodide, generating magnesium chloride and elemental iodine. Carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; hydrochloric acid protonates N,N‑diethylformamide leading to cleavage into formic acid and diethylamine. Typically refluxed in aqueous HCl (1–2 M) or a water‑ethanol mixture; no extra catalyst.

Reductive amination; 4‑aminobenzoic acid reacts with hexadecanal to form an imine that is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to give 4‑(hexadecylamino)benzoic acid, releasing water. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at pH 5‑6 (often buffered with acetic acid) at room temperature or mild heating; NaCNBH₃ serves as the reducing agent.

Redox oxidation of antimony metal by concentrated nitric acid; antimony is oxidized from 0 to +5 forming antimony(V) oxide while nitric acid is reduced to nitrogen dioxide gas and water. Typically carried out by slowly adding antimony to hot, conc. HNO3 in a fume hood; no catalyst needed; the acid itself acts as solvent.

Acid–base neutralization (esterification precursor). Lithium ethoxide reacts with acetic acid in ethanol or ether, producing ethanol and lithium acetate. Performed at 0‑25 °C; the mixture is typically cooled to control exotherm; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; potassium carbonate reacts with yttrium trichloride to give yttrium carbonate precipitate and potassium chloride in solution; conducted in water, often with gentle heating to dissolve carbonate; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Fischer esterification between benzoic acid and 1‑nonanol to give nonyl benzoate and water. Acid‑catalyzed condensation; usually refluxed with a catalytic amount of sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or benzene, employing a Dean‑Stark trap or excess alcohol to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction forming insoluble iron(II) molybdate precipitate and soluble potassium chloride. Mix equimolar solutions of FeCl2 and K2MoO4 at room temperature with stirring; the precipitate is filtered and washed. No special catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; lanthanum acetate reacts with sodium hydroxide to precipitate lanthanum hydroxide and generate soluble sodium acetate. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no additional reagents needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; purpose is anion exchange to isolate lead(II) bromide; key transformation: Pb²⁺ pairs with Br⁻ forming insoluble PbBr₂ precipitate while K⁺ pairs with BF₄⁻ to give soluble KBF₄; typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; common solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic halogenation of bromoacetonitrile with bromine, replacing the remaining hydrogen on the α‑carbon to give dibromoacetonitrile and hydrogen bromide as by‑product. Conducted in an inert, non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, protected from light; no catalyst required.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of elemental titanium and sulfur to give titanium disulfide; the reaction is carried out by intimately mixing Ti powder with S (1:2 molar ratio) and heating to 400–600 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) to avoid oxidation; no solvent or catalyst is required; the product is the layered sulfide TiS₂ used in batteries and lubricants.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) reaction where bromine oxidizes iodide in bismuth(III) iodide to elemental iodine while being reduced to bromide, yielding bismuth tribromide. Usually performed by grinding solid BiI3 with liquid Br2 or dissolving both in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) and gently heating; no catalyst needed.

Single‑displacement redox (metal displacement) reaction; reduction of mercuric bromide to elemental mercury. Solid Zn metal is added to an aqueous or ethanol solution of HgBr₂ and the mixture is heated gently (often reflux). Zn is oxidized to Zn²⁺ (forming ZnBr₂) while Hg²⁺ is reduced to Hg⁰, which deposits as liquid mercury. The process is carried out under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of Zn; no additional catalyst is needed.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; swaps the anions of manganese(II) chloride and calcium carbonate to give calcium chloride in solution and insoluble manganese(II) carbonate as a precipitate. Usually performed by adding solid CaCO₃ to an aqueous MnCl₂ solution with stirring at room temperature. No catalyst; water is the medium.

Nitration/esterification of 1,2‑propanediol with dinitrogen pentoxide to form propylene glycol dinitrate and nitric acid. Performed under dry, low‑temperature conditions (0–5 °C) in an aprotic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or acetonitrile; the reaction is moisture‑sensitive and does not require additional catalyst.

Hydrolysis (nucleophilic substitution, S_N2) of a sulfate ester. Diethyl sulfate reacts with water, cleaving the S–O bonds to generate ethanol and sulfuric acid (often observed as ethyl hydrogen sulfate in the reaction mixture). Typical conditions: excess water, heat (reflux, 80‑100 °C) or catalysis by dilute acid or base to accelerate the process. Water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a benzyl bromide by dimethylamine; the amine attacks the benzylic carbon displacing bromide to give 4‑[(dimethylamino)methyl]phenol and HBr. Usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, MeCN) at 0 °C to reflux, with excess amine serving as both nucleophile and base; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an α,β‑unsaturated ketone; H₂ reduces the C=C bond of cyclopent‑2‑en‑1‑one to afford cyclopentanone while the carbonyl remains intact. Typical conditions: 1–3 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd/C, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature ambient to 50 °C; reaction run under inert atmosphere.

Deoxy‑fluorination of a secondary alcohol with sulfur tetrafluoride; SF₄ replaces the hydroxyl group of isopropyl alcohol with fluorine, producing isopropyl fluoride while generating HF and thionyl fluoride (SOF₂) as by‑products. Conducted under anhydrous, inert conditions, often neat or in liquid SO₂ at –78 °C to 0 °C; no additional catalyst is.

Acid–base neutralization; magnesium oxide reacts with sulfurous acid to form magnesium sulfite and water; usually performed in a suspension of MgO in aqueous H2SO3 with gentle heating to improve contact; water serves as solvent; no special catalyst needed.

Oxidation (Pyridinium chlorochromate oxidation); converts the secondary alcohol of 1‑bromo‑2‑propanol to a ketone, yielding 1‑bromoacetone and water; typically carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature without additional catalyst.

Kumada‑type cross‑coupling (aryl‑alkyl coupling) of bromocyclodecane with phenylmagnesium bromide; purpose is to form a C(sp2)–C(sp3) bond (phenylcyclodecane). Key transformation: phenyl group transferred from the Grignard to the alkyl bromide with displacement of bromide. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere, anhydrous THF, catalytic NiCl2·dppp or Pd(PPh3)4 at 0 °C to rt. No stoichiometric catalyst; solvent is THF (or ether).

Acid–carbonate reaction; yttrium carbonate reacts with phosphoric acid, releasing CO₂ gas, forming water, and precipitating yttrium phosphate. Conducted in aqueous phosphoric acid (≈1 M) with gentle heating (50–80 °C); gas evolution indicates reaction progress, and the solid is filtered, washed and dried.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (Lewis‑acid‑catalyzed aromatic acylation). Methoxyacetyl chloride reacts with benzene in the presence of AlCl₃, giving 2‑methoxyacetophenone (phenyl 2‑methoxy‑acetyl) and HCl as by‑product. Performed under anhydrous conditions, usually in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, or dichloromethane, at 0 °C then warmed to reflux; excess AlCl₃ is later quenched with ice‑water.

Acid‑catalyzed decomposition of urea; protonation by HCl leads to loss of ammonia and formation of isocyanic acid, with the remaining chloride forming ammonium chloride. Typically carried out in aqueous HCl at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C); the reaction proceeds without external catalyst.

Alkaline hydrolysis of mercaptoacetic acid hydrazide; NaOH cleaves the acyl‑hydrazide bond, yielding hydrazine, sodium mercaptoacetate, and water. Reaction is performed in aqueous NaOH solution, heating to reflux (≈80 °C) for several hours; no additional catalyst is required.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification or acid‑catalyzed cleavage) of methyl cyclopropanecarboxylate; water attacks the carbonyl carbon, producing methanol and cyclopropecarboxylic acid. Commonly carried out with aqueous NaOH (base‑catalyzed) at reflux followed by acid work‑up, or with dilute aqueous acid (HCl) at reflux; solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture; no special catalyst beyond the acid or base.

Double‑replacement precipitation; potassium cyanide reacts with aqueous CoCl2·6H2O to form insoluble cobalt(II) cyanide and KCl; performed in cold water under controlled conditions because of cyanide toxicity; the solid cobalt cyanide is filtered and washed; no catalyst.

Reaction type: Bromination. Purpose: Synthesis of N-brominated amide products. Key transformation: Electrophilic bromination of acetamide nitrogen using bromine in the presence of a base. Condition: Aqueous solution; moderate temperature. Catalyst: Sodium carbonate acts as a base to neutralize HBr byproduct.

Alpha‑chlorination of butyric acid by chlorine gas; an electrophilic substitution at the carbon α to the carbonyl giving 2‑chlorobutanoic acid and hydrogen chloride as a by‑product; carried out under UV light or in the presence of a radical initiator, typically in a chlorinated organic solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) or in the gas phase at low temperature to avoid over‑chlorination.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aromatic heterocycle; purpose is to reduce N‑methylpyridine to the saturated N‑methylpiperidine. Hydrogen gas adds across the pyridine ring in the presence of a heterogeneous metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂, Raney Ni) under elevated pressure (5–50 bar) and moderate temperature (80–150 °C) in solvents like ethanol, methanol or acetic acid.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; nickel difluoride reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to precipitate nickel hydroxide and form soluble sodium fluoride; conducted at ambient temperature in water.

Reaction type: Ester aminolysis/condensation. Purpose: Synthesize amides from esters and primary amines. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack by methylamine on ester carbonyl, forming an amide bond. Conditions: Elevated temperature; no solvent required or aqueous/organic solvent.

Reaction type: Acylation. Purpose: Form phthalimide derivatives for synthesis or protection. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack by aniline on phthalic anhydride carbonyl groups. Conditions: Heating; solvent such as xylene or acetic acid.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis); converts the sulfonate ester to a primary alcohol and methanesulfonic acid. Water attacks the butyl carbon displacing the methanesulfonate group. Typically carried out in aqueous media or aqueous ethanol at reflux (50‑100 °C); no catalyst required; common solvent: water or water/ethanol.

Reaction type: Nitrosation. Purpose: Form N-nitrosocyanamide for nitrogen-containing heterocycle synthesis. Key transformation: Nitroso group (NO) addition via nitrous acid. Conditions: Aqueous acidic solution; low temperature to prevent side reactions.

Reaction type: Hydrolysis. Purpose: Convert acyl chlorides to carboxylic acids. Key transformation: Nucleophilic attack by water on 2-bromopropanoyl chloride. Conditions: Rapid hydrolysis under ambient conditions; no catalyst required. Solvent: Water.

Acid–base double displacement (metathesis) reaction; purpose is to liberate oxalic acid and precipitate strontium sulfate. Key transformation: proton transfer from H₂SO₄ to the oxalate anion, forming soluble H₂C₂O₄ and insoluble SrSO₄. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Oxidative cleavage of a polyol by periodic acid; purpose is to break glycerol into smaller carbonyl fragments. Key transformation: periodic acid oxidatively cleaves C–C bonds of the vicinal diols, yielding CO₂, HCOOH and H₂CO. Conducted in aqueous acidic medium, usually 0–25 °C; excess H₅IO₆ is used; no catalyst needed; water is the solvent.

Redox (halogen displacement) reaction; chlorine oxidizes iodide to iodine while being reduced to chloride. Key transformation: 2 I⁻ → I₂ + 2 e⁻; Cl₂ + 2 e⁻ → 2 Cl⁻. Usually carried out in dilute aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst; water (or dilute acid) as solvent.

Chlorination to generate phosphorus oxychloride. Dry hydrogen chloride gas (or concentrated HCl) is passed over heated phosphorus pentoxide (typically 100–150 °C) in an anhydrous system, yielding PO Cl₃ gas and water. The POCl₃ is distilled off, while water is removed by azeotropic distillation or trapped in a drying agent.

Acid‑catalyzed alkylation (alkylation of isobutane with isobutylene) to produce iso‑octane (2,2,4‑trimethylpentane). Key transformation: generation of tert‑butyl carbocation from isobutylene under strong acid, which then attacks isobutane. Typical conditions: strong acid catalyst such as H₂SO₄ or HF, temperature 0–50 °C, liquid phase; inert atmosphere may be used; sulfuric acid or HF acts as both catalyst and solvent.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of gallium and arsenic to afford gallium arsenide (GaAs), a III‑V semiconductor material. Usually performed in a sealed quartz ampoule under vacuum or inert gas, heating the elemental mixture to 600‑800 °C to allow interdiffusion and crystal formation; no solvent, purpose is bulk crystal growth.

Acid–base neutralization (formation of a fatty‑acid salt) between docosanoic acid and sodium methoxide. Key transformation: deprotonation of the carboxylic acid to give sodium docosanoate and methanol. Usually performed in methanol or mixed methanol/THF solvent at room temperature; stoichiometric NaOMe; no additional catalyst.

Williamson ether synthesis (phenolic methylation) of 3,4‑dihydroxybenzaldehyde with methyl iodide in the presence of potassium carbonate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of phenoxide anion on CH₃I to form methoxy groups. Typical conditions: aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or acetone, reflux or 60–80 °C, K₂CO₃ as base; no metal catalyst required.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl of isovaleric acid, forming the alkoxide which is protonated on work‑up to give isoamyl alcohol; performed under anhydrous conditions (dry ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, with careful quench to avoid violent reaction.

Oxidation; mild oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde using pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC). Converts the –CH2OH group of 3‑chloropropan‑1‑ol to a –CHO group, yielding 3‑chloropropanal while reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III) oxide and releasing HCl. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑mediated hydrolysis of acetyl chloride (nucleilic acyl substitution) with aqueous potassium hydroxide; produces potassium acetate and hydrogen chloride (which is neutralized to KCl in solution); reaction proceeds rapidly at 0‑25 °C in water or aqueous methanol, often used for quantitative conversion of acyl chlorides to carboxylate salts.

Single‑displacement redox where metallic sodium reduces mercuric bromide to elemental mercury and is itself oxidized to Na⁺; typically performed anhydrous in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere at ambient or gently refluxing temperature.

Oxidation of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid using chromic acid (Jones oxidation); pentanal is converted to pentanoic acid while Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III) oxide; reaction typically run in acetone/H2SO4 mixture at 0–25 °C, with stoichiometric Cr(VI) reagent, and produces water as by‑product.

Strong oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid with acidic potassium dichromate; butanol is oxidized to butanoic acid while dichromate is reduced to chromium(III) sulfate and potassium sulfate precipitates; carried out in dilute H2SO4, heated under reflux, aqueous medium; no additional catalyst required.

Acid chloride hydrolysis; nucleophilic acyl substitution where acetyl chloride reacts with water to give acetic acid and hydrogen chloride; typically performed in aqueous solution at 0‑25 °C, often with an excess of water; no catalyst required, HCl may be neutralized with base.

Reaction type: double displacement (metathesis). Purpose: synthesis of iron(III) pyrophosphate. Key transformations: sodium pyrophosphate reacts with iron(III) sulfate, forming iron(III) pyrophosphate precipitate and sodium sulfate. Conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature. Solvent: water.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; purpose is to introduce a second nitro group ortho to the existing one on 2‑nitrophenol yielding 2,3‑dinitrophenol; key transformation is generation of the nitronium ion (NO2⁺) from HNO3/H2SO4 and its substitution for a hydrogen atom on the aromatic ring; typical conditions involve concentrated H2SO4 as both solvent and catalyst, reaction temperature kept low (0–5 °C) to control over‑nitration; the mixed acid mixture itself acts as the reaction medium and water is produced as by‑product.

Esterification via acyl transfer from acetic anhydride to 3‑octanol; the alcohol attacks the anhydride to form octan‑3‑yl acetate and acetic acid; typically performed under reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base or catalyst such as pyridine or catalytic DMAP to scavenge the generated acid and accelerate the reaction.

Transesterification of methyl valerate with isopropanol to give isopropyl valerate and methanol; acid (H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (NaOCH₃) catalyst, reflux in anhydrous solvent (toluene, xylene) with removal of methanol to drive equilibrium.

Williamson ether synthesis with sodium methoxide; methoxide anion attacks ethyl methanesulfonate to afford ethyl methyl ether (methoxyethane) and sodium methanesulfonate; typical conditions involve anhydrous methanol or THF as solvent, mild heating (room temperature to 40 °C) under inert atmosphere; sodium methoxide serves as nucleophile; no additional catalyst needed.

E2 elimination; converts a secondary alkyl chloride to the corresponding alkene using a strong base; the base (ethoxide) abstracts a β‑hydrogen while chloride leaves, forming 2‑heptene, NaCl and ethanol; typically performed in refluxing ethanol or a polar aprotic solvent at 60–80 °C.

Acid‑base neutralization of butan‑2‑amine hydrochloride with sodium hydroxide; the strong base deprotonates the ammonium salt, liberating free butan‑2‑amine and forming NaCl and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stirring is sufficient.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration; hydantoic acid loses water to form the cyclic imide hydantoin; key formation of a five‑membered ring via dehydration; usually achieved by heating the acid neat or in a high‑boiling solvent, often with a dehydrating agent such as acetic anhydride or under reduced pressure.

Acid–base neutralization of vanadic acid with sodium carbonate; carbonate deprotonates the acid, releasing CO₂ and H₂O and forming sodium metavanadate (NaVO₃). Performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to evolve CO₂.
Hydrolysis of tantalum(V) bromide by water to produce hydrobromic acid and insoluble tantalum(V) oxide (Ta₂O₅). Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol, usually with heating; HBr remains in solution.

Type: oxidative ozonolysis of an alkene. Purpose: cleave the allyl side chain of 4‑allylphenol to afford 4‑hydroxybenzaldehyde and formaldehyde. Key transformation: O3 adds across the C=C bond forming a molozonide that fragments to carbonyl compounds. Typical conditions: Ozone bubbled through a solution of 4‑allylphenol in dry dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C until a persistent blue color, then work‑up with a mild reductive quench (e.g., Zn/AcOH) to isolate aldehydes; reaction time 15–30 min.

Oxidation of 1‑nonanol to nonanal using Dess‑Martin periodinane; mild, selective oxidation of a primary alcohol to an aldehyde, generating water as by‑product. Typical conditions: DMP (≈1.1 eq) in dry CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C to rt under N₂, reaction complete within 30 min.

Acyl transfer between benzoic anhydride and diethylzinc, yielding ethyl benzoate and zinc benzoate; organozinc reagent provides a nucleophilic ethyl group. Performed under inert atmosphere in dry THF or toluene at 0 °C to rt; zinc benzoate precipitates.

Metathesis/neutralization of calcium propionate with ammonium hydroxide forming soluble ammonium propionate and precipitating calcium hydroxide. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stir until Ca(OH)₂ precipitates, then filter.

Acid chloride hydrolysis; purpose is to convert a 3‑bromopropanoyl chloride to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbonyl carbon displaces chloride, yielding 3‑bromopropionic acid and HCl. Typically carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature to reflux; a base such as NaHCO₃ or NaOH is often added to neutralize the generated HCl. No special catalyst required.

Intramolecular cyclization to a cyclic carbonate using carbonyldiimidazole (CDI); purpose is synthesis of butylene carbonate from 1,2‑butanediol. CDI activates the diol by forming an imidazolyl carbonate intermediate; subsequent intramolecular attack closes the ring, releasing two equivalents of imidazole. Conducted in aprotic solvents (e.g., THF, CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed.

Sulfonylation/esterification of ethanol with pyrosulfuric acid (H₂S₂O₇); purpose is formation of ethyl hydrogen sulfate (ethyl sulfate). Ethanol attacks the electrophilic sulfur of pyrosulfuric acid, displacing a sulfate group and producing H₂SO₄ as by‑product. Performed at low temperature (0–25 °C) in a dry, sealed vessel; excess pyrosulfuric acid is used to drive the reaction. No catalyst required.

High‑temperature solid‑state oxidation to produce barium ferrite (BaFe₁₂O₁₉) nanopowder; purpose is preparation of magnetic ceramic material. Stoichiometric mixtures of BaO and Fe₂O₃ (or Fe₃O₄) are intimately ground, then heated in flowing O₂ or air at 1200–1300 °C for several hours, allowing diffusion and formation of the hexaferrite phase. No liquid solvents; the reaction relies on thermal energy and oxygen atmosphere.

Double‑displacement/precipitation (acid–base neutralization); purpose is to prepare insoluble lead arsenate while regenerating acetic acid; key transformation is exchange of acetate ions from lead acetate with arsenate ions from H3AsO4, forming solid lead arsenate (PbHAsO4 or related salt) and two equivalents of acetic acid; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent and no special catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed cyclodehydration (Friedel‑Crafts‑type intramolecular electrophilic aromatic substitution); purpose is conversion of diphenylmethane to fluorene. Concentrated H₂SO₄ protonates the benzylic carbon, generating a carbocation that undergoes intramolecular attack on the adjacent aromatic ring, forming the fused fluorene skeleton and releasing water. Reaction carried out at 150–200 °C in neat conc. H₂SO₄; no external Lewis acid is required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution; sodium fluoride exchanges anions with lithium nitrate to give sodium nitrate and lithium fluoride. Typically carried out by mixing aqueous solutions of NaF and LiNO₃ at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Strong reduction of an ester using lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH₄); isoamyl formate is cleaved to produce isoamyl alcohol from the alkoxy fragment and methanol from the formyl fragment. Conducted under inert atmosphere in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux, with LiAlH₄ added slowly; work‑up with aqueous acid quenches excess hydride.

Acid‑base proton transfer generating hydrofluoric acid; concentrated sulfuric acid protonates fluoride ions from sodium fluoride to give HF while forming sodium sulfate. Performed by adding solid NaF to cold concentrated H₂SO₄ (often < 10 °C) to control HF evolution; no catalyst required.

Reductive precipitation of copper metal by sodium borohydride; NaBH₄ reduces Cu²⁺ from copper(II) sulfate to Cu⁰, itself being oxidized to metaborate (BO₂⁻) while sulfate remains as sodium sulfate. Carried out in aqueous solution, typically at 0–25 °C; excess NaBH₄ is added to a stirred CuSO₄ solution, often with a mild base (e.g., NaOH) to stabilize the borohydride.

Acid‑carbonate reaction yielding a metal cyanide; cadmium carbonate reacts with hydrogen cyanide (a weak acid) to form cadmium cyanide, releasing carbon dioxide gas and water. Conducted in aqueous medium at ambient temperature; HCN is bubbled through a suspension of CdCO₃, and the evolution of CO₂ indicates completion. No catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of allyl bromide by hydrosulfide ion; NaSH provides HS⁻ which attacks the primary carbon of allyl bromide, displacing Br⁻ to give allyl mercaptan (prop-2-en-1-thiol) and sodium bromide. Typically performed in anhydrous ethanol or water/ether mixture at room temperature; reaction is fast and does not need a catalyst.

Acid‑base metathesis (neutralization). HBF₄ donates a proton to the sulfide ion of (NH₄)₂S, generating gaseous H₂S and forming the soluble salt NH₄BF₄. Typically performed in aqueous solution at 0 – 5 °C to control H₂S evolution; no catalyst required, water is the solvent.

Oxidative cleavage (ozonolysis with hydrogen peroxide) of the terminal double bond of 1‑decene; ozone adds across the C=C at low temperature (‑78 °C) in an inert solvent such as dichloromethane, followed by oxidative work‑up with aqueous H2O2. The terminal carbon is converted to formaldehyde and the remaining nine‑carbon chain to nonanoic acid.

Acid–base metathesis (salt formation) between nickel(II) acetate and perchloric acid in aqueous solution. The reaction exchanges the acetate and perchlorate anions, giving soluble nickel(II) perchlorate and acetic acid, which can be removed by distillation. Typically performed at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Hydride reduction of a 1,2‑diketone to the corresponding vicinal diol. Lithium aluminium hydride (LiAlH4) in anhydrous ether (e.g., THF or Et2O) at 0 °C to reflux reduces both carbonyl groups of 1,2‑cyclohexanedione to give 1,2‑cyclohexanediol. Reaction is quenched with water and acidwork‑up.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a ketone to a secondary alcohol. Benzophenone is reduced with H2 gas (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2, or Raney nickel in an alcohol solvent (ethanol or methanol) at room temperature or mild heating, affording diphenylmethanol.

Acid‑base neutralization followed by hydrolysis; the hydrazinium cation is deprotonated by NaOH, producing free hydrazine (NH₂NH₂), sodium nitrate, and water. Conducted in aqueous solution at low temperature (0–5 °C) to suppress oxidation; the hydrazine is typically extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., ether) or distilled.

O‑alkylation (SN2) of a phenolic hydroxyl; converts 2‑hydroxyestradiol to 2‑methoxyestradiol while generating HI. Used to protect or functionalize the phenol; typically performed with a base (K2CO3 or NaH) in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or DMSO, reflux temperature, under anhydrous conditions.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous calcium nitrate exchanges anions with sodium sulfate to give sparingly soluble calcium sulfate precipitate and soluble sodium nitrate. is to isolate CaSO4. Key: Ca^2+ + SO4^2– → CaSO4(s) and Na^+ + NO3^– → NaNO3(aq). Conducted by mixing aqueous solutions at ambient temperature; water is the medium, no catalyst.

Acid–base precipitation reaction; calcium acetate reacts with CO2 and water to release acetic acid and precipitate calcium carbonate. Employed for CO2 capture or acetic acid regeneration. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Copper(II)‑mediated aerobic oxidation of 2‑naphthol to 2‑hydroxy‑1,4‑naphthoquinone. The copper(II) acetate acts as a catalyst, using molecular oxygen as the oxidant. Reaction is carried out in refluxing acetic acid or pyridine, often under an O2 balloon, at 80–120 °C.

Thermal decomposition of an inorganic chlorate; heating barium chlorate causes it to decompose to barium chloride solid and liberate oxygen gas (≈3 O₂ per formula unit). Conducted at 300‑400 °C in a dry tube or crucible; no catalyst or solvent needed.

Transesterification (alcoholysis) of bornyl acetate with ethanol; ethanol attacks the acetate ester, yielding ethyl acetate and borneol. Acidic (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or basic (e.g., NaOCH3) catalysis is typical, with excess ethanol serving as solvent, refluxing temperature (≈78 °C) for several hours.

Acyl‑chloride esterification of tri‑n‑butyl citrate with acetyl chloride, producing mono‑acetylated tributyl citrate and HCl. Performed under anhydrous conditions, often in pyridine or with triethylamine as base to scavenge HCl, at 0 °C to room temperature; inert atmosphere (N2) is used.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of metipranolol acetate to give desacetylmetipranolol and acetic acid. Can be acid‑catalyzed (e.g., 1 M HCl, reflux) or base‑catalyzed (e.g., NaOH, 50 °C) in aqueous/ethanol mixture; reaction proceeds to completion with removal of acetic acid by extraction or evaporation.

Metal‑acid redox reaction between calcium metal and hydrogen bromide gas; calcium is oxidised to Ca²⁺ forming calcium bromide while H⁺ is reduced to H₂ gas. Typically carried out in a dry, inert environment (dry ether, liquid ammonia, or sealed tube) with gentle heating to initiate reaction; no solvent or catalyst required beyond the metal and HBr.

Double displacement precipitation reaction; aqueous mixing of barium chloride with zinc selenite exchanges anions to form soluble zinc chloride and insoluble barium selenite which precipitates; typically carried out in water at room temperature, no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of 2‑ethoxypropan‑1‑ol over palladium on carbon under H₂ pressure to give ethanol and 1‑propanol; purpose is cleavage of the ether C–O bond; typical conditions are H₂ 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–80 °C; no additional reagents required.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of potassium titanate; heating the solid at high temperature (≈800‑1000 °C) in air or inert atmosphere breaks the mixed oxide into titanium dioxide and potassium oxide; solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis (deprotection); p‑toluenesulfonic acid protonates 2‑methoxy‑1,3‑dioxane, leading to cleavage of the cyclic acetal to give ethylene glycol and methoxyacetaldehyde; performed in aqueous acidic medium, often with gentle heating or reflux, water/acetone as solvent.

Oxidation (sulfide to disulfide) using hydrogen peroxide; purpose: convert tetramethylthiuram monosulfide into the corresponding disulfide; key transformation: formation of an S–S bond with oxidation of the sulfur atom; typical conditions: 0 – 25 °C, aqueous or acetonitrile solution, stoichiometric H2O2; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage of an alkene (ozonolysis with oxidative work‑up); (Z)-hept‑3‑ene is exposed to ozone at –78 °C in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) to form an ozonide, which is then reduced/oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to yield butanoic acid and propanoic acid; no additional catalyst required.

Peracid oxidation of a trialkyl phosphine; tri‑n‑octylphosphine reacts with perbenzoic acid to give benzoic acid and tri‑n‑octylphosphine oxide; usually performed at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, proceeding spontaneously without extra catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (saponification) of benzyl prop‑2‑ynoate; water attacks the ester carbonyl to produce benzyl alcohol and prop‑2‑ynoic acid; typically carried out under aqueous acidic (e.g., HCl) or basic (e.g., NaOH) conditions with heating, often using a water/THF mixture as solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis; used to remove a methyl substituent from cyclohexane rings and generate methane as a gaseous by‑product; the C–C bond of methylcyclohexane is cleaved by hydrogen in the presence of a Raney nickel metal catalyst; typical conditions are high hydrogen pressure (50–100 atm) and elevated temperature (150–200 °C); the reaction is usually performed neat, using the liquid substrate as the reaction medium.

Halogen exchange (Finkelstein reaction); employed to replace bromine atoms with iodine to give 1,3‑diiodopropane; proceeds by SN2 substitution of each bromide by iodide from sodium iodide; carried out in anhydrous acetone (or another polar aprotic solvent) where NaBr precipitates, driving the reaction forward; refluxing the mixture for several hours is common; excess NaI is used to ensure complete conversion.

Thermal decomposition; regeneration of the constituent oxides from silver molybdate. Ag₂MoO₄ is heated strongly (typically >600 °C) in a furnace under air or inert gas, causing it to break down into Ag₂O (or metallic Ag at higher temperatures) and MoO₃. No solvent; the process is driven by heat alone.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to prepare soluble cobalt(II) chloride and to remove sulfate as insoluble barium sulfate; cobalt(II) sulfate solution is mixed with barium chloride solution; barium sulfate precipitates and is filtered off, leaving cobalt(II) chloride in the filtrate; performed in aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Direct combination (synthesis) of a metal sulfide; forms nickel(II) sulfide by reacting elemental nickel with elemental sulfur; the mixture is heated in a sealed tube or under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) to temperatures of 300–600 °C until a black NiS solid forms; no solvent is used; the reaction is often carried out in a furnace or tube furnace.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed transesterification. Phenol replaces the methyl group of methyl 2‑methylpropanoate, producing phenyl 2‑methylpropanoate and methanol. Commonly run with catalytic H₂SO₄ or NaOCH₃ in refluxing toluene or dimethyl carbonate; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium.

Double‑displacement/acid‑base complexation; converts lanthanum sulfate to the oxalate complex tri[oxalato(2‑)]dilanthanum while generating sulfuric acid; an aqueous solution of lanthanum(III) sulfate is treated with excess oxalic acid, the mixture is heated to reflux to promote ligand exchange; the metal oxalate complex may precipitate or remain in solution depending on concentration and temperature; after cooling, the product can be isolated by filtration; water is the solvent and no external catalyst is required.

Type: Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine). Purpose: convert the nitrile into the corresponding amine. Key transformation: hydrogen gas in the presence of Pd/C reduces the –C≡N group of 4‑fluorobenzyl cyanide to –CH₂NH₂, giving 4‑fluorobenzylamine. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, 5–10 % Pd on carbon catalyst, solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–80 °C, reaction time several hours.

Protonolysis (acid‑base reaction); ethyl lithium reacts with methanol, abstracting a proton from methanol to generate ethane and lithium methoxide; carried out in dry ether or THF, usually at 0 °C to room temperature, and serves as a standard quench step for organolithium reagents.

Halide exchange/acid‑base metathesis; swaps chloride ligands of tin(IV) chloride for fluoride to give tin(IV) fluoride and hydrogen chloride; anhydrous HF gas or concentrated hydrofluoric acid is added to SnCl₄, often at low temperature (0–25 °C) under an inert atmosphere to control exotherm; the reaction can be performed in a sealed PTFE reactor; the generated HCl gas is removed or scrubbed; no additional catalyst is needed.

Combustion reaction; oxidation of isobutanol by molecular oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water; highly exothermic, typically occurs at elevated temperature (flame conditions) in the presence of excess air or pure O₂; no solvent; often catalyzed by the heat of ignition.

Metathesis (double replacement) precipitation reaction; MgSO₄ exchanges anions with K₂CO₃ to produce sparingly soluble MgCO₃ precipitate and soluble K₂SO₄; conducted in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to enhance precipitation; no catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a nitro group; purpose: reduce the nitro substituent of 1‑chloro‑3‑nitrobenzene to an aniline while preserving the chloro group, giving 3‑chloroaniline. Key transformation: H₂ addition to the –NO₂ group forming –NH₂. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–3 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 25–50 °C, reaction time 1–4 h.

Oxidation of phosphine: Trimethylphosphine is oxidized by hydrogen peroxide to trimethylphosphine oxide with water as by‑product; PMe3 + H2O2 → OPMe3 + H2O. Usually performed in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to rt; no catalyst required.

Esterification (sulfonate ester formation); conversion of ethanol to ethyl p‑toluenesulfonate using p‑toluenesulfonic acid as the sulfonyl donor and sulfuric acid as a catalyst; acid‐catalyzed nucleophilic substitution where ethanol attacks the sulfonyl group, releasing water; performed at 0–25 °C to 50 °C in an inert organic solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene; water is removed (e.g., by azeotropic distillation) to drive the reaction to completion.

Salt neutralization/base extraction; alkaline deprotonation of the dihydrochloride salt of 1,5‑diaminopentane with aqueous sodium hydroxide yielding the free diamine, sodium chloride and water; typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the free base can be extracted into an organic solvent (e.g., ether) after basification.

Double‑displacement/metathesis (acid–base) reaction; lithium hydroxide reacts with ammonium chloride to give lithium chloride, ammonia gas, and water; carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating to evolve NH₃; ammonia is removed by gas venting; water is the solvent; no catalyst required.

Reductive gas‑phase reduction; carbon monoxide reduces Au₂O₃ to metallic gold while being oxidized to CO₂; key transformation is electron transfer from CO to Au³⁺; generally conducted in a tubular furnace under a flow of CO (or CO/N mixture) at 400‑600 °C; solid Au₂O₃ is packed in an alumina boat; no catalyst needed, but high temperature promotes complete reduction.

Ketal (acetal) formation; nucleophilic addition of two equivalents of ethanol to cyclopropanone to generate 1,1‑diethoxycyclopropane; acid‑catalyzed (commonly catalytic p‑TsOH or H₂SO₄) under reflux in anhydrous ethanol or a non‑protic solvent; removal of water (e.g., with molecular sieves) shifts equilibrium toward product.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchange of anions between ammonium chloride and silver nitrite forming insoluble silver chloride and soluble ammonium nitrite; performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; the silver chloride precipitate is filtered off, leaving ammonium nitrite in the filtrate.

Complexation/acid‑base precipitation; reaction of bismuth oxide with nitric acid and potassium citrate in aqueous medium to produce the water‑soluble bismuth subcitrate potassium complex (used pharmaceutically); typically carried out under gentle heating (30–60 °C) with stirring; the citrate ligates Bi³⁺, forming a soluble salt while water is generated as a by‑product.
