Conditions involve cooling to –78 °C in dry dichloromethane, sequential addition of oxalyl chloride, DMSO, the diol, then triethylamine, and gradual warming to –20 °C; the reaction is performed under inert atmosphere.

Oxidative dissolution of iron(II,III) oxide by concentrated nitric acid; type: redox/acid dissolution; purpose is to convert Fe₃O₄ to soluble iron(III) nitrate and iron(II) nitrate while reducing nitrate to nitrogen oxides; key transformation: Fe₃O₄ + HNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₃ + Fe(NO₃)₂ + H₂O (plus NO₂/NO gases); typical conditions: reflux Fe₃O₄ with conc. HNO₃ (≈68 %) at 80‑120 °C; solvent is concentrated nitric acid; no additional catalyst.

Oxidation; converts 1‑naphthol to 1,4‑naphthoquinone using hydrogen peroxide; a two‑electron oxidation forming two carbonyl groups and water; typically performed in aqueous or mixed solvent at 0–25 °C, often catalyzed by Fe²⁺, MoO₄²⁻ or under acidic conditions.

Acid‑base neutralization; phosphoric acid reacts with basic calcium oxide to transfer protons to the oxide, forming water and the calcium dihydrogen phosphate salt. Used to prepare Ca(H2PO4)2 (fertilizer). Typically carried out in aqueous medium with gentle heating and stirring; water acts as solvent.

Alkaline hydrolysis of an amide (amidic bond cleavage); NaOH attacks the carbonyl of acetoacetanilide, breaking the C–N bond to give aniline and the sodium salt of acetoacetic acid. Employed to liberate aniline and generate sodium acetoacetate. Conducted in aqueous NaOH, reflux (~100 °C) for 1–2 h; water (often with a miscible organic co‑solvent such as ethanol) is the reaction medium.

Coordination‑complex synthesis via ligand exchange; ammonium hydroxide deprotonates acetylacetone to form acac⁻, which replaces chloride ligands on HfCl4, yielding hafnium(IV) acetylacetonate and producing NH4Cl and water as by‑products. Provides Hf(acac)4 as a precursor for CVD/sol‑gel routes. Performed in refluxing ethanol or methanol with excess NH4OH; the mixture is then cooled and the solid complex isolated.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; barium hydroxide reacts with ammonium sulfate, exchanging ions to form insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble ammonium hydroxide (or in solution, NH4⁺ and OH⁻). Used to remove sulfate ions from solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; no special catalyst required.

Halide exchange (metathesis) reaction; iridium(III) bromide reacts with hydrochloric acid, swapping bromide for chloride ligands and releasing hydrogen bromide gas. Converts IrBr3 to IrCl3. Typically performed in aqueous HCl under gentle heating to evolve HBr; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2, Finkelstein‐type) reaction; iodide ion from NaI attacks the carbon bearing chlorine in 1‑chloro‑3‑iodopropane, displacing chloride to afford 1,3‑diiodopropane and precipitating NaCl. Used to replace a chloride with iodine. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, often refluxed; NaCl precipitates and is filtered off.

Alcoholysis (metal halide to metal alkoxide) – substitution of chloride ligands of TiCl₄ by methanol to give titanium tetramethoxide and hydrogen chloride; used to prepare metal alkoxides. Typically performed under anhydrous conditions with excess dry methanol at 0 – 25 °C under nitrogen; HCl evolves as gas. No catalyst; solvent is methanol.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation of copper(II) carbonate from copper(II) acetate and sodium carbonate; purpose is to produce CuCO₃; key equation Cu(CH₃COO)₂(aq) + Na₂CO₃(aq) → CuCO₃(s) + 2 NaCH₃COO(aq); conducted at room temperature in aqueous solution with mixing; no additional catalyst.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation – calcium acetate reacts with copper(II) sulfate to exchange anions, forming soluble copper(II) acetate and insoluble calcium sulfate precipitate. Carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; filtration isolates CaSO₄. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis – hydrochloric acid hydrolyzes the amide bond of acetanilide, yielding aniline and acetic acid. Conducted by refluxing acetanilide in concentrated aqueous HCl (often with ethanol as co‑solvent) for several hours. Strong acid (HCl) serves as catalyst; water/ethanol mixture is the solvent.

Double‑displacement precipitation – potassium cyanide reacts with mercuric nitrate to precipitate mercuric cyanide while forming soluble potassium nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution, usually at 0 – 25 °C, with careful control of pH (neutral to slightly basic) to avoid cyanide volatilization. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide by ammonia – ammonia displaces bromide from 6‑bromohexanoic acid to afford 6‑aminohexanoic acid, with hydrogen bromide generated as by‑product. Usually carried out in aqueous or ethanol solution containing excess NH₃, heated to 50‑80 °C. No catalyst; solvent is water or ethanol; excess ammonia drives the reaction.

Redox reaction (oxidative chlorination): titanium(III) chloride is oxidized by molecular oxygen to titanium dioxide while chloride ions are reduced to chlorine gas. Typically carried out at high temperature (≈400–600 °C) in the solid state or under flow of O₂; no solvent, inert atmosphere may be used.

Acidic redox oxidation: iodide ions from potassium iodide are oxidized to elemental iodine by potassium permanganate in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid. Reaction proceeds in aqueous solution under reflux; acid medium supplies H⁺ and maintains Mn in +2 state as MnSO₄. No additional catalyst required.

Formation of calcium bicarbonate by dissolution of calcium carbonate in water under carbon dioxide pressure (CO2 + H2O), a reversible carbonation reaction; occurs in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or slightly elevated CO2 pressure, no catalyst or solvent beyond water.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a sulfate ester: ethanol attacks methyl sulfate, displacing a methyl group as methanol and forming ethyl sulfate. Generally performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or dimethylformamide at 0–50 °C, often with a base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize the generated acid.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis: 2‑chloronicotinonitrile is hydrolyzed by aqueous hydrochloric acid to give 2‑chloronicotinic acid and ammonium chloride. Conducted by refluxing the substrate in concentrated HCl solution (6–12 M) for several hours; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitrile; purpose is to convert the nitrile group of 2‑aminopropanenitrile into a primary amine, giving 1,2‑diaminopropane. Key transformation: C≡N → CH2NH2 while the existing α‑amino group remains unchanged. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–10 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Raney Ni, Pd/C or Pt, in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, methanol or water) at 50–150 °C.

Acid‑base neutralization/decomposition: sodium bicarbonate reacts with sodium bisulfate, yielding carbon dioxide, water, and sodium sulfate. Occurs at ambient temperature in aqueous solution; mixing of the solid reagents provides rapid effervescence without need for a catalyst.

Strong oxidation of an alkyl side chain: 2‑methylthiophene is oxidized by sodium dichromate in concentrated sulfuric acid to afford 2‑thiophenecarboxylic acid. Typical conditions involve refluxing the substrate in (≈150 °C) sulfuric acid with Na₂Cr₂O₇ as the oxidant; the reaction proceeds via Cr(VI) reduction to Cr(III).

Same sulfinate alkylation as above but using iodomethane, which is more reactive; yields dimethyl sulfone and NaI. Conditions analogous to reaction 3 (DMF or DMSO, rt to mild heating), stoichiometric reagents, no catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction. Aqueous solutions of barium acetate and manganese(II) sulfate are mixed, leading to the formation of insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble manganese(II) acetate in the solution. Typical conditions: water as solvent, ambient temperature, stirring; no catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction in aqueous solution. Potassium carbonate reacts with lithium sulfate to exchange cations, producing lithium carbonate (which may precipitate due to limited solubility) and potassium sulfate remaining in solution. Conditions commonly involve dissolving the salts in water, heating gently to promote crystallization of Li2CO3; no catalyst is needed.

Halogenation (chlorination) of a partially chlorinated cyclobutene to give the fully chlorinated cyclobutane. Chlorine gas adds across the remaining double bond(s) of hexachlorocyclobutene, converting it to octachlorocyclobutane. Typical conditions: chlorine bubbled through the substrate in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, under UV light or moderate heat (40–80 °C) to initiate radical chlorination; no catalyst required.

Oxidative desulfurization; purpose is to convert 4‑thiouracil back to uracil by oxidizing the thio‑carbonyl; key transformation is C=S → C=O with water as by‑product; carried out by treating 4‑thiouracil with aqueous hydrogen peroxide at ambient temperature (0–25 °C), often in water or a water‑acetone mixture, sometimes with a mild base to buffer the solution.

Hydration (oxide hydrolysis) reaction; arsenic pentoxide hydrolyzes to give arsenic acid. As2O5 + 3 H2O → 2 H3AsO4(aq). Performed by adding As2O5 to water, often with gentle heating or reflux; water is the solvent, no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduction of the C=C double bond of maleic acid to yield succinic acid. The reaction uses a heterogeneous metal catalyst such as Raney nickel, Pd/C, or PtO₂ under H₂ pressure1–5 atm) in an aqueous or alcoholic solvent at 50–100 °C. After completion, the mixture is filtered to remove catalyst and the succinic acid is recovered by crystallization.

Halogen exchange (metathesis) reaction between antimony pentafluoride and thiazyl chloride. Fluoride ions are transferred from SbF5 to thiazyl chloride, producing antimony pentachloride and thiazyl fluoride. The reaction is performed under strictly anhydrous conditions, usually in a dry, non‑coordinating solvent such as liquid SO2 or in the gas phase, at low temperature (0–25 °C) to control reactivity; no additional catalyst is employed.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an isocyanate. Hydrogen gas in the presence of Raney nickel reduces 2,6‑dimethylphenyl isocyanate, cleaving the –N=C=O group to give 2,6‑dimethylaniline and carbon monoxide as a by‑product. Typical conditions: hydrogen pressure of 1–5 atm, temperature 80–150 °C, solvent such as ethanol or THF; Raney Ni serves as the heterogeneous catalyst.

Acid hydrolysis reaction; transforms nitrile group into amide via nucleophilic attack by water under acidic conditions. Uses hydrochloric acid as both reactant and proton source, aqueous solution as solvent. Produces chloroacetamide and ammonium chloride.

Carbonation of glycerol catalyzed by potassium carbonate under supercritical CO2 conditions. Converts glycerol into glycerol carbonate via cyclization, utilizing high-pressure CO2 as solvent and reactant.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; aqueous mixture of magnesium sulfide and potassium hydroxide; Mg²⁺ exchanges with K⁺ yielding precipitated magnesium hydroxide and soluble potassium sulfide; carried out at room temperature or with mild heating; water as solvent, no catalyst.

Acid‑base reaction of a metal sulfide with carbonic acid; CO2 in water generates carbonic acid which reacts with solid MnS, precipitating MnCO3 and liberating H2S gas; carried out in aqueous suspension at room temperature or with gentle heating, no catalyst, water as solvent.

Electrophilic nitration of 2,4-Dinitrophenol in concentrated nitric and sulfuric acid. Adds a third nitro group to form Picric Acid, with sulfuric acid acting as acid catalyst and dehydrating agent. Typically requires controlled heat.

Alkylation (quaternization) of the two pyridine nitrogens in 4,4′‑bipyridine with methyl chloride in the presence of hydrogen chloride, forming the bis‑methylated pyridinium salt N,N′‑dimethyl‑4,4′‑bipyridinium dichloride. Conducted in anhydrous polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or nitromethane, usually under reflux; excess HCl serves both as solvent and counter‑ion source; no catalyst needed.

Metathesis reaction between perchloric acid and silver oxalate. Exchanges anions to yield oxalic acid and silver perchlorate, driven by solubility differences. Proceeds in aqueous conditions without additional solvents.

Precipitation/neutralization of thulium trichloride with ammonium hydroxide; aqueous TmCl₃ reacts with NH₄OH to produce thulium(III) hydroxide precipitate and ammonium chloride in solution; performed at room temperature in aqueous NH₄OH, no additional reagents needed.

Acid–base reaction; HF reacts with magnesium oxide to produce magnesium fluoride (MgF₂) and water; key transformation is substitution of Mg‑O by Mg‑F; performed by adding solid MgO to aqueous HF, often under reflux; no catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

General type: Fischer esterification. Purpose: Convert cinnamic acid to methyl cinnamate. Key transformation: The carboxylic acid reacts with methanol to form the methyl ester and water. Typical conditions: Reflux cinnamic acid in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., sulfuric acid or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) for several hours; removal of water by a Dean–Stark trap or azeotropic distillation drives the equilibrium toward the ester.

Protonolysis (acidolysis) of a metal alkyl with hydrogen iodide; affords gallium triiodide and methane. Performed in dry ether or THF, typically at 0 °C to ambient temperature under nitrogen; HI gas (or a solution in THF) is added to the trimethylgallium solution. No catalyst is needed.
Halogen addition of chlorine to 1-pentene. Adds Cl2 across the double bond to form 1,2-dichloropentane. Typically occurs under ambient conditions in inert solvents like CCl4 or dichloromethane.

Acid–base neutralization; calcium hydroxide reacts with chloric acid to form calcium chlorate and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Catalytic hydrogenation (heterogeneous) of the cyclic disulfide in lipoic acid to give dihydrolipoic acid. Reaction uses H₂ gas (1–3 atm) over 5–10 % Pd/C in a protic solvent (EtOH, MeOH or water/acetone) at ambient temperature to 50 °C. The disulfide ring is reduced to the open‑chain dithiol, providing the biologically active reduced form.

Esterification (condensation) forming a chlorogenic acid ester between the carboxyl group of caffeic acid and a hydroxyl of quinic acid. Can be performed chemically using a coupling agent (e.g., DCC/DMAP) in anhydrous dichloromethane or dimethylformamide at 0 °C to room temperature, producing chlorogenic acid and dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Enzymatic (plant) biosynthesis also occurs under aqueous conditions.

Carbodiimide‑mediated amide coupling. DCC activates chloroacetic acid to form an O‑acylisourea intermediate, which then reacts with dimethylamine to give N,N‑dimethylchloroacetamide; dicyclohexylurea precipitates as a by‑product. Conducted in aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or DMF, usually at 0 °C to room temperature; optional catalytic DMAP can accelerate acyl transfer.

Acid–base (salt formation) reaction; copper(II) carbonate reacts with hydrobromic acid to dissolve the carbonate, releasing CO₂ gas and forming aqueous copper(II) bromide and water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with excess HBr; no catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Electrophilic α‑bromination of a ketone. Pyridinium tribromide serves as a solid source of bromine, brominating acetone at the α‑position to afford α‑bromoacetone; pyridinium bromide is generated as the counter‑ion. Reaction typically performed in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, with stoichiometric amounts of the brominating reagent.

Type: Metal‑alkoxide formation (acid‑base deprotonation). Purpose: Generate the sodium alkoxide of 2‑butoxyethanol for use as a nucleophile or base. Key transformation: Na metal donates an electron to the O‑H bond, forming sodium 2‑butoxyetholate and releasing H₂ gas. Typical conditions: Anhydrous, aprotic solvent (dry THF or diethyl ether), inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), 0 °C to room temperature. No catalyst required.

Acid–base neutralization (metal hydroxide with strong oxidizing acid); zinc dihydroxide reacts with chloric acid to afford soluble zinc chlorate and water; carried out in dilute aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature to avoid decomposition of chloric acid; no catalyst is used.

Hydrolysis with hydrochloric acid; benzocaine is cleaved by aqueous HCl to afford p‑aminobenzoic acid and ethanol. Reaction carried out under reflux, often in a mixture of HCl (conc. or 6 M) and water; the acid both protonates the carbonyl and provides the nucleophilic water.

Reductive amination (hydrogenation) of a β‑keto amine precursor to give 3‑methoxymethcathinone. 3‑Methoxyphenylacetone reacts with methylamine to form an imine, which is reduced in situ by H₂ over palladium on carbon (1–5 atm) in ethanol or methanol at room temperature, yielding the secondary amine (methcathinone analogue) with water as the only by‑product.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration (electrophilic addition) of (E)-3‑methylhept‑3‑ene to give the tertiary alcohol 3‑methylheptan‑3‑ol. The double bond is protonated by H₂SO₄ to form a tertiary carbocation, water attacks, and loss of a proton yields the alcohol. Typically performed at 0–50 °C in aqueous sulfuric acid (often 1–2 M) or in a mixture of water and dilute H₂SO₄; no additional catalyst required.

Redox oxidation; converts toxic hydrogen selenide to selenium dioxide and nitrogen monoxide while forming water; H2Se is oxidized to SeO2 (Se +4) and NO2 is reduced to NO (N +2); typically carried out as a gas‑phase reaction at elevated temperature (≈100–200 °C) under a flow of NO2 or air; no solvent or catalyst required.

Solid‑state chalcogen exchange (metathesis) between sodium sulfide and elemental selenium to afford sodium selenide and elemental sulfur. Na₂S + Se → Na₂Se + S. Usually carried out by heating the powdered reagents together (150–300 °C) under an inert atmosphere; occasionally performed in polar aprotic solvents such as DMF or NMP to improve mixing.

Halide exchange (double‑displacement) producing tetrabutylammonium fluoride from tetrabutylammonium chloride and silver fluoride. AgF precipitates AgCl, and the soluble TBAF remains in solution. Conducted at room temperature in dry acetonitrile, acetone or THF under nitrogen; the mixture is filtered to remove AgCl.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (esterification) of phenol with trichloroacetyl chloride to give phenyl trichloroacetate (a phenol protecting group) and HCl. Usually performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to room temperature, in the presence of a base (pyridine, triethylamine, etc.) to scavenge the generated HCl.

Benzylic oxidation using chromium(VI) reagents; purpose: oxidize the methyl group of 2‑chlorotoluene to a carboxylic acid; key transformation: conversion of the –CH₃ side chain to –CO₂H by chromic acid (H₂CrO₄) or potassium dichromate in acidic medium; typical conditions: reflux in aqueous sulfuric acid with excess Cr(VI) oxidant, often with a co‑solvent such as acetic acid; the reaction proceeds under strongly oxidizing, acidic conditions.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) between diphenylmethanol (deprotonated to the alkoxide by NaOH) and 2‑chloro‑N,N‑dimethylethylamine, giving phenbenzamine together with NaCl and water. Conducted in aqueous or alcoholic NaOH at 0–50 °C, often using a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO to promote the SN2 step.

Acylation of an amino acid (formation of an N‑acetyl derivative); purpose is to protect the amino group of L‑leucine as an acetamide; the primary amine reacts with acetic anhydride, releasing acetic acid; commonly performed in pyridine or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, with pyridine acting as a base to absorb the generated acid; the reaction is usually carried out under nitrogen with no metal catalyst.

Carbothermal reduction of gadolinium phosphate with carbon to afford gadolinium phosphide and carbon monoxide. A solid mixture of GdPO₄ and carbon is heated to 1200–1500 °C in an inert (Ar) or reducing (H₂) atmosphere; the high temperature drives the reduction: GdPO₄ + 4 C → GdP + 4 CO. No solvent is used; gaseous CO is removed, and the solid GdP is collected after cooling.

Hydrolysis of metal sulfide: Magnesium sulfide reacts with water (often with mild heating) to form magnesium hydroxide precipitate and evolve hydrogen sulfide gas; performed in aqueous medium, the solid Mg(OH)₂ is isolated and H₂S is vented or captured.

Transesterification of methyl cyanoacrylate with ethanol to give ethyl cyanoacrylate and methanol; generally catalyzed by a small amount of acid (p‑TsOH) or base (NaOEt) in refluxing ethanol; purpose: exchange of ester alkoxy group.

Reaction type: solid‑state reduction/nitridation. Purpose: preparation of vanadium nitride (VN) from vanadium(III) chloride using hydrogen as a reducing agent and nitrogen as the nitride source. Key transformation: VCl₃ is reduced by H₂ to V, which then reacts with N₂ to form VN; HCl gas is liberated. Typical conditions: high temperature (≈800–1200 °C) in a flow of H₂/N₂ or under a nitrogen atmosphere in a tubular furnace. No solvent; reagents are gases and solid.

Reaction type: base‑catalyzed ester saponification. Purpose: cleavage of the acetate to give the allylic alcohol and the acetate salt. Key transformation: hydroxide ion attacks the carbonyl carbon, generating a carboxylate and an alkoxide; the alkoxide is protonated to afford the alcohol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux, usually in water/ethanol; after reaction the mixture is acidified to isolate the alcohol and the sodium acetate remains in solution.

Reaction type: base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Purpose: conversion of an ester (ethyl salicylate) to the corresponding carboxylate salt and recovery of the alcohol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O ester bond by KOH, giving potassium salicylate and ethanol. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous ethanol or methanol with excess KOH, 60–80 °C. No catalyst; solvent is a polar protic alcohol/water mixture.

Catalytic hydrogenation of nitrile; cyclohexanecarbonitrile is reduced to cyclohexylamine using H₂ and Pd/C; typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, ethanol or methanol solvent, 25–80 °C; purpose is synthesis of a primary amine from the nitrile.

General type: conversion of an alcohol to an alkyl bromide using phosphorus tribromide (Appel‑type halogenation). Purpose: obtain geranyl bromide, a useful alkylating agent. Key transformation: PBr₃ reacts with the hydroxyl group of geraniol to form a phosphite intermediate, which collapses to give geranyl bromide and phosphorous acid (H₃PO₃). Typical conditions: anhydrous conditions, dry dichloromethane or diethyl ether, 0 °C to ambient temperature, addition of PBr₃ dropwise to a solution of geraniol under nitrogen; reaction finishes within 30 min to 1 h. Common solvents/catalysts: dry CH₂Cl₂ or Et₂O; no external catalyst required.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: preparation of strontium selenate from selenic acid. Key transformation: two equivalents of H₂SeO₄ donate protons to Sr(OH)₂, yielding SrSeO₄ and two molecules of water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; stirring until complete dissolution. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Reaction type: acyl‑chloride esterification (Schotten‑Baumann type) with pyridine as acid scavenger. Purpose: synthesis of allyl phenylacetate from phenylacetyl chloride and allyl alcohol. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of allyl alcohol on phenylacetyl chloride forming the ester; pyridine abstracts the released HCl, forming pyridinium chloride. Typical conditions: pyridine used as solvent/base, temperature 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; reaction usually completed in 1–2 h. No additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: direct halogenation (synthesis of phosphorus pentachloride). Purpose: formation of PCl₅ by chlorination of elemental phosphorus. Key transformation: chlorine adds to P₄, breaking the P–P bonds and forming four equivalents of PCl₅. Typical conditions: dry Cl₂ gas passed over heated P₄ in a sealed, moisture‑free vessel (≈200–300 °C); reaction performed under anhydrous conditions. No solvent; inert atmosphere often employed.

Direct reduction of an aromatic azide to an amine with lithium aluminium hydride; performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) under inert atmosphere, typically at 0 °C then reflux; strong reducing conditions; purpose: synthesis of 2‑amino‑1,3‑dimethylbenzene.

Electrophilic nitration/esterification of methanol by nitronium tetrafluoroborate; the nitronium ion transfers a nitrate group to methanol forming methyl nitrate, while the BF4 counter‑anion yields boron trifluoride and hydrogen fluoride as by‑products. Conducted under anhydrous, low‑temperature conditions (0–‑20 °C) in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often under nitrogen.

Acyl substitution (nucleophilic acyl substitution) of a di‑acid chloride with ammonia, producing the diamide succinamide and HCl; performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature, using excess gaseous or aqueous ammonia, with HCl gas evolved.

Oxidation; oxidative dehydrogenation of an α‑hydroxy acid to the corresponding α‑keto acid (mandelic acid → phenylglyoxylic acid); purpose is regeneration of the acid or analytical oxidation; key transformation is oxidation of the benzylic alcohol to a carbonyl with formation of NaCl and H2O; typical conditions use aqueous sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) at 0‑5 °C, pH 7‑9, often buffered; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening of ethylene carbonate by phenol (catalytic K2CO3) to afford phenoxyethanol and release CO2. This carbonate‑to‑alcohol conversion is used to synthesize the preservative phenoxyethanol. Typical conditions: K2CO3 (10–20 mol %) as base, temperature 80‑120 °C, solvent‑free or in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dimethyl carbonate or toluene); reaction driven by removal of CO2.

Reduction of an N‑carbamate ester; LiAlH4 converts ethyl pyrrolidine‑1‑carboxylate (a carbamate) to the secondary amine pyrrolidine while the ethoxy group is reduced to ethanol. Typical conditions: LiAlH4 (1–2 eq) in dry ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by careful aqueous work‑up (water then dilute acid) to destroy excess hydride.

Simple double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange in aqueous solution: KBr + NaPF6 ⇌ NaBr + KPF6. Employed to prepare potassium hexafluorophosphate, a common electrolyte salt. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; the products are isolated by crystallisation or evaporation; no catalyst required.

Partial reduction of a carboxylic acid to an aldehyde. Purpose: prepare 4‑(dimethylamino)benzaldehyde from 4‑(dimethylamino)benzoic acid. Key transformation: DIBAL‑H delivers a single hydride to the acid carbonyl, forming a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses to the aldehyde upon work‑up. Typical conditions: dry THF (or Et₂), –78 °C under nitrogen, 1‑2 equiv DIBAL‑H added slowly, then quench with methanol or aqueous Rochelle’s salt at low temperature, followed by warming to rt and extraction.

Nucleophilic SN2 quaternization of triethylamine with ethyl bromide to form tetraethylammonium bromide, a quaternary ammonium salt. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (acetonitrile, DMF) at reflux or 50‑80 °C; excess triethylamine serves both nucleophile and base; no additional catalyst needed.

Electrophilic demethylation of the aryl methyl ether (7‑methoxycoumarin) by boron tribromide. BBr₃ cleaves the methoxy group, releasing methyl bromide and yielding the phenolic product umbelliferone. Standard conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), solvent dichloromethane or CH₂Cl₂; reaction quenched with methanol or water after completion.

Transesterification of dimethyl phthalate with isobutanol to give diisobutyl phthalate and methanol; acid (e.g., p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe) catalyzed, reflux (~120 °C), excess isobutanol serves as solvent, continuous removal of methanol drives equilibrium toward product.

Thermal decomposition (redox) of bismuth triiodide; heating BiI₃ releases elemental iodine and yields metallic bismuth. Typically performed by strong heating (≈300‑400 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (aqueous). Samarium(III) hydroxide reacts with nitric acid to form soluble samarium(III) nitrate and water: Sm(OH)3 + 3 HNO3 → Sm(NO3)3 + 3 H2O. Conducted in water at room temperature with stirring; no additional reagents required.

Carbothermal reduction of arsenic(V) oxide with carbon to elemental arsenic; high‑temperature redox (≈900–1100 °C) in a graphite or metal furnace under inert atmosphere, solid‑state reaction, no solvent or catalyst required.

Halide exchange (metathesis) of gold(III) bromide with hydrochloric acid producing gold(III) chloride and hydrobromic acid; performed in aqueous HCl (concentrated) at room temperature, no additional catalyst, useful for converting AuBr₃ to AuCl₃.

Esterification of ethylene glycol with methacrylic anhydride yielding ethylene glycol dimethacrylate and methacrylic acid; catalyzed by pyridine or DMAP, carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, by‑product acid removed by aqueous wash.

Grignard addition of methylmagnesium bromide to butyronitrile followed by aqueous work‑up to afford pentan‑2‑one; reaction in anhydrous ether (THF or Et₂O) at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere, then quenched with dilute acid to hydrolyze the imine intermediate to the ketone.

Combination (synthesis) reaction: elemental strontium reacts with bromine vapor to give strontium bromide (SrBr₂). The process is similarly exothermic and occurs readily upon contact of the metal with Br₂, typically at ambient or mildly heated conditions in a sealed container. No solvent or catalyst is needed; the reaction proceeds in the gas phase.

Double‑displacement precipitation; replaces the sulfate anion with hydroxide to give Gd(OH)3 and soluble Na2SO4; typically performed by adding aqueous NaOH to a dissolved gadolinium(III) sulfate solution under stirring at room temperature; the resulting Gd(OH)3 precipitates, is filtered, washed with water and dried; water is the solvent, no catalyst needed.

Direct fluorination; elemental sulfur reacts with fluorine gas to form sulfur hexafluoride (SF6). Conducted at elevated temperature (200‑500 °C) in a fluorine‑resistant reactor, often under pressure; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis). Silver benzoate reacts with sodium sulfide in aqueous solution to form insoluble silver sulfide precipitate and soluble sodium benzoate. Performed at ambient temperature in water; the Ag₂S precipitate is filtered off, leaving the benzoate salt in solution.

Esterification (acetylation) of a secondary alcohol; borneol reacts with acetic anhydride to form the acetate ester (bornyl acetate) and acetic acid as by‑product. Typically performed at 0 °C to room temperature then warmed, often in dichloromethane or pyridine with catalytic DMAP or a small amount of pyridine as base to scavenge the generated acid.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; forms scandium(III) fluoride (ScF₃) from scandium metal and fluorine gas. The highly exothermic reaction is usually performed at low to moderate temperatures (0–50 °C) in a controlled F₂ flow, often in a fluorinated‑glass apparatus, with no solvent or catalyst; an inert carrier gas may be used to dilute the fluorine.

Thermal/cracking of a long‑chain alkane; n‑octadecane undergoes high‑temperature pyrolysis to cleave C–C bonds, yielding a smaller linear alkane (propane) and a cyclic alkane (cyclopentadecane). Conducted at 450–800 °C, usually in the gas phase or over a solid acid catalyst such as zeolite or alumina, under inert atmosphere.

Reduction of an aldehyde hydrate; chloral hydrate (trichloroacetaldehyde hydrate) is reduced by sodium borohydride to give trichloroethanol, with water formed as the only by‑product. Reaction is carried out in a polar protic solvent (e.g., methanol, ethanol, or aqueous THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; NaBH₄ is used in slight excess.

Base‑ or acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; 4‑hydroxybutyramide reacts with water to cleave the amide bond, producing 4‑hydroxybutyric acid and ammonia. Typically performed with aqueous acid (e.g., 6 M HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) at reflux (80–120 °C), followed by neutralization to isolate the acid and release NH₃ gas.

Redox oxidation of arsenous acid (As(III)) to arsenic acid (As(V)) by bromine; bromine is reduced to hydrobromic acid. Aqueous reaction, usually performed in dilute acidic solution at room temperature; no additional catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed ester saponification; ethyl N‑methylglycinate (ethyl N‑methylglycinate) is hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH, giving sarcosine (N‑methylglycine) and ethanol. Reaction proceeds under reflux in aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), then the mixture is acidified (e.g., with HCl) to precipitate the free amino acid.

Oxidative fluorination; Ge(II) fluoride is oxidized by elemental fluorine to the higher valent Ge(IV) fluoride; performed in the gas phase or in sealed tube at elevated temperature (≈150‑300 °C) under anhydrous conditions; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Acid–base double‑displacement (salt metathesis); aqueous HCl reacts with ammonium sulfate to protonate the sulfate ion, forming ammonium hydrogen sulfate and ammonium chloride in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature in water; the reaction is quantitative and does not require additional catalysts.

Acidic ether cleavage with hydroiodic acid. Purpose: deprotect the methyl ether and generate the corresponding alkyl iodide. Key transformation: protonation of the ether oxygen by HI followed by SN2 attack of I⁻ at the methyl carbon, yielding methanol and isobutyl iodide. Typical conditions: excess anhydrous HI (48 % w/w) refluxed in a tube or heated oil bath (100‑120 °C) for several hours. The reaction is performed neat or in a small amount of ethanol as a co‑solvent; no catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (amination) on a heteroaryl bromide. Purpose: replace the bromine on 2‑bromo‑1,3,4‑thiadiazole with an amino group to afford 2‑amino‑1,3,4‑thiadiazole. Key transformation: attack of NH₃ on the electron‑deficient carbon bearing bromine, displacement of Br⁻ as HBr. Typical conditions: aqueous ammonia (≈ 25 % NH₃) heated under reflux (80‑100 °C) for 2‑6 h, often in a mixed solvent system (water/ethanol). The reaction proceeds without added catalyst; the generated HBr may be neutralized by excess ammonia.

Catalytic hydrogenation of a trinitrile; reduces each –C≡N to a primary amine giving a triamine. Typically performed with H2 (50–100 atm) over Raney Ni, Pd/C or Pt at 50–100 °C in ethanol or methanol; purpose is conversion of nitriles to amines.

Phosgenation/cyclization to form isatoic anhydride. Purpose: convert anthranilic acid into the cyclic isatoic anhydride, a useful intermediate for heterocycle synthesis. Key transformation: triphosgene (ClCO)₃ reacts with the amine and carboxyl groups of anthranilic acid, forming a carbamoyl chloride intermediate that cyclizes to the anhydride, releasing six equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: dichloromethane or THF as solvent, low temperature (0 °C) during addition of triphosgene, followed by gentle warming to rt. A base such as triethylamine or pyridine (2‑3 equiv per acid) is employed to scavenge HCl. Reaction is carried out under inert atmosphere.

Solid‑state synthesis / reduction; purpose is to prepare iron boride (FeB) as a hard refractory material; key transformation is reduction of boron trichloride by hydrogen and simultaneous alloying of iron with boron, forming FeB and releasing HCl gas; typically conducted at elevated temperatures (500–1000 °C) under an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen); no solvent, gaseous H2 used as reductant.

Oxidative condensation (hydrazone oxidation); purpose is to construct a diphenylcarbazone linkage from an aldehyde and phenylhydrazine; key steps involve formation of a phenylhydrazone with benzaldehyde followed by oxidation by peretic acid to generate the azo‑hydrazone (carbazone) bond; usually performed in an acidic organic medium (e.g., dichloromethane or ethanol) at 0 °C to ambient temperature; peracetic acid acts as the oxidant, no metal catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of N‑[2-(1H‑imidazol‑4‑yl)ethyl]acetamide to regenerate the primary amine and acetic acid. Conducted by heating the amide in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) at reflux for several hours; the reaction mixture is then neutralized to isolate the free amine.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to convert 2‑chlorobenzoic acid into its methyl ester; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methanol on the protonated carboxyl group, followed by elimination of water to give methyl 2‑chlorobenzoate; carried out by refluxing excess methanol with catalytic sulfuric acid (≈1–5 mol %) for several hours; methanol serves both reactant and solvent; water is removed by azeotropic distillation or by using a Dean–Stark trap.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation; purpose is to synthesize insoluble manganese(II) sulfide and remove manganese from solution; key transformation is exchange of anions between Na2S and MnSO4 yielding Na2SO4 (soluble) and MnS (precipitate); carried out in water at ambient temperature with vigorous stirring; the mixture is filtered to isolate MnS; no catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement precipitation; purpose is to prepare barium tungstate (BaWO4) as a white insoluble salt; key transformation is exchange of chloride and tungstate ions between BaCl2 and Na2WO4, producing soluble NaCl and precipitated BaWO4; performed by mixing aqueous solutions of the two salts at room temperature, often with gentle heating to improve crystallinity; the BaWO4 is filtered, washed, and dried; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base metathesis (salt‑acid exchange); used to convert insoluble europium(III) phosphate into soluble nitrate and recover phosphoric acid; key transformation is replacement of PO4³⁻ by NO3⁻; typically performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to aid dissolution; no special catalyst required.

Henry (nitro‑aldol) condensation; forms β‑nitroalkene 1‑phenyl‑2‑nitropropene from benzaldehyde and nitroethane; key step is nucleophilic addition of nitronate to the aldehyde followed by dehydration (water loss); usually base‑catalyzed (NaOH, K2CO3, or NH4OAc) in ethanol or methanol at 0 °C to rt; no metal catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization of ammonium sulfide with sodium hydroxide; liberates ammonia gas and generates sodium sulfide in water; key transformation is proton transfer from NH4⁺ to OH⁻ producing NH3 and H2O; carried out in aqueous solution, often with heating to drive off NH3; no catalyst required.

Oxidative sulfone formation; thioanisole is oxidized to methyl phenyl sulfone by sodium persulfate, a strong oxidizing agent; key transformation is conversion of the sulfide to a sulfone (S⁰ → S⁺⁴) with evolution of water and formation of sodium sulfate; typically performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., MeCN/H2O) at reflux temperature; no additional catalyst.

Reaction type: thermal decarboxylation (spontaneous decomposition) of a carbamic acid. Purpose: generate the free secondary amine (dimethylamine) and release CO2. Key transformation: cleavage of the N‑C(O)‑O bond with loss of carbon dioxide, yielding dimethylamine. Typical conditions: mild heating (50–100 °C) or even ambient temperature, as N,N‑dimethylcarbamic acid is unstable; often performed in aqueous solution or under reduced pressure to remove CO2. No catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (acid‑chloride esterification); ethanol reacts with 4‑chlorobenzoyl chloride to give ethyl 4‑chlorobenzoate and HCl. Conducted under similar conditions as the methanol version: anhydrous solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂), low temperature, and a base (pyridine, TEA) to neutralize the generated HCl.

Raney‑nickel reductive amination; acetaldehyde reacts with methylamine under hydrogen to give N‑methyl‑ethyl‑amine, with water as by‑product; key steps are formation of an imine intermediate followed by hydrogenation on Raney Ni surface; conditions: Raney nickel catalyst, H₂ pressure (10–30 bar), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature 50–100 °C; catalyst provides both hydrogen activation and reduction.

Acid‑base neutralization of tellurium dioxide with potassium hydroxide; analogous to the sodium case, yielding potassium tellurite; key transformation: TeO₂ + 2 KOH → K₂TeO₃ + H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous KOH solution, ambient temperature or gentle heating, stirring; aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Dess‑Martin periodinane oxidation of a secondary alcohol; cyclodecanol is oxidized to cyclodecanone; key transformation is transfer of oxygen from the hypervalent iodine(V) reagent to the alcohol, yielding the ketone; by‑products are acetic acid and iodobenzene; typically run in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; no metal catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ether cleavage to generate bromomethyl methyl ether; dimethoxymethane reacts with dry HBr gas, giving BrCH₂OCH₃ and methanol; conducted in dry ether or dichloromethane at low temperature (0–25 °C), optionally with a Lewis acid catalyst.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous neutralization of cadmium acetate with sodium hydroxide to form insoluble cadmium hydroxide precipitate and soluble sodium acetate; typically performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Sulfonylation (formation of a sulfonate ester). Purpose: convert the hydroxyl group into a good leaving group (mesylate) for subsequent substitution reactions. Key transformation: the hydroxyl oxygen of isopropanol attacks the electrophilic sulfur of methanesulfonic anhydride, displacing methanesulfonic acid and forming isopropyl methanesulfonate. Typical conditions: 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere, often in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine which also acts as a base to scavenge the generated acid.

Single‑displacement redox (metathesis) reaction. Purpose: reduction of Bi³⁺ to elemental bismuth while oxidizing iron to Fe³⁺. Key transformation: iron metal donates electrons to bismuth(III) chloride, producing iron(III) chloride and elemental bismuth. Typical conditions: high temperature (≈400–500 °C) in the molten state or in a sealed tube; no solvent is required, and an inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) is used to prevent oxidation by air.

Acid–base (proton transfer) reaction; HF protonates the formate anion of ammonium formate, yielding formic acid and ammonium fluoride. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Acid‑metal reaction (redox dissolution). Purpose: preparation of zirconium(IV) sulfate from the metal. Key transformation: zirconium metal is oxidized to Zr⁴⁺, while protons from concentrated sulfuric acid are reduced to hydrogen gas, giving Zr(SO₄)₂ in solution. Typical conditions: use of concentrated (≈95–98 %) H₂SO₄, heating to 150–200 °C under reflux; reaction performed in a glass or PTFE reactor resistant to hot acid.

Carboxylation (formation of an alkyl carbonate); purpose is to generate lithium ethyl carbonate as a carbonate source; key transformation is insertion of CO₂ into the LiOEt bond forming the ethyl carbonate anion paired with Li⁺; typical conditions involve bubbling CO₂ gas (1–5 atm) through a solution of lithium ethoxide in dry THF or DMF at 0–25 °C; reaction proceeds without added catalyst, but moisture must be excluded.

Ester reduction (LiAlH4 reduction): A strong hydride reduces methyl hexanoate (an ester) to the corresponding primary alcohol, hexanol, while the methoxy group is released as methanol. Performed under anhydrous conditions in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, using excess LiAlH4; work‑up with aqueous acid quenches the reagent.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; citronellal is hydrogenated to citronellol. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, 5 % Pd/C (or PtO2, Raney Ni) in ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate at room temperature to 40 °C. The C=O double bond is reduced while the isolated alkene remains unchanged under mild conditions.

Hydride reduction of an acid chloride. Purpose: synthesize a primary alcohol (1‑propanol) from the corresponding acid chloride. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers a hydride to the carbonyl carbon of propanoyl chloride, collapsing to release chloride and forming the alkoxide, which is then protonated upon work‑up to give 1‑propanol. Typical conditions: dry ether solvent (diethyl ether or THF), temperature 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar); reaction quenched carefully with water or dilute acid after completion.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt‑acid exchange). Purpose: liberate free gluconic acid from its magnesium salt and generate soluble MgCl₂. Key transformation: proton transfer from HCl to the gluconate anion, forming gluconic acid and MgCl₂ as the ionic by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, excess dilute or concentrated HCl, temperature at ambient to mild heating (≤60 °C); stirring until dissolution is complete.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration; purpose is synthesis of picric acid (2,4,6‑trinitrophenol). Key transformation is generation of the nitronium ion (NO2⁺) from concentrated HNO₃ (often assisted by H₂SO₄) which attacks the activated phenol ring at the ortho and para positions, installing three nitro groups and releasing three molecules of water. Typical conditions are low to moderate temperature (0‑50 °C) under careful temperature control to avoid runaway reaction. Reaction is usually performed in the concentrated acid mixture itself; no additional solvent or catalyst is required beyond the acid system that generates NO2⁺.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction between magnesium sulfate and calcium bromide in aqueous solution. The exchange of the anions produces insoluble calcium sulfate, which precipitates, and soluble magnesium bromide remains in solution. Purpose can be isolation of CaSO₄ or removal of Ca²⁺ from a mixture. Conditions are ambient temperature, medium, vigorous stirring; the reaction proceeds spontaneously without catalyst. Water serves as the solvent.

Deoxygenation (reduction) of an aromatic amine N‑oxide with phosphorus trichloride; PCl₃ transfers Cl to the oxygen, producing phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and regenerating N,N‑dimethylaniline; carried out under anhydrous conditions, often in dichloromethane or toluene at 0 °C to reflux; inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) is recommended.

Base‑promoted nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether synthesis) where phenol is deprotonated by sodium carbonate to give phenoxide ion, which attacks the benzylic carbon of 2‑chloroacetophenone, displacing chloride and forming 2‑phenoxyacetophenone. Carbonate decomposition yields CO₂ and water, and NaCl is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF, or ethanol; excess sodium carbonate to maintain basic conditions. No metal catalyst is required.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive amination) of 2,6‑dinitrotoluene in the presence of excess HCl to give the dihydrochloride salt of 2,6‑diaminotoluene. The two nitro groups are reduced to amines by H₂ gas on a metal catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni) while the amine product is immediately protonated by HCl to form the salt. Typical conditions: 3–5 MPa H₂ pressure, 100–150 °C, catalytic loading 5–10 % metal, solvent such as ethanol or methanol. Acidic medium is essential to obtain the dihydrochloride.

Enzymatic/biochemical dehydrogenation – oxidation of hydroquinone coupled to reduction of NAD⁺. In aqueous phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) and in the presence of a suitable dehydrogenase enzyme, hydroquinone transfers two electrons and two protons to NAD⁺, forming p‑benzoquinone and NADH. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature under aerobic or anaerobic conditions as required by the enzyme.

Hydrolysis of tungsten(VI) hexachloride. Water attacks WCl₆, replacing two chloride ligands with an oxo group and releasing two equivalents of HCl, yielding tungsten(VI) oxychloride (WOCl₄) and HCl gas. This is a non‑redox hydrolysis of a metal halide. It proceeds readily at room temperature under ambient conditions; the reaction is usually carried out in an inert, dry atmosphere to avoid uncontrolled moisture exposure. No catalyst is required; the solvent may be absent or an inert organic solvent (e.g., CS₂) can be used to dissolve WCl₆.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; silver acetate and potassium chromate exchange ions to give insoluble silver chromate precipitate and soluble potassium acetate. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1 elimination) of cyclohexanol to cyclohexene using p‑toluenesulfonic acid as the protic acid. The reaction removes water from the secondary alcohol to form the alkene. Typically carried out by heating the alcohol with a catalytic amount of p‑TsOH in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, often under reflux with a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Acid‑base proton transfer (metathesis) between sulfuric acid and sodium benzenesulfonate, yielding benzenesulfonic acid and sodium bisulfate. Conducted in aqueous medium at room temperature or with mild heating; water serves as the solvent and no external catalyst is needed.

Condensation (hydrazone formation) of phenylhydrazine with cyclohexanone to afford cyclohexanone phenylhydrazone. The carbonyl carbon of the ketone reacts with the nucleophilic –NH2 of phenylhydrazine, eliminating water. Usually performed in ethanol or methanol under reflux, often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid to promote imine formation.

Kumada cross‑coupling (nickel‑catalyzed coupling of an aryl halide with a Grignard reagent); purpose: form a C‑C bond to install a methyl substituent; 2‑bromothiophene reacts with methylmagnesium bromide in the presence of NiCl2 (often as NiCl2·DME) to afford 2‑methylthiophene and magnesium bromide salts; carried out in dry THF at reflux or 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen.

Prins reaction (acid‑catalyzed addition of an aldehyde to an alkene) where formaldehyde adds to isobutylene producing 3‑methyl‑‑buten‑1‑ol, a homoallylic alcohol. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature, using a Lewis or Brønsted acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄, BF₃·OEt₂) to activate the aldehyde.

Aqueous hydrolysis of 2‑aminopropanenitrile (α‑aminopropionitrile) to DL‑alanine with release of ammonia. The nitrile undergoes acid‑ or base‑catalyzed addition of two equivalents of water, converting the –C≡N group to a carboxylate while the amino group is liberated as NH₃. Typical conditions involve refluxing the nitrile in aqueous HCl or NaOH, followed by neutralization and isolation of the racemic alanine; water is the solvent and the acid or base serves as the catalyst.

Ester hydrolysis (acid‑ or neutral‑catalyzed) of tri(2‑ethylhexyl) phosphate; water attacks a P–O bond, cleaving one alkyl group to give 2‑ethylhexanol and bis(2‑ethylhexyl) phosphate; usually performed in aqueous acidic medium (e.g., 1 M HCl) at reflux or elevated temperature.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of 2‑methylthiophene in glacial acetic acid; bromine adds at the 3‑position giving 3‑bromo‑2‑methylthiophene and HBr as by‑product. Reaction run at 0–5 °C to minimize polybromination; acetic acid serves as solvent and weak acid to generate the bromonium electrophile.

Condensation (amidation) of nicotinic acid with hydrazine to afford nicotinic hydrazide with loss of water; typical procedure involves refluxing the acid with excess hydrazine in ethanol or methanol, sometimes using a coupling agent (e.g., DCC) or azeotropic removal of water to drive the reaction.

Acylation of taurine’s amino group with acetyl chloride in the presence of triethylamine; triethylamine captures the generated HCl forming triethylammonium chloride, yielding N‑acetyltaurine; carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Acid‑base/carbonation of tricalcium phosphate with CO₂ and water to produce phosphoric acid and precipitate calcium carbonate; conducted in aqueous suspension of the phosphate at elevated temperature (≈50–80 °C) under CO₂ pressure (1–10 atm), often with vigorous stirring to promote conversion.

Metathesis (acid‑base exchange) between hydroiodic acid and tetrabutylammonium acetate, giving acetic acid and tetrabutylammonium iodide; proceeds readily in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of butyl 2‑methylpropanoate with sodium hydroxide, forming sodium 2‑methylpropanoate and n‑butanol. Conducted in aqueous NaOH (often with a co‑solvent such as ethanol) and heated to reflux; after reaction the mixture may be acidified to isolate the free acid if desired.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑methyl‑2‑pentene to 2‑methylpentane; adds H₂ across the C=C bond; typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm), palladium on carbon (Pd/C) or platinum catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, temperature 25–80 °C.

Reduction of an ester with lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to cleave the ester into two primary alcohols. LiAlH4 (1–2 equiv) donates hydride to the carbonyl carbon of methyl fluoroacetate, breaking the C–O bond; the alkoxy fragment is released as methanol and the acyl fragment is reduced to fluoroethanol. Typical conditions: dry ether (diethyl ether or THF), inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous acidic work‑up.

Redox disproportionation of permanganate by hydrogen peroxide in water; purpose is to decompose KMnO₄ while generating oxygen gas and insoluble manganese dioxide. H₂O₂ reduces Mn(VII) to Mn(IV) (MnO₂) and is itself oxidized to O₂; K⁺ is neutralized to KOH. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often with excess H₂O₂; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of calcium cyanide; water reacts with Ca(CN)₂ to produce calcium hydroxide and hydrogen cyanide gas. Conducted in aqueous medium, typically with gentle heating to drive HCN evolution; no catalyst required.

General type: nucleophilic acyl substitution (acylation of an amine). Purpose: mono‑acetylation of m‑phenylenediamine to afford 3‑aminoacetanilide. Key transformation: one –NH2 attacks acetyl chloride, yielding the amide and HCl. Typical conditions: anhydrous solvent such as pyridine, dichloromethane or THF, temperature 0 °C to rt, with a stoichiometric base (pyridine, triethylamine) to trap HCl; reaction performed under inert atmosphere.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of a 3‑bromoindolizine with phenylboronic acid; purpose is to install a phenyl group at the C‑3 position of the indolizine core. The aryl bromide undergoes palladium‑catalyzed transmetallation with the boronic acid in the presence of a base (K2CO3). Typical conditions: Pd(0) or Pd(OAc)2 (5–10 mol %), PPh3 or other phosphine ligand, K2CO3 as base, mixed solvent DMF/H2O or dioxane/H2O, heated 80–100 °C under nitrogen. By‑products are potassium bromide and boric acid.

Metal‑hydride reduction (dehalogenation) of benzyl bromide using lithium triethylborohydride (Superhydride); purpose is to replace the benzylic bromine with hydrogen to afford toluene. LiEt₃BH transfers a hydride to the benzylic carbon, displacing bromide as LiBr; the resulting triethylborane is generated as a by‑product. Reaction is run in anhydrous THF under nitrogen or argon, typically at 0 °C to room temperature.

Carboxylation of phenyl lithium with carbon dioxide; purpose is to synthesize benzoic acid from an organolithium reagent. Phenyl lithium adds to CO₂ to form lithium benzoate, which is protonated during aqueous work‑up to give benzoic acid. Conditions: dry ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether), low temperature (‑78 °C to ‑20 °C) under inert atmosphere, CO₂ supplied as gas or dry ice, followed by acidic quench.

Boron‑tribromide mediated demethylation of 2‑methoxynaphthalene. BBr3 coordinates to the ether oxygen, cleaving the C‑O bond and forming 2‑naphthol while methyl bromide is released as a volatile by‑product. Conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) in anhydrous CH2Cl2 under nitrogen; the mixture is quenched with methanol or water after completion.

High‑temperature solid‑state metathesis to prepare terbium phosphide; purpose is to obtain TbP from readily available salts. Terbium(III) chloride reacts with sodium phosphide (Na₃P) exchanging Cl⁻ for P³⁻ to give TbP and NaCl. Carried out in a sealed tube or furnace under argon, heated to 800–1000 °C; no solvent, sometimes a slight excess of Na₃P is used to drive the reaction.

Base‑promoted condensation of acetylene with carbon disulfide to form 1,2‑dithiole‑3‑thione; purpose is the synthesis of a heterocyclic thione. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates acetylene to generate the acetylide ion, which attacks CS₂; subsequent cyclization and protonation afford the dithiole ring. Reaction is performed in aqueous NaOH (often with ethanol as co‑solvent) at 60–80 °C while bubbling acetylene gas, followed by acid work‑up to isolate the thione.

Double displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction; purpose is to replace Na⁺ with Li⁺ in the tungstate salt; key transformation is exchange of Na⁺ and Li⁺ ions producing Li₂CO₃ and Na₂WO₄; generally carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Fluorination / halogen‑exchange synthesis of phosphorus pentafluoride; purpose is to generate PF₅ gas from solid P₂O₅; key transformation replaces the five O atoms of P₂O₅ with fluorine, releasing H₂O; conducted in anhydrous hydrogen fluoride gas, often in a fluorination apparatus at controlled temperature (0–50 °C); no solvent other than HF and no catalyst needed.

Halide exchange (metathesis) reaction to prepare gold(III) bromide; purpose is to convert AuCl₃ to AuBr₃; key transformation is substitution of chloride ligands by bromide, forming HCl as by‑product; typically performed in aqueous or non‑aqueous HBr solution under reflux or gentle heating; no catalyst required.

Carbothermal reduction / carburization of molybdenum dioxide; purpose is to synthesize molybdenum carbide; key transformation: carbon reduces MoO₂, oxygen leaves as CO while carbon incorporates into Mo to form MoC (or Mo₂C); carried out at high temperature (≈900–1200 °C) in an inert or reducing atmosphere; solid‑state reaction with no solvent and no catalyst.

Metal‑mediated reductive dehalogenation using zinc dust; purpose is to remove one bromine atom from 1,2‑dibromo‑1‑nitroethane giving 1‑bromo‑1‑nitroethane; key transformation involves single‑electron transfer from Zn to the C–Br bond forming ZnBr₂ and the monobromo product; usually performed in dry ethanol or THF under reflux with inert atmosphere; zinc dust acts as the reductant, no additional catalyst.

Strong oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid with potassium permanganate in basic aqueous medium; 2-(4‑chlorophenoxy)ethanol is converted to 2-(4‑chlorophenoxy)acetic acid, MnO2 precipitates, and KOH is generated; typically reflux in water or aqueous NaOH with solid KMnO4 added portionwise.

Double displacement/complexation precipitation to form trilead dicitrate; purpose is to synthesize a lead citrate coordination complex; key transformation exchanges Na⁺ for Pb²⁺, producing NaCl and the Pb₃(citrate)₂ complex; carried out in aqueous solution, often with slight heating to dissolve lead(II) chloride; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Grignard addition to a nitrile (methylmagnesium bromide). The methyl nucleophile attacks benzonitrile, forming a magnesium imine that, after aqueous work‑up, furnishes acetophenone (C₆H₅‑CO‑CH₃). Purpose: synthesize aryl‑alkyl ketones from nitriles. Conditions: dry ether (THF or diethyl ether), −78 °C to 0 °C during addition, then quench with dilute acid or water; excess Grignard often used. No catalyst.

Direct nitridation (solid‑gas reaction) producing tantalum nitride; purpose: preparation of conductive/hard ceramic TaN; key transformation: 2 Ta (s) + N₂ (g) → 2 TaN (s); typical conditions: 1200–1500 °C under flowing N₂ or NH₃ atmosphere; inert carrier gas may be used; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Oxidation (hydroxylation) of cyclobutane; purpose is to introduce a hydroxyl group forming cyclobutanol; key transformation is insertion of an OH from H₂O₂ into a C–H bond with concomitant formation of water; typically carried out in the presence of a metal catalyst such as Fe‑ or Ti‑based species (e.g., Fe‑EDTA, Ti‑silicalite) under mild acidic or neutral aqueous conditions, often with an organic co‑solvent like acetonitrile.

Oxidative conversion of manganese dioxide to permanganate; purpose is to generate rubidium permanganate in solution; key transformation is oxidation of Mn(IV) in MnO₂ to Mn(VII) by ozone in basic medium, producing water; usually performed in aqueous rubidium hydroxide at ambient temperature with ozone gas bubbled through the solution; no additional catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction; purpose is to exchange the anions and form an insoluble lead(II) molybdate precipitate; key transformation swaps sulfate and molybdate ions, yielding soluble sodium sulfate and solid PbMoO₄; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature, often with gentle stirring; no special solvent beyond water is needed.

Acid–base reaction of a carbonate with chromic acid; purpose is to neutralize the acid and generate calcium chromate while releasing CO₂; key transformation converts CaCO₃ to CaCrO₄, producing carbon dioxide gas and water; typically performed in aqueous solution with dilute H₂CrO₄ at ambient temperature; water serves as the solvent.

Catalytic of a sulfide to a sulfone; purpose is to convert diethyl sulfide into diethyl sulfone; key transformation oxidizes the sulfur from the +2 to the +4 oxidation state using H₂O₂, with sodium tungstate acting as the catalyst and water as the by‑product; commonly conducted in a mixed aqueous‑organic medium (e.g., water–acetone or water–acetonitrile) at mild temperatures (0–40 °C) under neutral to slightly acidic conditions.

Anisole + N,N‑Dimethylformamide + Phosphorus oxychloride → 4‑Methoxybenzaldehyde  
General type: Vilsmeier–Haack formylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution). Purpose: introduce a formyl group para to the methoxy substituent on the aromatic ring. Key transformation: POCl₃ reacts with DMF to generate the Vilsmeier reagent (Cl‑CH=NMe₂⁺ Cl⁻); this electrophile attacks the activated anisole ring preferentially at the para position, followed by hydrolysis to give 4‑methoxybenzaldehyde. Typical conditions: anisole dissolved in dry DMF (2–3 M), cooled to 0 °C, POCl₃ added dropwise, then stirred 1–2 h at 0–25 °C; work‑up with ice‑water and neutralization. Common solvents/catalysts: DMF (solvent & reagent), POCl₃ (reagent); reaction performed under nitrogen to exclude moisture.

Suzuki‑Miyaura coupling of phenylboronic acid pinacol ester with 4‑bromoacetophenone; reaction type: palladium‑catalyzed C–C cross‑coupling; purpose: synthesis of 4‑acetylbiphenyl; key transformations: same catalytic cycle as in (1) but the aryl bromide bears an acetyl substituent; typical conditions: Pd(PPh₃)₄ (5 mol %), K₂CO₃ (2 eq) in water/THF or dioxane, 80‑100 °C under nitrogen; no additional catalyst needed.

High‑temperature hydrogen reduction of tellurium dioxide; purpose is to produce hydrogen telluride gas; key transformation reduces Te(IV) in TeO₂ to Te(−II) as H₂Te while oxidizing H to; typically carried out in a sealed reactor at elevated temperatures (300–500 °C) under a flow of H₂ gas; inert gas diluent such as N₂ may be used, and the reaction is gas‑phase with no solvent.

Solid‑state synthesis of a metal chalcogenide by thermally decomposing tungsten hexacarbonyl in the presence of elemental tellurium; heating W(CO)6 with 2 equiv Te at 200‑300 °C under inert atmosphere gives tungsten telluride (likely WTe2) while liberating six molecules of CO gas; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Palladium‑catalyzed Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 3‑bromoaniline with phenylboronic acid using Pd(OAc)2 and the bidentate phosphine ligand dppf, with Na2CO3 as base; typically performed in a mixed aqueous/organic solvent such as ethanol/water or toluene at 80‑100 °C under nitrogen; the reaction forms a new C‑C bond delivering 3‑aminobiphenyl as the product.

Thermal dehydration of thallium(I) hydroxide; solid TlOH is heated to about 300 °C in the absence of moisture, causing two equivalents to condense and release water vapor while forming thallium(I) oxide (Tl2O); the process proceeds without added catalyst or solvent.

Direct combination (oxidation) reaction; used to synthesize terbium(III) oxide from the elemental metal. Terbium metal reacts with molecular oxygen, converting Tb⁰ to Tb³⁺ and forming Tb₂O₃. Typically carried out by heating terbium powder or turnings in a stream of dry air or pure O₂ at 300–500 °C. No solvent or catalyst is required; the reaction occurs in the solid state.

Acid or base‑catalyzed hydrolysis of N‑isobutylformamide; the amide is treated with aqueous acid (e.g., HCl) or aqueous base (e.g., NaOH) and heated to reflux (≈100 °C), often in water or a water/THF mixture, resulting in cleavage of the C–N bond to give formic acid and isobutylamine.

Partial reduction of a nitrile to an aldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL) – a metal‑hydride mediated reduction; typically performed at −78 °C in an aprotic solvent such as THF or toluene, followed by aqueous work‑up to give ethanal.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑methylpyridine (2‑picoline) to 2‑methylpiperidine; the aromatic pyridine ring is saturated, converting the heteroarene into a saturated secondary amine. Reaction uses H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with 5–10 % Pd/C as catalyst, in an alcohol solvent such as ethanol or methanol, at 50–100 °C. The purpose is to reduce aromaticity and generate a saturated cyclic amine.

Metathesis (acid‑base) reaction forming a silver salt; purpose: generate the insoluble silver benzoate for isolation or further use. Key transformation: exchange of the nitrate anion of AgNO₃ with the benzoate anion of benzoic acid, producing AgC₆H₅COO and HNO₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution at ambient temperature, stirring; no special solvent beyond water; reaction proceeds readily.

Acyl‑transfer esterification of the allylic alcohol linalool using acetylimidazole as the acetyl donor, catalyzed by 4‑dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP); the reaction is typically carried out at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, producing linalyl acetate and releasing imidazole as a by‑product.

Complete combustion of 2,5‑dimethylheptane in excess oxygen; performed in the gas phase at flame temperatures, the hydrocarbon reacts with 14 mol O2 to yield 9 mol CO2 and 10 mol H2O according to the balanced equation; no solvent or catalyst is involved.

Condensation (amide formation) of ethylamine with L‑glutamic acid to give L‑theanine; the primary amine attacks the γ‑carboxyl carbonyl forming an amide bond and releasing water; typically performed in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic media, often under mild heating (50 °C) and pH control (neutral to slightly basic) to facilitate dehydration.

Reductive coupling (Wurtz‑type) of chlorotrimethylsilane with sodium metal yielding hexamethyldisilane; sodium metal reduces the Si–Cl bond and promotes Si–Si bond formation; carried out under inert atmosphere in dry ether or THF, usually at reflux temperature, with excess sodium to drive the reaction to completion.

Selective reduction of the C‑6 ketone of oxymorphone to the corresponding secondary alcohol (hydromorphone) using lithium aluminium hydride; LiAlH₄ transfers hydride to the carbonyl, converting it to a hydroxyl group; performed in anhydrous (ethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux, followed by careful aqueous work‑up to quench excess reagent.

N‑alkylation of 2‑propylpiperidine with methyl iodide via an SN2 nucleophilic substitution, producing 1‑methyl‑2‑propylpiperidine and HI; the secondary amine attacks the methyl carbon displacing iodide; usually carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF, with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaHCO₃) to neutralize the generated HI, at ambient temperature or gentle heating.

Oxidative coupling of L‑selenocysteine to L‑selenocystine (diselenide) using ferric chloride as the oxidant; FeCl₃ oxidizes two selenol groups to a Se–Se bond, being reduced to FeCl₂ and releasing HCl; typically performed in aqueous buffer (pH ≈ 6‑7) at room temperature, with stoichiometric FeCl₃ and gentle stirring.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2,3‑dichloronitrobenzene to 2,3‑dichloroaniline using H₂ gas and palladium on carbon; Pd/C activates hydrogen, reducing the nitro group to an amine while water is formed as by‑product; conducted in an alcoholic solvent (ethanol or methanol) under 1‑5 atm H₂ pressure at 25‑50 °C, often with continuous stirring.

Type: Nucleophilic substitution (conversion of phenol to aryl chloride); Purpose: Replace the hydroxyl group with chlorine to obtain an aryl chloride; Key transformation: OH of 4‑bromophenol is substituted by Cl, forming 4‑bromophenyl chloride with release of SO2 and HCl gases; Typical conditions: Add thionyl chloride dropwise to a solution of the phenol at 0 °C then warm to reflux; Solvent/Catalyst: Anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine is commonly used, pyridine also scavenges HCl.

Acid‑base neutralization forming a metal fluoride; hydrogen fluoride reacts with strontium oxide to give water and strontium fluoride; typically performed in liquid or aqueous HF at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Rosenmund‑von Braun cyanation (nucleophilic substitution with CuCN); copper(I) cyanide transfers a cyanide ion to 1‑iodohexane, forming hexanenitrile and precipitating CuI. The reaction is performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere; sometimes a catalytic amount of CuCl is added to facilitate the process.

2-chlorobenzamide + lithium aluminium hydride → 2-chloroaniline  
Type: strong reduction of an amide to a primary amine. Purpose: reduction of the carbonyl group and removal of the carbonyl oxygen, yielding the corresponding aniline. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, then subsequent work‑up converts the intermediate to the amine, eliminating oxygen as Al‑containing by‑products. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), low temperature addition (0 °C) followed by reflux (≈70 °C) for 2–4 h under nitrogen. Quench carefully with water or dilute acid.

Copper‑catalyzed Ullmann aryl amination; converts 2‑bromobiphenyl to 2‑aminobiphenyl using ammonia as nucleophile and potassium carbonate as base; typical conditions: CuI (5–10 mol %), K2CO3, polar aprotic solvent (DMF or DMSO), heat 120–150 °C under inert atmosphere; purpose is to introduce an aryl amine functionality.

Acid‑base neutralisation forming thorium(IV) nitrate; purpose is to generate a highly soluble nitrate salt used in fuel‑cycle chemistry; OH− groups are protonated by nitric acid to give water and Th4+ combines with four nitrate anions; carried out in aqueous HNO3 (often 1–3 M) with heating to 50–80 °C to ensure dissolution; water is the solvent, no catalyst is needed.

Fischer esterification of borneol with acetic acid to produce bornyl acetate; acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) is used; reflux in toluene or excess acetic acid as solvent; water is removed (e.g., by Dean‑Stark) to drive the equilibrium.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation: sodium oxalate and barium nitrate exchange ions to precipitate insoluble barium oxalate while forming soluble sodium nitrate; carried out at room temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst required.

Oxidation of thioanisole to methyl phenyl sulfoxide with perbenzoic acid; selective oxygen transfer to sulfur affording the sulfoxide and benzoic acid; carried out in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, using a stoichiometric amount of peracid and often a slight excess to avoid over‑oxidation to the sulfone.

Acid‑halide exchange synthesis; germanium dioxide reacts with concentrated hydrobromic acid (or HBr gas) to give germanium tetrabromide and water; usually refluxed in excess HBr or in a sealed tube at 150–200 °C to drive off water; no additional solvent needed, though the reaction medium is essentially aqueous or neat HBr.

Type: Williamson ether synthesis (SN2). Purpose: preparation of ethyl phenyl ether. Key transformation: phenoxide O‑ attacks ethyl bromide, displacing Br⁻; lithium bromide precipitates. Typical conditions: anhydrous THF or DMF, 0 °C to reflux, inert atmosphere; phenoxide formed from phenol and a strong base. No catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis (alkaline saponification); acetamide reacts with aqueous NaOH, water attacks the carbonyl giving sodium acetate and liberating ammonia (which may escape as NH₃ gas); performed by heating the mixture under reflux, often with excess NaOH, and then acidifying if needed to isolate acetic acid.

Ester hydrolysis (acid-catalyzed). Purpose: convert a methyl ester into the corresponding carboxylic acid and recover methanol. Key transformation: cleavage of the C–O ester bond by water, forming trifluoroacetic acid and methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or base, reflux 1–2 h. Common solvent: mixture of water and an organic co‑solvent (e.g., THF) if needed; neutralization after reaction.

Mitsunobu reaction converting phenethyl alcohol into a pyrrolidine derivative; reagents are triphenylphosphine and diethyl azodicarboxylate, pyrrolidine acts as nucleophile; by‑products are triphenylphosphine oxide and diethyl hydrazodicarboxylate; performed in anhydrous THF or dioxane at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of magnesium silicide by direct combination of elemental silicon and magnesium; mixture heated to 600‑800 °C under an inert atmosphere (argon) to prevent oxidation; no solvent or catalyst required.

Catalytic dehydrogenation; converts tetrahydroquinoline to quinoline by removing two hydrogen atoms. Pd/C (5–10 wt %) serves as the catalyst under an inert nitrogen atmosphere; the reaction is heated (≈100–150 °C) often in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene or performed neat, releasing H₂ gas.

Acid–base neutralization forming apomorphine hydrochloride; purpose is to convert the free base into a more water‑soluble and stable salt; key transformation is protonation of the amine nitrogen by HCl; typically performed by adding aqueous or ethanolic HCl to apomorphine at room temperature; common solvent is ethanol or isopropanol with water; no catalyst required

Metal dissolution in acid (acidic leaching); scandium metal reacts with aqueous sulfuric acid to produce scandium(III) sulfate and hydrogen gas. The overall transformation is oxidation of Sc⁰ to Sc³⁺ with concurrent reduction of protons to H₂. Typically performed with dilute to concentrated H₂SO₄ (e.g., 1–6 M) under reflux or heating (~80–120 °C) to accelerate the reaction; aqueous solution is the solvent, and no external catalyst is required.

α‑Halogenation of a carboxylic acid via the Hell‑Volhard‑Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction. Acetic acid is first converted to the acyl bromide by catalytic phosphorus tribromide; bromine then α‑brominates the acyl bromide, and hydrolysis regenerates the α‑bromo acid (2‑bromoacetic acid) with HBr as a by‑product. Usually carried out in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, under reflux, with catalytic PBr₃ and stoichiometric Br₂.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2); sodium methanethiolate acts as a nucleophile displacing iodide from methyl iodide to give dimethyl sulfide and sodium iodide; usually performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO, or acetone at 0‑25 °C; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis/neutralization with ammonium base; GaI₃ is added to an aqueous solution of NH₄OH (typically 1‑2 M) at room temperature. Gallium hydroxide precipitates while ammonium iodide (NH₄I) remains dissolved; aqueous medium, gentle stirring, optional mild heating.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; transforms ethyl 2‑chloro‑2‑methylpropanoate into the corresponding carboxylic acid (2‑chloro‑2‑methylpropionic acid) and ethanol; carried out in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) under reflux; water is the reaction medium.

Acylation of phenethylamine with acetic anhydride to give N‑acetylphenethylamine and acetic acid; reaction type is nucleophilic acyl substitution (amide formation); purpose is protection/derivatization of the amine; key step is nucleophilic attack of the amine on the anhydride carbonyl; usually carried out in anhydrous pyridine or dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, often with catalytic DMAP; no additional catalyst beyond the base/solvent

Metathesis/precipitation of scandium trichloride with ammonium hydroxide yielding scandium hydroxide precipitate and ammonium chloride; reaction type is double‑replacement (salt‑metathesis); purpose is isolation of Sc(OH)₃; key transformation is exchange of Cl⁻ for OH⁻ ions; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature by adding aqueous NH₄OH to a ScCl₃ solution; water is the solvent; no catalyst required

Free‑radical bromination of cycloheptane with bromine to give bromocycloheptane and HBr; reaction type is radical substitution; purpose is introduction of a bromine substituent; key steps involve homolytic cleavage of Br₂ under UV light or peroxide, hydrogen abstraction from cycloheptane, and recombination to form the alkyl bromide; typically run in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane under reflux with light or a radical initiator; no catalyst other than the initiator

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; converts the nitrile group of benzoyl cyanide to a carboxylic acid. Key transformation is cleavage of the C≡N bond to give benzoic acid while cyanide is released as hydrogen cyanide. Typical conditions: aqueous hydrochloric acid, reflux or heating at 60–100 °C; water serves as solvent and acid provides the catalyst.
