Swern oxidation of 1,1,1‑trifluoro‑2‑propanol using oxalyl chloride and dimethyl sulfoxide; purpose is to convert the secondary alcohol to the corresponding ketone (1,1,1‑trifluoroacetone) without over‑oxidation; key steps are activation of DMSO by oxalyl chloride at –78 °C to form a chlorosulfonium intermediate, addition of the alcohol, then deprotonation with triethylamine to give the ketone; typical conditions use CH₂Cl₂ as solvent, low temperature (–78 °C to –30 °C), and TEA as base; by‑products are CO, CO₂, and dimethyl sulfide.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride with aqueous ammonia; used to convert 1‑chloro‑3‑methoxypropane into the primary amine 1‑amino‑3‑methoxypropane. The chlorine is displaced by NH3, yielding the amine and chloride ion. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous NH3 (often 5–25 % solution) optionally with a co‑solvent such as ethanol; reaction proceeds at 50–80 °C until completion, then the product is isolated by extraction or distillation.

Acid‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; used to deprotect the N‑acetyl group and liberate the free aniline. The C–N bond of the N‑acetyl moiety is cleaved, giving 3‑methoxyaniline and acetic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous hydrochloric acid (6 M or 1–2 M HCl) at 80–100 °C, solvent water or aqueous ethanol; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed condensation/cyclization (Friedel‑Crafts‑type) of hydroquinone (1,4‑dihydroxybenzene) with phthalic anhydride in the presence of methanesulfonic acid; purpose is the synthesis of the anthraquinone dye quinizarin. The reaction forms two new C–C bonds and an internal quinone ring, converting the phenolic substrate into 1,4‑dihydroxy‑9,10‑anthraquinone. Typical conditions: melt or heat the mixture to 180–220 °C under nitrogen, using excess methanesulfonic acid as catalyst; no separate solvent is required, but the acid also acts as a high‑boiling medium. After cooling, the product precipitates and is filtered, washed, and recrystallized.

Acid‑base reaction/precipitation with hydrofluoric acid forming aluminum fluoride; purpose is to produce AlF3 for material synthesis or etching; key transformation: Al(OH)3 + 3 HF → AlF3 + 3 H2O (often as hydrated AlF3·3H2O); typical conditions: aqueous HF at low to ambient temperature, careful handling due to HF hazard; solvent: water; no catalyst, but excess HF may be used to drive complete conversion.

Alcoholysis (ligand exchange) of a metal alkoxide; titanium(IV) ethoxide reacts with isopropanol to replace ethoxy groups with isopropoxy groups, generating titanium(IV) isopropoxide and ethanol as by‑product. This transesterification is employed to prepare titanium isopropoxide for sol‑gel or polymerization processes. Typical conditions: excess isopropanol, reflux (≈80 °C) under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) to avoid moisture; reaction proceeds quantitatively and the ethanol formed is removed by distillation or azeotropic removal.

Redox reaction; iodine oxidizes Sn(II) in sodium stannite to Sn(IV) producing sodium stannate, while iodine is reduced to iodide, forming sodium iodide. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Acidolysis of cadmium sulfide with hydrobromic acid; the sulfide is protonated to release hydrogen sulfide gas and form cadmium bromide. Typically carried out in aqueous acid under reflux to ensure complete conversion; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation in aqueous solution; copper(II) sulfate reacts with sodium arsenate to form insoluble copper arsenate precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. The purpose is the preparation or removal of copper arsenate as a pigment or corrosion‑inhibitor. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in water at ambient temperature, stir vigorously; the copper arsenate precipitates as a green‑blue solid, which is filtered and washed. No special catalysts are required; the reaction is driven by the low solubility product of copper arsenate.

Conversion of 3‑methylthiophene‑2‑carboxylic acid to its acyl chloride using thionyl chloride; a chlorination of a carboxylic acid that releases SO₂ and HCl gases; usually performed under reflux or at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine (pyridine scavenges HCl); catalytic DMF may be added to accelerate; purpose is activation of the acid for subsequent amide or ester formation.

Acidification of an ammonium salt; concentrated or dilute H₂SO₄ protonates the adipate anion of ammonium adipate, yielding solid adipic acid and ammonium sulfate in solution; carried out in water at low to moderate temperature (0–50 °C) to avoid decomposition; the mixture may be cooled, the adipic acid crystallizes out and is filtered, the aqueous layer contains (NH₄)₂SO₄; no catalyst needed.

Transesterification of phthalic anhydride with methanol to produce methyl phthalate; C6H4(CO)2O + CH3OH → CH3OOC‑C6H4‑COOH; typically reflux methanol (70–120 °C) with an acid catalyst (H2SO4) or catalytic amount of DMAP; removal of phthalic acid (or water) shifts equilibrium toward ester.

Catalytic hydrogenation; Pd/C‑mediated addition of H₂ across the terminal double bond of 2-methylpent-1-ene to produce the saturated alkane 2-methylpentane. Standard protocol: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm), 5 % Pd/C (5–10 wt % relative to substrate) in ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient temperature to gentle reflux; reaction time ranges from 1–4 h.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (reductive dehalogenation); hydrogen in the presence of Pd/C reduces the C–Cl bond to a C–H bond, forming ethane and HCl; performed under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in solvents such as ethanol or ethyl acetate at mild temperature (room to 50 °C).

Alcoholysis of dichlorosilane with methanol; each Si–Cl bond is converted to a Si–OCH₃ group yielding dimethoxysilane and HCl; performed in anhydrous methanol, frequently in the presence of a tertiary amine base to capture the liberated HCl; carried out at 0–25 °C under inert atmosphere.

Thermal decomposition of an organic azide (azide reduction) in water; benzyl azide undergoes thermolysis to generate benzylamine and molecular nitrogen. The azide loses N₂, forming a transient nitrene that abstracts a proton from water (or solvent) to give the primary amine. This reaction provides a simple route to primary amines from azides. Typical conditions: heat an aqueous solution of benzyl azide to 80–120 °C (often under reflux) for 1–2 h; nitrogen gas evolves, and the amine remains in solution. The reaction is generally performed without additional catalysts, though a sealed system or vented apparatus is required for safe N₂ release.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization and double‑displacement precipitation. Purpose: preparation of lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO₄), a cathode material for Li‑ion batteries. Key transformation: phosphoric acid reacts with lithium hydroxide and iron(II) carbonate to give LiFePO₄ while CO₂ is liberated and water formed. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, heating to 80–100 °C to evolve CO₂ and drive the reaction to completion, pH controlled near neutral. Common solvent: water; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: metathesis (double‑replacement) ionic exchange. Purpose: synthesis of thallium(I) iodide and potassium carbonate. Key transformation: thallium carbonate exchanges its carbonate anion with iodide from potassium iodide, precipitating sparingly soluble TlI and leaving K₂CO₃ in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, stirring at ambient temperature or with mild heating to improve solubility. Solvent: water; no catalyst needed.

Reaction type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitro group to an amine. Purpose: conversion of 3‑nitrobenzaldehyde to 3‑aminobenzaldehyde. Key transformation: H₂ gas reduces the –NO₂ functionality to –NH₂ in the presence of palladium on carbon. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % wt), solvent such as ethanol or methanol, temperature from room temperature to reflux (~50–80 °C) for several hours. No additional reagents required.

Reaction type: alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of an ester. Purpose: preparation of gemfibrozil (2‑(4‑chlorophenoxy)‑2‑methylpropanoic acid) from its ethyl ester and generation of ethanol as by‑product. Key transformation: NaOH attacks the carbonyl of the ethyl ester, yielding the carboxylate which upon acid work‑up gives the acid, while the ethoxy group is released as ethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–2 h, followed by acidification (e.g., dilute HCl) to precipitate the product. Solvent: water/ethanol mixture; no catalyst required.

Copper‑catalyzed oxidative decarboxylation (decarboxylative hydroxylation); anthranilic acid reacts with copper(II) acetate under reflux, releasing CO₂ and forming 2‑aminophenol; usually performed in refluxing acetic acid or a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF) with Cu(OAc)₂ as catalyst, sometimes with added base; temperature around 120–150 °C.

Radical halogenation of tetrahydrofuran with bromine to give 2‑bromotetrahydrofuran and HBr. Performed under UV light or heat in a non‑polar solvent (CCl₄, CH₂Cl₂); bromine serves as both reagent and source of HBr.

Acidic decomposition of cadmium carbonate with hydrobromic acid; the carbonate reacts to form cadmium bromide, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or with gentle heating to promote CO₂ evolution; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; converts 2‑phenylpropanenitrile to 2‑phenylpropanoic acid; key steps: protonation of the nitrile, nucleophilic attack by water to give an imidic acid, tautomerization to an amide, and further hydrolysis to the carboxylic acid while releasing ammonia which is captured as ammonium chloride; typical conditions: reflux in aqueous hydrochloric acid (6 M) for 2–6 h; solvent is water/HCl mixture.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis. Purpose: conversion of ecgonine methyl ester to ecgonine (free acid) with methanol as the leaving alcohol. Key transformation: protonated ester carbonyl is attacked by water, effecting cleavage of the C‑O bond and releasing methanol. Typical conditions: conc. HCl (1–6 M), reflux 80–100 °C for several hours in aqueous medium. Solvent: water (often with a co‑solvent); no additional catalyst needed.

Reaction type: redox (reduction) reaction. Purpose: reduction of methylarsonic acid (As V) to monomethylarsonous acid (As III). Key transformation: Fe²⁺ from iron(II) sulfate donates electrons to As(V), reducing it to As(III) while Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, mildly acidic to neutral pH, ambient to 60 °C, reaction proceeds under stirring. Solvent: water; no external catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction. Oxalic acid exchanges anions with manganese(II) acetate in water, producing insoluble manganese(II) oxalate precipitate and acetic acid. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient or gently heated temperature; no catalyst required; product manganese oxalate is filtered off.

Free‑radical halogenation (substitution). Chlorine gas reacts with 2,3‑dimethylpentane under UV light or heat, abstracting a hydrogen atom and forming 3‑chloro‑2,3‑dimethylpentane together with hydrogen chloride. Conducted in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or neat alkane, with UV irradiation or thermal initiation; no additional catalyst.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; aqueous potassium carbonate reacts with YbBr₃, precipitating ytterbium carbonate and leaving potassium bromide in solution. Conducted in water with mild heating to complete precipitation; no catalyst necessary.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal formation. Acetaldehyde reacts with excess ethanol in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid to give acetaldehyde diethyl acetal, water being eliminated. Typically carried out in ethanol (or in toluene with a Dean‑Stark trap) at reflux; catalytic H₂SO₄ (≈0.1 equiv) and removal of water drive the equilibrium.

Strong reduction of a diester with LiAlH4; lithium aluminium hydride reduces both carbonyls of diethyl succinate to primary alcohols, giving 1,4‑butanediol (ethanol is liberated on work‑up). Purpose: convert a diester to a diol. Conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere; quench with water then dilute acid, no additional catalyst.

Transfer hydrogenation (catalytic reduction) of nitro groups. Formic acid serves as a hydrogen donor; palladium on carbon decomposes it to generate hydrogen that reduces the two nitro groups of 2,4‑dinitrotoluene to the corresponding diamine, producing 2,4‑diaminotoluene, CO₂ and water. Usually performed in aqueous or alcoholic solvent at 80–120 °C under inert atmosphere; Pd/C (5–10 % wt) is the catalyst.

Acid‑base neutralization/salt formation. Phenylmercuric hydroxide reacts with acetic acid to form phenylmercuric acetate and water. Conducted in water or a water/organic solvent mixture (e.g., water/acetone) at room temperature; no additional catalyst required; the organomercury acetate often precipitates.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of paraldehyde. Dilute sulfuric acid in water protonates paraldehyde, cleaving the cyclic acetal to regenerate acetaldehyde. Performed under reflux in aqueous dilute H₂SO₄; acetaldehyde can be distilled off or extracted. No other reagents are needed.

Acid‑base precipitation (neutralization) of a metal nitrate; produces scandium hydroxide precipitate and sodium nitrate in solution. Performed in aqueous medium at room temperature by adding aqueous NaOH to a scandium nitrate solution with vigorous stirring. Water is the solvent; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol with hydrogen gas and palladium on carbon; a hydrogenolysis that reduces the C=O of nonaldehyde to a C‑OH group yielding nonanol; generally carried out in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate at 1–5 atm H₂ and ambient or slightly elevated temperature, using a Pd/C catalyst and filtered off after completion.

Acid‑carbonate reaction; used to generate carbon dioxide and a nitrite salt; the carbonate ion reacts with nitrous acid, releasing CO₂ and H₂O while forming barium nitrite; performed in aqueous solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; water is the solvent.

Sodium borohydride reduction of a β‑keto ester; selectively reduces the ketone carbonyl of ethyl acetoacetate to give the β‑hydroxy ester ethyl 3‑hydroxybutanoate. Purpose: obtain a β‑hydroxy ester for further functionalisation. Typical conditions: NaBH4 (1‑2 equiv) in methanol or ethanol, 0 °C to room temperature, reaction complete within 1‑2 h. No additional catalyst required.

Oxidative cleavage of a 1,8‑diol to a dicarboxylic acid using sodium hypochlorite and hydrogen peroxide; both oxidants convert the primary alcohol groups into carboxyl groups, yielding suberic (octanedioic) acid, water and NaCl; conducted in aqueous basic solution (often with NaOH) at 0–25 °C; water is the reaction medium.

Halogen‑exchange fluorination of thiophosphoryl bromide; three bromine atoms are substituted by fluorine atoms, producing phosphorothioic trifluoride and bromine monofluoride as by‑product; the reaction requires anhydrous conditions, low temperature, and an inert fluorinated solvent such as liquid HF or a perfluoroalkane; no catalyst is typically needed.

Acetylation reaction; forms phenyl acetate (ester) and acetic acid; ester bond formation via nucleophilic attack by phenol and proton transfer; typically conducted with acetic anhydride as acylating agent in presence of acid/base catalysts (e.g., sulfuric acid, pyridine) in anhydrous solvents like pyridine or chloroform.

Catalytic hydrogenation of dimethyl fumarate to dimethyl succinate; Pd/C catalyst under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) in a solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, typically at 25‑50 °C; reduces the C=C double bond to a saturated ester.

Electrophilic addition of chlorine across a cis‑1,2‑difluoroethylene double bond; each chlorine atom adds to a carbon of the C=C, giving 1,2‑dichloro‑1,2‑difluoroethane while retaining the fluorine substituents; performed in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, usually in the dark (thermal) or under UV for a radical pathway.

Hydrolytic deamination of aminomethylphosphonic acid; water attacks the C‑N bond, releasing ammonia and converting the aminomethyl group to a methyl group, yielding methylphosphonic acid; carried out in aqueous solution with gentle heating (≈50–80 °C), under neutral or slightly acidic conditions; water serves as the solvent.

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) in which hydrogen telluride (a weak acid) reacts with zinc bromide to form hydrobromic acid and insoluble zinc telluride; usually carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature, with the HBr evolving as gas.

precipitation metathesis between lead(II) chloride and sodium molybdate producing soluble sodium chloride and insoluble lead(II) molybdate precipitate; performed in water at room temperature with stirring, no special catalyst required.

catalytic aerobic oxidation of thezylic C–H bond of toluene to benzaldehyde, mediated by N‑hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) as a radical co‑oxidant and cobalt(II) acetylacetonate as the metal catalyst; conducted under an O₂ atmosphere, typically in acetonitrile or a high‑boiling solvent at 80–120 °C, yielding water as the only by‑product.

Metal‑halogen exchange (organolithium formation). n‑Butyllithium abstracts the bromide from 1‑bromohexane, generating hexyl lithium (a primary organolithium reagent) and 1‑bromobutane as the by‑product. Performed under inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at low temperature (−78 °C) in dry ethereal solvents such as tetrahydrofuran (THF) or diethyl ether. No additional catalyst is required.

redox (oxidation) reaction where chlorine oxidizes ferrocyanide to ferricyanide while being reduced to chloride; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often in the presence of excess potassium chloride to maintain ionic strength; no additional catalyst is required.

Halogenation (alcohol to alkyl chloride) using phosphorus pentachloride; converts a tertiary alcohol to the corresponding chloride via an SN1‑type substitution; typically performed neat or in a non‑coordinating solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene under reflux; phosphorus pentachloride acts as the chlorinating agent and generates phosphorus oxychloride and hydrogen chloride as gaseous by‑products; no additional catalyst is required.

acid‑base metathesis wherein acetic acid reacts with lithium sulfite to give lithium acetate and sulfurous acid (which exists in equilibrium with dissolved SO₂ and water); typically performed in aqueous solution at low to moderate temperature, with stirring; no catalyst is needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (aminolysis) of the cyclic anhydride diketene by ammonia; the reaction opens the four‑membered anhydride ring and installs an amide group, producing acetoacetamide. Typically carried out in a polar protic solvent (water or aqueous methanol) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base complexation to form a palladium(II) β‑diketonate. Triethylamine deprotonates two equivalents of 2,4‑pentanedione, generating the acetylacetonate anion which chelates Pd(II)Br₂, yielding bis(acetylacetonato) palladium(II) and triethylammonium bromide as a by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous ethanol or methanol under reflux, inert atmosphere, with triethylamine as the base; the product precipitates on cooling.

Transesterification; replaces the methyl group of methyl heptanoate with a tert‑butyl group to give tert‑butyl heptanoate, generating methanol. Typically catalyzed by a Brønsted acid (e.g., H2SO4, p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or a catalytic amount of base (NaOMe) under reflux in anhydrous solvent such as toluene or benzene; removal of methanol (e.g., azeotropic distillation) drives the equilibrium. Used to install a tert‑butyl ester protecting group.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Copper(II) sulfate exchanges anions with magnesium oxalate, producing insoluble copper oxalate (precipitate) and soluble magnesium sulfate. Performed in water at ambient temperature; stirring is sufficient, and the copper oxalide is collected by filtration. No catalyst required.

Double‑displacement precipitation forming iron(II) molybdate. Sodium molybdate reacts with iron(II) nitrate in aqueous solution; the iron(II) cation combines with molybdate anion to give sparingly soluble FeMoO₄ ((II) molybdate) while sodium nitrate remains in solution. Typically carried out in water at room temperature or slight warming; the solid is filtered off. No catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed trans‑etherification; methanol attacks the vinyl ether carbon of 2‑chloroethyl vinyl ether, swapping the alkoxy groups to afford 2‑chloroethanol and methyl vinyl ether. Typical conditions use a protic acid catalyst (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid, 5 mol %) in refluxing toluene or dichloromethane, often with removal of the volatile methyl vinyl ether to drive the equilibrium.

Hydrolysis (acid‑ or base‑catalyzed) of 4‑methylphenyl acetate to regenerate 4‑methylphenol and produce acetic acid. Conducted in aqueous HCl or NaOH at reflux; after acidic work‑up the phenol is isolated.

Electrophilic aromatic iodination (halogen exchange) of 5‑chloro‑8‑hydroxyquinoline in pyridine. Iodine acts as the electrophile, substituting at the 7‑position of the quinoline ring to give clioquinol (5‑chloro‑7‑iodo‑8‑hydroxyquinoline); pyridine scavenges the generated hydrogen iodide, forming pyridinium iodide. Conducted in pyridine solvent at 0 °C to reflux, often under nitrogen; the reaction without additional catalyst.

Condensation (heterocycle formation) of phenylglyoxal with ammonium acetate to produce 2‑phenyl‑1,3‑oxazole and water. The 1,2‑dicarbonyl reacts with ammonia (generated from NH₄OAc) in a cyclodehydration step, forming the five‑membered oxazole ring. Conducted by heating phenylglyoxal with excess ammonium acetate in ethanol or glacial acetic acid at 80–120 °C for several hours; no external catalyst is required.

Reaction type: redox reduction of a triarylmethane dye. Purpose: to convert the colored Malachite green into its colorless leuco form for analytical or decolorization purposes. Key transformation: electrophilic carbon of the dye is reduced by sulfite, breaking the conjugated quinonelike system and adding two electrons/hydrogens to give Leucomalachite green; sulfite is oxidized to sulfate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, mildly alkaline (often pH ≈ 8–10), ambient temperature; excess Na₂SO₃ is commonly used. Common solvent/catalyst: water; no additional catalyst required.

Reaction type: acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: to prepare the inorganic salt ammonium perrhenate, a precursor for rhenium chemistry. Key transformation: perrhenic acid (HReO₄) donates a proton to the hydroxide of ammonium hydroxide, forming water and the perrhenate anion, which pairs with NH₄⁺. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, room temperature, stoichiometric 1 : 1 molar ratio. Common solvent/catalyst: water; the reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Reaction type: radical‑mediated hydroperoxidation/oxidative transfer. Purpose: to generate cyclohexyl hydroperoxide and reduce cumene hydroperoxide to the corresponding alcohol, useful in peroxide synthesis and in chain‑transfer studies. Key transformation: thermal or metal‑catalyzed homolysis of cumene hydroperoxide yields cumyloxyl radicals; these abstract hydrogen from cyclohexene, forming cyclohexyl radicals that recombine with •OOH to give cyclohexyl hydroperoxide, while the cumyl radical abstracts hydrogen from another cumene hydroperoxide molecule, producing 2‑methyl‑1‑phenyl‑1‑propanol. Typical conditions: high temperature (≈120–150 °C) in bulk or in an inert organic solvent, with a small amount of radical initiator (e.g., AIBN) if not using the hydroperoxide itself to initiate. Common solvents: toluene, xylene, or bulk reaction; no metal catalyst is required, though trace iron can accelerate initiation.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of a tertiary amide. Purpose: cleave N,N‑dimethylbenzamide to the corresponding carboxylate and liberate dimethylamine. Key transformation: amide C–N bond hydrolyzed by NaOH to give sodium benzoate and dimethylamine (as its hydroxide salt). Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M), reflux 1–4 h (often in EtOH/H₂O mixture). After cooling, acidify if free benzoic acid is desired; otherwise isolate sodium benzoate directly.

Reaction type: oxidative homocoupling of terminal alkynes (Glaser coupling). Purpose: to form the symmetric diyne diphenylacetylene from phenylacetylene, a key step in polymer synthesis and construction of conjugated systems. Key transformation: two molecules of phenylacetylene are deprotonated, coordinated to Cu(I) to give copper acetylide intermediates; molecular oxygen re‑oxidizes Cu(I) to Cu(II), coupling the two acetylide units and releasing Cu(I) again, yielding diphenylacetylene. Typical conditions: ambient to mild heating (25–80 °C), aerobic atmosphere, often under nitrogen/oxygen balance. Common solvent/catalyst: pyridine, dimethylformamide (DMF) or dichloromethane; CuCl (or CuCl·2H₂O) is the catalyst, sometimes in the presence of a ligand such as TMEDA or 1,10‑phenanthroline.

α‑Alkylation (enolate alkylation) of acetophenone: sodium hydride deprotonates acetophenone to give the enolate, which undergoes SN2 methylation with methyl iodide to afford 2‑methylacetophenone (sodium iodide as by‑product). Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as THF at 0 °C to rt under nitrogen.

Oxidation‑reduction preparation of platinum dioxide (Adams’ catalyst). Aqueous hydrogen peroxide oxidizes chloroplatinic acid (H2PtCl6), reducing chloride to HCl and precipitating PtO2. Conducted in water at ambient to mild temperatures (0–25 °C) under acidic conditions; no additional solvent or catalyst required.

General type: salt metathesis (anion exchange) reaction. Purpose: replace the chloride counter‑ion of 1,3‑dimethylimidazolium with the non‑coordinating hexafluorophosphate anion to afford a more stable ionic liquid. Key transformation: double displacement producing 1,3‑dimethylimidazolium hexafluorophosphate and sodium chloride. Typical conditions: dissolve both salts in a polar aprotic solvent (acetonitrile, methanol or water) at ambient temperature, stir until complete, then isolate the product by filtration or precipitation. Common solvents/catalysts: acetonitrile or methanol; no catalyst required; often the mixture is filtered to remove NaCl precipitate.

Reaction type: intramolecular cyclization to form a 1,2‑benzisoselenazol‑3(2H)‑one (heterocycle formation). Purpose: synthesis of Ebselen, a selenium‑based antioxidant and pharmacophore. Key transformation: phenylselenyl bromide electrophilically attacks the ortho‑amino group of anthranilic acid, generating a seleno‑amide intermediate; triethylamine scavenges HBr, and subsequent intramolecular attack of the carbonyl oxygen on the selenium center closes the five‑membered ring, followed by oxidation to give Ebselen. Typical conditions: anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), stoichiometric TEA (1 equiv) to neutralize HBr. Common solvent/catalyst: dichloromethane; triethylamine acts as base, no metal catalyst is required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (hydrolysis of ethyl glycolate). Ethyl 2‑hydroxyacetate is refluxed with water and a catalytic amount of mineral acid (e.g., HCl) to cleave the ester bond, yielding glycolic acid and ethanol. Solvent is typically aqueous mixture; reaction proceeds at 80‑100 °C.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (chlorination of phenol). Purpose: convert a phenolic OH into an aryl chloride for further coupling or protection. Key transformation: the OH of pentafluorol is replaced by Cl, producing pentafluorophenyl chloride while generating HCl and SO2 as gaseous by‑products. Typical conditions: reflux or gentle heating in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform, often with a base (pyridine or DMF) to scavenge HCl. No metal catalyst required.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (alcohol to alkyl chloride). Purpose: synthesize a primary alkyl chloride useful as an electrophile. Key transformation: the primary alcohol group of 4‑bromobutanol is converted to a chloride, yielding 4‑bromo‑1‑chlorobutane with release of HCl and SO2. Typical conditions: addition of thionyl chloride neat or in a solvent like CH2Cl2, gentle reflux; excess pyridine or triethylamine may be used to neutralize HCl. No catalyst needed.

Type: Williamson ether synthesis / epoxy resin monomer formation. Purpose: prepare the diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA), the primary building block for epoxy thermosets. Key transformation: bisphenol A is deprotonated by NaOH to form phenoxide ions, which attack epichlorohydrin; subsequent ring‑closure yields two glycidyl (epoxy) groups attached to the bisphenol core, releasing NaCl and water. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at 60–80 °C, often in a solvent such as diphenyl ether or acetone; after reaction, the mixture is washed, and the epoxy product is isolated by vacuum distillation or precipitation. No metal catalyst required.

Type: double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose: exchange the chloride anion of cobalt(II) chloride for nitrate, producing a water‑soluble cobalt(II) nitrate salt. Key transformation: Na⁺ pairs with Cl⁻ to form NaCl, while Co²⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to form Co(NO₃)₂. Typical conditions: aqueous solutions of the two salts mixed at ambient temperature with stirring; the reaction proceeds to completion without heating. No catalyst needed.

Type: ester aminolysis (ammonolysis). Purpose: convert a methyl ester of oleic acid into the corresponding amide (oleamide), a surfactant or polymer precursor. Key transformation: ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon of methyl oleate, displacing methanol and forming the amide bond of oleamide. Typical conditions: excess gaseous or aqueous NH₃, elevated temperature (120–180 °C) in a sealed reactor or high‑pressure autoclave; sometimes a small amount of base (e.g., NaOH) is added to accelerate the reaction. No metal catalyst required.

Type: ligand exchange / alcoholysis of a metal alkoxide. Purpose: prepare titanium(IV) acetate, a precursor for sol‑gel processes or catalyst supports. Key transformation: the ethoxy groups of Ti(OEt)₄ are protonated by acetic acid and displaced as ethanol, while acetate ligands coordinate to titanium, giving Ti(OAc)₄. Typical conditions: reflux of Ti(OEt)₄ with excess glacial ac acid in a solvent‑free setup or in a non‑coordinating solvent (e.g., toluene); ethanol by‑product is removed by distillation. No external catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation); used to prepare the perbromate anion as a stable ammonium salt. The reaction converts perbromic acid (HBrO₄) and ammonia (NH₃) into ammonium perbromate (NH₄BrO₄) with loss of a proton. Typically carried out in cold aqueous solution (0–5 °C) to minimise decomposition of the perbromate; water is the solvent and no catalyst is required.

Catalytic dehydrogenation; employed to obtain the fully aromatic naphthalene from its partially saturated analogue tetralin (1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene). The process removes two equivalents of hydrogen to give naphthalene and molecular H₂. Conducted in the gas phase over a metal catalyst such as Pt, Pd, or Raney Ni at 300–400 °C under an inert carrier gas; the hydrogen produced is removed by a sweep gas or trapped. No additional solvents or reagents are needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (aminolysis) of phosphorus oxychloride; used to synthesize phosphoramide [(NH₂)₃PO] while generating ammonium chloride as a by‑product. Six equivalents of NH₃ replace three Cl atoms of POCl₃, forming the P‑N bonds of phosphoramide and three NH₄Cl molecules. The reaction is usually performed at 0–5 °C in anhydrous liquid ammonia or in a dry solvent such as ether, with excess ammonia to drive the reaction to completion; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑salt double‑displacement; silver chromate reacts with nitric acid, converting the Ag+ into soluble silver nitrate (AgNO3) while the chromate is protonated to chromic acid (H2CrO4). Usually carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature; water as solvent; no catalyst required.

Direct nitridation of gadolinium metal with nitrogen gas to afford gadolinium nitride; performed at elevated temperature (≈900–1200 °C) under a flow of N₂ (or NH₃ as nitrogen source), solid‑state, no solvent, inert atmosphere.

Single‑displacement/redox reaction of a metal with a non‑oxidizing acid; serves to dissolve nickel metal and produce nickel(II) iodide while liberating hydrogen gas. Nickel metal reacts with 2 equivalents of hydroiodic acid (HI) to give NiI₂ and H₂. The reaction is carried out in aqueous HI solution, typically under reflux to ensure complete dissolution; no catalyst is needed.

Oxidation of a sulfide to a sulfoxide using a peracid; employed to convert thianthrene (a diaryl sulfide) into its S‑oxide. m‑Chloroperbenzoic acid (mCPBA) transfers an oxygen atom to the sulfur, yielding thianthrene S‑oxide and reducing the peracid to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Standard conditions involve stirring the substrate in dichloromethane (or chloroform) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is required.

Reaction type: Nucleophilic substitution (SN2). Purpose: Synthesis of ethers. Key transformation: Methoxide ion displaces bromide from ethyl bromide. Conditions: Polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dimethylformamide, DMSO), typically at elevated temperatures.

Halogenation of phenolic OH groups via chlorination with thionyl chloride; used to replace the two hydroxyl groups of 2,5‑dichloro‑1,4‑dihydroxybenzene with chlorine atoms, producing 1,2,4,5‑tetrachlorobenzene. Each OH is converted to Cl with loss of HCl and SO₂ from SOCl₂. The reaction is typically performed under reflux in an inert solvent such as pyridine or dichloromethane; pyridine acts as a base to scavenge HCl. No external catalyst is needed.

Redox (oxidation‑reduction) reaction; sulfite ion is oxidized to sulfate while hydrogen peroxide is reduced to water. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often under neutral or mildly acidic conditions; no special catalyst required.

Reaction type: acylation (esterification) of an alcohol with an anhydride. Purpose: protect the hydroxyl group as an acetate or generate the bromoethyl acetate ester. Key transformation: the hydroxyl of 2‑bromoethanol attacks acetic anhydride, forming 2‑bromoethyl acetate and releasing one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: catalytic base such as pyridine or DMAP, reflux in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or chloroform) for 1–3 h. The reaction is often performed under nitrogen to avoid moisture; the by‑product acetic acid can be neutralized by the base.

Simple acid–base metathesis (salt hydrolysis) where sodium formate reacts with aqueous HCl to generate formic acid and sodium chloride; performed at room temperature in aqueous solution, no special catalyst needed.

Metal‑halogen exchange (transmetalation) between n‑butyl bromide and tert‑butyl lithium, giving n‑butyl lithium and tert‑butyl bromide. Performed in anhydrous ether solvents (THF or diethyl ether) under inert atmosphere, usually at –78 °C to –20 °C to control reactivity.

Nucleophilic addition (hydroamination/Michael addition) of ammonia to the electron‑deficient C=C bond of maleonitrile, yielding diaminomaleonitrile. Conducted in excess liquid or gaseous ammonia, often at elevated pressure or mild heating; transition‑metal catalysts (e.g., Pd, Rh) can be employed to facilitate the addition.

Ligand exchangeamine‑alkoxide substitution) to form tris(dimethylamido)aluminum(III). Aluminum isopropoxide reacts with dimethylamine, exchanging isopropoxide ligands for dimethylamido groups and releasing isopropanol. Typically performed under inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar) in anhydrous solvent such as toluene or THF, refluxing 60–80 °C until gas evolution ceases; yields Al(NMe2)3 as a moisture‑ensitive solid.

Esterification with diazomethane (Diazomethane methylation). Two equivalents of diazomethane react with the two carboxyl groups of pimelic acid to give dimethyl pimelate and nitrogen gas. Carried out in dry diethyl ether or anhydrous hexane at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is rapid and does not require a catalyst.

Electrophilic iodination of indole. Purpose: obtain 3‑iodoindole. Key transformation: I⁺ (generated from I₂ with an oxidant or from N‑iodosuccinimide) attacks C‑3, liberating HI. Typical conditions: I₂ (1.2 equiv) in glacial acetic acid or DMF at rt, or N‑iodosuccinimide (1.1 equiv) in DMF, often with a catalytic amount of acid; reaction time 30 min–2 h.

Acid‑base neutralization (double displacement). Carbonic acid reacts with two equivalents of lithium hydroxide in aqueous solution to form lithium carbonate and water. Performed at ambient temperature; no catalyst is needed.

NaBH₄ reduction of 2‑chlorobenzaldehyde to 2‑chlorobenzyl alcohol; a chemoselective mild hydride reduction of an aromatic aldehyde. The reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature in protic solvents such as methanol, ethanol, or a mixed MeOH/THF system, using 1.1–1.5 equiv of NaBH₀₄. The mixture is quenched with water or dilute acid after completion, and the alcohol is isolated by extraction.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt‑acid exchange). Sulfuric acid protonates the salicylate ligands of bismuth subsalicylate, liberating salicylic acid while forming insoluble bismuth sulfate. Usually carried out in aqueous solution, often with heating (reflux) to drive completion. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Acid‑metal reaction; europium metal dissolves in hydrochloric acid to afford europium(II) chloride and hydrogen gas. Provides a straightforward route to EuCl₂ in solution. Conducted at ambient temperature or mild heating (0–50 °C) in aqueous HCl (1–3 M); the reaction mixture is stirred under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation of Eu²⁺ to Eu³⁺. No special catalyst required.

Selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol with sodium borohydride; purpose is to convert 2‑iodoacetaldehyde into 2‑iodoethanol. Hydride transfer reduces the carbonyl to a hydroxyl group while preserving the iodine substituent. Reaction is carried out in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or a mixed THF/water system at 0 °C to room temperature; NaBH₄ is the reagent, no catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification). Lithium hydroxide attacks the carbonyl of butyl acetate, producing butanol and lithium acetate. Typically performed in a water/ethanol mixture under reflux; stoichiometric LiOH; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidation of a heteroaromatic nitrogen to N‑oxide. Hydrogen peroxide transfers an oxygen atom to 3,5‑dimethylpyridine, giving the N‑oxide and water. Conducted in a polar solvent such as acetonitrile or a water‑acetone mixture, often at 0‑25 °C; acidic or catalytic additives (e.g., acetic acid) may be used to accelerate the reaction.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkyne. Raney nickel mediates addition of two equivalents of H₂ across the C≡C bond of but‑3‑yn‑1‑amine, yielding saturated butan‑1‑amine. Reaction is run under H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in ethanol or methanol at ambient to moderate temperature (25–60 °C).

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification. Ethanol attacks propyl acetate, exchanging alkoxy groups to give ethyl acetate and 1‑propanol. Typically performed with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid) under reflux in excess ethanol; removal of the generated propanol drives the equilibrium.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a haloacid by a primary amine. Methylamine displaces bromide of 2‑bromoacetic acid, forming N‑methylglycine (sarcosine) and HBr. Usually carried out in an aqueous or ethanol solution at room temperature; the reaction may be buffered or performed with a base (e.g., Na₂CO₃) to neutralize the released HBr.

Reaction type: selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Purpose: obtain cinnamyl alcohol from cinnamaldehyde. Key transformation: carbonyl carbon of the aldehyde is reduced to a hydroxyl group. Typical conditions: sodium borohydride (1‑1.5 eq) is added to a solution of cinnamaldehyde in methanol, ethanol, or isopropanol at 0 °C to ambient temperature; stirring for 30‑60 min. Reaction is quenched with water and extracted with an organic solvent (e.g., ethyl acetate).

Esterification (acetylation) of trimethylolpropane with acetic anhydride to give the triacetate; purpose is to protect the three hydroxyl groups as acetate esters. Key transformation: three –OH groups converted to –OCOCH3 groups, producing three equivalents of acetic acid as by‑product. Typical conditions: trimethylolpropane is mixed with excess acetic anhydride, often in the presence of a catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP, at 0 °C to room temperature then gently heated (50–80 °C) until completion. The reaction can be run neat or in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) and the product is isolated by aqueous work‑up and distillation.

Oxidative conversion of 2‑(pyridin‑2‑yl)ethanol to pyridine‑2‑carboxylic acid (picolinic acid) using potassium permanganate; a strong oxidizing reaction that cleaves the primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid. Key transformation: CH₂CH₂OH side chain is oxidized to –COOH, with reduction of Mn(VII) to MnO₂ precipitate and formation of KOH in solution. Typical conditions: aqueous alkaline medium (K₂CO₃ or NaOH) with KMnO₄ added portionwise, heating under reflux (60–80 °C). The mixture is then acidified to precipitate MnO₂ and isolate the acid, which is extracted with a non‑polar solvent (e.g., ethyl acetate).

Radical bromination of pentane (1‑pentane) under UV light with bromine; a free‑radical halogenation that substitutes a hydrogen atom with bromine. Key transformation: formation of a carbon‑centered radical followed by capture of Br·, giving mainly 2‑bromopentane (secondary bromide) together with hydrogen bromide as a side product. Typical conditions: dilute Br₂ in an inert such carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, irradiation with UV light (hν) at ambient temperature; reaction is stopped once desired conversion is reached and the mixture is quenched with aqueous sodium sulfite.

Acid–base precipitation reaction between lead(II) oxide and hydroiodic acid; purpose is to generate lead(II) iodide as an insoluble salt. Key transformation: PbO + 2 HI → PbI₂ (yellow precipitate) + H₂O. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of HI (often 2 M) added to a suspension of PbO at room temperature with stirring; the mixture is allowed to stand so that PbI₂ precipitates, which is then filtered, washed with cold water, and dried. No catalyst required.

3-Ethylpent-1-ene reacts with hydrogen in a hydrogenation reaction. The purpose is to saturate the carbon-carbon double bond, forming 3-ethylpentane. Key transformation involves hydrogen addition across the double bond. Reaction conditions typically use a catalyst like palladium on carbon (Pd/C) or platinum under hydrogen pressure at room temperature.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination of quinoxaline to give 6‑chloroquinoxaline; introduces a chlorine substituent at the C‑6 position; usually carried out with Cl₂ gas in an inert halogenated solvent (e.g., CHCl₃ or CCl₄) in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃; temperature ranges from 0 °C to reflux; HCl is formed as by‑product.

O‑methylation (Williamson ether synthesis) of 5‑hydroxypsoralen with dimethyl sulfate in the presence of potassium carbonate to afford isopimpinellin (5‑methoxypsoralen). Key transformation: phenolic –OH is deprotonated by K₂CO₃ and then methylated by the sulfonate methyl donor, forming a methoxy group. Typical conditions: suspension of 5‑hydroxypsoralen and K₂CO₃ in dry acetone (or DMF) cooled to 0 °C, dimethyl sulfate added dropwise, then the mixture is stirred at reflux (≈60 °C) for several hours. The reaction is quenched with ice‑water, extracted with ethyl acetate, and the product purified by recrystallization or chromatography.

Esterification of propionic acid with diazomethane to produce methyl propionate. Same type as reaction 3 (carboxylic‑acid methyl ester formation). Conditions: propionic acid in dry ether or DCM, 0 °C addition of dilute diazomethane, stirring to rt; nitrogen evolution signals progress; no additional reagents required.

Selective reduction of a ketone to a secondary alcohol using sodium borohydride; NaBH₄ reduces 1‑phenylhexan‑1‑one to 1‑phenylhexan‑1‑ol; reaction proceeds in protic solvents such as methanol or ethanol, usually at 0 °C to room temperature.

Acid‑catalyzed transesterification between isobutanol (2‑methyl‑1‑propanol) and propyl acetate; purpose is to exchange the alkoxy groups, yielding propanol and isobutyl acetate. Key transformation: the ester –OCH₂CH₂CH₃ is replaced by –OCH₂CH(CH₃)₂, producing propyl alcohol as the leaving alcohol. Typical conditions: excess 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol, catalytic amount of strong acid (e.g., 1–2 % H₂SO₄), reflux in toluene or xylene with a Dean–Stark trap to remove formed water, for 3–6 h. After completion the mixture is cooled, neutralized with sodium bicarbonate, and the two phases are separated; the organic phase contains isobutyl acetate, and the aqueous phase contains propanol, both of which can be purified by distillation.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of one hydroxyl group of propylene glycol with chloride to afford 1‑chloro‑2‑propanol; typically carried out with excess aqueous or concentrated HCl, reflux at 80‑100 °C, often with ZnCl₂ (Lucas reagent) to accelerate the SN1/SN2 displacement; water is liberated as by‑product.

Enzymatic methyl‑transfer reaction; SAM (S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine) donates its methyl group to hydrogen selenide yielding methyl‑selenol (CH3SeH) and S‑adenosylhomocysteine; occurs in aqueous physiological buffer at neutral pH in the presence of a specific SAM‑dependent methyltransferase; no external solvents or catalysts beyond the enzyme.
Direct oxidation of samarium metal; samarium heated in dry O₂ (or air) at 500‑800 °C forming Sm₂O₃; combustion‑type oxidation used to produce samarium(III) oxide.

Acid‑catalyzed ether formation (Fischer ether synthesis); methanol and n‑propyl alcohol undergo dehydration to give methyl n‑prop ether and water; typically performed with conc. H2SO4 (10–20 % catalyst) at 140–180 °C, the alcohols act as both reactants and solvent; water is removed to drive equilibrium.

High‑temperature solid‑state reduction/halide exchange; lithium metal reduces UF4, abstracting a fluoride as LiF and converting uranium() fluoride to uranium(III) fluoride (UF3); carried out under inert atmosphere (Ar or N2) at 500–800 °C in a sealed tube or molten‑salt bath; no solvent, the reactants are solids.

Fischer esterification of β‑alanine (3‑aminopropanoic acid) with ethanol; the carboxyl group reacts with ethanol to form ethyl 3‑aminopropanoate (ethyl β‑alan) and water; reflux in excess ethanol with catalytic H2SO4 or p‑TsOH (1–5 mol %); water is removed (Dean–Stark trap) to shift equilibrium ethanol serves as solvent and reactant.

This metathesis reaction generates beryllium hydroxide precipitate and potassium chloride. Purpose is hydroxide formation; requires excess aqueous potassium hydroxide. Beryllium hydroxide may dissolve in excess strong base by amphoteric behavior.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) alkylation of morpholine by 2‑chloroethanesulfonic acid; the morpholine nitrogen attacks the chloro‑ethyl carbon, forming 4‑morpholineethanesulfonic acid (MES buffer) and releasing HCl; carried out in aqueous or mixed water/ethanol medium at 0–25 °C, often with a base (NaOH or Na2CO3) to neutralize the generated HCl; product isolated by crystallization or ion‑exchange.

Steam‑gasification (hydrolysis) of molybdenum carbide. Mo2C reacts with high‑temperature steam (600–900 °C) to oxidize the carbide, producing carbon monoxide, hydrogen, and molybdenum dioxide (MoO2). No solvent; reaction carried out in a flow reactor with controlled steam feed; serves as a route to synthesis‑gas generation and MoO2 preparation.

Transmetallation (organometallic methyl transfer); dimethylzinc donates methyl groups to silicon tetrachloride to form tetramethylsilane and zinc chloride; performed under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) using dry, aprotic solvents such as diethyl ether or THF; typically at 0 °C to room temperature to avoid decomposition; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of a ketone; water adds across the carbonyl of 2‑butanone to give 2‑butanol via protonated carbonyl intermediate; carried out with dilute mineral acid (e.g., 5 % H₂SO₄) at 70–80 °C; aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent; reaction driven by excess.

Chlorination (halogenolysis) of phosphorus pentasulfide; Cl₂ attacks P₄S₁₀, cleaving P–S bonds and generating thiophosphoryl chloride (PSCl₃) and disulfur dichloride (S₂Cl₂) in a 4 : 3 molar ratio; reaction is exothermic, performed in a cooled glass apparatus at 0–25 °C dry inert gas purge; no additional catalyst; by‑products are filtered or distilled.

Nucleophilic substitution of an alcohol with phosphorus pentabromide; 2‑propanol reacts PBr₅ to give 2‑bromopropane, hydrobromic acid, and phosphorus oxybromide (POBr₃); carried out anhydrously in a non‑protic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to reflux; excess PBr₅ or PBr₃ often used; reaction proceeds via formation of alkoxy‑phosphonium intermediate.

Enzymatic methyl transfer using S‑adenosyl‑L‑methionine (SAM); the sulfonium methyl group of SAM is transferred to the thiol of 6‑mercaptopurine, producing 6‑methylmercaptopurine and S‑adenosyl‑L‑homocysteine; catalyzed by a specific methyltransferase in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at physiological temperature (37 °C); requires Mg²⁺ or other cofactors depending on the enzyme; occurs in vivo or can be reconstituted in vitro with recombinant enzyme.

0.: carbamate formation (amine protection) using di‑tert‑butyl dicarbonate (Boc2O). Purpose: install a Boc protecting group on 3‑bromopropylamine. Key transformation: the amine attacks the carbonyl of Boc2O, releasing CO₂ and tert‑butanol and yielding N‑Boc‑3‑bromopropylamine. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, dichloromane or THF as solvent, triethylamine (or another tertiary amine) as base to scavenge the generated acid. No metal catalyst required.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene (diene). Purpose: to fully saturate the carbon–carbon double bonds, producing the corresponding alkane. Key transformation: addition of H₂ across each C=C bond of 1,9‑decadiene, yielding decane. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1‑5 atm, catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Raney Ni, solvent like ethanol, ethyl acetate or cyclohexane, temperature 25‑60 °C. Reaction is usually performed in a sealed autoclave or hydrogenation flask.

Type: nucleophilic substitution (2) hydrolysis of a primary alkyl halide. Purpose: convert 1‑iododecane to the corresponding primary alcohol. Key transformation: water attacks the carbon bearing iodine, displacing I⁻ and forming 1‑decanol and hydrogen iodide. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous alcohol or mixed solvent (e.g., ethanol/water), often with a base (NaHCO₃ or pyridine) to neutralize HI. No special catalyst needed.

Redox (oxidation) reaction: metallic zinc reduces hydrogen peroxide, being oxidized to zinc oxide while H₂O₂ is reduced to water. The reaction is performed in aqueous hydrogen peroxide solution (commonly 3 % H₂O₂) at ambient temperature, sometimes with gentle heating. No external catalyst is necessary; the reaction proceeds efficiently in neutral to mildly alkaline aqueous media, where ZnO precipitates as the product.

Type: ozonolysis of an alkene with reductive work‑up. Purpose: cleave the C=C bond of methylenecyclohexane to generate carbonyl fragments. Key transformation: ozone adds across the double bond forming a molozonide that fragments to give formaldehyde (from the exocyclic methylene) and cyclohexanone (from the ring carbon). Dimethyl sulfide serves as the reductive quench, converting ozonides to carbonyls. Typical conditions: ozone bubbled through a solution of the alkene in dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C, followed by addition of excess DMS, then work‑up at rt.

Type: acid‑base double displacement (metathesis). Purpose: generate copper(II) sulfate and recover acetic acid. Key transformation: the proton of sulfuric acid protonates the acetate ligands of cupric acetate, releasing two molecules of acetic acid and forming copper(II) sulfate. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at ambient temperature; no heating or catalyst required.

Metal‑acid reduction (Sn/HCl) of a nitro acid; converts 2‑nitropropionic acid to 2‑aminopropanoic acid. Key transformation: tin metal reduces the nitro group in aqueous hydrochloric acid, generating the amine, tin(IV) chloride and water. Typical conditions: excess tin powder (5–10 equiv) added to a solution of the nitro acid in concentrated HCl (6 M), heated to reflux (≈80 °C) for 1–3 h. After cooling, the mixture is basified, and the free amine is extracted or crystallized.

Type: Prilezhaev epoxidation (peracid epoxidation). Purpose: convert 1‑butene to the corresponding epoxide. Key transformation: peracetic acid transfers an oxygen atom to the C=C bond, producing 1,2‑epoxybutane and acetic acid as the by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert solvent such as dichloromethane or chloroform; reaction is often performed under nitrogen to avoid over‑oxidation. No metal catalyst is needed.

Metathesis reaction between cobalt(II) thiocyanate and sodium sulfite; the thiocyanate anion pairs with sodium while sulfite pairs with cobalt, giving sodium thiocyanate in solution and cobalt(II) sulfite, which may precipitate. Usually performed in aqueous medium with gentle heating and stirring; the solid cobalt sulfite can be isolated by filtration.

Type: nucleophilic ring‑opening of an epoxide by organolithium. Purpose: extend the carbon chain and form a primary alcohol after work‑up. Key transformation: methyllithium attacks the less hindered carbon of ethylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to give a lithium alkoxide intermediate, which upon aqueous protonation yields 1‑propanol. Typical conditions: dry THF, –78 °C to –20 °C under inert atmosphere, followed by careful quench with water or ammonium chloride. No additional catalyst required.

Oxidative deamination; converts a benzylic amine bearing a phenolic OH into the corresponding aldehyde while releasing ammonia and water. Typically performed with aqueous hydrogen peroxide under mildly acidic or neutral conditions, often at 25–60 °C; metal catalysts such as Fe II/Fe III or Cu II may be employed to accelerate oxidation.

S‑Methylation (alkylation) of a thiol; dimethyl sulfate transfers a methyl group to thiophenol to give phenyl methyl sulfide via an SN2 mechanism. The reaction is usually carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (acetone, DMF, or acetonitrile) with a base (e.g., NaOH, K₂CO₃) to deprotonate the thiol, at 0 °C to room temperature, under an inert atmosphere.

Hydrolysis of a primary alkyl chloride to regenerate the corresponding alcohol; nucleophilic substitution (S_N2) where Cl is displaced by water to give 2‑methylbutan‑1‑ol. Employed to convert halides back to alcohols or to obtain alcohols from inexpensive halides. Conditions: aqueous medium, heating (reflux) or room temperature, sometimes acid‑ or base‑catalyzed. Common solvent: water or a water/ethanol mixture.

Nitration (esterification) of cyclopropanol with nitric acid; purpose is to convert the alcohol into the corresponding alkyl nitrate (fuel additive). Key transformation: the hydroxyl hydrogen is replaced by a nitrooxy group (–O–NO2) producing cyclopropyl nitrate and water. Typical conditions: cold (0‑5 °C) dilute HNO₃, often with a catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄ as a dehydrating agent. Common solvent: carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, reaction performed under inert atmosphere.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; anisole (methoxybenzene) undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with allyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ to afford para‑allylanisole (estragole) and HCl. Conducted under dry conditions, typically in dichloromethane or carbon disulfide at 0 °C → reflux, with careful exclusion of moisture.

Salt hydrolysis reaction; purpose is to convert samarium(III) sulfide into the hydroxide while liberating hydrogen sulfide gas; key transformation: Sm2S3 + 6 H2O → 2 Sm(OH)3(s) + 3 H2S(g); carried out by adding water to the solid sulfide, often with gentle heating or reflux; aqueous medium; no catalyst required.

Thermal hydrolysis of 1,2‑dibromoethane to ethylene glycol. Under refluxing aqueous conditions (≥150 °C) water attacks the carbon atoms of 1,2‑dibromoethane, displacing bromide ions and forming ethylene glycol while liberating two equivalents of HBr. Acidic or neutral is common; the reaction may be assisted by a base to capture HBr. No organic solvent is essential, though a biphasic system (water/acetone) can improve mixing.

The reaction is a Knoevenagel condensation. Purpose: to form α,β-unsaturated carboxylic acids. Key transformation: 4-methylbenzaldehyde condenses with malonic acid at the activated methylene group under basic conditions. Conditions: piperidine acts as a base/catalyst, typically refluxed in a solvent like ethanol.

Single‑displacement redox (metal reduction of Cu²⁺). Iron metal reduces cupric acetate to metallic copper while being oxidized to iron(II) acetate. The reaction proceeds in refluxing glacial acetic acid or aqueous acetic acid solution, often under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of Fe; no additional catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis; sodium isopropoxide attacks isopropyl bromide in an SN2 step to give diisopropyl ether and sodium bromide. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to moderate temperature, under anhydrous conditions to avoid elimination side reactions.

Nitrite ester formation (alkyl nitrite synthesis); n‑butanol reacts with nitrous acid generated in situ from NaNO₂ and H₂SO₄ to produce n‑butyl nitrite, water, and sodium bisulfate. The mixture is kept cold (0–5 °C) in aqueous acidic medium, then the organic nitrite is extracted; the reaction proceeds via protonation of nitrite to HNO₂ followed by O‑alkylation of the alcohol.

Sulfide precipitation (double‑displacement) reaction; hydrogen sulfide gas reacts with aqueous arsenic trichloride to replace chloride ions with sulfide, producing insoluble arsenic sulfide (commonly As₂S₃) and releasing hydrochloric acid into solution. Performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature or mild heating; typically no catalyst is required.

Oxidative cyclization heterocycle formation; converts o‑phenylenediamine, elemental sulfur and iodine into the aromatic 1,2,3‑benzothiadiazole ring; iodine acts as oxidant and sulfur source; typically performed by refluxing the reagents in ethanol or glacial acetic acid (often 80–120 °C) under an inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

Condensation (oximation) of a ketone with hydroxylamine; acetone reacts with free hydroxylamine (generated from hydroxylamine hydrochloride and base) to give acetone oxime with loss of water; carried out in aqueous‑ethanol at 0–25 °C to 80 °C, using NaOH, pyridine or NaHCO₃ as base; solvent usually ethanol or methanol.

Acid‑base/precipitation reaction of calcium arsenite with CO₂ and water. Dissolved calcium arsenite reacts with dissolved CO₂ (forming carbonic acid) and water, protonating the arsenite to arsenous acid (H₃AsO₃) while calcium precipitates as calcium carbonate (CaCO₃). Conducted at ambient temperature and pressure in aqueous solution; stirring ensures complete conversion.

Solid‑state adduct formation (percarbonate synthesis); hydrogen peroxide is added to an aqueous solution of sodium carbonate at 0–5 °C, maintaining pH around 10, and the mixture is crystallized to afford sodium percarbonate (Na₂CO₃·1.5H₂O₂) with water as by‑product; reaction proceeds under stirring, often under a nitrogen blanket to prevent peroxide decomposition; solvent is water.

Thermal pyrolysis of a sulfonium salt; heating trimethylsulfonium bromide (150–200 °C) under reduced pressure or inert atmosphere induces cleavage to dimethyl sulfide and methyl bromide; performed as a neat solid‑phase reaction, sometimes in a sealed tube; no solvent or catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl bromide by formate; sodium formate provides the formate anion which attacks isoamyl bromide to give isoamyl formate and sodium bromide; typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetone at reflux temperature; a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) may be employed to enhance reaction rate.

Nucleophilic substitution of a sulfonyl chloride by a primary amine to give a sulfonamide; used for preparing sulfonamide derivatives or protecting amines. The amine attacks the electrophilic sulfur, displacing chloride which is captured as HCl. Typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, with a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) to neutralize HCl.

Acid–base/complexation reaction forming ammonium hexafluorogallate from gallium(III) oxide in hydrofluoric acid media. Gallium oxide is dissolved by HF, and ammonium fluoride supplies NH4⁺ to precipitate (NH₄)₂GaF₆. Conducted in aqueous HF/NH₄F mixtures at elevated temperature (often 80–120 °C) in a Teflon‑lined autoclave; no external catalyst is required.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) halide exchange producing iron(II) fluoride and sodium iodide. Iron(II) iodide reacts with sodium fluoride in aqueous solution, precipitating the less‑soluble FeF₂ while NaI remains in solution. Usually carried out at room temperature or with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Partial combustion (incomplete oxidation) of 2‑methylhexane with oxygen, yielding carbon monoxide and water. The hydrocarbon is oxidized under limited oxygen or low temperature conditions that prevent full conversion to CO₂, producing CO as the major carbon product. Typical of flame‑type reactors operating at high temperature; no catalyst other than the flame itself.

Carbothermal reduction and nitridation of vanadium(V) oxide in a nitrogen atmosphere to form vanadium nitride. Carbon reduces V₂O₅ to lower oxidation states while nitrogen inserts into the lattice, giving VN and CO as the gaseous by‑product. Conducted at very high temperatures (≈1500–1700 °C) in a furnace under flowing N₂; no additional catalyst is required.

Lipase‑catalyzed transesterification/acyl transfer: the primary allylic alcohol of linalool attacks vinyl acetate, forming linalyl acetate (an ester) and releasing acetaldehyde from the vinyl group. Performed under mild conditions (20–40 °C) using Candida antarctica lipase B, often solvent‑free or in a low‑polarity organic solvent (e.g., tert‑butyl methyl ether); the enzyme acts as the catalyst.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of a vinyl ether; water attacks the protonated vinyl ether, cleaving the C–O bond to afford acetaldehyde and n‑propyl alcohol. Typically carried out in aqueous mineral acid (e.g., 1 M H₂SO₄) at 0–50 °C, often in a water/organic mixture as solvent.

Fischer esterification; converts (E)-but-2-enoic acid (crotonic acid) to ethyl (E)-but-2-enoate; key transformation is condensation of the carboxylic acid with ethanol forming an ester and water; typically performed under reflux with catalytic amount of a strong acid such as sulfuric acid or p‑tosic acid; excess ethanol serves as solvent and drives equilibrium, water may be removed with a Dean‑St trap.

Fischer esterification between benzyl alcohol and mandelic acid forming benzyl mandelate with loss of water. Conducted under reflux with an acid catalyst such as p‑TsOH or H₂SO₄, commonly in toluene or benzene using a Dean‑Stark trap to remove water.

Nucleophilic ring‑opening alkylation of adenine with glycidol under basic conditions. NaOH deprotonates adenine, allowing attack on the less‑substituted carbon of the epoxide, yielding 9‑(2,3‑dihydroxypropyl)adenine. Performed in aqueous NaOH (0–25 °C) then neutralized; water or aqueous methanol serves as solvent.

Hydrolysis of 3‑aminopropionitrile to 3‑aminopropionic acid with release of ammonia. Either acidic (HCl, reflux) or basic (NaOH, reflux) conditions convert the nitrile first to the amide then to the acid, liberating NH₃. Reaction carried out in water, heated to reflux.

Metallothermic reduction; calcium reduces thulium trichloride to metallic thulium while forming calcium chloride; performed as a high‑temperature solid‑state reaction (≈800–1000 °C) under inert atmosphere, usually in a sealed crucible with no solvent or catalyst.

Direct solid‑state synthesis of germanium(II) telluride by heating elemental germanium and tellurium together. The powders are mixed and heated under an inert atmosphere (argon) at 400–600 °C to form GeTe. No solvent; sometimes a sealed tube is employed.

Aqueous metathesis/precipitation reaction forming nickel carbonate and ammonium acetate. Solutions of nickel(II) acetate and ammonium carbonate are mixed at room temperature; insoluble NiCO₃ precipitates while NH₄OAc remains in solution. No catalyst required; water is the solvent.

O‑methylation of a primary alcohol using diazomethane; nucleophilic substitution (alkylation) of the hydroxyl oxygen with the methylene group of diazomethane, liberating nitrogen gas. Purpose is to convert the alcohol to a methyl ether (protecting group or structural modification). Typically carried out in dry ether or dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; diazomethane is added dropwise, no additional catalyst required.

Double‑displacement acid‑base precipitation; sodium hydroxide reacts with terbium(III) bromide to form precipitated terbium(III) hydroxide and soluble sodium bromide; carried out in aqueous NaOH, usually with cooling to control precipitation.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (neutral water alone is very slow). Purpose: cleave the ester to recover the parent fatty acid and the corresponding alcohol. Key transformation: protonation of the carbonyl oxygen of butyl octanoate, water attack, collapse of tetrahedral intermediate, and release of butan‑1‑ol, yielding octanoic acid. Typical conditions: reflux in a mixture of water and a non‑co‑solvent (e.g., toluene or dioxane) with 1–2 equiv of a strong acid such as H₂SO₄ or HCl (0.5–1 M) at 100 °C for 2–6 h. The acid acts as catalyst; no additional solvent is required beyond the water/co‑solvent mixture.

Oxide‑base neutralization; zinc oxide is slaked with aqueous sodium hydroxide (typically heated to 60–80 °C) to generate sodium zincate and water. Conducted in water; heating accelerates dissolution, no catalyst required.

This is a free radical substitution reaction, used for halogenation of alkanes. Key transformation is the replacement of a hydrogen atom with a bromine atom. Typical conditions include UV light or heat to initiate the reaction. Common solvents are none required, as it often occurs in the gas phase or neat, but can use CCl4 if needed.

Reaction type: Grignard addition to a tertiary amide (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Purpose: formation of a tertiary amine (N,N‑dimethylisopropylamine). Key transformation: methylmagnesium bromide adds a methyl nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon of dimethylacetamide, generating a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses and, after acidic work‑up, yields the desired tertiary amine. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether solvent (THF or diethyl ether), 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by quenching with dilute acid; no additional catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of a primary alcohol with hydrobromic acid (SN1/SN2); 4‑bromobenzyl alcohol is protonated, water leaves, and bromide attacks to give 4‑bromobenzyl bromide. Performed in concentrated HBr (often 48 % aq.) or in HBr generated in situ (NaBr/H2SO4) at 50‑80 °C. No special solvent required; aqueous medium is common. Provides a straightforward route to the benzyl bromide.

Transfer hydrogenation of the stilbene double bond in Combretastatin A‑4 to afford Combretastatin B‑1. Formic acid acts as a hydrogen donor in the presence of palladium on carbon, reducing the C=C bond to a saturated C–C linkage. Gives the hydrogenated analogue useful for biological studies. Performed with Pd/C (5–10 % loading) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, formic acid (excess), at 25–80 °C, usually under nitrogen; the catalyst is recovered after reaction.

Reaction type: oxidative conversion of a phenolic monoterpene to a quinone. Purpose: synthesis of thymoquinone from thymol. Key transformation: sodium dichromate oxidizes the phenolic moiety ofol, removing two hydrogen atoms and forming the quinone carbonyl groups; sulfuric acid provides the acidic medium and proton balance. Typical conditions: aqueous sulfuric acid (≈ 1–2 M), sodium dichromate added at 50–80 °C, reaction time 1–3 h; water is the solvent; no extra catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; NaI exchanges anions with lead(II) acetate, producing insoluble lead(II) iodide (yellow precipitate) and soluble sodium acetate; usually performed in water at room temperature with stirring; the precipitated PbI2 is filtered off; no catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed epoxide ring‑opening of 1,2‑epoxycyclohexane with aqueous NaOH to give 1,2‑cyclohexanediol. Hydroxide attacks the less hindered carbon of the epoxide, opening the ring and forming a vicinal diol. Reaction occurs in water or water/ethanol mixture at ambient or mild heating (0–50 °C). No additional catalyst required; after completion, the diol is isolated by extraction and drying.

Acid‑base neutralization (double displacement). Oxalic acid donates a proton to bicarbonate, forming carbonic acid (which decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O) and the mono‑sodium salt, sodium hydrogen oxalate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

Reaction type: alkaline hydrolysis of an acetal. Purpose: obtain ethylene glycol and formaldehyde from 1,3-dioxolane. Key transformation: OH⁻ attacks the acetal, leading to ring opening and formation of the diol and aldehyde. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1 M), heating at 60‑80 °C. Solvent: water. No additional catalyst.

Grignard addition of phenylmagnesium bromide to acetaldehyde forming the secondary alcohol 1‑phenyl‑1‑propanol after acidic work‑up; carried out in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to room temperature.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) – O‑alkylation (Williamson ether synthesis). The phenolic OH of catechol is deprotonated (often with a mild base such as K₂CO₃) and attacks methyl iodide to give 2‑methoxyphenol, releasing HI. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents (acetone, DMF) at reflux; base scavenges the generated hydrogen iodide.

Metathesis (double‑replacement) ion exchange. Ammonium chloride exchanges its anion with rubidium nitrite, producing ammonium nitrite and rubidium chloride in aqueous solution. Performed at low temperature (0–5 °C) to limit decomposition of the unstable ammonium nitrite; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution – acylation of an amine. Acetyl chloride reacts with the primary amino group of 5‑amino‑1,3,4‑thiadiazole‑2‑sulfonamide to form the amide linkage of acetazolamide, liberating HCl. Typically run in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine at 0 °C to room temperature; pyridine or a similar base neutralizes the generated HCl.

Metal‑catalyzed epoxidation (oxidation). Hydrogen peroxide, in the presence of sodium tungstate as a catalyst, transfers an oxygen atom to the carbon‑carbon double bond of acrylamide, yielding the epoxide glycidamide and water. Conducted in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic buffer (pH 7–9) at 0–25 °C; tungstate facilitates formation of a peroxotungstate oxidant.

Alcohol chlorination (substitution) using thionyl chloride. The hydroxyl group of 2,2‑difluoroethanol is converted to a chloride, producing 2,2‑difluoroethyl chloride with concomitant generation of gaseous HCl and SO₂. Performed under anhydrous conditions, often in dry dichloromethane or pyridine, at reflux or room temperature; pyridine acts as acid scavenger.

Reaction type: halide metathesis (acid–base exchange). Purpose: preparation of chromium(II) fluoride. Key transformation: fluoride from hydrogen fluoride replaces chloride ligands on chromium(II) chloride, generating chromium(II) fluoride and releasing hydrochloric acid. Typical conditions: anhydrous HF gas or aqueous HF solution mixed with a suspension of CrCl₂ at low to moderate temperature (0–25 °C) under inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Redox (oxidation) reaction; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes ammonium thiosulfate to elemental sulfur and ammonium sulfate, with water as a by‑product. Conducted in aqueous solution, often at ambient temperature and slightly acidic pH; no additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of the alkene moiety in 1‑hexen‑3‑ol to give the saturated hexan‑3‑ol. Uses H₂ gas and Pd/C (5–10 % Pd on carbon) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, typically at 1–5 atm H₂ and 20–60 °C.

Oxidative dehydrogenation (redox) of (S)-reticuline using potassium ferricyanide as a mild one‑electron oxidant, producing (‑)-nuciferine and reducing ferricyanide to ferrocyanide. Reaction is carried out in aqueous buffer (pH 7–8) at room temperature; no metal catalyst is required.

Ullmann‑type copper‑catalyzed cyanation (nucleophilic substitution) of 3‑iodophenol to form 3‑cyanophenol. Involves KCN as cyanide source and CuCN as the catalyst, heated in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., DMF or DMSO) at 150–200 °C under inert atmosphere.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) reaction between a metal halide and a strong acid; magnesium chloride reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, usually under heating, to produce magnesium sulfate and gaseous hydrogen chloride; performed in a dry apparatus to collect HCl gas, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis precipitation reaction; used to generate insoluble zirconium silicate from aqueous solutions; silicic acid exchanges its silicate anion with the sulfate of zirconium(IV) sulfate, precipitating ZrSiO4 and liberating sulfuric acid into solution; typically carried out in water at ambient to modest temperature; no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration with nitronium tetrafluoroborate (NO₂⁺ BF₄⁻); delivers the same 2‑nitro product from 1,3,5‑trimethylbenzene. Conducted at –10 to 0 °C in dry dichloromethane or nitromethane; the strongly ion‑paired nitronium reagent eliminates the need for external Lewis acids.

Fischer esterification; tert‑butanol reacts with acetic acid in the presence of catalytic sulfuric acid to afford tert‑butyl acetate and water. Conducted under reflux (~100 °C), often with removal of water (e.g., azeotropic distillation) to drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Oxidation of a secondary alcohol; 2‑nonanol is oxidized to 2‑nonanone while potassium dichromate (Cr(VI)) is reduced to chromium(III) sulfate; performed in aqueous acidic medium using H2SO4 and K2Cr2O7 as oxidant; typically refluxed at 80‑100 °C; water serves as solvent; no additional catalyst required.

Metathesis/precipitation (double‑displacement); potassium phosphate and magnesium chloride exchange ions to form insoluble magnesium phosphate and soluble potassium chloride; carried out in aqueous solution with stoichiometric amounts of K3PO4 and MgCl2; mixture is stirred at ambient temperature; water is the solvent; the solid magnesium phosphate is isolated by filtration.

Aqueous disproportionation/neutralization; purpose: to convert nitrogen dioxide into a mixture of nitrite and nitrate ions while neutralizing the acidic NO₂; key transformation is redox disproportionation of NO₂ in the presence of OH⁻ yielding NaNO₂, NaNO₃, and water; performed in water at ambient temperature with excess NaOH; no catalyst is needed.

Reaction type: acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1/E2 elimination). Purpose: synthesis of 1‑pent from pentan‑1‑ol. Key transformation: phosphoric acid protonates the hydroxyl group, producing water as a leaving group; subsequent removal of a β‑hydrogen forms the C=C double bond, yielding 1‑pentene. Typical conditions: excess concentrated phosphoric acid, heating to 140–180 °C (often in a distillation apparatus), using the alcohol neat or in a high‑boiling solvent; no additional catalyst needed.

Chlorination (conversion to sulfonyl chloride); transforms benzenesulfinic acid into the reactive electrophile benzenesulfonyl chloride, releasing SO2 and HCl gases; thionyl chloride provides the chlorine and acts as a dehydrating agent; usually carried out under reflux in anhydrous inert solvent such as dichloromethane, chloroform or carbon tetrachloride; reaction proceeds at ambient to reflux temperature (20–80 °C); gases are removed by venting or trapped.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of nitrate ester; sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes propylene glycol dinitrate to give propylene glycol, sodium nitrate, and water. Conducted in aqueous NaOH solution, usually heated to reflux to ensure complete conversion.

Alkylation/esterification (Williamson ester synthesis); the carboxylate of (-)-jasmonic acid, generated by deprotonation with triethylamine, attacks methyl iodide to afford (-)-methyl jasmonate, while triethylammonium iodide is formed as by‑product; carried out in anhydrous aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF; reaction is performed at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst is required.

Reaction type: double‑displacement (metathesis) salt reaction. Purpose: generation of antimony(III) chloride from antimony sulfate. Key transformation: chloride ions from ammonium chloride replace sulfate ligands on antimony, forming SbCl₃ and ammonium sulfate as by‑product. Typical conditions: aqueous solution or solid‑state mixture heated gently (~80 °C) to promote ion exchange; stoichiometric amounts as written; no extra catalyst required.

Double‑displacement/metathesis; calcium hydroxide reacts with potassium metaphosphate to exchange cations, yielding calcium metaphosphate and potassium hydroxide; performed in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to improve solubility; water is the solvent; the calcium metaphosphate precipitates and can be filtered off.

Transesterification; catalytic exchange of alkoxy groups between ethanol and 2‑methylpropyl acetate to give 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol and ethyl acetate; purpose is to modify ester composition; typically performed with an acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOMe) catalyst at reflux in a non‑water‑solvent such as toluene or xylene, often removing the formed ethanol to drive equilibrium.
