Halogenation of a primary alcohol using phosphorus pentachloride; propargyl alcohol reacts with PCl₅, replacing the hydroxyl group with chloride to give 3‑chloroprop‑1‑yne (propargyl chloride) while generating phosphorus oxychloride (POCl₃) and hydrogen chloride as by‑products; the reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions, often in dichloromethane or chloroform, at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst is required, and the volatile by‑products are removed by gas evolution, with the chloride isolated after aqueous work‑up.

Halide exchange (salt metathesis) of a platinum(II) halide; platinum(II) chloride reacts with two equivalents of potassium iodide, exchanging chloride for iodide to afford platinum(II) iodide and potassium chloride; typically carried out in aqueous or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetonitrile) at ambient temperature with stirring; the insoluble PtI₂ precipitates and is collected by filtration; no catalyst is involved.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; exchanges acetate and chloride ions to form beryllium acetate while insoluble silver chloride precipitates; typically performed in aqueous or polar aprotic solvent (water, acetonitrile) at ambient temperature; product isolated by filtration; no catalyst required.

Swern oxidation; converts the secondary alcohol of ecgonine methyl ester to the corresponding ketone (ecgonone methyl ester) using DMSO activated by oxalyl chloride and triethylamine as base; carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere; produces dimethyl sulfide as by‑product; no metal catalyst.

Hydrogen reduction of a metal oxide; RhO₂ is reduced by hydrogen gas to metallic rhodium with formation of water; performed at elevated temperature (≈300–500 °C) under a flow of H₂, often in a tubular furnace; solid‑gas reaction, no solvent or catalyst needed.

Jones oxidation; primary allylic alcohol (10‑undecen‑1‑ol) is oxidized to the corresponding carboxylic acid (undecylenic acid) using chromium(VI) oxide in aqueous sulfuric acid (Jones reagent); reaction conducted in acetone/water at 0–25 °C; chromium(VI) acts as oxidant, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base/metal‑salt metathesis; lead chromate reacts with nitric acid to generate soluble lead(II) nitrate and chromic acid; carried out in aqueous solution, often with heating to aid dissolution; no catalyst required.

High‑temperature chlorination (redox) of indium(III) oxide; chlorine gas oxidizes In₂O₃ to give indium(III) chloride while releasing oxygen; typically performed in a sealed tube or furnace at temperatures above 400 °C; gas‑phase reaction, no solvent or catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution at silicon (desilylation). Tetrabutylammonium fluoride attacks the Si–OEt bond of ethoxy(dimethyl)silane, displacing the ethoxy group as ethanol and forming fluorodimethylsilane. Typically carried out at room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as THF; TBAF is used as both fluoride source and phase‑transfer catalyst.

Hydrolysis of N‑acetylpiperazine back to piperazine and acetic acid; an amide cleavage reaction. Water (often with added acid like HCl or base such as NaOH) attacks the carbonyl carbon, leading to cleavage of the C–N bond and formation of the free amine and carboxylic acid. Conducted at reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours in aqueous acid or base, followed by neutralization to isolate the products.

Chlorination/oxidation of a phosphite; chlorine oxidizes dimethyl phosphite from P(III) to P(V) and introduces a chlorine substituent, giving dimethyl chlorophosphate and hydrogen chloride; useful for preparing chlorophosphate reagents for further substitution reactions; carried out at low temperature (0 °C to 25 °C) in non‑protic solvents such as carbon tetrachloride, dichloromethane or chloroform; a base (e.g., pyridine) is added to trap the HCl formed.

Acyl substitution (ester formation from an acid chloride). Ethanol attacks the carbonyl carbon of 4‑methylbenzoyl chloride, giving ethyl 4‑methylbenzoate and releasing HCl. The reaction is usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HCl.

Acid‑base neutralization and hydrolysis of a pyrophosphate. Pyrophosphoric acid reacts with potassium hydroxide in water, producing phosphoric acid, dipotassium hydrogen phosphate, and water. The process is carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; stoichiometry can be adjusted to favor the desired phosphate salt.

Side‑chain oxidation (Jones oxidation). 1‑Ethyl‑4‑methylbenzene is oxidized by chromic acid (generated from CrO₃ and H₂SO₄) to convert the benzylic ethyl group into a carbonyl, yielding 4‑methylacetophenone and water. Reaction is performed in acetone (or dichromate in aqueous sulfuric acid) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under reflux for complete conversion.

Partial reduction of a nitro group to a hydroxylamine. Nitrobenzene is reduced in ethanol with zinc dust and ammonium chloride, delivering N‑phenylhydroxylamine as the main product. The mixture is refluxed under nitrogen; ammonium chloride provides a mildly acidic medium that moderates the reduction, preventing over‑reduction to aniline.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of 1,2‑dibromooctane to octane; a reductive dehalogenation using H2 gas and Pd/C catalyst; typical conditions 1–5 atm H2, Pd/C (10 % loading), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient to mild heating.

Nucleophilic substitution of organolithium reagents on phosphorus trichloride; purpose: prepare 1,2‑bis(dichlorophosphino)benzene as a bis‑phosphine ligand precursor; key transformation: two C–Li bonds attack PCl₃, forming two C–P bonds and releasing LiCl, leaving –PCl₂ groups ortho to each other on the benzene ring; typical conditions: –78 °C to –20 °C in dry THF under N₂ or Ar, slow addition of PCl₃, then warm to rt; no catalyst required.

Acid–carbonate reaction; zinc carbonate is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, yielding zinc chloride, carbon dioxide gas, and water. Conducted in dilute to concentrated HCl solution at room temperature or with mild heating; no catalyst needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation in aqueous solution. Trisodium phosphate reacts with nickel(II) chloride to exchange ions, forming insoluble nickel(II) phosphate precipitate and soluble sodium chloride. The reaction is carried out in water at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the solid product is filtered and washed.

Dehydration of an amide to a nitrile (Arbuzov-type amide‑to‑nitrile conversion). Thionyl chloride acts as a dehydrating agent, converting 2,6‑dichlorobenzamide into 2,6‑dichlorobenzonitrile (Dichlobenil) while releasing HCl and SO₂. Typically performed under reflux in anhydrous non‑protic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane, toluene) or neat SOCl₂, often with a base such as pyridine to trap HCl; reaction temperature 60–80 °C.

Reaction type: Thermal decarboxylation. Purpose: Remove the carboxyl group of picolinic acid to afford the parent heterocycle pyridine and release CO₂. Key transformation: C‑CO₂ bond cleavage, converting pyridine‑2‑carboxylic acid into pyridine. Typical conditions: Heating the neat acid or its salt at 200‑250 °C, often in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., diphenyl ether) or in the presence of a metal oxide catalyst such as CuO or Ag₂O to facilitate CO₂ evolution. No special solvents or catalysts are required if performed neat; otherwise, dry pyridine or quinoline can be used as solvent.

Solid‑state ceramic synthesis of the ferroelectric perovskite Pb(Zr,Ti)O₃ (lead zirconate titanate, PZT). Powders of NaCl (flux), PbO, TiO₂ and ZrO₂ are intimately mixed, then calcined and sintered at high temperature (≈800–1200 °C) in air or oxygen. The process yields a crystalline PZT solid solution; no liquid solvents are used, but occasional ball‑milling in dry media improves homogeneity.

Michaelis‑Arbuzov rearrangement (phosphonate synthesis). Ethyl chloroacetate reacts with triethyl phosphite under reflux (120–150 °C) to give triethyl phosphonoacetate and ethyl chloride as the by‑product. The reaction is usually conducted neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., xylene) under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is required.

Nucleophilic substitution of a benzylic chloride by a secondary amine. Benzhydryl chloride undergoes SN1/SN2 attack by pyrrolidine to afford 2‑(diphenylmethyl)pyrrolidine and HCl. The transformation is carried out in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature, often with an added base (triethylamine, NaHCO₃) to neutralize the generated HCl.

Acid‑catalyzed epoxide opening (cyanolysis) of ethylene oxide with hydrogen cyanide. HCN adds to the less hindered carbon of the oxirane, producing 2‑hydroxyacetonitrile (glycolonitrile). The reaction is performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution at 0 °C to 25 °C, sometimes in the presence of a weak base (e.g., NaHCO₃) to control acidity; no metal catalyst is required.

Acid‑base/redox reaction of sodium peroxide with hydrochloric acid; peroxide reacts with HCl to give sodium chloride and hydrogen peroxide; carried out in cold aqueous medium to prevent decomposition of H2O2; stoichiometric amounts of acid are added slowly with stirring; no catalyst; useful for in‑situ preparation of dilute hydrogen peroxide.

Formation of chloroformate from an alcohol using triphosgene (triphosgene‑mediated chlorocarbonylation). Each equivalent of 1‑chloroethanol reacts with one carbonyl chloride unit of triphosgene to give 1‑chloroethyl chloroformate while releasing HCl. The reaction is carried out in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to ambient temperature, with a stoichiometric base (pyridine or triethylamine) to capture the liberated HCl.

Hydrolysis of nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate; acid‑base reaction used to generate nitrous acid in situ; NO⁺BF₄⁻ reacts with H₂O to give HNO₂ and HBF₄; typically performed in aqueous solution at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no additional solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ether formation (Fischer ether synthesis) of phenetole; phenol is alkylated by ethanol in the presence of catalytic H₂SO₄, producing ethyl phenyl ether and water; carried out by refluxing excess ethanol with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (≈140–180 °C); ethanol serves as both reactant and solvent.

Acid–base neutralization forming a pyrrolidinium tetrafluoroborate salt. The lone‑pair on the secondary amine of pyrrolidine is protonated by HBF4, giving the pyrrolidinium cation paired with BF4–. Usually carried out at 0–25 °C in anhydrous ether, MeCN or dichloromethane; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethyl hydrogen sulfate with thiocyanate; KSCN provides SCN⁻ which attacks the ethyl group, displacing HSO₄⁻ to afford ethyl thiocyanate and KHSO₄; generally conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone or DMF at 40–80 °C; no additional catalyst required.

Oxidative conversion of xanthene to xanthone (chromium(VI) oxidation); potassium dichromate in concentrated H₂SO₄ oxidizes the benzylic carbon of xanthene, forming xanthone, water, and reducing Cr(VI) to Cr(III) which complexes as chromium(III) sulfate; reaction is performed under reflux in aqueous sulfuric acid; no extra catalyst beyond the dichromate oxidant.

Selective reduction of the aldehyde group in 5‑methylfurfural to the corresponding alcohol; NaBH₄ in methanol transfers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, yielding 5‑methylfurfuryl alcohol; reaction is carried out at 0 °C to room temperature with stoichiometric NaBH₄, methanol serving as solvent; quench with water after completion.

Thermal dehydrohalogenation (elimination) of a gem‑dichloride. Heating 1,1,2‑trichloroprop‑1‑ene promotes loss of HCl to give the conjugated alkene 1,2‑dichloroprop‑1‑ene. The transformation can be performed neat or in an inert solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride) at 100–150 °C; sometimes a weak base such as pyridine is added to scavenge the liberated HCl.

Thermal (or flash photolytic) decomposition of methyl azide; the azide eliminates N₂ and undergoes a rearrangement to give methyl isocyanide; performed by heating the neat azide (≈150–200 °C) or by rapid flash photolysis under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid–base neutralization where sulfuric acid protonates cesium chloride to release hydrogen chloride gas and form cesium bisulfate; typically carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to evolve HCl; no catalyst required.

Allylic double‑bond isomerization (Safrole → Isosafrole); converts the terminal propenyl side chain to the internal isopropenyl isomer. Often achieved with a base (NaOH or K₂CO₃) in ethanol or with a Lewis acid (AlCl₃) or a Pd‑catalyzed isomerization at 50–100 °C. The reaction shifts the C=C= double bond without changing the aromatic methylenedioxy group.

Acid‑catalyzed substitution of tertiary alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol with concentrated HBr (SN1 mechanism) to afford 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane and water; reflux in concentrated HBr or HBr/AcOH mixture at 60–80 °C; polar protic solvent.

Base‑promoted E2 dehydrohalogenation of 3‑chloro‑2‑butanone using potassium hydroxide to give methyl vinyl ketone, water and potassium chloride; performed in aqueous or alcoholic KOH, heated under reflux; no specific catalyst.

Acylation of N‑methylaniline with acetic anhydride forming N‑methyl‑N‑phenylacetamide and acetic acid; usually conducted at room temperature in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dichloromethane or pyridine, sometimes with a catalytic amount of DMAP; no metal catalyst.

Oxidation (combustion) reaction; converts cobalt(II) sulfide to cobalt(II) oxide and generates sulfur dioxide. Solid CoS is heated in a flow of oxygen or air at 400–600 °C. No solvent; solid‑state heating in a furnace provides the necessary activation energy.

Redox reaction; ferricyanide ion is reduced to ferrocyanide while thiosulfate is oxidized to tetrathionate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required. Used in analytical chemistry to assess oxidizing power or to generate ferrocyanide.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of 1‑bromononane with water to form 1‑nonanol and HBr; typically performed by refluxing the alkyl bromide in water (or aqueous acid) at elevated temperature, proceeding via an SN2 mechanism for the primary bromide.

Palladium‑catalyzed Buchwald‑Hartwig amination of 2‑bromopyridine with ammonia to afford 2‑aminopyridine; uses Pd(OAc)₂ (5–10 mol %), tri‑tert‑butylphosphine ligand, sodium tert‑butoxide base, in a polar aprotic solvent (toluene, dioxane or THF) under inert atmosphere at 80–120 °C.

Povarov (imino‑Diels‑Alder) multicomponent reaction of aniline, formaldehyde and ethylene catalyzed by boron trifluoride etherate to produce 1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroquinoline; typically run in dichloromethane or ether at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; BF₃·OEt₂ acts as Lewis acid catalyst.

Protonolysis of methyllithium by ethanol giving lithium ethoxide and methane; carried out under anhydrous conditions in ether (THF or Et₂O) at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C); no additional catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation; reduces the carbonyl group of oxcarbazepine to a secondary alcohol, yielding licarbazepine (the active metabolite). Performed with H₂ gas and Pd/C as catalyst in a protic solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at room temperature to 50 °C under 1–5 atm pressure.

Cannizzaro disproportionation of a non‑α‑hydrogen aldehyde; one molecule is oxidized to the corresponding carboxylic acid and another is reduced to the primary alcohol; carried out with concentrated sodium hydroxide in water or aqueous alcohol, typically 0–25 °C; provides both 2‑nitrobenzoic acid and 2‑nitrobenzyl alcohol in a single step.

Gas absorption/neutralization reaction. Aqueous potassium hydroxide absorbs carbon dioxide gas, converting it to potassium carbonate and water. CO2 is bubbled through a chilled or room‑temperature KOH solution with stirring; the reaction proceeds readily without. No catalyst; water is the solvent.

Partial neutralization (acid‑base) where one equivalent of NaOH neutralizes one proton of H₂SO₄, forming water and sodium hydrogen sulfate (NaHSO₄). Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of ethyl 3‑cyanopropanoate with methanol, exchanging the ethoxy group for a methoxy group to give methyl 3‑cyanopropanoate and ethanol. Typically refluxed in excess methanol with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOMe); removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium.

Acid–base salt formation; 1‑Phenylpropan‑2‑amine reacts with hydrochloric acid to give the ammonium chloride salt (1‑phenylpropan‑2‑amine·HCl); typically performed in anhydrous ether, dichloromethane, or directly in aqueous HCl at 0 °C to room temperature, with stirring to ensure complete protonation.

Methanolysis (transesterification) of diphenyl carbonate with methanol giving methyl phenyl carbonate and phenol; typically refluxed in methanol with a catalyst such as potassium carbonate or a weak acid (p‑TsOH); phenol is removed to drive the equilibrium; serves to prepare mixed carbonates stepwise.

Acylation (acetylation) of one amino group of 4,4′‑diaminodiphenyl sulfone using acetic anhydride, producing N‑acetyl‑4,4′‑diaminodiphenyl sulfone and acetic acid as by‑product. Usually carried out neat or in pyridine at 0 °C to reflux, allowing the acetic acid formed to be neutralized by the pyridine.

Reaction type: Hydrogenation. Purpose: Industrial production of cyclohexane. Key transformation: Benzene ring undergoes catalytic hydrogenation to form a saturated cyclohexane. Conditions: High pressure (H₂ gas), elevated temperature (~100-200°C). Catalyst: Palladium or nickel supported on carbon. Solvent: Liquid phase reaction or gas-phase.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) hydrolysis of a primary alkyl bromide; converts the bromomethyl group to a hydroxymethyl group; purpose is to obtain the corresponding alcohol; key transformation is Br → OH; typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv), heating ( reflux or 60–80 °C ) in water or water/ethanol mixture, neutral work‑up gives 2‑(hydroxymethyl)pyridine.

Crossed aldol addition (base‑catalyzed). Benzaldehyde (non‑enolizable) reacts with acetaldehyde enolate to afford the β‑hydroxyaldehyde 3‑hydroxy‑3‑phenylpropanal. Performed with aqueous NaOH (0.1‑0.5 M) at 0 °C to 25 °C for 1 h, then quenched with dilute acid. Common solvents are water/ethanol mixtures; the reaction proceeds via the acetaldehyde enolate attacking the benzaldehyde carbonyl.

Acid‑base/metathesis reaction where lithium fluoride reacts with hexafluorosilicic acid to generate hydrofluoric acid and lithium hexafluorosilicate (Li₂SiF₆). Performed in aqueous solution, often at low to ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Reaction type: halogen exchange/acid‑base fluorination. Purpose: preparation of molybdenum tetrafluoride from the oxide. Key transformation: MoO3 reacts with HF, oxygen is transferred to water and Mo is converted to MoF4. Typical conditions: anhydrous HF (liquid or gas) passed over MoO3 at 150‑250 °C, often under reflux in a PTFE‑lined apparatus; inert atmosphere may be used. No special catalyst; common solvent is molten HF or an HF–pyridine mixture.

Double‑displacement precipitation: aqueous bismuth nitrate reacts with ammonium carbonate to precipitate insoluble bismuth carbonate while forming soluble ammonium nitrate in solution. Conducted at room temperature in water; the bismuth carbonate is collected by filtration.

Type: Hydride reduction of an acid chloride to a primary alcohol. Purpose: Convert phenoxyacetyl chloride into phenoxyethanol by removing the carbonyl functionality. Key transformation: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, reducing the acyl chloride first to the aldehyde intermediate and then to the alcohol; chloride is displaced as LiCl and the aluminum by‑product is hydrolyzed to Al(OH)3 on work‑up. Typical conditions: Anhydrous ether or THF, 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; addition of LiAlH4 to a cooled solution of the acyl chloride, followed by careful quench with dilute acid or water. Common solvents/catalysts: Diethyl ether or THF; no catalyst required.

Type: Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (amide deacetylation). Purpose: Remove the N‑acetyl protecting group from N‑acetyl‑DL‑aspartic acid to regenerate the free amino acid. Key transformation: Water attacks the amide carbonyl, assisted by acid, yielding acetic acid and the free aspartic acid; the reaction proceeds through a tetrahedral intermediate that collapses with loss of acetate. Typical conditions: Aqueous HCl (pH ≈ 1) heated to reflux (≈ 100 °C) for several hours. Common solvents/catalysts: Pure water or dilute mineral acid; no additional catalyst needed.

Type: Double‑displacement (metathesis) halide exchange. Purpose: Exchange chloride for fluoride to prepare copper(II) fluoride from copper(II) chloride. Key transformation: CuCl₂ + 2 KF ⇌ CuF₂ + 2 KCl; fluoride ions replace chloride ions around Cu²⁺, precipitating the sparingly soluble CuF₂ while KCl remains in solution. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution at elevated temperature (≈ 80 °C) to drive precipitation of CuF₂; solid‑state grinding can also be used. Common solvents/catalysts: Water or mixed aqueous/ethanol; no catalyst required.

Alkaline hydrolysis (saponification) of the N‑acetyl amide back to the free amine. Refluxing the amide in aqueous NaOH1–2 M) for several hours cleaves the amide bond, yielding α‑methylbenzylamine and sodium acetate. The reaction may be carried out in a mixed water/ethanol solvent to improve solubility. After cooling, the amine is extracted or acidified to isolate the free base. This step is used for de‑protection of the amide.

Type: Redox oxidation of a phosphine by a nitroxyl radical. Purpose: Convert triphenylphosphine to its oxide while reducing TEMPO to the corresponding hydroxylamine (TEMPO‑H). Key transformation: PPh₃ + TEMPO → PPh₃=O + TEMPO‑H; the phosphorus atom is oxidized by accepting an oxygen atom from the nitroxyl group, which is reduced to the hydroxylamine. Typical conditions: Room temperature, inert atmosphere, in a non‑protic polar solvent such as dichloromethane or acetonitrile; reaction proceeds rapidly without additional reagents Common solvents/catalysts: CH₂Cl₂, MeCN; no catalyst required.

Type: Controlled hydrolysis of a trialkyl aluminum compound leading to aluminoxane formation. Purpose: Generate methylaluminoxane (MAO) and release methane gas, a key step in preparing cocatalysts for olefin polymerization. Key transformation: (CH₃)₃Al + H₂O → CH₄↑ + [(CH₃)AlO]ₙ (MAO) + minor Al(OH)₃. The water protonates an Al–C bond, liberating CH₄ and forming Al–O–Al linkages that oligomerize to aluminoxane. Typical conditions: Anhydrous, oxygen‑free solvent (toluene, hexane) at 0–25 °C; water added dropwise under vigorous stirring, temperature controlled to manage exotherm. Common solvents/catalysts: Inert hydrocarbon solvents; no external catalyst, but the reaction is often performed in a Schlenk line or glovebox.

Type: Acid–base neutralization with gas evolution (carbonate decomposition). Purpose: Convert calcium carbonate and arsenic acid into soluble calcium arsenate while releasing carbon dioxide. Key transformation: 2 H₃AsO₄ + 3 CaCO₃ → Ca₃(AsO₄)₂ + 3 CO₂↑ + 3 H₂O; protons from arsenic acid react with carbonate to form CO₂ and water, the remaining anions combine with Ca²⁺ to give calcium arsenate. Typical conditions: Aqueous solution, moderate heating (≈ 60–80 °C) to accelerate CO₂ evolution and ensure complete reaction. Common solvents/catalysts: Water; no catalyst required.

Redox (halogen exchange) reaction: Fluorine oxidizes hydrogen bromide, reducing to bromine while forming hydrogen fluoride. Key transformation: HBr → Br2 (oxidation) and F2 → HF (reduction). Typically carried out in the gas phase; reactions are conducted in a dry, inert atmosphere (e.g., glass tube) at room temperature or with slight cooling to control the highly exothermic process. No solvent; often performed in a flow of inert gas (N2) to avoid moisture.
Combustion/oxidation of arsine; 2 AsH3 + 3 O2 → As2O3 + 3 H2O; occurs upon ignition of arsine in air or pure O2, converting toxic gas to solid arsenic trioxide; flame conditions, no catalyst.

Reduction; LiAlH4 acts as a strong hydride donor to reduce both aldehyde groups of 2,5‑diformylfuran to primary alcohols, yielding 2,5‑bis(hydroxymethyl)furan. Typical conditions are anhydrous ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; excess LiAlH4 is used and the reaction is quenched with water or dilute acid after completion.

Combustion (oxidation); complete oxidation of 2‑methoxy‑2‑methylbutane in the presence of excess oxygen yields carbon dioxide and water. Requires high temperature (flame or furnace conditions), sufficient O2 supply, and often occurs in atmospheric air; no solvent or catalyst is needed.

Gas‑solid reduction by carbon monoxide; purpose: reduce Tb₄O₇ to Tb₂O₃ while oxidizing CO to CO₂; key transformation: CO + O (from Tb₄O₇) → CO₂, overall Tb₄O₇ + CO → 2 Tb₂O₃ + CO₂; typical conditions: CO gas flow at 800–1000 °C over solid Tb₄O₇, solid‑state, no solvent, inert atmosphere optional.

High‑temperature redox (carbothermic reduction and halogenation); elemental bromine oxidizes carbon to CO while carbon reduces vanadium(III) oxide, forming vanadium(III) bromide. Conducted in a sealed tube or furnace at 800–1000 °C in the absence of solvent; solid reactants are intimately mixed and heated under an inert atmosphere.

Acyl substitution (esterification) of an acyl fluoride with an alcohol; propanoyl fluoride reacts with methanol to give methyl propionate and HF as a by‑product. Usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, often in the presence of a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine) to capture HF.

Nucleophilic epoxide ring‑opening: ethanol attacks the less‑substituted carbon of propylene oxide, opening the three‑membered ring to give 2‑ethoxypropan‑1‑ol; typically performed in excess ethanol or a mixed ethanol/ether solvent, often catalyzed by a weak acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) or base (e.g., NaOH) at reflux temperatures.

Double‑displacement (acid–salt) metathesis; purpose is to exchange sulfate and nitrate ions to form cadmium sulfate and nitric acid; key transformation is H2SO4 + Cd(NO3)2 → CdSO4 + 2 HNO3; carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; water is the solvent; cadmium sulfate may precipitate depending on concentration; no catalyst needed.

Intramolecular cyclodehydration (condensation) to form an oxazoline; the β‑amino alcohol 2‑amino‑1‑phenylethanol reacts with acetic anhydride, acetylating both the amine and the alcohol and then cyclizing to 2‑phenyloxazoline, with acetic acid generated as a by‑product. Typical conditions: reflux in an aprotic solvent such as toluene or dichloromethane, often with pyridine or triethylamine as an acid scavenger, at 80–120 °C for 1–3 h.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; purpose: synthesis of cobalt(II) thiocyanate with removal of sulfate as insoluble barium sulfate; key transformation: CoSO4 + Ba(SCN)2 → Co(SCN)2 (in solution) + BaSO4 (ppt); typically performed in water by mixing the two aqueous solutions; BaSO4 precipitates and is filtered off; aqueous medium, no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation; naphthalene is hydrogenated on one aromatic ring to give tetralin (1,2,3,4‑tetrahydronaphthalene). Reaction uses H2 gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst (Pd/C, PtO2, Raney Ni), in a solvent like ethanol or ethyl acetate, at 50–100 °C under stirring until the desired conversion is achieved.

Cyclodehydration/heterocycle formation using carbonyldiimidazole (CDI). The carbonyl group of CDI activates the amine of 2‑aminothiophenol, allowing intramolecular attack by the thiol to close a five‑membered ring, giving 1,2‑benzisothiazol‑3(2H)‑one and releasing two molecules of imidazole. Purpose: preparation of the benzisothiazolinone scaffold (used as preservative). Typical conditions: stoichiometric CDI in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Enzymatic oxidative deamination (histamine oxidase/diamine oxidase pathway). Molecular oxygen serves as the terminal electron acceptor, oxidizing the primary amine of histamine to the corresponding aldehyde (imidazole‑4‑acetaldehyde) while reducing O₂ to H₂O₂ and releasing NH₃. Purpose: physiological catabolism of histamine. Conditions: aqueous buffer at physiological pH (≈7.4), 37 °C, in the presence of the appropriate flavin‑containing oxidase enzyme; copper or FAD cofactors are required for activity.

General type: nucleophilic alkylation (SN2) of a carboxylate (Williamson ester synthesis). Purpose: formation of methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen) from potassium salicylate. Key transformations: the salicylate anion attacks methyl iodide, displacing I⁻ and forming the methyl ester. Typical conditions: reflux in acetone or DMF, often with a phase‑transfer catalyst (e.g., tetrabutylammonium bromide) at 50‑80 °C. Common solvent/catalyst: acetone or DMF; phase‑transfer catalyst optional.

Oxidation of an α‑hydroxy acid to an α‑keto acid. Lactic acid is converted to pyruvic acid by removal of two electrons and two protons from the hydroxyl‑bearing carbon. The reaction can be carried out enzymatically with NAD⁺ (catalyzed by lactate dehydrogenase) or chemically with oxidants such as CrO₃, KMnO₄, or Dess‑Martin periodinane. Typical conditions: enzymatic route – aqueous buffer, pH 7–8, 25–37 °C, catalytic NAD⁺/NADH recycle; chemical route – anhydrous solvent (e.g., acetone or dichloromethane), low temperature (0 – 25 °C) for selective oxidation, stoichiometric oxidant, inert atmosphere.

Oxidation (combustion) of MgB₂; purpose: thermal decomposition or removal of MgB₂ by converting it to stable oxides; key transformation: MgB₂ reacts with O₂ to yield magnesium oxide (MgO) and boron trioxide (B₂O₃); typical conditions: heating in air or flowing oxygen at temperatures above 500 °C; no solvent; reaction is usually performed in a furnace under ambient pressure.

N‑benzylation of morpholine with benzyl bromide (SN2 alkylation); purpose is to attach a benzyl group to nitrogen; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of morpholine on the benzylic carbon, displacing bromide and forming N‑benzyl‑morpholine and HBr; commonly performed in dry DMF or acetonitrile at room temperature to reflux, with a mild base such as K₂CO₃, NaH, or triethylamine to scavenge the generated HBr; benzyl bromide’s good leaving ability makes the reaction efficient.

Halide metathesis (chloride‑fluoride exchange). Solid NaF reacts with NbCl₅ to replace chloride ligands with fluoride, producing NbF₅ and NaCl. The reaction is driven by the formation of the more volatile NbF₅ and the lattice energy of NaCl. Typically performed under dry, inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) at elevated temperature (≈200–300 °C) in a sealed tube or melt; no solvent is usually employed, though a high‑boiling inert solvent such as sulfolane can be used to improve mixing.

Double‑displacement (acid‑salt) reaction. Gaseous HCl reacts with strontium nitrate to exchange anions, yielding strontium dichloride and nitric acid. In practice the reaction is carried out in aqueous solution: Sr(NO₃)₂ is dissolved, HCl gas is bubbled in, and the resulting SrCl₂ remains soluble while HNO₃ stays in the aqueous phase (or can be distilled). Conditions: aqueous medium, ambient temperature, excess HCl to drive the equilibrium; no catalyst required.

Cyanohydrin formation (nucleophilic addition of HCN to an aldehyde). Propanal adds HCN across the carbonyl, giving 2‑hydroxypropanenitrile (the corresponding cyanohydrin). The reaction is usually conducted in a polar aprotic or alcoholic solvent (e.g., methanol, ethanol, or THF) at low temperature (0 – 5 °C) to suppress side reactions, with catalytic amounts of base (NaCN or KCN) to generate the cyanide nucleophile. The mixture is quenched with acid after completion to neutralize excess cyanide.

Acid‑base salt formation; converts gaseous hydrogen cyanide and solid calcium oxide into calcium cyanide with release of water; typically performed at elevated temperature (150‑200 °C) under dry conditions, often in a sealed tube or furnace; no solvent required, solid‑gas reaction.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration (mixed‑acid nitration) of anisole to give 2,4‑dinitroanisoleDNAN); purpose is synthesis of an energetic material; key transformation is substitution of two hydrogen atoms on the aromatic ring by nitro groups at the ortho and para positions relative to the methoxy group; carried out with fuming HNO₃ and conc. H₂SO₄ at 0‑5 °C then warmed to ~30 °C; anisole acts as both substrate and solvent; reaction mixture is usually stirred under an ice bath and then quenched into ice water.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution of a primary benzylic mesylate by cyanide ion to afford benzyl cyanide; purpose is preparation of a nitrile; key step is displacement of the methanesulfonate leaving group by CN⁻; performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetonitrile at 0‑50 °C; excess KCN or phase‑transfer catalyst may be used; potassium methanesulfonate is formed as the by‑product.

Halogen exchange/acyl‑chloride generation using phosphorus pentachloride and a potassium carboxylate; converts potassium trifluoroacetate into trifluoroacetyl chloride while producing POCl₃ and KCl; purpose is preparation of a reactive acyl chloride; typically carried out in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C to reflux; POCl₃ evolves as a gas and is removed; the reaction is moisture‑sensitive.

SN2 alkylation of ammonia with a primary alkyl chloride to give a primary amine; transformation replaces the chloride by an amino group, releasing HCl; performed in excess gaseous or liquid NH₃ dissolved in a polar protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, often under reflux (80‑100 °C); the HCl formed is either scavenged by a base or removed as gas; the reaction yields hexylamine.

Ether formation (Williamson-type) of ethanol with methyl fluorosulfate; O‑alkylation gives ethyl methyl ether (methoxyethane) and fluorosulfonic acid; carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to rt; a tertiary amine base (pyridine, triethylamine) is typically employed to trap the acid and drive the reaction.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification of ethyl levulinate with sodium methoxide to give methyl levulinate; key transformation is exchange of the ethoxy group for a methoxy group; typically run in methanol (or neat) with catalytic NaOMe at reflux (65‑70 °C) under inert atmosphere; sodium ethoxide is generated in situ as the by‑product; the reaction proceeds to equilibrium, often driven to completion by removal of ethanol.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; reduction of the C=C bond to give a saturated hydrocarbon. Key transformation: (E)-3‑methylhept‑3‑ene → 3‑methylheptane. Typical conditions: H₂ gas (1–5 atm) with a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO₂, or Ni in a solvent like ethanol or THF, temperature 25–100 °C.

Acid‑base reaction of lithium carbonate with hydrofluoric acid; carbonate is protonated, releasing CO₂ gas and forming lithium fluoride and water; performed in aqueous HF solution, typically at room temperature or mild heating; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement/precipitation (metathesis) in aqueous solution; carbonate ion reacts with calcium sulfide to precipitate calcium carbonate while forming soluble ammonium sulfide. Conditions: aqueous medium at room temperature with stirring; the CaCO₃ solid is filtered off. No catalyst required.

Base‑induced conversion of dichromate to chromate (acid‑base equilibrium); dichromate ion reacts with excess cesium hydroxide to give potassium chromate, cesium chromate and water. Conditions: aqueous solution with excess CsOH, ambient to moderate temperature (≤60 °C). No catalyst needed.

This is a Grignard addition reaction, used to synthesize alcohols from carbonyl compounds. The key transformation involves the nucleophilic addition of the methyl group from methylmagnesium bromide to the ketone carbonyl of ethyl levulinate, forming a magnesium alkoxide intermediate that hydrolyzes to ethyl 4-hydroxy-3-methylpentanoate. Typical conditions include anhydrous ether solvents like diethyl ether, low temperatures around 0°C, and an aqueous acid workup for protonation.

DCC‑mediated esterification (Steglich condensation) to synthesize piperocaine. Carboxylic acid (p‑aminobenzoic acid) reacts with 2‑(piperidin‑1‑yl)ethanol in the presence of dicyclohexylcarbodiimide, producing piperocaine and dicyclohexylurea as a precipitated by‑product. Typical conditions: dry dichloromethane or THF, 0 °C then rt, inert atmosphere (N₂), often with catalytic DMAP; by‑product filtered off.

Esterification of 2‑phenylpropan‑1‑ol with benzoyl chloride (acyl‑chloride acylation). The alcohol attacks the acid chloride to give 2‑phenylpropyl benzoate, HCl is scavenged by a base (e.g., pyridine or triethylamine). Conducted in CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C→rt under inert atmosphere.

SN2 cyanation of 2‑(bromomethyl)pyridine with sodium cyanide to give 2‑(cyanomethyl)pyridine and NaBr. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO, typically at 50–80 °C, using NaCN (1.5–2 eq). No metal catalyst is required; reaction is quenched with aqueous work‑up to remove inorganic salts.

Acid‑base neutralization (saponification) of a carboxylic acid; 3‑methylpentanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to give sodium 3‑methylpentanoate and water. Conditions: aqueous NaOH solution, room temperature or gentle heating, stirring until completion. No catalyst required.

Nucleophilic halogenation of an organolithium; prepares chlorobenzene from phenyl lithium; phenyl lithium attacks chlorine gas forming chlorobenzene and lithium chloride; performed in dry ether or THF at low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C) under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst needed.

Direct fluorination (halogenation/oxidation) to form tellurium(VI) fluoride; used to obtain volatile TeF6. Anhydrous TeO2 is exposed to F2 gas, often at 0 °C to –78 °C, sometimes in a dry inert fluorinating medium (e.g., CCl4 or BrF5). The reaction produces TeF6 and O2. No catalyst, but strict moisture‑free conditions are essential.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of the primary amine in tryptamine with allyl bromide to give N,N‑diallyltryptamine; typically performed with a mild base (e.g., K2CO3 or NaH) in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 0 °C to room temperature; purpose is to install two allyl groups for protection or further functionalization.

Nucleophilic addition of phenyl lithium to the carbonyl of acetone, followed by aqueous work‑up to afford 2‑phenyl‑2‑propanol (a tertiary alcohol). This is a classic organolithium addition (Grignard‑type) reaction. Conducted at low temperature (‑78 °C) in dry THF under nitrogen; after addition, the reaction mixture is quenched with dilute acid or NH₄Cl to protonate the alkoxide.

Acid‑base neutralization of n‑butylammonium acetate with sodium hydroxide, yielding free n‑butylamine, sodium acetate and water. Typically carried out in an aqueous solution at ambient temperature; the reaction proceeds spontaneously as the strong base deprotonates the ammonium ion.

Protonation of hydrazine by hydrobromic acid to form hydrazine hydrobromide (hydrazinium bromide). This is a straightforward acid‑ salt formation, performed in aqueous HBr (often cold to limit side reactions) at 0 °C to room temperature; the solid saltitates on cooling.

Acid‑base exchange; dipotassium molybdate reacts with phosphoric acid to give molybdic acid and dipotassium phosphate; carried out in water by mixing the two aqueous solutions, usually at room temperature or gentle heating; no catalyst needed, water is the reaction medium.

Reductive hydride reaction; sodium borohydride reduces methylseleninic acid (RSeO₂H) to methylselenol (RSeH), generating sodium borate and water as by‑products; usually run in an aprotic solvent such as THF or ethanol under inert atmosphere, often at 0 °C to rt, no additional catalyst.

The synthesis of ruthenium(III) fluoride via direct combination of metallic ruthenium and fluorine gas. This is a combustion/oxidative reaction where fluorine acts as a strong oxidizing agent, converting Ru(0) to Ru(+3). High temperatures (typically >300°C) are required to overcome activation energy. The reaction occurs in a non-aqueous environment to prevent hydrolysis of RuF3.

Halide metathesis (double‑displacement) between bismuth(III) chloride and sodium bromide to give bismuth(III) bromide and sodium chloride. Usually performed by mixing the solid reagents in a polar solvent such as water or ethanol, with gentle heating to promote ion exchange; the product bismuth bromide precipitates and can be isolated by filtration.

Palladium‑catalyzed decarboxylative arylation of 1‑naphthoic acid with iodobenzene to produce 1‑phenyl‑naphthalene, releasing CO₂ and forming potassium iodide as a by‑product. The reaction uses a base (K₂CO₃) and a Pd(II) source (e.g., Pd(OAc)₂) with a phosphine ligand, carried out in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 150–200 °C under inert atmosphere. This transformation couples an aromatic carboxylic acid to an aryl halide via decarboxylation.

Selective reduction of glutaraldehyde to 1,5‑pentanediol using sodium borohydride; each aldehyde carbonyl is reduced to a primary alcohol. Conducted in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature, with NaBH4 added portionwise; reaction quenched with water or dilute acid, then purified to afford the diol.

Williamson ether synthesis; phenol is deprotonated by sodium hydride to give phenoxide, which undergoes an SN2 attack on allyl chloride forming allyl phenyl ether; generates hydrogen gas and sodium chloride as by‑products; typically carried out in dry aprotic solvents such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to rt under inert atmosphere.

Strong hydride reduction (dehalogenation); lithium aluminium hydride supplies hydride that replaces the chlorine atom of 4‑chloroheptane, yielding heptane and aluminium chloride species; performed in dry ether solvents (diethyl ether or THF) at low temperature followed by reflux; moisture‑free conditions required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) in aqueous solution exchanging calcium and lithium ions; calcium carbonate reacts with lithium sulfate to precipitate calcium sulfate while lithium carbonate remains dissolved; carried out by stirring aqueous suspensions of the salts at ambient temperature.

Metallothermic reduction (high‑temperature redox); metallic sodium reduces vanadium(V) oxide to vanadium(II) oxide while being oxidized to sodium oxide; performed at elevated temperatures (often >300 °C) in sealed tubes or molten sodium media under inert atmosphere; no solvent is used.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogenation) of a primary alkyl iodide; 2‑iodo‑1,3‑propanediol is reduced on palladium on carbon under H₂ pressure to give glycerol (1,2,3‑propanetriol) and hydrogen iodide; typical conditions are 1–5 atm H₂, Pd/C catalyst, solvent such as ethanol or water, temperature 25–50 °C.

Base‑promoted E2 dehydrohalogenation; potassium hydroxide abstracts a β‑hydrogen from 3‑iodoheptane, eliminating hydrogen iodide and forming the internal alkene 2‑heptene; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic KOH, often heated to reflux; KI and water are generated as by‑products.

Oxidative side‑chain oxidation (benzylic oxidation). KMnO₄ in hot aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes the methyl group of 1‑methylnaphthalene to a carboxyl group, yielding 1‑naphthoic acid while MnO₄⁻ is reduced to MnO₂ precipitate and KOH is formed. Typical conditions: dilute KMnO₄ solution, reflux, aqueous medium; work‑up with acid to isolate product.

Thermal decomposition (calcination) of lithium carbonate; employed to generate lithium oxide and release CO2 for ceramic or battery material preparation. Requires strong heating (≈800‑900 °C) of solid Li2CO3 in a furnace, often under air or inert atmosphere. No solvent or catalyst is used.

Ester aminolysis (nucleophilic acyl substitution). Ammonia attacks methyl acetate, displacing methanol and forming acetamide. Usually carried out by refluxing excess NH₃ (gaseous or aqueous) with the ester, often in a sealed tube or in methanol/water solvent. No additional catalyst required; excess ammonia drives the reaction.

Free‑radical halogenation of a Si–H bond. Chlorine adds across the Si–H bond of trimethylsilane to give chlorotrimethylsilane. Reaction is initiated by UV light or heat in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane, typically at 0–25 °C to control radical formation. No catalyst is required beyond the light source.

Acid–base neutralization (gas‑evolving). Trifluoroacetic acid reacts with sodium bicarbonate in aqueous solution ambient temperature, producing sodium trifluoroacetate, water and carbon dioxide gas. The reaction proceeds readily without catalyst; stirring in water ensures complete gas evolution.

Halogen exchange (nucleophilic substitution) to generate trimethylsilyl fluoride; fluoride ion attacks trimethylsilyl chloride, displacing chloride and forming Me3SiF and NaCl; performed in dry polar aprotic solvents such as acetonitrile, THF, or dichloromethane, often with crown ether or phase-transfer catalyst to solubilize NaF; inert atmosphere and mild heating may be used.

Condensation of propylamine with urea to afford N‑propylurea and water; nucleophilic attack of the amine on the carbonyl of urea followed by elimination of water; usually performed under reflux in a polar solvent such as ethanol or in the melt, often with continuous removal of water (Dean‑Stark) to drive the equilibrium forward.

Fischer esterification (acid‑catalyzed ester formation). Phenol acts as the alcohol component and reacts with acetic acid under catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or HCl) at reflux, forming phenyl acetate and water. Removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark trap) drives the equilibrium toward ester formation; solvent is usually excess acetic acid or toluene.

Metathesis (acid displacement) in aqueous medium. Sulfuric acid protonates the chromate anion of cobalt(II) chromate, converting it to chromic acid (H₂CrO₄) while cobalt(II) sulfate remains dissolved. Reaction is performed in water at room temperature or mild heating; no additional reagents are required.

Acid–base neutralisation; converts the carboxylic acid meclofenamic acid into its sodium salt (meclofenamate sodium). Key transformation is deprotonation of the acid and formation of water. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often by simply stirring the acid with an aqueous solution of NaOH; no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (acidic saponification). Purpose: convert the ethyl ester into the free hydroxycarboxylic acid. Key transformation: protonation of the carbonyl oxygen followed by nucleophilic attack of water, leading to cleavage of the C–OEt bond and formation of 2‑hydroxybutanoic acid plus ethanol. Typical conditions: aqueous HCl (≈ 2–6 M) with the ester heated under reflux (80–100 °C) for several hours. Solvent system: mixture of water and the ester; no external catalyst other than the acid.

High‑temperature solid‑gas reduction; hydrogen gas reduces niobium(V) oxide (Nb2O5) to niobium(II) oxide (NbO). The key transformation is the gain of electrons by Nb5+ and formation of water as the only by‑product. Conducted in a flow of H2 at 900–1200 °C in a tubular furnace; inert support (e.g., quartz) may be used, no catalyst other than the metal oxide itself.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of 2‑bromoethyl acetate; aqueous sulfuric acid protonates the ester carbonyl, water attacks, yielding acetic acid and 2‑bromoethanol; typical conditions: excess water, 1–2 M H2SO4, reflux for 1–3 h; solvent can be water or a water‑organic biphasic mixture.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamoylation); dimethylamine attacks phosgene to form N,N‑dimethylcarbamoyl chloride with concomitant release of HCl; carried out at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to trap the generated HCl and prevent polymerization.

Direct fluorination. Selenium reacts with fluorine gas to produce selenium tetrafluoride. Conducted similarly to the sulfur case: F₂ passed over solid Se at 150–300 °C in a fluoropolymer or nickel vessel, often with a slight excess of fluorine to drive the reaction to completion. The volatile SeF₄ is condensed in a cooled trap; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Reductive conversion of TEMPO to the hydroxylamine by ascorbic acid; ascorbic acid acts as a mild aqueous reducing agent, being oxidized to dehydroascorbic acid while TEMPO is reduced. Performed in water or aqueous buffer at pH ≈ 7, ambient temperature; commonly used in catalytic cycles to regenerate TEMPO in situ.

N‑alkylation (Williamson‑type SN2) of N‑methylpiperazine with benzyl bromide using sodium hydride as base. NaH deprotonates the secondary amine, generating a nucleophilic anion that displaces bromide to give 1‑benzyl‑4‑methyl‑piperazine, with evolution of H2 gas and formation of NaBr. Conducted in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or THF under inert atmosphere, usually at 0 °C to room.

Acid‑base exchange; concentrated H2SO4 protonates sodium oxamate, producing oxamic acid and sodium bisulfate (NaHSO₄). Usually carried out in aqueous or neat sulfuric acid with gentle heating; no catalyst needed.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2) between phenoxide (generated in‑situ from phenol and a base such as NaOH K2CO3) and 2‑chloroethanol to afford phenoxyethanol with release of HCl (or NaCl if sodium base is used). Reaction performed in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone, DMF) at reflux or 60–80 °C; base is required to deprotonate phenol.

Acidification of a disodium tartrate salt to the free d‑tartaric acid; two equivalents of HCl protonate the carboxylate groups, yielding tartaric acid and sodium chloride. Carried out in aqueous solution by adding aqueous HCl to the disodium salt at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑base reaction; samarium(III) carbonate is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, producing soluble samarium(III) chloride, carbon dioxide gas, and water; performed at room temperature or with gentle heating; aqueous HCl is the solvent.

Redox (halogen oxidation) of cyanide; converts cyanide to cyanogen while reducing chlorine to chloride; NaCN + Cl2 → NaCl + (CN)2; carried out in aqueous solution, often at 0–5 °C with chlorine gas bubbled through; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Carbodiimide‑mediated esterification (DCC coupling). Purpose: convert pyridine‑2,4‑dicarboxylic acid into its diethyl ester. Key transformation: DCC activates the two carboxyl groups to O‑acyl‑urea intermediates, which are attacked by ethanol; DMAP acts as a nucleophilic acyl‑transfer catalyst, giving diethyl pyridine‑2,4‑dicarboxylate and dicyclohexylurea as by‑product. Typical conditions: 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere, dichloromethane or THF as solvent; reaction stirred 1–12 h.

Precipitation (metathesis) reaction; used to isolate manganese(II) sulfide as an insoluble solid. Hydrogen sulfide gas is bubbled into an aqueous solution of manganese(II) chloride, forming a black MnS precipitate and releasing hydrochloric acid into the solution. Typically carried out at room temperature in water under an H₂S atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Double displacement/precipitation reaction; similarly employed to precipitate gallium hydroxide using a weaker, volatile base. Gallium nitrate solution is treated with aqueous ammonium hydroxide (NH₄OH) dropwise at room temperature, maintaining pH around 7‑9. Ga³⁺ combines with OH⁻ to afford a gelatinous Ga(OH)₃ precipitate, and NH₄⁺ pairs with NO₃⁻ to form soluble NH₄NO₃. Reaction proceeds in water; no catalyst is needed.

Homolytic C–H bond cleavage of acetaldehyde to generate an acetyl radical and a hydrogen atom; typically initiated by UV photolysis or radical initiators (e.g., AIBN) in an inert solvent such as benzene or carbon tetrachloride. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base double displacement (metathesis) reaction. Purpose: exchange of anions between nitric acid and copper(II) acetate. Key transformation: protonation of acetate to give acetic acid while nitrate replaces acetate as the copper(II) anion, yielding copper(II) nitrate and acetic acid. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, room temperature to gentle heating, no special catalyst; often performed in dilute acid.

Direct amidation of pentanoyl chloride with methylamine; type: acyl substitution (amide formation); purpose: synthesize N‑methylpentanamide; key transformation: chloride of the acid chloride is displaced by the amine, releasing HCl; typical conditions: add methylamine (often as a solution in ether or dichloromethane) to a cold solution of pentanoyl chloride at 0 °C to 5 °C under nitrogen; optionally include a base such as triethylamine to scavenge HCl; solvent: dry CH₂Cl₂, THF, or Et₂O.

Decomposition (redox) of perbromic acid; yields a lower oxidation‑state bromic acid and molecular. Unstable HBrO₄ spontaneously breaks down to HBrO₃ (bromic acid) plus O₂, especially upon heating, exposure to light, or in concentrated solutions. Conducted in aqueous solution under controlled temperature (often 0–25 °C) to limit runaway reaction. No solvent beyond water; no catalyst, though acidic conditions promote the pathway.

Redox (disproportionation) reaction of bromide and bromate in acidic medium. Purpose: generate elemental bromine from bromide/bromate mixture. Key transformation: bromate (BrO₃⁻) oxidizes bromide (Br⁻) in the presence of strong acid (H₂SO₄) to produce Br₂, water, and the corresponding hydrogen sulfate salts (NaHSO₄, KHSO₄). Typical conditions: concentrated H₂SO₄, aqueous medium, reflux or heating to ~80 °C; reaction proceeds rapidly once mixed.

General type: acid–base double displacement (neutralization). Purpose: generate soluble aluminum nitrate and sodium nitrate, often for nitrate sourcing or waste neutralization. Key transformation: Al(OH)₄⁻ + HNO₃ → Al(NO₃)₃ + NaNO₃ + H₂O (overall stoichiometry yields Al needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (amidation) of chlorosulfonyl fluoride with ammonia to produce fluorosulfonamide (FSO₂NH₂) and HCl. Ammonia attacks the sulfonyl chloride, displacing chloride as HCl. Reaction is performed at 0 °C to 5 °C in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF, with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) present to scavenge the generated HCl. The purpose is preparation of a primary sulfonamide containing a fluorine substituent.

Chlorination / halogen‑exchange with phosphorus pentachloride. Purpose: replace the alkoxy group of a methyl ester with chloride and convert the remaining carbonyl to an acid chloride, while also generating methyl chloride. Key transformation: PCl₅ converts the ester carbonyl into bromodifluoroacetyl chloride and simultaneously chlorinates the methoxy group to give methyl chloride; POCl₃ is formed as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂), 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; reaction completed within 1–2 h.

Selective reduction of an aromatic aldehyde with sodium borohydride. Purpose: reduce the aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol without affecting the phenolic OH. Key transformation: NaBH₄ delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon of 4‑hydroxybenzaldehyde, forming 4‑hydroxybenzyl alcohol; the borohydride is oxidized to sodium borate. Typical conditions: protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or aqueous‑ethanol mixture, 0 °C to rt, short reaction time (minutes to 1 h).

Solid‑state metathesis (cation exchange) synthesis of copper(II) selenide. Purpose: produce CuSe from inexpensive precursors. Key transformation: Cu²⁺ from CuCl₂ exchanges with Ca²⁺ from CaSe, yielding CuSe (insoluble black solid) and CaCl₂ as a by‑product. Typical conditions: intimate grinding of powders followed by heating at 800–900 °C in an inert atmosphere or sealed tube; sometimes performed in molten salt flux to improve diffusion.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of an alkene; converts cyclobutene to cyclobutanol by Markovnikov addition of water; typically performed in aqueous dilute H₂SO₄ or HCl at 0–50 °C; water acts as solvent and proton source.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; used to convert soluble magnesium salt to insoluble magnesium hydroxide while generating soluble calcium chloride. Key transformation: Mg²⁺ exchanges anions with Ca²⁺, precipitating Mg(OH)₂. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating; water is the solvent, no catalyst required.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride using phosphorus pentachloride; acrylic acid is transformed to acryloyl chloride with release of HCl and POCl₃; carried out in anhydrous organic solvent such as CH₂Cl₂ or toluene under reflux; inert atmosphere recommended.

A double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; mercuric cyanide exchanges anions with lead(II) nitrate producing soluble mercury(II) nitrate and insoluble lead cyanide which precipitates; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special catalyst required.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of a metal sulfide; Sc₂S₃ reacts with O₂ to form Sc₂O₃ and SO₂. Carried out in flowing air or oxygen at >500 °C; solid‑state reaction, no solvent; sometimes a quartz tube furnace is used.

Base‑promoted intramolecular dehydrohalogenation yielding an epoxide; 1,3‑dichl‑2‑propanol reacts with calcium hydroxide to give epichlorohydrin, water and calcium chloride; heated (≈120–150 °C) in solid or molten Ca(OH)₂, sometimes with a small amount of water as medium.

Hydride reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol while retaining the bromine substituent; LiAlH₄ reduces 2‑bromobutanoic acid to 2‑bromo‑1‑butanol; performed in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) under nitrogen at 0 °C to reflux, followed by aqueous work‑up that yields Al(OH)₃ as a by‑product.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis (calcination) forming calcium titanate; calcium carbonate and titanium dioxide are mixed and heated above ~1000 °C, releasing CO₂ and producing CaTiO₃; conducted in a crucible under air or inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Metal‑halide reduction/comproportionation; magnesium reduces boron trichloride and couples two BCl₃ units to form diboron tetrachloride (B₂Cl₄) while being oxidized to MgCl₂. The reaction is performed in anhydrous ether or THF under nitrogen, using finely powdered Mg and gaseous BCl₃, generally at reflux temperature.

Reductive dehalogenation (hydrogenolysis) of an aryl bromide; catalytic hydrogenation using H₂ gas and palladium on carbon removes the bromine atom, converting 1‑bromo‑4‑nitrobenzene to nitrobenzene while hydrogen bromide. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure (1–5 atm) in an alcohol solvent (e.g., ethanol or methanol) at room temperature to 50 °C under an inert atmosphere.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) salt formation; sodium sulfate reacts with aluminum sulfate in aqueous solution to give the mixed alum salt sodium aluminum sulfate, NaAl(SO₄)₂. The reaction proceeds at ambient temperature; the product often crystallizes upon cooling or evaporation of water.

This is an elimination reaction, specifically E2 dehydrohalogenation, used to form alkynes from haloalkenes. Key transformation is the removal of HCl to create a triple bond. Typical conditions include strong base and heat, such as reflux with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Common solvents are water or ethanol.

Acid‑base neutralization; phosphoric acid protonates dicalcium phosphate (CaHPO₄) to afford calcium dihydrogen phosphate, Ca(H₂PO₄)₂, with release of water if hydrated forms are used. Conducted in aqueous medium, typically at room temperature with stirring until the pH reaches the target range.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide by cyanide; NaCN attacks cyclohexylmethyl iodide to replace I with CN, yielding cyclohexylacetonitrile and NaI. Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF, DMSO or acetonitrile, often at 50–80 °C; a phase‑transfer catalyst may be employed when using solid NaCN.

Thermal decomposition of a chlorate; heating strontium chlorate causes it to break down into strontium chloride and oxygen gas (3 O₂). The decomposition occurs at temperatures above ~250 °C, sometimes accelerated by a catalyst such as MnO₂, in an open crucible or furnace with proper venting for the released O₂.

Acid–base neutralization; used to convert picric acid into its sodium salt (sodium picrate). The carbonate deprotonates the phenolic OH groups of picric acid, forming sodium picrate and releasing CO₂ and H₂O. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient or mild heating with stirring; no catalyst required.

Esterification (acetylation) of a primary allylic alcohol; purpose is to protect the hydroxyl group as an acetate ester. The hydroxyl of pent‑4‑en‑1‑ol attacks acetic anhydride, transferring an acetyl group and releasing acetic acid. Typically performed at 0 °C to rt in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base/DMAP or pyridine as catalyst; mild heating may be applied if needed.

SN2 hydrolysis of benzyl chloride with aqueous NaOH to give benzyl alcohol and NaCl. Conducted in water or aqueous ethanol, heated to reflux (50‑100 °C) for several hours; the reaction proceeds cleanly with excess hydroxide and no catalyst.

Fischerification; synthesis of isobutyl acetate from acetic acid and isobutanol. The carboxylic acid and alcohol undergo condensation, eliminating water to give the ester. Conducted under reflux in excess alcohol or a non‑polar solvent (toluene) with a strong acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid; water is often removed by azeotropic distillation (Dean–Stark).

High‑temperature solid‑state sulfide formation (carbothermic reduction/sulfurization). Thorium dioxide is reduced by carbon in the presence of elemental sulfur, yielding thorium disulfide (ThS₂) and carbon monoxide gas. Performed in a sealed quartz tube or high‑temperature furnace at 1200–1600 °C under inert atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst is used.

Chlorination (thionyl chloride mediated substitution). Dimethyl phosphorodithioic acid reacts with SOCl₂, replacing the –SH group with a chlorine atom to give dimethyl phosphorochloridothionate, while HCl and SO₂ are liberated as gases. The reaction is run in anhydrous, inert solvent such as dry dichloromethane or chloroform, typically at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen; no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination; introduction of a third chlorine onto 1,2‑dichlorobenzene to afford 1,2,3‑trichlorobenzene. Chlorine gas is activated by FeCl₃ (Lewis acid catalyst), generating the Cl⁺ electrophile that attacks the aromatic ring; HCl is formed as a by‑product. Conducted in a non‑polar chlorinated solvent (e.g., carbon tetrachloride or chloroform) at reflux temperature, with catalytic FeCl₃ and careful temperature control.

Acid‑base metathesis (acid dissolution of a phosphate). Hydrochloric acid protonates praseodymium(III) phosphate, converting it to phosphoric acid and forming soluble praseodymium(III) chloride. Carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to improve solubility; no catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: generate the sodium salt of diglycolic acid for easier handling or further reactions. Key transformation: the carboxylic acid proton is deprotonated by sodium hydroxide, forming sodium diglycolate and water. Typical conditions: aqueous solution of diglycolic acid mixed with stoichiometric NaOH at 0–25 °C, stirring until dissolution; no special catalyst required.

Solid‑state double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; purpose is to convert tin(IV) bromide to tin(IV) oxide while forming calcium bromide; key transformation is replacement of bromide ligands on tin by oxide from CaO, precipitating insoluble SnO₂ and generating soluble CaBr₂; typically carried out by heating the solid mixture to 600‑800 °C in a furnace; no solvent or catalyst is employed.

Phase‑transfer catalyzed O‑alkylation (SN2) of dihydroartemisinin with bromoethane to give Arteether; NaOH serves as the base to deprotonate the hydroxyl, tetrabutylammonium bromide shuttles the anion into the organic phase; typically performed in a biphasic water/organic system (e.g., dichloromethane or toluene) at reflux temperature under inert atmosphere.

Fischer esterification of menthol with isovaleric acid to afford menthyl isovalerate; acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄ or p‑toluenesulfonic acid is used, the reaction is heated (reflux) in an aprotic solvent like toluene or benzene with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water and drive the equilibrium toward ester formation.

Reaction type: metal‑acid reduction of a nitro group. Purpose: obtain 2,5‑dichloroaniline from the nitro precursor without using hydrogen gas. Key transformation: tin metal in concentrated HCl reduces the nitro group to an amine, generating tin(IV) chloride and water as by‑products. Typical conditions: reflux the substrate in a mixture of ethanol‑water with excess tin powder and conc. HCl for 2–4 h; after completion the mixture is basified, extracted and the product purified. No external catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement acid‑base precipitation forming strontium phosphate from phosphoric acid and strontium chloride; aqueous solutions of the reagents are mixed at ambient temperature, the insoluble Sr₃(PO₄)₂ precipitates and is filtered, while the by‑product HCl remains in solution; no special catalyst is required.

SN2 methylation of the phenolic hydroxyl of naringenin using methyl iodide in the presence of potassium carbonate as base; reaction is carried out in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or acetone at 50‑80 °C, generating isosakuranetin and potassium iodide as the only by‑product; the base deprotonates the phenol, allowing nucleophilic attack on MeI.

Nucleophilic addition of phenylmagnesium bromide (Grignard reagent) to formaldehyde followed by acidic work‑up with HCl to yield benzyl alcohol; the Grignard reaction is performed in dry ether (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere, and the reaction mixture is quenched with dilute HCl to protonate the alkoxide intermediate, giving the alcohol.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (halogenation); chlorine adds ortho to the phenolic OH of para‑cresol producing 2‑chloro‑4‑methylphenol and HCl as by‑product; typically carried out in glacial acetic acid as solvent at 0–5 °C to limit poly‑chlorination; acid medium provided by acetic acid promotes formation of the electrophilic Cl⁺ species.

Transesterification / carbonate formation; tert‑butyl alcohol reacts with diphenyl carbonate to give di‑tert‑butyl dicarbonate (a Boc protecting reagent) and phenol; usually performed under reflux in anhydrous toluene (or xylene) with removal of phenol by azeotropic distillation; catalytic amounts of pyridine or DMAP may be added to accelerate the exchange.

Thermal solid‑state decompositionion‑exchange dissociation) of trisodium hexafluoroaluminate (cryolite) into aluminium fluoride and sodium fluoride; requires heating above ~500 °C in the absence of solvent; no catalyst is needed.

Nophilic substitution (SN2) of bromoethane by lithium thiocyanate to afford ethyl thiocyanate and lithium bromide; conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone or DMF at reflux or ambient temperature; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation producing copper(II) phosphate; phosphoric acid reacts with copper(II) oxide, generating water and insoluble Cu₃(PO₄)₂; carried out in aqueous medium with heating (reflux) and stirring to ensure complete reaction; no special catalyst is needed.

Acid‑carbonate reaction (neutralization); lead(II) carbonate reacts with sulfuric acid to generate carbonic acid that decomposes to CO₂ and water, leaving insoluble lead(II) sulfate as a precipitate. Conducted in water at ambient to mild heating (≤60 °C) using dilute H₂SO₄. No catalyst required.

Condensation (Schiff‑base formation) of acetone with thiosemicarbazide to give acetone thiosemicarbazone; water eliminated; usually carried out by refluxing acetone and thiosemicarbazide in ethanol or methanol, often with a few drops of acetic acid as catalyst; ambient to reflux temperature.

Hydride reduction of the sulfoxide group in alliin to give S‑allyl‑L‑cysteine; sodium borohydride supplies hydride, being oxidized to sodium metaborate; typically performed in a methanol‑water mixture or phosphate buffer at 0–4 °C to avoid over‑reduction; no additional catalyst required.

Activation / coupling to give an NHS ester; CDIs reacts with benzoic acid to form an imidazolide intermediate which is attacked by N‑hydroxysuccinimide, generating N‑succinimidyl benzoate plus imidazole and CO₂; typical conditions: aprotic solvent (DMF or DCM), 0 °C to rt, inert atmosphere; CDI serves as the activating reagent; purpose: produce an activated ester for later amide bond formation.

Thionation of an amide; the carbonyl oxygen of acetamide is replaced by sulfur to give thioacetamide while phosphorus pentasulfide is reduced to phosphoric acid. Conducted by heating solid P2S5 with the amide, often in an inert high‑boiling solvent such as pyridine or xylene under a nitrogen atmosphere.

Metal‑free reduction of aldehydes via pinacolborane‑hydrogen peroxide (hydroboration–oxidation): Benzaldehyde is reduced by pinacolborane (HBpin) in the presence of aqueous hydrogen peroxide to give benzyl alcohol, with boric acid as the benign by‑product. The process involves hydroboration of the carbonyl (formation of a benzylic alkoxy‑boron intermediate) followed by oxidative work‑up with H₂O₂ to release the alcohol. Reactions are usually performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as THF or MeCN; H₂O₂ (30 % aq.) is added dropwise, and no metal catalyst is required. Reaction completes within 30 min to 2 h, after which the mixture is quenched, extracted, and the alcohol is isolated.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (mixed ester interchange); ethanol attacks the carbonyl carbon of chloromethyl acetate, displacing chloromethanol and forming ethyl acetate. Typically carried out in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetone or THF) with a catalytic amount of base or acid at reflux temperatures to accelerate the substitution.

Hydrolysis of a tetrahalide; tellurium tetrabromide reacts with water, converting the Te–Br bonds to Te–O bonds to afford tellurium dioxide and releasing hydrobromic acid. The reaction proceeds readily in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating or reflux; no catalyst is required.

Reductive decolorization (redox) of phenolphthalein; sodium dithionite (Na2S2O4) reduces phenolphthalein in a strongly basic solution (NaOH), converting the colored lactone to its colorless leuco form while being oxidized to sulfite (Na2SO3) and generating water. Performed in aqueous NaOH at ambient temperature, typically under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of dithionite.

Acid‑base metathesis of zinc thiocyanate with hydrochloric acid; HCl protonates the thiocyanate ligand, releasing hydrogen thiocyanate (HSCN) and converting Zn²⁺ to zinc chloride. Carried out in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating or reflux to ensure complete conversion; the HSCN can be distilled or used in situ.

Acid‑ or base‑catalyzed amide hydrolysis; n‑Hexylformamide reacts with water to cleave the amide bond, yielding n‑hexylamine and formic acid. The reaction is usually heated in aqueous acid (e.g., 2 M HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) and then neutralized; reflux for several hours is common to drive complete hydrolysis.

Iron(II)‑catalyzed radical N‑acetylation; N‑acetoxyphthalimide serves as an acetyl radical precursor, which under Fe(II) reduction generates an acetyl radical that acylates the primary amine of serotonin to give N‑acetylserotonin, with phthalimide released as the by‑product. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or DMF at room temperature, using a soluble Fe(II) salt (e.g., FeSO4·7H2O) under an inert atmosphere.

Carbonylation of aryl azides; a transition‑metal‑catalyzed insertion of CO into the nitrene formed from phenyl azide, yielding phenyl isocyanate with loss of N2. Typically performed under CO pressure (1–10 atm) using Rh(I) or Pd(0) catalysts such as RhCl(PPh₃)₃ in THF or toluene at 50–100 °C.

Acid‑base/oxide‑anion exchange; copper(II) oxide reacts with acetic anhydride to give copper(II) acetate and acetic acid. Usually carried out by heating neat acetic anhydride or in glacial acetic acid at reflux (≈120 °C); no additional solvent or catalyst required.

Aqueous neutralization/ion exchange; choline sulfate is treated with two equivalents of NaOH to form choline hydroxide (a quatern ammonium base) and sodium sulfate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the reaction is exothermic and proceeds to completion without added catalyst.

Hydrolysis of 2‑chloroacetophenone with aqueous sodium hydroxide; a nucleophilic substitution (SN1/SN2) where OH⁻ displaces chloride at the benzylic carbon to give 2‑hydroxyacetophenone (an α‑hydroxy ketone) and NaCl. Conducted in water/ethanol mixture, refluxing for several hours. Provides a route to phenolic analogues of acetophenone.

Intramolecular Michael (aldol) cyclization of a chalcone to a flavanone; naringenin chalcone undergoes base‑ or acid‑catalyzed cyclisation to form the flavanone ring of naringenin. Typical conditions use aqueous NaOH or dilute HCl inethanol, refluxing for 1–3 h, followed by acid work‑up and crystallisation.

SN2 alkylation (nucleophilic substitution). Lithium ethoxide acts as a nucleophile toward iodomethane in anhydrous ethyl acetate or THF, displacing iodide to give ethyl methyl ether (methoxyethane) and lithium iodide. Reaction is carried out under inert atmosphere at 0‑25 °C; polar aprotic solvent (e.g., THF, DMF) improves yield.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction; sulfurous acid (H2SO3) reacts with silver nitrate (AgNO3) in water, exchanging anions to precipitate silver sulfite (Ag2SO3) while forming nitric acid (HNO3) in solution; performed at ambient temperature, aqueous medium.

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis); lead(II) acetate in aqueous solution reacts with ammonium sulfate, precipitating insoluble lead(II) sulfate while forming soluble ammonium acetate. Performed at room temperature in water; the solid PbSO₄ is filtered and washed, and the filtrate contains the acetate salt.

Sequential O‑demethylation and catalytic hydrogenation; boron tribromide cleaves the 3‑methoxy group of codeine to give the phenolic intermediate (morphine), and Raney‑nickel under hydrogen pressure reduces the 7,8‑double bond to afford dihydromorphine. Commonly executed by adding BBr₃ in CH₂Cl₂ at 0 °C, quenching, then hydrogenating the crude mixture with Raney Ni in ethanol under 1–3 atm H₂ at 25–50 °C.

Nucleophilic addition of phenylmagnesium bromide to an in‑situ generated benzyne intermediate; a Grignard aryl anion attacks benzyne to form the C‑C bond of biphenyl after protonation. Used for biaryl construction. Typically performed in dry ether or THF under nitrogen at low to ambient temperature; no external catalyst required.

Acid‑base salt formation (protonation of a basic amine). Molindone free base is treated with aqueous or ethanolic hydrochloric acid, protonating the amine nitrogen to give Molindone hydrochloride salt. This improves solubility and handling for pharmaceutical use. Conducted at room temperature with stirring; the salt is isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) of copper(I) iodide with potassium thiocyanate. Cu⁺ exchanges its iodide for SCN⁻, precipitating copper(I) thiocyanate while potassium iodide remains soluble. Reaction is carried out in water at room temperature with stirring; the CuSCN solid is filtered and washed. No catalyst needed.

Base‑induced E2 elimination of 1‑methyl‑1‑chlorocyclopropane with sodium ethoxide. NaOEt abstracts a β‑hydrogen, chloride departs, yielding 1‑methylcyclopropene; sodium chloride and ethanol are formed as by‑products. Conducted in dry ethanol, often under reflux or mild heating, under inert atmosphere to avoid side reactions.

Electrophilic aromatic bromination of 2‑methylthiophene with N‑bromosuccinimide (NBS) to give 3‑bromo‑2‑methylthiophene. Purpose: regioselective halogenation at the 3‑position of the thiophene ring. Key transformation: generation of Br⁺ from NBS, electrophilic attack on the aromatic system, loss of a proton, and formation of succinimide as a by‑product. Typical conditions: NBS (≈1.1 eq) in dry dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, 0 °C to room temperature, protected from light.

Metath/precipitation reaction; sulfide-induced precipitation of a heavy‑metal sulfide. Sodium sulfide in water displaces bromide from mercuric bromide, yielding soluble sodium bromide and black, insoluble mercuric sulfide (HgS). Conducted in aqueous solution, often at room temperature.

Reaction type: radical reduction (hydrogen‑atom transfer). Purpose: dehalogenation of 1‑iodobutane to give n‑butane. Key transformation: tributyltin hydride donates a hydrogen atom to the alkyl radical generated after homolytic cleavage of the C–I bond, producing butane and tributyltin iodide. Typical conditions: inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar), reflux in toluene or benzene, with a catalytic amount of radical initiator such as AIBN or thermal initiation at 80‑110 °C. No additional catalyst beyond the tin hydride; solvent is toluene or benzene.

Acid–base protonation; purpose is to generate hydrogen thiocyanate (thiocyanic acid); key transformation proton transfer from HNO₃ to SCN⁻ yielding HSCN and KNO₃; typical conditions: dilute nitric acid, low to moderate temperature to avoid decomposition, aqueous medium; no catalyst.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of a cyclic ketone; peracetic acid (ethane‑peroxoic acid) inserts an oxygen adjacent to the carbonyl of cyclohexanone, expanding the ring to the seven‑membered ε‑caprolactone and producing acetic acid as by‑product; performed at 0 °C to room temperature in an inert organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with catalytic amounts of acid or base to control the rate.

Transesterification; exchanges the alkoxy group of 2‑methylpentan‑2‑yl acetate with methanol to afford methyl acetate and 2‑methylpentan‑2‑ol. Typically performed with catalytic acid (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) or base (e.g., NaOCH₃) in excess methanol as solvent, refluxing 60–80 °C until equilibrium is reached; removal of methanol drives the reaction forward.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of oct‑2‑yne (oxymercuration of an alkyne) using mercuric sulfate as catalyst in aqueous sulfuric acid. Hg²⁺ adds to the triple bond, forming a vinyl‑mercury intermediate that is hydrolyzed to an enol which tautomerizes to 2‑octanone. Typical conditions: dilute H₂SO₄, catalytic HgSO₄, temperature 50‑80 °C, stirring; no additional solvent required.
