Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling of 4‑iodophenol with phenylboronic acid in the presence of Pd(OAc)₂, triphenylphosphine, and potassium carbonate. Oxidative addition of Pd(0) into the C–I bond, transmetalation with the boronic acid, and reductive elimination forge the C–C bond of 4‑phenylphenol; KI and water are by‑products. Usually run in a polar aprotic solvent such as dioxane/water or THF/water, at 80‑100 °C under nitrogen or argon atmosphere.

Double displacement (metathesis) acid‑base reaction; sulfuric acid protonates the bromide ion of mercuric bromide, producing insoluble mercury(II) sulfate as a solid precipitate and gaseous hydrogen bromide. Typically carried out in aqueous solution with dilute to concentrated H2SO4 at reflux; HBr gas is evolved and can be collected. No catalyst required.

Base‑catalyzed nitrile hydrolysis; NaOH hydrolyzes trifluoroacetonitrile to give sodium trifluoroacetate and ammonia. Key transformation: CN → CO2– (as Na+ salt) + NH3. Typically carried out in aqueous NaOH solution, heated under reflux (80‑100 °C) for several hours. No special catalyst; water is the solvent.

Hydrolysis of sodium aluminum hydride; the strong reducing agent NaAlH₄ reacts with water to yield sodium hydroxide, aluminum hydroxide precipitate, and hydrogen gas; typically conducted cautiously at 0–25 °C in a dry, inert atmosphere, then quenched with cold water or dilute acid; purpose is safe disposal or generation of H₂ gas.

Halide exchange (Finkelstein SN2 reaction); iodide ion substitutes the chloride in ethyl chloroacetate to form ethyl iodoacetate, precipitating NaCl. Usually performed in dry acetone where NaCl is insoluble driving the reaction forward. Conditions: reflux in acetone, excess NaI, inert atmosphere. No catalyst required.

Acid‑base (oxide protonation) producing gaseous BF₃; purpose is to generate boron trifluoride from boron oxide; key transformation: B–O bonds cleaved, B–F bonds formed and water produced; typical conditions: anhydrous hydrofluoric acid at 0–50 °C with gas evolution; solvent: HF itself; no catalyst needed.

Acid‑catalyzed trans‑etherification / alkylation of phenol; phenol attacks the isobutyl group of isobutyl methyl ether, displacing methanol and forming isobutyl phenyl ether. Typical conditions: strong Brønsted acid (e.g., 90 % H₂SO p‑TsOH) as catalyst, reflux in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as toluene or xylene. Reaction proceeds via an SN1‑type cleavage of the secondary isobutyl‑oxygen bond.

Electrophilic addition of hydrogen bromide (hydrohalogenation); HBr adds across the double bond of 1‑heptene in a Markovnikov fashion, delivering hydrogen to C‑1 and bromine to C‑2 to give 2‑bromoheptane. Usually carried out by bubbling HBr gas or adding aqueous HBr at 0 °C to room temperature, often in a non‑polar solvent like dichloromethane. No catalyst needed unless radical (anti‑Markovnikov) pathway is desired.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous potassium sulfate reacts with strontium nitrate to exchange anions, producing insoluble strontium sulfate precipitate and soluble potassium nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature with stirring; the solid SrSO₄ is filtered off. No catalyst required.

SN2 O‑methylation (Williamson ether synthesis); converts the phenolic OH of 5‑hydroxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine to a methoxy group to give 5‑methoxy‑N,N‑dimethyltryptamine. Key transformation is nucleophilic attack of the phenoxide on iodomethane, forming a C–O bond and releasing HI. Typically performed with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃, NaH, or triethylamine) in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, DMF or DMSO, at 0 °C to reflux, under inert atmosphere if desired. No metal catalyst required.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges counter‑ions of cobalt(II) carbonate and cadmium nitrate in aqueous solution to precipitate the insoluble cadmium carbonate while soluble cobalt(II) nitrate remains in solution; performed in water at ambient temperature, often with stirring.

Acid–base neutralization (salt metathesis); hydroxide ion deprotonates the 3‑methylpiperidinium chloride salt, liberating free 3‑methylpiperidine, generating water and sodium chloride; typically carried out in aqueous medium at room temperature, optionally with gentle heating to aid removal of the organic base.

Direct fluorination (radical halogen exchange); fluorine gas replaces two hydrogen atoms of chloromethane, yielding chlorodifluoromethane and hydrogen fluoride; conducted under rigorously controlled conditions, often at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in a flow reactor with inert diluent gas; HF is captured or scrubbed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution (carbamoylation) to form a substituted urea; the aniline nitrogen attacks dimethylcarbamoyl chloride, displacing chloride and giving 3‑(3,4‑dichlorophenyl)‑1,1‑dimethylurea; reaction is typically carried out in an aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) at 0 °C to room temperature in the presence of a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to neutralize the generated HCl.

Base‑catalyzed condensation (glycidylation) to produce bisphenol A diglycidyl ether, the main component of epoxy resins; tetramethylammonium hydrox deprotonates the phenolic OH groups of bisphenol A, which then attack epichlorohydrin to form glycidyl ether linkages, releasing water and tetramethylammonium chloride; executed at 50–80 °C in a polar aprotic solvent (e.g., isopropanol or dimethyl sulfoxide) under nitrogen, followed by work‑up to isolate the epoxy product.

Conversion of 2‑butoxyacetic acid to 2‑butoxyacetyl chloride using thionyl chloride; purpose is to generate the reactive acyl chloride for subsequent acylation steps. Key transformation: the carboxylic OH is replaced by Cl, releasing SO₂ and HCl gases. Typical conditions: addition of SOCl₂ (1.2 eq) to a solution of the acid in dry dichloromethane or chloroform at 0 °C, then stirring at room temperature for 1–2 h. Pyridine or triethylamine may be added as an HCl scavenger.

General type: redox acid‑metal dissolution. Purpose: convert elemental erbium into soluble erbium(III) nitrate while reducing nitrate to nitrogen monoxide gas. Key transformations: Er metal is oxidized from 0 to +3, nitrate ion is reduced from +5 to +2 (NO), and water is formed from hydrogen of the acid. Typical conditions: reflux in aqueous nitric acid (often 6 M to conc.) at 80‑120 °C. Sol: water (as the nitric acid solution). No external catalyst required.

General type: nucleophilic addition of a Grignard reagent to a carbonyl (addition to strained cyclopropanone). Purpose: synthesize 1‑methyl‑cyclopropanol. Key transformations: methyl‑MgBr adds to the carbonyl carbon of cyclopropanone forming an alkoxide intermediate; after aqueous work‑up the alkoxide is protonated to give the secondary alcohol, while MgBr₂ remains as a by‑product. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF), 0 °C to room temperature, inert atmosphere (₂ or Ar). Work‑up with dilute NH₄Cl or water. No additional catalyst.

General type: acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Purpose: prepare sodium methanesulfinate from methanesulfinic acid. Key transformations: carbonate deprotonates two equivalents of methanesulfinic acid, releasing CO₂ and H₂O; the resulting sodium cations pair with the methanesulfinate anions. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stir at ambient or slightly elevated temperature to drive off CO₂. Solvent: water. No catalyst needed.

General type: catalytic hydrogenation (reduction of a nitrile to a primary amine). Purpose: convert phenoxyacetonitrile into 2‑phenoxyethanamine. Key transformations: H₂ adds across the C≡N triple bond in the presence of Pd/C, reducing it sequentially to an imine and then to the primary amine; palladium on carbon acts as the catalyst. Typical conditions: H₂ pressure 1–5 atm, Pd/C (5–10 % Pd loading), solvent ethanol or methanol, temperature 25‑50 °C, reaction time 2‑12 h. No other reagents required.

General type: acid‑base metathesis (proton transfer) forming pyrophosphoric acid and ammonium sulfate. Purpose: generate free pyrophosphoric acid and neutralize excess sulfate as ammonium sulfate. Key transformations: ammonium pyrophosphate is protonated by sulfuric acid to give H₄P₂O₇; the displaced ammonium ions combine with sulfate to form (NH₄)₂SO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, gentle heating to dissolve salts and promote exchange, followed by concentration if isolation is desired. No catalyst required.

General type: double‑displacement (metathesis) ion‑exchange reaction. Purpose: prepare samarium(III) acetate from samarium nitrate and sodium acetate. Key transformations: nitrate anions pair with sodium cations to give NaNO₃, while acetate anions coordinate to Sm³⁺ to form Sm(OAc)₃. Typical conditions: aqueous solution, stirring at room temperature or mild heating; the solid samarium acetate may precipitate and be filtered. Solvent: water. No catalyst needed.

Double displacement (metathesis) reaction; aqueous medium; mercuric chloride reacts with ammonium sulfate to precipitate sparingly soluble mercuric sulfate while forming soluble ammonium chloride; typically carried out at room temperature or with gentle heating; no special catalyst required; water is the solvent.

Fischer esterification of an α‑amino acid. Purpose: convert glycine into its methyl ester (methyl 2‑aminoacetate). Key transformation: the carboxylic acid of glycine reacts with methanol, losing water and forming the methyl ester; the amine group remains unchanged. Typical conditions: excess methanol as solvent, catalytic amount of concentrated H₂SO₄, reflux (≈65 °C) for several hours. Common solvent: methanol itself; sulfuric acid acts as catalyst.

Double displacement (precipitation) reaction; performed in aqueous solution; silver nitrate combines with ammonium sodium phosphate to produce insoluble silver phosphate precipitate and soluble ammonium nitrate and sodium nitrate; usually conducted at ambient temperature; water serves as the reaction medium; no catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an anhydride by a carboxylate; propionic anhydride reacts with sodium acetate to exchange acyl groups, yielding acetic acid and sodium propionate; generally carried out in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., water/ethanol) at room temperature or mild heating; no additional catalyst required.

Alcoholysis of propionic anhydride with ethanol; purpose is to form ethyl propionate while releasing one equivalent of propionic acid. Key transformation: anhydride + EtOH → ethyl propionate + propionic acid. Typical conditions: reflux ethanol (often the solvent) with the anhydride, optionally with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) to accelerate; reaction proceeds to completion in several hours.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification;1‑nonanol reacts with acetic acid in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid, which acts both as catalyst and dehydrating agent, to form 1‑nonyl acetate and water; reflux conditions are typical, with removal of water to drive equilibrium; the reaction mixture often consists solely of the alcohol and acid, sometimes with a small amount of inert solvent such as toluene.

Oxidation/hydrolysis of phenylborinic acid by hydrogen peroxide; yields phenylboronic acid and water; a mild oxidation performed in water or water/alcohol mixture at room temperature to ~50 °C; no catalyst required.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution of an acyl chloride by an alkoxide; 1‑decanoyl chloride reacts with sodium ethoxide to give ethyl decanoate (an ester) and sodium chloride as by‑product; performed in ethanol (which also serves as the solvent) at low to moderate temperature (0 °C to reflux); no additional catalyst is required.

Benzyne trimerization (a [2+2+2] cycloaddition) leading to formation of triphenylene; three benzyne intermediates combine under high‑temperature, solvent‑free conditions (often in a sealed tube or flash‑vacuum pyrolysis setup) to generate the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon triphenylene; typically requires inert atmosphere and may be promoted by metal catalysts such as nickel or copper, though uncatalyzed thermal pathways are also reported.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 1,3‑dinitrobenzene in aqueous HCl using Pd/C under H₂ pressure; each nitro group is reduced to an amine and protonated, yielding m‑phenylenediamine dihydrochloride and water. Typical conditions: 1–5 atm H₂, Pd on carbon (5–10 wt %), aqueous HCl (1–3 M), reflux or room temperature, sometimes with ethanol as co‑solvent.

Reduction of the aldehyde functional group of 4‑isopropylbenzaldehyde to the primary alcohol 4‑isopropylbenzyl alcohol. Common methods: NaBH₄ (1–2 eq) in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to rt, or catalytic hydrogenation (H₂, Pd/C) in ethanol. No stoichiometric by‑products other than water (NaBH₄ route) or H₂O (hydrogenation).

L‑Lysine + NAD⁺ → L‑Pipecolic acid + NADH + ammonia (NH3). Enzymatic oxidative deamination (dehydrogenase) in lysine catabolism. Removes the α‑amino group as NH3 while oxidizing the carbon skeleton; NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH and a cyclic secondary amino acid is formed. Happens in aqueous buffer at physiological pH (~7.5), 30–37 °C, in the presence of a lysine dehydrogenase enzyme; no external solvents or catalysts beyond the enzyme and NAD⁺.

O‑methylation of glycolic acid (HO‑CH₂‑COOH) with dimethyl sulfate under basic conditions. The glycolate anion attacks dimethyl sulfate, displacing methyl hydrogen sulfate forming 2‑methoxyacetic acid (CH₃O‑CH₂‑COOH). Typical conditions: NaOH (1‑2 eq) in aqueous or mixed aqueous‑organic solvent (e.g., THF/H₂O) at 0 °C to rt; dimethyl sulfate added dropwise; work‑up yields methyl hydrogen sulfate as the acidic by‑product.

Oxymercuration–demercuration of 4‑methyl‑1‑pentene. Mercuric acetate adds across the C=C to a organomercury intermediate; subsequent reduction with NaBH₄ replaces the HgOAc group with hydrogen, delivering the Markovnikov alcohol 4‑methyl‑2‑pentanol. Conditions: CH₂Cl₂ or THF, Hg(OAc)₂ (0.5–1 eq), H₂O (excess), 0 °C to rt, followed by NaBH₄ (2–3 eq) in methanol at 0 °C to rt.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation; aqueous barium nitrate reacts with potassium tellurate, producing insoluble barium tellurate and soluble potassium nitrate; performed in water, often with gentle heating to improve crystallization, no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (deoxygenation) of 2‑pentanol to pentane. The secondary alcohol is reduced in the presence of H₂ and a metal catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni, Pd/C, or PtO₂), generating pentane and water as the only by‑product. Typical conditions: H₂ 20–50 atm, catalyst loading 5 wt %, temperature 80–120 °C in a suitable solvent (e.g., ethanol or cyclohexane).

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction of dysprosium nitrate with sodium hydroxide. In aqueous solution, three equivalents of NaOH neutralize the nitrate salt, forming soluble NaNO₃ and insoluble dysprosium(III) hydroxide precipitate, Dy(OH)₃. Conducted at ambient temperature with aqueous media; the solid is filtered and washed.

Metallothermic reduction (single‑displacement) of zirconium tetrabromide by aluminum; purpose is to obtain metallic zirconium and aluminum bromide; key transformation is Zr^4+ reduced to Zr⁰ while Al is oxidized to Al^3+; performed at high temperature (≈800‑1000 °C) in a sealed tube or furnace under inert atmosphere; solid‑state reaction, no solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of phenethyl bromide by hydrazine to give phenelzine (phenethylhydrazine) with HBr as by‑product; typically refluxed in ethanol or isopropanol; a base such as pyridine or triethylamine is often added to scavenge the released HBr; no external catalyst required.

Double‑displacement/precipitation; purpose: removal of iodide as insoluble AgI and conversion of mercury(II) to nitrate salt. In aqueous solution, dipotassium tetraiodomercurate(II) exchanges its potassium ions with nitrate from AgNO3; insoluble AgI precipitates while Hg(NO3)2 and KNO3 remain dissolved. Carry out at ambient temperature in water; no special solvent or catalyst required, filtration isolates AgI.

Metal‑acid reduction of the nitro group in 2‑amino‑4‑nitrophenol using tin(II) chloride in hydrochloric acid; converts the –NO₂ to –NH₂ yielding 2,4‑diaminophenol; carried out in aqueous acidic solution, heated to 60‑80 °C; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Oxidative halogenation of tetramethyllead with bromine gas, producing methyl bromide and lead(II) bromide; key step is oxidation of Pb(IV) to Pb(II) while each methyl group is halogenated; performed in an inert organic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform at 0‑5 °C under stirring; no catalyst needed.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 4‑phenylphenol using a mixture of concentrated nitric acid and sulfuric acid; installs a nitro group para to the existing phenyl substituent to give 4‑(4‑nitrophenyl)phenol; reaction mixture kept at 0‑5 °C during addition then warmed to 50‑70 °C; the mixed acids act as both solvent andating medium; purpose is aromatic functionalisation.

Direct oxidation of iridium metal by ozone to form iridium dioxide with concomitant release of oxygen; Ir⁰ is oxidized to Ir⁴⁺ in IrO₂; carried out by passing a stream of O₃ over heated Ir (≈200‑300 °C); gaseous reagents only, no solvent; provides a route to high‑purity IrO₂.

Acid displacement/halogenation; concentrated hydrochloric acid protonates and chlorinates arsenic triselenide, yielding volatile arsenic trichloride (AsCl3) and hydrogen selenide gas (H2Se); carried out by adding solid As2Se3 to hot 6–12 M HCl, often under reflux; water/HCl solution as medium, no catalyst.

Base‑promoted dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination) of 2‑bromobutanamide with potassium tert‑butoxide; purpose is to form the α,β‑unsaturated amide (2‑butenamide). Key transformation: abstraction of the β‑hydrogen by t‑BuO⁻ and concomitant loss of Br⁻ to give the C=C double bond, producing potassium bromide and tert‑butanol as by‑products. Performed in aprotic polar solvents such as THF or DMF at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; stoichiometric KOt‑Bu (1.1–1.5 eq) is used.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation: aqueous ammonium hydroxide reacts with cadmium sulfate, the hydroxide ions replace the sulfate, precipitating cadmium hydroxide while forming soluble ammonium sulfate. Performed in water at ambient temperature, stirring; no catalyst required.

Thermal dehydration of formamide; a high‑temperature decomposition that converts formamide into hydrogen cyanide and water. Typically performed by heating neat formamide to 200–300 °C, often under reduced pressure to remove the gaseous HCN; no additional solvent or catalyst is required.

Acid–base salt formation (hydrochloride): protonation of the basic amine group of tulobuterol by hydrochloric acid yields tulobuterol·HCl salt. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution, often at 0 °C to 25 °C, followed by solvent removal to isolate the hydrochloride; no catalyst needed.

Acid quench of sodium borohydride (redox/acid‑base): dilute sulfuric acid protonates the borohydride anion, releasing hydrogen gas and oxidizing BH₄⁻ to boric acid while forming sodium sulfate. Conducted in ice‑cold water to control vigorous H₂ evolution; no catalyst required.

Redox oxidation of hydrazine by sodium hypochlorite (bleach); employed for wastewater treatment or laboratory destruction of hydrazine. In aqueous alkaline solution, N₂H₄ + NaOCl → N₂ + NaCl + 2 H₂O (overall stoichiometry may vary). Reaction is carried out at low temperature (0–25 °C) to avoid runaway; basic conditions (NaOH added) help control the reaction; water is the solvent and NaOCl solution provides the oxidant.

Metathesis precipitation: aqueous sodium sulfate exchanges anions with lead(II) chloride, producing insoluble lead(II) sulfate precipitate and soluble sodium chloride. Performed at room temperature in water with stirring; no catalyst.

Halide‑thiocyanate exchange (metathesis) precipitation: copper(I) bromide reacts with potassium thiocyanate in water or aqueous ethanol, swapping ligands to give insoluble copper(I) thiocyanate and soluble potassium bromide. Mild heating may aid precipitation; no catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation of lanthanum carbonate; aqueous lanthanum(III) nitrate reacts with sodium carbonate, yielding solid La₂(CO₃)₃ and soluble sodium nitrate; done in water with stirring at room temperature, no catalyst.

Base‑mediated deprotonation (formation of a lithium phosphide): lithium diisopropylamide abstracts the phosphorus‑bound hydrogen of diphenylphosphine, producing lithium diphenylphosphide and diisopropylamine. Typically carried out in dry THF at –78 °C under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Redox acid-base reaction. Purpose is generating sodium alkoxide and hydrogen gas. Key transformation: Deprotonation of 1-butanol by sodium metal, forming sodium butoxide. Conducted at room temperature, typically in anhydrous ammonia or ethanol as solvent. Hydrogen gas evolved.

This is an acid-base neutralization reaction to regenerate hydrogen cyanide (HCN) from its salt (lithium cyanide) using a strong acid (HCl). Key transformation includes protonation of the cyanide ion. Reaction occurs in aqueous solution under ambient conditions with no catalyst needed.

Thionation (sulfurization) of the carbonyl group: Lawesson’s reagent converts 1,1’-carbonyldiimidazole to its thio analogue (1,1’-thiocarbonyldiimidazole) while dimethyl sulfide is liberated; typically performed under inert atmosphere at reflux in anhydrous toluene or THF, no additional catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of 2‑ethylpyridine using mixed nitric/sulfuric acids. Generates the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) which substitutes the hydrogen at the 3‑position of the pyridine ring, yielding 2‑ethyl‑3‑nitropyridine. Conducted at 0–5 °C then warmed to room temperature; concentrated H₂SO₄ serves as solvent and catalyst; no additional catalyst required.

Single‑displacement redox (metal displacement) reaction; zinc reduces Pb(II) to metallic lead while being oxidized to Zn(II), yielding zinc acetate; Pb(CH3COO)2·3H2O + Zn → Pb(s) + Zn(CH3COO)2 + 3 H2O; carried out in aqueous lead acetate solution, often heated or under reflux to enhance rate; no catalyst, water solvent.

Oxidative dissolution of germanium by hot concentrated sulfuric acid; redox oxidation yielding GeO₂ and sulfur dioxide. Key transformation: Ge → Ge⁴⁺ (GeO₂) and H₂SO₄ → SO₂. Performed with 95–98 % H₂SO₄, heating to 150–200 °C (often in a reflux apparatus). Aqueous/acidic medium; no catalyst required.

Radical benzylic bromination with N‑bromosuccinimide; purpose is to replace the benzylic hydrogen of 1‑methyl‑4‑nitrobenzene with bromine, yielding 4‑(bromomethyl)nitrobenzene. Key transformation: NBS provides a source of Br· radicals that abstract the benzylic H, forming a benzylic radical that recombines with Br· to give the bromomethyl product; succinimide is formed as by‑product. Typical conditions: CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂ solvent, ambient or reflux temperature, with a radical initiator (light or AIBN); reaction performed under nitrogen to avoid side oxidation.

Acid‑base neutralization/precipitation: Phosphoric acid reacts with aluminum hydroxide to form aluminum tris(dihydrogen phosphate) and water; carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to dissolve reactants, no catalyst needed.

Metathesis (double‑displacement) precipitation. Reacts gadolinium sulfate with ammonium fluoride to precipitate insoluble gadolinium trifluoride while forming soluble ammonium sulfate in solution. Performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature or with gentle heating (50–80 °C) to improve crystallization. No catalyst; water serves as solvent.

Oxidation of a thioether to a sulfone; excess m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) oxidizes allyl methyl sulfide to allyl methyl sulfone, producing m‑chlorobenzoic acid as the reduced by‑product; usually run in anhydrocarbon solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; the reaction proceeds through a sulfoxide intermediate but excess oxidant gives the sulfone directly.

Lewis‑acid mediated ether cleavage (dealkylation): Boron tribromide cleaves tert‑butyl phenyl ether to give phenol and tert‑butyl bromide; usually conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in anhydrous dichloromethane under nitrogen, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Ligand exchange/complexation precipitation; NiCl2·6H2O is treated with acetylacetone and NaOH (typically 2 equivalents) to deprotonate the β‑diketonate, producing nickel(II) acetylacetonate Ni(acac)2, NaCl and water; commonly carried out in ethanol/water mixture under reflux; no additional catalyst needed.

Duff ortho‑formylation of phenols: Hexamethylenetetramine and trifluoroacetic acid convert phenol to salicylaldehyde, generating ammonium trifluoroacetate and water; the reaction is run neat in excess TFA at 80–100 °C (reflux), no metal catalyst required.

Nucleophilic substitution/hydrolysis of a dihaloalkane: 1,1′‑Dichlorononane reacts with aqueous NaOH to give 1,9‑nonanediol and sodium chloride; performed in aqueous solution at reflux, sometimes with a phase‑transfer catalyst to enhance rate.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an alkyl bromide: Hydrogen gas reduces cyclooctyl bromide to cyclooctane with concomitant formation of HBr; typically carried out under H₂ pressure (10–50 atm) using a Pd/C, Raney Ni or Pt catalyst in ethanol or methanol at ambient or mild elevated temperature.

Finkelstein halogen exchange (SN2) converting a secondary bromide to the corresponding iodide. NaI provides I− which attacks the carbon bearing Br, displacing Br− to give 1‑iodo‑2‑methoxypropane; NaBr precipitates out. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as dry acetone, often refluxed; removal of NaBr drives the reaction to completion.

Fischer esterification; purpose is to form the ester 2‑ethylbutyl benzoate from benzoic acid and 2‑ethylbutanol; key transformation is condensation of the carboxylic acid and the primary alcohol with loss of water; typically performed under reflux with a catalytic amount of a strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) in a non‑polar solvent such as toluene or benzene, often using a Dean‑Stark apparatus to continuously remove water.

Hydrolysis of phenylacetyl chloride to phenylacetic acid; a classic acid‑chloride hydrolysis. Conducted in aqueous medium, often at 0 °C to room temperature, sometimes with a two‑phase system (ether/water) to control HCl evolution; the reaction may be quenched with dilute acid after completion.

Fischer esterification between propylene glycol and stearic acid yielding propylene glycol monostearate and water; acid catalyst such as H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, heated to 150‑180 °C with continuous removal of water (Dean‑Stark) in a non‑polar solvent like toluene or xylene; the mono‑ester serves as a surfactant.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of N‑methylformamide to methylamine and formic acid; purpose: cleavage of the amide bond to recover the amine; key transformation: water attacks the carbonyl carbon, followed by loss of formic acid; typical conditions: reflux in aqueous HCl (1–2 M) or NaOH (base hydrolysis) for several hours, solvent is water or water/ethanol mixture.

Conversion of phenol to aryl chloride (chlorination via thionyl chloride); thionyl chloride reacts with 4‑hydroxyphenylacetone to replace the hydroxyl with chlorine, yielding 4‑chlorophenylacetone. Typical procedure: add SOCl₂ (excess) dropwise to a solution of the phenol in dry pyridine (or dichloromethane) at 0 °C, then stir at rt for 1–2 h; pyridine acts as base and solvent, and the reaction gases (SO₂, HCl) are vented.

Nucleophilic alkylation (Williamson‑type ester synthesis) of the benzoate anion with benzyl bromide using a phase‑transfer catalyst. Benzoic acid is deprotonated (often in situ with aqueous base), the benzoate is transferred into the organic phase by a quaternary ammonium salt (e.g., TBAB) and reacts SN2 with benzyl bromide to afford benzyl benzoate, releasing HBr. Conducted in a biphasic system (water/organic solvent such as toluene) at mild heating (50–80 °C).

Acid‑base neutralization forming a basic salt; aluminum hydroxide reacts with acetic acid to give basic aluminum acetate (hydroxy‑diacetate) and water. Conducted in aqueous media, often at ambient temperature with stirring; no special reagents required.

Double‑displacement acid‑base metathesis; calcium lactate reacts with sodium hydroxide to exchange cations, precipitating calcium hydroxide and forming sodium lactate in solution. Key transformation is ion exchange: Ca²⁺ pairs with OH⁻ to give Ca()₂ (insoluble) while Na⁺ pairs with lactate anion. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with vigorous stirring; the calcium hydroxide can be filtered off after formation.

Thermal decomposition of a metal nitrate; yields a basic oxide and gaseous products; Ba(NO3)2 → BaO + 2 NO2 + ½ O2 (balanced as 2 Ba(NO3)2 → 2 BaO + 4 NO2 + O2); performed by strong heating (≈500‑600 °C) in a furnace; no solvent required.

Curtius rearrangement (amine synthesis) of 2‑(furan‑2‑yl)acetic acid. The carboxylic acid reacts with diphenylphosphoryl azide (DPPA) in the presence of triethylamine to generate an acyl azide, which thermally rearranges to an isocyanate and is subsequently hydrolyzed to give 2‑(furan‑2‑yl)ethan‑1‑amine. Typical conditions: aprotic solvent (e.g., THF or CH₂Cl₂), 0 °C to rt, followed by aqueous work‑up.

Reductive dehalogenation (sodium metal reduction); converts 1,2-dichlorocyclopropane to cyclopropene by eliminating two chloride atoms as NaCl; typically performed in dry ether under reflux with excess Na metal; no catalyst required; purpose is to generate a strained alkene from a vicinal dihalide.

Acid–base reaction with carbonate; benzoic acid reacts with potassium carbonate, producing potassium benzoate, water, and CO₂ gas. Carried out in aqueous medium, usually with mild heating to evolve CO₂; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction between zinc selenite and sodium hydroxide. Two equivalents of NaOH convert ZnSeO₃ to soluble Na₂SeO₃ while insoluble Zn(OH)₂ precipitates. Performed in aqueous medium at ambient temperature with stirring.

Transfer hydrogenation (reductive amination) of 4‑nitrosalicylic acid using formic acid as hydrogen donor in the presence of Pd(II) chloride. Formic acid decomposes to CO₂ and H₂ on Pd, reducing the nitroso group to an amino group to afford 4‑aminosalicylic acid, while Pd(II) is reduced to Pd(0). Conducted in a polar solvent (e.g., water/ethanol), typically at 70–90 °C under inert atmosphere.

Oxidative dissolution (redox) of iron selenide with dilute nitric acid; the acid oxidizes FeSe, converting iron to soluble iron(III) nitrate and selenium to selenous acid while nitrogen monoxide gas is released. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient to moderately elevated temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Mitsunobu esterification; converts a primary alcohol to an ester using a carboxylic acid, triphenylphosphine and a dialkyl azodicarboxylate (DEAD). The alcohol is activated as a phosphonium intermediate, then displaced by the benzoate anion, giving 4‑bromobenzyl benzoate with inversion of configuration (if stereogenic). Typical conditions: dry THF (or dioxane), 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; stoichiometric PPh₃ and DEAD, benzoic acid (1.1 eq). No additional catalyst required.

Peracid oxidation of a thioether; m‑chloroperbenzoic acid (m‑CPBA) oxidizes ethyl phenyl sulfide to the corresponding sulfone (ethyl phenyl sulfone) while being reduced to m‑chlorobenzoic acid. Conducted in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is usually quenched with aqueous sodium sulfite before work‑up.

Aqueous metathesis/precipitation (double‑replacement) between phosphoric acid and yttrium(III) chloride. The strong acid protonates chloride, forming hydrochloric acid, while yttrium combines with phosphate to give insoluble yttrium phosphate (YPO₄) which precipitates. Performed in water, often with gentle heating and stirring; the solid is isolated by filtration and washing.

Thermal decomposition of molybdenum hexacarbonyl to elemental molybdenum and carbon monoxide. Conducted by heating Mo(CO)₆ under vacuum or inert gas (e.g., N₂ or Ar) at temperatures above ~200 °C (often 300–400 °C), resulting in clean liberation of CO and deposition of fine Mo metal.

Reduction of N‑(4‑bromophenyl)acetamide with lithium aluminium hydride; yields 4‑bromoaniline and ethanol (from the hydride reacting with the carbonyl); performed in dry ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere (N₂); excess LiAlH₄ is quenched with careful addition of water then dilute acid during work‑up.

Pechmann condensation of 4‑methylphenol with ethyl acetoacetate to afford 4‑methylumbelliferone (a coumarin) and ethanol as by‑product. Requires a strong Brønsted acid catalyst (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH, or methanesulfonic acid) and heating (80–120 °C). Reaction can be run neat or in a high‑boiling solvent such as toluene; removal of ethanol drives the equilibrium forward.

Reductive metal‑mediated preparation of a zero‑valent nickel complex; Zn metal reduces NiCl₂ in the presence of excess 1,5‑cyclooctadiene (COD) to give bis(1,5‑COD)nickel, Ni(COD)₂, with ZnCl₂ as the by‑product; the reaction is run in dry THF or diethyl ether under nitrogen or argon at rt.

Schiff‑base formation (imine condensation) between benzaldehyde and aniline to give N‑benzylideneaniline. Conducted in a polar protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) or under solvent‑free conditions with reflux; a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., acetic acid) facilitates imine formation. Water formed is removed by azeotropic distillation (Dean‑Stark apparatus) or by using molecular sieves.

Double displacement precipitation; synthesis of indium(III) phosphate from indium(III) chloride and sodium phosphate; key transformation InCl₃ + Na₃PO₄ → InPO₄↓ + 3 NaCl; performed in water with stirring at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; solvent water; no catalyst

Oxidative nitration; converts trinitromethane to tetranitromethane, a high‑energy oxidizer. Performed with excess fuming (concentrated) nitric acid, which acts as both solvent and nitrating/oxidizing agent; typically carried out at 0 °C to 25 °C under stirring to control exotherm.

Acid‑mediated ionization; protonates triphenylmethanol and eliminates water to generate the trityl cation, which is trapped as the hexafluorophosphate salt. Conducted with hexafluorophosphoric acid (or HPF6) in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as dry dichloromethane or acetonitrile at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere.

Halogen exchange / Grignard preparation; lithium chloride abstracts the iodide from isopropylmagnesium iodide to give the more reactive mixed halide isopropylmagnesium chloride (chloroisopropylmagnesium). Reaction is run in anhydrous ether (THF or Et₂O) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen or argon.

Photocatalytic aerobic oxidation; TiO₂ (usually P‑25) under UV illumination activates molecular oxygen to oxidize 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural to 2,5‑furandicarboxaldehyde (dialdehyde). Typically performed as a suspension of TiO₂ in acetonitrile or water, O₂ bubbled through, with irradiation at 350 nm; temperature kept at 25–40 °C.

Thermal cracking (beta‑scission) of a branched alkane; high‑temperature pyrolysis cleaves 2,3‑dimethylbutane to give ethane (alkane) and 2‑methylpropene (alkene). Conducted in a tubular furnace at 500–800 °C under inert gas (e.g., N₂ or He) to prevent oxidation.

Acid–base salt formation; glycine reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to give the crystalline salt triglycine sulfate. Key transformation: protonation of the amino group and formation of the sulfate di‑anion complex. Usually performed by adding solid glycine to cold, concentrated H2SO4, stirring at 0–30 °C, then evaporating or cooling to crystallize the triglycine sulfate. No catalyst; water is the medium.

Exothermic oxidation (combustion) of hydrazine; hydrazine is oxidized by O2 to nitrogen gas and water. Serves as a high‑energy propellant reaction and as a laboratory method for generating N2. Conducted in the gas phase at elevated temperature (often >200 °C) or catalyzed on metal surfaces (Pt, Pd, Cu); no solvent, no added catalyst if heating is sufficient.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis (saponification); water attacks the carbonyl of 2‑propoxyethyl acetate, yielding acetic acid and 2‑propoxyethanol. Performed in aqueous acid (e.g., 1 M HCl) or dilute base, refluxing for several hours in a mixed solvent (water/ethanol or water/acetone).

Metathesis (double displacement) reaction used to prepare ammonium salicylate; ion exchange converts Na⁺ to NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻ to Na⁺. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; the products are soluble NaCl and sparingly soluble ammonium salicylate which can be crystallized.

Acidolysis (protonolysis) of a metal‑acetylacetonate complex; concentrated HNO₃ protonates the β‑diketonate ligands of europium(III) acetylacetonate, liberating 2,4‑pentanedione (acetylacetone) and forming soluble europium nitrate. Usually carried out by refluxing the complex in aqueous nitric acid; water is the solvent and no additional catalyst is required.

Hydrolysis of a sulfonyl chloride; benzenesulfonyl chloride reacts with water to regenerate benzenesulfonic acid and release HCl. This is a classic acyl‑chloride hydrolysis. Performed in aqueous medium, often at 0‑25 °C to control exotherm; the resulting acid can be neutralized with a base if desired.

Double‑displacement precipitation to obtain copper(II) oxalate. Sodium oxalate solution is mixed with copper(II) sulfate solution, producing insoluble copper(II) oxalate precipitate and soluble sodium sulfate. Reaction is conducted in water at room temperature with stirring; the solid is filtered and washed.

N‑alkylation (SN2) of tryptamine with 1‑bromobutane in the presence of potassium carbonate base, yielding N,N‑dibutyltryptamine and KBr. Performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as DMF or acetonitrile, under reflux or gentle heating; K₂CO₃ neutralizes the released HBr and drives the substitution.

Acid‑catalyzed ether formation (Fischer ether synthesis). Cyclopentanol reacts with methanol in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄, producing cyclopentyl methyl ether and water. The mixture is refluxed, water is removed (e.g., by azeotropic distillation), and the ether is isolated by extraction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of ethylene glycol with n‑butyl bromide under basic conditions, forming 2‑butoxyethanol (butyl cellosolve) and NaBr, with water as by‑product. Carried out in aqueous NaOH (often with excess ethylene glycol) at elevated temperature (50‑80 °C); phase‑transfer catalysts may be used to improve yield.

Oxidative cyclization (iodine‑mediated) – converts o‑aminothiophenol into benzothiazole by simultaneous formation of C–N and C–S bonds; iodine acts as oxidant and is reduced to hydrogen iodide. Typically carried out in refluxing ethanol or glacial acetic acid, sometimes with a catalytic amount of base (e.g., pyridine) to neutralize HI.

Nucleophilic substitution of phenolic OH with chlorine using thionyl chloride – replaces the hydroxyl group of 2,4‑dinitrophenol with chloride to give 2,4‑dinitrophenyl chloride, generating HCl and SO₂ as gaseous by‑products. Conducted underhydrous conditions, often in pyridine (which serves as solvent and HCl scavenger) or dichloromethane, with reflux or gentle heating while nitrogen is purged.

Acid‑base decomposition of sodium hexafluorosilicate – aqueous hydrochloric acid protonates the SiF₆²⁻ anion, releasing silicon tetrafluoride gas and hydrofluoric acid while forming NaCl. Performed in aqueous HCl at room temperature or with mild heating; no catalyst required, water is the solvent and the reaction is usually conducted in a sealed apparatus to capture SiF₄.

Base‑promoted formation of a dithiocarbamate salt – dimethylamine attacks carbon disulfide in the presence of sodium ethoxide, yielding sodium dimethyldithiocarbamate; the ethoxide is protonated to give ethanol as a by‑product. Typical conditions involve stirring the reagents in dry ethanol at 0 °C to ambient temperature under nitrogen; no additional catalyst is needed.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution) of benzene with 2‑phenylacetyl fluoride using AlCl₃; purpose is to install a phenylacetyl carbonyl onto benzene, yielding 2‑phenylacetophenone. Key transformation: AlCl₃ activates the acyl fluoride to generate an acylium ion, which attacks benzene to form the aryl ketone, releasing HF. Typical conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1.2–2 equiv) in a dry, non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane, CS₂, or nitrobenzene, under nitrogen, at 0 °C to reflux. Reaction is quenched with ice‑water to hydrolyze the Al‑complex and isolate the ketone.

Reaction type: metal‑catalyzed cyclopropanation an alkene using a diazo compound (carbene transfer). Purpose: construction of a three‑membered cyclopropane ring bearing a carboxylate ester and two phenyl substituents. Key transformation: ethyl diazoacetate loses N₂ to generate a metal‑carbene which adds across the C=C double bond of 1,1‑diphenylethylene, forming ethyl 2,2‑diphenylcyclopropane‑1‑carboxylate. Typical conditions: 1–5 mol % Rh₂(OAc)₄ (or Cu(I) salts such as CuOTf) in dry dichloromethane, 0 °C to rt, under nitrogen; reaction time 1–4 h. Solvent: anhydrous CH₂Cl₂; sometimes addition of a base (e.g., triethylamine) to scavenge acid.

Direct combination (synthesis) of lithium sulfide – elemental lithium reduces elemental sulfur to form Li₂S (Li⁰ → Li⁺, S⁰ → S²⁻). Usually carried out in dry, aprotic solvents such as THF or diethyl ether under inert atmosphere; the mixture may be gently heated to initiate the reaction, and no catalyst is employed.

Solid-state redox synthesis; combines FeO (iron(II) oxide) and Fe2O3 (iron(III) oxide) at high temperature (≈1000 °C) in the solid phase to form mixed‑valence Fe3O4 (magnetite); no solvent or catalyst, often performed in air or inert atmosphere.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 2‑methylquinoline – platinum oxide (Adams catalyst) facilitates addition of hydrogen across the aromatic ring, giving 2‑methyl‑1,2,3,4‑tetrahydroquinoline. Conducted under hydrogen pressure (1–5 atm) in a solvent like ethanol or acetic acid at 25–80 °C; PtO₂ is the catalyst and the reaction proceeds via stepwise reduction of the heteroaromatic system.

Condensation (Debus‑Radziszewski) of 2‑aminoacetaldehyde with glyoxal to afford 2‑methylimidazole, eliminating water; cyclodehydration forms the imidazole ring; typically performed under acidic conditions (e.g., HCl or acetic acid) at reflux in ethanol or methanol, with acid catalyst promoting cyclization.

Nucleophilic substitution (Williamson ether synthesis) where morphine’s phenolic OH is deprotonated by NaOH and alkylated with ethyl chloride to give ethylmorphine; water and NaCl are by‑products; carried out in aqueous or alcoholic medium, often refluxing NaOH solution; base serves as the catalyst.

Oxidation of platinum(II) oxide (PtO) by molecular oxygen to form platinum(IV) oxide (PtO₂); solid‑state redox reaction performed by heating the mixture in an O₂ atmosphere at several hundred °C; no solvent or additional catalyst required.

Thermite (aluminothermic) redox reaction: elemental aluminum reduces iron(II,III) oxide (Fe₃O₄) to metallic iron while being oxidized to aluminum oxide (Al₂O₃); highly exothermic, initiated by ignition of mixed powders, carried out without solvent.

Acyl‑substitution forming a thioester: acetyl chloride reacts with butyl mercaptan to produce butyl thioacetate and HCl; usually conducted at 0 °C to room temperature in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, with a base (pyridine or triethylamine) to neutralize the released HCl.

Esterification (acetylation) of an allylic alcohol with acetic anhydride. Purpose: form the acetate ester 3‑hexenyl acetate. Key transformation: hydroxyl group → acetate ester, with formation of one equivalent of acetic acid. Typical conditions: reagents mixed in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, catalytic amount of pyridine or DMAP as base, 0 °C to rt, often under nitrogen.

Catalyzed anhydride synthesis: butyric acid reacts with acetic anhydride in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst (ZnCl₂) to give butyric anhydride and acetic acid; typically performed under reflux, often solvent‑free or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent like toluene; ZnCl₂ accelerates the acyl transfer.

Reaction type: Nucleophilic addition to a Weinreb amide (Grignard‑mediated ketone synthesis). Purpose: generate acetone from the Weinreb amide. Key transformation: methylmagnesium bromide adds to the carbonyl, the O‑Me‑NMe group chelates the Mg, preventing over‑addition and after work‑up releases acetone and N‑methoxy‑N‑methylamine. Typical conditions: anhydrous ether or THF, -78 °C to 0 °C, nitrogen atmosphere, 1–2 h. No additional catalyst.

Methanolysis (transesterification) of 2,2,2‑trifluoroethyl acetate; methanol attacks the ester carbonyl, displacing the trifluoroethyl alcohol and forming methyl acetate while releasing 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol. Carried out with excess methanol, often with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., p‑toluenesulfonic acid) or base (e.g., NaOMe), at reflux (65 °C) in methanol as both reactant and solvent.

Esterification of an acyl chloride with ethanol: yields ethyl 4‑methylpentanoate and HCl; performed analogously to the methanol case using dry ethanol (often with pyridine/Et₃N) at 0 °C to rt; the reaction is fast and the product is isolated by aqueous work‑up and distillation.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene; reduces the carbon–carbon double bond of 4‑ethylstyrene to give a fully saturated para‑diethylbenzene. Typically carried out with H2 (1–5 atm) over a metal catalyst such as Pd/C, PtO2 or Raney Ni in a protic solvent (ethanol, methanol) at 25–80 °C.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN1) hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl chloride; water attacks the carbocation formed from 3‑chloro‑3‑methylheptane to produce the tertiary alcohol 3‑methyl‑3‑heptanol and HCl. Usually performed by refluxing the chloride in aqueous acid or aqueous NaOH, followed by acid work‑up; temperature about 80–100 °C.

Acid‑induced decomposition of sodium germanate. Purpose: to recover germanium as germanium dioxide precipitate while converting sodium to soluble nitrate. Key transformation: Na₂GeO₃ reacts with HNO₃, producing solid GeO₂, NaNO₃ in solution, and water. Typical conditions: aqueous medium, excess HNO₃, gentle heating (50–80 °C) to promote precipitation. Solvent: water (nitric acid solution). No catalyst.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution) of 2‑isopropyl‑naphthalene with 2‑chloropropane in the presence of the Lewis acid AlCl₃. The reaction installs a second isopropyl group at the 6‑position, yielding 2,6‑diisopropylnaphthalene. Conducted under anhydrous conditions in a non‑coordinating solvent such as dry CH₂Cl₂ or CS₂, at 0 °C to reflux, with excess AlCl₃.

Strecker synthesis of an α‑amino acid; the aldehyde 5‑hydroxyvaleraldehyde reacts with NaCN and ammonium carbonate to form theitrile intermediate, which is then hydrolyzed (usually acid‑catalyzed) to give 2‑amino‑5‑hydroxyvaleric acid. Typical conditions: aqueous or alcoholic solution, ambient to reflux temperature for the cyanation step, followed by acidic hydrolysis (HCl, 60–100 °C).

Double‑displacement precipitation (metathesis) reaction; aqueous solutions of BaCl₂ and Ag₂SeO₃ exchange partners to precipitate insoluble AgCl (white solid) while forming soluble BaSeO₃. Carried out at room temperature in water; the AgCl precipitate is filtered off to isolate the product.

Acid anhydride exchange (acyl transfer); benzoic acid reacts with acetic anhydride to form benzoic anhydride while releasing acetic acid. Typically performed by refluxing the acids in an inert solvent such as toluene or chloroform, often with removal of the volatile acetic acid to drive the equilibrium; no metal catalyst required, though pyridine or DMAP can be used to accelerate the reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of an alkyl halide by sulfide ion to generate a thiol; 1‑chloropropane is displaced by HS⁻ (generated from Na₂S/H₂O) to give 1‑propanethiol and NaCl. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents like DMF, DMSO or ethanol at moderate temperatures (50‑80 °C); no additional catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ester hydrolysis; ethyl valerate is hydrolyzed by aqueous HCl to afford valeric (pentanoic) acid and ethanol. The reaction is refluxed in a mixture of water and the ester (or in an aqueous/alcoholic solvent) under strong acidic conditions; HCl itself serves as the catalyst.

Redox oxidation; hydrogen peroxide oxidizes lead(II) acetate to brown lead(IV) oxide (PbO₂) while acetic acid and water are formed. Usually carried out in aqueous medium, often mildly acidic, at 0–25 °C; H₂O₂ acts as the oxidant, no additional catalyst required.

Amide formation via acylation of an amine with an acid anhydride (Schotten‑Baumann type); N‑methylglycine (sarcosine) reacts with lauric anhydride to give N‑lauroylsarcosine (a surfactant) and liberates lauric acid. Usually carried out in a basic aqueous medium (e.g., NaHCO₃) or in anhydrous organic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane) with a base such as pyridine to neutralize the released acid.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (Friedel‑Crafts chlorination); tert‑butylbenzene undergoes para‑selective chlorination in the presence of chlorine gas and catalytic FeCl₃, producing p‑tert‑butylchlorobenzene and hydrogen chloride as a by‑product. Typical conditions are low temperature (0‑25 °C) in an inert solvent like carbon tetrachloride or dichloromethane; FeCl₃ acts as a Lewis‑acid catalyst.

Haloform (iodoform) reaction; converts a methyl ketone (methyl ethyl ketone) into triiodomethane (iodoform) and a carboxylate (sodium acetate). Performed in aqueous NaOH with elemental iodine; the mixture is stirred at 0 °C to reflux, often in water or aqueous ethanol. The base deprotonates the ketone, iodine halogenates the α‑methyl repeatedly, and the triiodomethyl anion collapses to CHI₃ while the carbonyl becomes acetate.

Neutralization (acid‑base) reaction; converts a strong base (RbOH) and a weak acid (acetic acid) into the corresponding salt (rubidium acetate) and water. Key transformation is proton transfer from acetic acid to hydroxide. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the solvent.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride; purpose is to convert the acidic functional group into an alcohol; the carbonyl of 2‑ethylhexanoic acid is reduced to give 2‑ethylhexanol; typically carried out in anhydrous ether (diethyl ether or THF) at 0 °C to reflux under nitrogen, followed by aqueous acidic work‑up.

Nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr); replaces the chloro substituent on a pyrazine ring with a cyano group to give cyanopyrazine. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at elevated temperature (80‑120 °C). Sodium cyanide provides the nucleophilic CN⁻; sodium chloride is the by‑product.

Carbamate formation via phosgene chemistry; methylamine reacts with phosgene to generate N‑methyl carbamoyl chloride, which then couples with 1‑naphthol to afford 1‑naphthyl N‑methylcarbamate. Conducted in an inert, non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at 0 °C to room temperature, often with a base such as pyridine or triethylamine to scavenge the liberated HCl.

Strong oxidative degradation of a thioether; potassium permanganate oxidizes the methyl group of methyl phenyl sulfide to carbon dioxide while converting the sulfide to benzenesulfonic acid. Carried out in aqueous alkaline medium (excess KOH formed in situ), typically under reflux. Manganese dioxide precipitates as the reduced MnO₂ by‑product.

Electrophilic demethylation of aryl methyl ethers; boron tribromide cleaves the three methoxy groups of 1,3,5‑trimethoxybenzene, yielding phloroglucinol (tri‑hydroxybenzene) and three equivalents of methyl bromide. Reaction is performed under anhydrous conditions in a non‑coordinating solvent such as CH₂Cl₂, starting at –78 °C and warming to 0 °C, with BBr₃ as the Lewis acid reagent.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an aromatic lactam; molecular hydrogen reduces the aromatic 4‑pyridone to the saturated lactam 4‑piperidone. Typically uses a heterogeneous catalyst (e.g., Pd/C, Raney Ni) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, under H₂ pressure of 20–50 bar at 50‑100 °C.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction; aqueous silver nitrate exchanges anion with gadolinium bromide, forming insoluble silver bromide precipitate and soluble gadolinium nitrate. Conducted in water at ambient temperature; the silver bromide can be filtered off, leaving the nitrate salt in solution.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation). Proton transfer from hydrochloric acid to the primary amine generates the ammonium chloride salt of 2‑phenylethylamine. Used to isolate or purify the amine as a water‑soluble solid. Typically carried out in aqueous or alcoholic solution (e.g., water, ethanol) at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Nitrosation via trans‑nitrosation (nitrosamine synthesis). The alkyl nitrite transfers a nitrosyl group (NO⁺) to aniline, forming N‑nitrosoaniline, while the alkoxy fragment is released as n‑pentanol. Conducted in a non‑aqueous organic solvent such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride, often at 0 °C to room temperature; no additional catalyst is needed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Sulfate anion from sodium sulfate exchanges with hydroxide from barium hydroxide, producing soluble sodium hydroxide and insoluble barium sulfate, which precipitates out. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature; no catalyst required.

Oxidation (redox) of mercury(I) to mercury(II). Chlorine gas oxidizes Hg₂Cl₂, breaking the Hg–Hg bond and yielding mercury(II) chloride; chloride ions are retained. Typically carried out in aqueous HCl or water with chlorine bubbled through the suspension; no catalyst needed.

Acid–metal displacement reaction of elemental erbium with aqueous hydrochloric acid; generates erbium(III) chloride and hydrogen gas; serves to prepare the soluble lanthanide chloride salt; usually performed in dilute HCl solution at 0 °C to reflux, with vigorous gas evolution; water is the solvent.

Halogen displacement (redox) reaction. Chlorine oxidizes bromide in nickel(II) bromide to molecular bromine while chloride replaces it, forming nickel(II) chloride and liquid bromine. Conducted in aqueous solution by passing Cl₂ gas over the nickel bromide solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Barium cation exchanges with lithium to give insoluble barium arsenate, which precipitates, while lithium nitrate remains in solution. Performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of a metal carbide; magnesium carbide reacts with water, cleaving the C≡C bond to give magnesium hydroxide precipitate and acetylene gas; carried out at room temperature or with mild heating, using water as both reagent and solvent; acetylene is collected as a gas, Mg(OH)₂ precipitates.

Electrophilic aromatic chlorination (substitution). Purpose: convert a trichlorobenzene to the fully chlorinated hexachlorobenzene. Key transformation: each chlorine atom from Cl2 replaces a hydrogen on the aromatic ring, generating three equivalents of HCl. Typical conditions: excess chlorine gas, elevated temperature (150‑250 °C) and often a Lewis‑acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃; reactions may be performed in a sealed tube under inert atmosphere. Common solvent: none required (gas‑phase) or inert liquid such as CCl₄ for slurry.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a primary alkyl chloride by cyanide ion. Purpose synthesize cyanomethyl methyl ether. Key transformation: NaCN attacks the electrophilic carbon bearing chlorine, displacing Cl⁻ to form the C‑CN bond; NaCl is produced as by‑product. Typical conditions: polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at 0 °C to ambient temperature, stoichiometric NaCN (often aqueous or in slight excess). No catalyst required; reaction may be monitored by TLC or GC.

Decarboxylation; removes the 2‑carboxyl group of 5,6‑dihydroxyindole‑2‑carboxylic acid to give 5,6‑dihydroxyindole and CO₂. Usually performed by heating the acid (150–200 °C) in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., diphenyl ether) or under aqueous reflux; no catalyst required, though metal salts (Cu²⁺) can accelerate.

Alcoholysis (trans‑silylation) with isopropanol; the ethoxy group is replaced by an isopropoxy group to give isopropoxytrimethylsilane and ethanol. Reaction proceeds by heating ethoxytrimethylsilane in isopropanol, sometimes with a catalytic amount of a Brønsted acid or a base such as imidazole; no special solvent is required beyond the alcohol.

Formation of an alkyl nitrite via nitrosylation of an alcohol. Purpose: generate isobutyl nitrite, a nitrite ester. Key transformation: nitrosyl chloride (NOCl) reacts with the hydroxyl group, producing isobutyl nitrite and HCl. Typical conditions: low temperature (0‑5 °C) to control side reactions, inert organic solvent such as CCl₄ or CH₂Cl₂; a base (e.g., pyridine or NaHCO₃) is often added to neutralize the liberated HCl. Reaction proceeds without catalyst.

Electrophilic addition of chlorine across a carbon–carbon double bond. Purpose: install two vicinal chlorine atoms on the alkene. Key transformation: Cl₂ adds anti across the C=C of 2,3‑dimethyl‑2‑butene to give 2,3‑dichloro‑2,3‑dimethylbutane. Typical conditions: room temperature, inert solvent (CCl₄, CHCl₃, or dichloromethane). No catalyst needed; reaction is rapid and may be stopped by addition of sodium thiosulfate to quench excess chlorine.

Chlorination with phosphorus pentachloride; similar to reaction 1, benzenesulfinic acid is converted to benzenesulfonyl chloride while generating POCl3 and HCl as by‑products; PCl5 supplies chloride and abstracts oxygen; typical conditions: dry, non‑protic solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2, CS2) at 0 °C to room temperature, often under nitrogen; reaction mixture is stirred until gas evolution ceases.

Acid‑base hydrolysis (neutralization) of a metal nitride. Purpose: generate ammonia gas and a soluble sulfate salt. Key transformation: strontium nitride reacts with sulfuric acid; nitride ions are protonated to release NH₃, while Sr²⁺ combines with SO₄²⁻ to precipitate SrSO₄. Typical conditions: aqueous H₂SO₄ (conc. or 2‑6 M), controlled addition of solid Sr₃N₂ with stirring; gentle heating (50‑80 °C) speeds gas evolution. No catalyst required; solid SrSO₄ is insoluble and can be filtered off.

Redox (halogen–sulfide exchange); purpose: convert magnesium sulfide to magnesium iodide and elemental sulfur; key transformation: I2 oxidizes S²⁻ to S⁰ while forming MgI2; conditions: dry solid‑state or reflux in dry ether/THF, inert atmosphere; no catalyst required.

Reductive amination of an aromatic aldehyde; purpose: synthesize vanillylamine from vanillin; key transformation: condensation of vanillin with ammonium acetate to an imine followed by reduction with sodium triacetoxyborohydride to the primary amine, generating acetic acid; typical conditions: room temperature, dichloromethane or acetonitrile, inert atmosphere; NaBH(OAc)3 is the reducing agent.

Acid‑catalyzed hydration of (E)-oct‑2‑ene: water adds across the double bond in the presence of a strong Brønsted acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, p‑TsOH) to give 2‑octanol (Markovnikov product). Conducted at 50–80 °C in a mixed aqueous/organic medium (often water with a co‑solvent like methanol or dichloromethane). The acid protonates the alkene, forming a carbocation that is captured by water, followed by deprotonation to afford the alcohol.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; purpose: convert isobutyl alcohol to isobutyric acid; key transformation: KMnO4 oxidizes the alcohol first to aldehyde then to the acid, with MnO2 precipitating; typical conditions: aqueous KMnO4, reflux, neutral to mildly basic pH; water is the solvent, no additional catalyst.

Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis (thiourea cleavage). N‑(2‑chlorophenyl)thiourea is treated with aqueous NaOH (5–10 % w/v) and heated to reflux (80–100 °C) for 1–3 h. The thiourea bond is hydrolysed, affording 2‑chloroaniline, sodium thiocyanate and water as the products. No additional catalyst is required; water is the solvent.

Double‑displacement metathesis (precipitation) reaction; aqueous lithium chloride reacts with silver nitrate to precipitate insoluble silver chloride while forming soluble lithium nitrate; performed in water at room temperature; no catalyst needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of a nitro aromatic; purpose: reduce p‑nitroacetanilide to p‑aminoacetanilide; key transformation: H2/Pd‑C reduces –NO2 to –NH2, producing water as by‑product; typical conditions: 1–5 atm H2, 10 % Pd on carbon, ethanol or methanol solvent, 25–50 °C; palladium on carbon is the catalyst.

Acid‑base deprotonation to form a metal acetylide; purpose: generate sodium acetylide for use as a nucleophile; key transformation: NaNH2 abstracts the terminal proton of acetylene, yielding NaC≡CH and NH3; typical conditions: liquid ammonia or THF, low temperature (‑78 °C to 0 °C), inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst.

Base‑induced dehydrohalogenation (E2 elimination); potassium hydride abstracts a β‑hydrogen from allyl chloride forming propene and potassium chloride. Typically performed in dry polar aprotic solvents such as THF or DMF under inert atmosphere; solid K‑H is added to a solution of allyl chloride at ambient to reflux temperatures.

Acid‑carbonate neutralization; hydrochloric acid reacts with rubidium hydrogen carbonate, releasing carbon dioxide gas, forming water and rubidium chloride. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; no special catalyst required.

Nucleophilic halogen exchange (SN2 substitution); fluoride ion from potassium fluoride displaces chloride on methyl chloroacetate to give methyl fluoroacetate and potassium chloride. Often carried out in polar aprotic solvents (acetone, DMF, DMSO) at reflux or elevated temperature; excess KF may be used to drive the reaction.

Hydrolytic ring opening of (4S)-1,3‑thiazolidine‑4‑carboxylic acid back to L‑cysteine and formaldehyde; a reverse of the thiazolidine formation. Conducted in water with either dilute acid (pH ≈ 2–3) or dilute base (pH ≈ 9–10) under gentle heating (50–80 °C) to accelerate cleavage.

Metallothermic (aluminothermic) reduction; solid aluminum reduces uranium trioxide to metallic uranium while being oxidized to aluminum oxide. Conducted at high temperature (typically >1500 °C) in an inert or vacuum atmosphere; no solvent or catalyst, reaction proceeds as a solid‑state thermite process.

Oxidation; converts the aldehyde group of 1H‑pyrrole‑2‑carbaldehyde to a carboxylic acid. Key transformation: –CHO → –COOH. Typically performed with 30 % aqueous hydrogen peroxide in glacial acetic acid, 0 °C to room temperature, stirring for 1–2 h. Acetic acid acts as solvent and acid catalyst; water is generated as by‑product.

Proton transfer (acid‑base) between a super‑acid and a strong non‑nucleophilic amide base; trifluoromethanesulfonic acid protonates lithium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide, yielding bis(trimethylsilyl)amine and lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate. Performed in dry aprotic solvents such as THF or toluene at 0 °C to rt under inert gas; no additional catalyst required.

Sulfonation of an amine (formation of cyclamic acid); cyclohexylamine reacts with chlorosulfonic acid to produce cyclohexylsulfonic acid (cyclamic acid) and hydrochloric acid. The addition is done at 0 °C to control exotherm, then the mixture is allowed to warm to ambient temperature. The reaction is typically carried out in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane or directly in the chlorosulfonic acid; no catalyst is required. The product is the sulfonic acid form of the amine, used in acid‑base chemistry.

Chlorination of a primary alcohol with thionyl chloride; replaces the –OH of 3‑hydroxypropanenitrile by chlorine to give 3‑chloropropionitrile. Key transformation: HO–CH₂–CH₂–C≡N + SOCl₂ → ClCH₂–CH₂–C≡N + SO₂ + HCl. Typical conditions: addition of SOCl₂ dropwise to a solution of the substrate in anhydrous dichloromethane or pyridine, 0 °C to room temperature, stirring 1–2 h. By‑product gases (SO₂, HCl) are vented.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; purpose is preparation of thallium(I) sulfide, a binary metal sulfide. Elemental thallium reacts with elemental sulfur in a 2:1 molar ratio to give Tl₂S. Performed by heating the solid reactants together, often in a sealed quartz tube or under an inert atmosphere (argon) at temperatures above the melting point of thallium (~304 °C) to ensure intimate contact and complete reaction.

Oxidation reaction using Dess‑Martin periodinane; purpose is selective oxidation of ferruginol (a phenolic diterpene) to sugiol (a ketone). The periodinane transfers an oxygen atom to the secondary alcohol of ferruginol, converting it to a carbonyl while being reduced to 2‑iodobenzoic acid. Typically carried out in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to room temperature, under nitrogen, with 1.1–1.5 equivalents of DMP and mild stirring; no additional catalyst is required.

Acid‑carbonate reaction between hydrogen bromide and sodium bicarbonate; purpose is gas evolution and salt formation; key transformation: HBr + NaHCO₃ → NaBr + H₂CO₃, which immediately decomposes to CO₂ + H₂O; overall: HBr + NaHCO₃ → NaBr + CO₂↑ + H₂O; typical conditions: aqueous solution at room temperature; water as solvent, no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution (nitration); purpose is introduction of two nitro groups onto benzoic acid to afford 3,5‑dinitrobenzoic acid. The mixed acid (conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄) generates the nitronium ion (NO₂⁺) which attacks the aromatic ring meta to the carboxyl group. Conducted by adding benzoic acid to the chilled acid mixture (0–5 °C), then allowing the temperature to rise to 40–50 °C for completion. The reagents themselves serve as solvent; no external catalyst is needed.

Acid–base (salt formation) reaction; purpose is production of calcium bisulfite, an intermediate in SO₂ scrubbing, with concomitant release of CO₂. Sulfur dioxide dissolves in water to form sulfite/bisulfite, which reacts with calcium carbonate to give Ca(HSO₃)₂ and CO₂ gas. Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, often in a gas‑absorption tower; stirring and excess water aid dissolution and conversion. No catalyst required.

Strong reduction; ketone reduction to secondary alcohol using lithium aluminium hydride. LiAlH4 (1–2 eq) in dry ether (THF or diethyl ether) reduces the carbonyl of 1‑hydroxybutan‑2‑one to afford 1,2‑butanediol. Reaction is performed under nitrogen at 0 °C then refluxed gently; after completion the mixture is cautiously quenched with water then dilute acid and the diol is isolated.

Acid–base displacement (protonation of a formate salt); used to generate formic acid from its sodium salt. The reaction proceeds by proton transfer from sulfuric acid to the formate anion, yielding formic acid and sodium hydrogen sulfate. Typically carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; excess dilute H₂SO₄ is often used, and the mixture is stirred until gas evolution ceases.

Acidic hydrolysis of scandium nitride; ScN is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, the nitride is protonated to release ammonia gas and form soluble scandium chloride; typically carried out at room temperature to mild heating in water, no catalyst, used to convert ScN back to ScCl3 and generate NH3.

Suzuki–Miyaura cross‑coupling; palladium‑catalysed C–C bond formation between an aryl chloride and phenylboronic acid to give 4‑chlorobiphenyl. Base K2CO3 deprotonates the boronic acid forming potassium aryl‑borate; Pd(PPh3)4 is the catalyst and is oxidised to triphenylphosphine oxide. Typically run in refluxing polar aprotic solvent (toluene, dioxane or DMF) with aqueous K2CO3 under nitrogen.

Catalytic thermal cracking of isopentane to propane and ethylene; high‑temperature (500–800 °C) pyrolysis over solid acid catalysts such as zeolites or silica‑alumina; typically conducted in the gas phase without solvent.

Direct combination (synthesis) reaction; chlorine gas oxidises sodium metal to give sodium chloride. Highly exothermic redox process, usually performed in a dry, inert atmosphere or sealed vessel. No solvent required; reaction proceeds at ambient temperature once initiated, often with controlled addition of Cl2.

Complete combustion of 3‑ethylhexane; oxidation of the hydrocarbon to CO2 and H2O. Provides maximal energy release and yields gaseous products. Requires ignition and excess O2, typically at high temperature in open flame or combustion chamber; no catalyst or solvent needed.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reductive) of o‑dinitrobenzene to o‑phenylenediamine; each nitro group is reduced to an amine with H2, producing water as by‑product. Conducted with Pd/C (10–20 % loading) in a protic solvent such as ethanol or methanol, under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 25–50 °C.

Double‑displacement metathesis; copper(II) chloride reacts with sodium acetate exchanging anions to form copper(II) acetate and sodium chloride. Usually performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; no catalyst required. The product may precipitate upon cooling.

Sulfonylation of a diol to give a bis‑tosylate; a dehydration/activation of alcohols. Triethylene glycol is treated with p‑toluenesulfonyl chloride in dry dichloromethane (or pyridine) with an added base (pyridine or triethylamine) at 0 °C to rt. The reaction yields triethylene glycol bis(p‑toluenesulfonate) and HCl, which is scavenged by the base.

Metathesis (salt exchange) between potassium malate and calcium hydroxide; potassium ions exchange with calcium to give calcium malate and potassium hydroxide. Conducted in aqueous medium, often at ambient temperature; stirring until equilibrium is reached. No catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed crossed aldol (Claisen‑Schmidt) condensation; NaOH deprotonates 2,4‑dihydroxyacetophenone to give an enolate that adds to benzaldehyde, followed by dehydration to afford the (E)‑α,β‑unsaturated chalcone. Typically run in ethanol or methanol/water at 0 °C to reflux; work‑up with acid neutralization and recrystallization.

Reductive metal precipitation (redox) where hydroxylamine sulfate reduces AuCl₃ (Au³⁺) to elemental gold while being oxidized to nitrous oxide; acidic by‑products (HCl, H₂SO₄) are formed. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient to moderately elevated temperature (≈50 °C); excess hydroxylamine ensures complete reduction; no additional catalyst required.

Thermal cracking (pyrolysis) of cyclobutane to two ethylene molecules via C–C bond scission. Requires high temperatures (≈600–800 °C) in the gas phase, often with an inert carrier gas (N₂ or He); low pressure; no solvent or catalyst.

Hydrolysis (quench) of lithium aluminum hydride. Purpose: safely decompose LiAlH₄ and generate hydrogen gas. Key transformation: LiAlH₄ reacts with water to form lithium hydroxide, aluminum hydroxide precipitate, and H₂ gas. Conditions: ambient temperature, excess liquid water acting as solvent; typically performed in a glass vessel. No catalyst required.

Direct combination (solid‑state synthesis) of elemental chromium and phosphorus to afford chromium phosphide (CrP). Performed by mixing powders and heating under inert atmosphere (Ar) at 800–1000 °C to promote intermetallic formation; no solvent or catalyst.

Metathesis/precipitation where oxalic acid displaces acetate from chromium(III) acetate, forming insoluble chromium(III) oxalate and liberating acetic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous solution at room temperature or mild heating; product precipitates and is filtered; no special catalyst.

Electrophilic nitrosation (nitrosylation) of tert‑butyl alcohol with nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate to give tert‑butyl nitrite and tetrafluoroboric acid. Performed in anhydrous aprotic solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂ or MeCN) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; temperature control is important; no additional catalyst.

Redox chlorination; chlorine oxidizes osmium dioxide to give osmium tetrachloride while releasing oxygen gas; typically performed by heating a mixture of OsO2 and Cl2 gas in a sealed tube or reflux apparatus at elevated temperature (200‑300 °C); no solvent needed, inert atmosphere often used.

Swern oxidation; converts the primary alcohol functional group of 4-(hydroxymethyl)pyridine into the corresponding aldehyde (4‑pyridinecarboxaldehyde) using DMSO activated by oxalyl chloride, with triethylamine as base; carried out at –78 °C to 0 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane; addition of TEA quenches the intermediate and furnishes the aldehyde.

Metathesis/precipitation reaction; silver chloride and potassium bromide exchange halides to form soluble potassium chloride and insoluble silver bromide, which precipitates out; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special reagents or catalysts required.

Oxidative cleavage of a vicinal diol using sodium periodate (periodate oxidation). The two adjacent hydroxyl groups are oxidized to carbonyls, breaking the C‑C bond and yielding acetone from the more substituted carbon and formaldehyde from the primary carbon; NaIO4 is used in aqueous medium (often THF/H2O) at 0–25 °C, no additional catalyst required.

Nucleophilic ring opening of an epoxide by ammonia. Ammonia attacks the less‑substituted carbon of propylene oxide, yielding 2‑aminopropan‑1‑ol (a β‑amino alcohol). Usually performed in aqueous or alcoholic ammonia at low to moderate temperature (0 °C to 50 °C), often in methanol or ethanol as solvent.

Acid–base neutralization; hydrochloric acid reacts with potassium carbonate, generating carbonic acid (which rapidly decomposes to CO₂ and H₂O) and potassium chloride; performed in aqueous solution, often with excess acid to drive CO₂ evolution; no catalyst needed.

Grignard addition to an ester; phenylmagnesium bromide attacks ethyl benzoate forming a tetrahedral intermediate, expelling ethoxide and then a second phenyl addition; after aqueous work‑up yields diphenylmethanol (benzhydrol) and ethanol; performed in dry ether or THF under inert atmosphere, 0 °C to reflux, no catalyst required.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (Finkelstein-type halide exchange); replaces the methanesulfonate leaving group with iodide to give 1‑iodopropane; typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone (or DMF) under reflux, where NaI is soluble and NaMSO3 precipitates, driving the reaction forward.

Grignard addition to a nitrile followed by hydrolysis; methylmagnesium bromide adds a methyl group to hexanenitrile, forming an imine magnesium salt that on aqueous work‑up yields heptan-2-one (a methyl ketone). Performed in anhydrous ether/THF at –78 °C to 0 °C, then warmed and quenched with water.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange) between ammonium hydroxide and sodium arsenite; purpose is to generate the ammonium arsenite salt while producing sodium hydroxide; key transformation is exchange of the cations (NH4⁺ ↔ Na⁺); carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no special solvent or catalyst required beyond water.

Ligand exchange/complex formation; preparation of bis(acetonitrile)dichloropalladium(II) from palladium(II) acetate by reacting with HCl and acetonitrile; acetic acid is generated as the acetate leaving group; typically performed in refluxing acetonitrile with gaseous or aqueous HCl under inert atmosphere.

Uncatalyzed hydrolysis (SN2) of ethyl bromide with water, giving ethanol and hydrobromic acid. Reaction proceeds slowly; accelerated by heating (reflux) or by a mild acid/base catalyst. Carried out in aqueous medium, often under reflux for several hours; no external catalyst required.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis (hydrogen reduction) of an alkyl bromide; purpose is to remove the bromine from 2‑bromopropanoic acid, yielding propionic acid while retaining the carboxyl group. Hydrogen gas reduces the C–Br bond on the surface of palladium on carbon (Pd/C). Typical conditions: 1 atm H₂, Pd/C (5‑10 % Pd), solvent such as ethanol or ethyl acetate, ambient to 50 °C, stirring for 1‑4 h. The by‑product HBr is absorbed by the solvent or neutralized by added base if necessary.

Reaction type: acetylation (acylation) of a secondary alcohol with an anhydride. Purpose: to protect the hydroxy group of propyl lactate as an acetoxy ester, giving propyl 2‑acetoxypropanoate. Key transformation: nucleophilic attack of the alcohol oxygen on one carbonyl of acetic anhydride, forming the acetoxy ester and releasing acetic acid. Typical conditions: stir propyl lactate with 1.2–1.5 equiv acetic anhydride in dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt for 1–2 h, using a catalytic base such as pyridine or DMAP to scavenge the generated acetic acid. Solvent: CH₂Cl₂, sometimes THF. No metal catalyst required.

Electrophilic bromination of oxazole (heteroaromatic substitution). N‑bromosuccinimide supplies Br⁺ that replaces the hydrogen at the C‑2 position of oxazole, yielding 2‑bromo‑1,3‑oxazole and succinimide. Typical conditions: oxazole (1 equiv) and NBS (1 equiv) in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as carbon tetrachloride, chloroform or DMF, 0 °C to room temperature, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base neutralization (protonation of phenolate); converts sodium phenolate back to phenol while forming sodium hydrogen sulfate; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent.

Redox titration reaction: permanganate oxidizes Fe(II) to Fe(III) while itself being reduced to Mn(II); Na+ and sulfate ions form Na2SO4. Usually performed in aqueous sulfuric acid (0.5–1 M) at room temperature; mixture appears pink initially and decolorizes as MnO4‑ is consumed.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; exchanges carbonate and sulfate anions to give soluble sodium carbonate and insoluble barium sulfate which precipitates; conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature; water is the solvent.

Acid‑base salt formation; protonation of the secondary amine 2‑methylamino‑1‑phenylbutane by hydrochloric acid to give its hydrochloride salt; usually performed in aqueous or ethanol solution at ambient temperature; water/ethanol mixture is typical solvent.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of a propargylic chloride by hydroxide ion; chloride is displaced to afford propargyl alcohol (prop‑2‑yn‑1‑ol) and sodium chloride; carried out with aqueous NaOH, often under reflux; water or water/ethanol is used as solvent.

Acid–base (neutralization) reaction; sulfuric acid protonates cadmium silicate, breaking Si–O bonds to give silica (SiO2) and forming cadmium sulfate; typically carried out in aqueous solution with heating to promote dissolution; no special catalyst, water acts as solvent.
