Transesterification with ethanol (ethanolysis); purpose is to form ethyl propionate and n‑propyl alcohol; key transformation analogous to methanolysis, with ethanol as nucleophile; typical conditions include refluxing the ester in excess ethanol (solvent) with a catalytic amount of acid (e.g., H₂SO₄, 1 %) or a base (e.g., NaOEt), often 60–80 °C for 2–6 h; removal of ethanol or continuous azeotropic distillation can shift equilibrium.

Direct combination (synthesis) redox reaction; elemental aluminum is oxidized from 0 to +3 while chlorine gas is reduced from 0 to –1, yielding aluminum chloride (AlCl3); performed at elevated temperatures (often 600–800 °C) in a furnace under dry conditions; no solvent or catalyst required.

Carbylamine (isocyanide) synthesis; chloroform is dehydrohalogenated by strong base (KOH) in the presence of methylamine, generating methyl isocyanide, with potassium chloride and water as by‑products; conducted in aqueous/ethanolic KOH solution under reflux or vigorous stirring, usually at ambient to moderate temperature; no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration of phenol using nitronium tetrafluoroborate; purpose is to install a nitro group ortho/para to the hydroxyl group; key transformation is formation of a σ‑complex followed by loss of a proton to give nitrophenol; BF₃·CF₄ is generated as a Lewis‑acid byproduct along with HF; performed in anhydrous, non‑nucleophilic solvents such as dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature; reaction is typically quenched with ice‑water.

Formation of an acyl chloride from a carboxylic acid using thionyl chloride; the acid reacts with SOCl₂, releasing HCl and SO₂ gases and converting the carboxyl group to the 2,2‑dichloroacetyl chloride; carried out under reflux in an inert atmosphere, often in solvents like dichloromethane or chloroform; excess SOCl₂ drives the reaction, no additional catalyst needed.

Catalytic transfer hydrogenation of 5‑methylfurfural to 5‑methylfurfuryl alcohol; formic acid serves as hydrogen donor, decomposing on a Ru on carbon (Ru/C) surface to generate H₂ in situ, reducing the aldehyde to the corresponding alcohol; typically run at 80–120 °C in a polar solvent (e.g., water, ethanol) under sealed conditions; Ru/C is the heterogeneous catalyst.

Carbothermal reduction; reduces tungsten(VI) oxide to tungsten(IV) oxide while oxidizing carbon to carbon monoxide. Solid‑state high‑temperature reaction (≈900–1100 °C) under inert atmosphere or vacuum; no solvent, no catalyst required.

Williamson ether synthesis (SN2 alkylation); sodium ethoxide attacks the bromomethyl carbon of 2‑bromoethyl acetate, displacing bromide to form 2‑ethoxyethyl acetate and NaBr. Conducted in anhydrous ethanol or dry THF with NaOEt (1 equiv) at 0 °C to rt; the reaction is usually complete within 30 min to 2 h and requires exclusion of moisture.

Oxidative sulfone synthesis; converts a thioether (diphenyl sulfide) to the corresponding sulfone (diphenyl sulfone) using sodium persulfate as the oxidant. Typically carried out in aqueous medium (often water or dilute NaOH) at reflux; sodium persulfate supplies sulfate byproduct and drives oxidation; no additional catalyst needed.

Acid‑base neutralization; calcium oxide reacts with hydroiodic acid to give calcium iodide and water; oxide O^2‑ is protonated to H2O, Ca2+ pairs with I‑; conducted in aqueous solution with dilute HI, often with gentle heating to ensure dissolution; water solvent, no catalyst.

Catalytic hydrogenation of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol; isobutyraldehyde is reduced to isobutanol using H₂ gas and palladium on carbon; conducted in ethanol, methanol or ethyl acetate under 1–5 atm H₂ at 25–50 °C; Pd/C (5–10 % wt) serves as catalyst and the reaction stops at the alcohol stage.

Williamson ether synthesis (O‑alkylation); phenolic hydroxyl of salicyl alcohol is deprotonated by potassium carbonate and alkylated with methyl iodide to give 2‑methoxybenzyl alcohol. Conducted in polar aprotic solvents such as acetone or DMF, reflux conditions, under nitrogen; potassium carbonate acts as base, no metal catalyst required.

Friedel‑Crafts alkylation; electrophilic aromatic substitution of benzene with diphenylmethyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous aluminum chloride, forming triphenylmethane and releasing HCl. Performed in dry non‑coordinating solvents (e.g., carbon disulfide, dichloromethane, or nitrobenzene) at 0 °C to reflux under inert atmosphere; AlCl₃ is the Lewis acid catalyst.

Direct combination (synthesis) of zinc phosphide; elemental zinc reacts with tetraphosphorus (P₄) to give zinc phosphide (Zn₃P₂). High‑temperature solid‑state reaction (300–500 °C) in a sealed tube or under inert gas to prevent oxidation; no solvent or catalyst.

Direct fluorination oxidation; cobalt(II) fluoride is oxidized by elemental fluorine to cobalt(III) fluoride. Typically carried out at elevated temperature (200–400 °C) in an anhydrous, fluorine‑resistant vessel (e.g., nickel or Monel). No solvent is used; the reaction proceeds in the gas phase under a flow of dry F₂. Purpose: synthesis of the high‑valent CoF₃ which is a powerful fluorinating agent.

Aqueous metathesis/acid‑base reaction; arsenic pentoxide reacts with sodium sulfide in water, forming arsenic pentasulfide precipitate and sodium hydroxide in solution. Typically carried out at room temperature to gentle heating with stirring; water serves as solvent, no additional catalyst required.

SN2 alkylation of aniline by ethyl methanesulfonate; nucleophilic substitution on a primary sulfonate ester to give N‑ethyl aniline and methanesulfonic acid. Typically performed in a polar aprotic solvent (DMF, DMSO, MeCN) at 50‑80 °C, often with a mild base (e.g., K₂CO₃) to deprotonate the amine and drive the reaction to completion.

Direct amidation (condensation) of cyclopropanecarboxylic acid with ammonia to afford cyclopropanecarboxamide and water. Because simple carboxylic acids are poor acyl donors, the reaction usually requires high temperature (150‑200 °C) under gaseous or aqueous NH₃ pressure, or activation with a coupling reagent (e.g., DCC, EDC) in the presence of a base such as pyridine or triethylamine.

Thioester formation via activation of acrylic acid with carbonyl diimidazole (CDI). CDI converts the carboxylic acid into an acrylic‑imidazolide intermediate, which is then attacked by methanethiol to give S‑methyl thioacrylate and liberate imidazole. The reaction is carried out at 0‑25 °C in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF, and no additional catalyst is required.

Baeyer‑Villiger oxidation of cyclobutanone using hydrogen peroxide in the presence of an acid catalyst (e.g., trifluoroacetic acid, H₂SO₄, or a peracid generated in situ) to produce γ‑butyrolactone and water. Typical conditions involve 1–5 equiv H₂O₂, 1 equiv acid, in a solvent like dichloromethane or acetone at 0‑30 °C, with the reaction often accelerated by a phase‑transfer catalyst or a Lewis acid (e.g., SnCl₄).

O‑silylation (protecting group formation) of phenol; the phenolic OH attacks the silicon center, displacing ethanol and forming phenyl‑trimethylsilyl ether. Typically carried out in a dry aprotic solvent (e.g., dichloromethane or THF) at 0 °C to rt with a catalytic base such as imidazole, pyridine, or DMAP to neutralize the released ethanol and promote the silyl transfer.

Copper‑catalyzed cyanation (Rosenmund‑von Braun type) of 3‑chloro‑1‑iodobenzene with CuCN to afford 3‑chlorobenzonitrile and precipitated CuI. Conducted in a high‑boiling polar aprotic solvent (DMF, NMP, DMSO) at 150‑200 °C under inert atmosphere; the copper cyanide acts as both cyanide source and catalyst, and the by‑product CuI is removed by filtration.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of an aldehyde; applied to convert butanal to n‑butanol. Key transformation: addition of H₂ across the carbonyl, reducing the aldehyde to a primary alcohol. Performed with H₂ gas (1–5 atm) over 5–10 % Pd/C in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol, or THF, generally at room temperature to 50 °C under stirring. Pd/C acts as the catalyst.

Nucleophilic substitution of thiophosgene (Cl₂C=S) by methanethiolate generated in situ from methanethiol, yielding dimethyl trithiocarbonate (CS(SMe)₂) and two equivalents of HCl. The reaction is performed at 0‑25 °C in anhydrous dichloromethane or chloroform, often in the presence of a base such as triethylamine or pyridine to scavenge the liberated HCl and drive the substitution to completion.

Oxidative chlorination; preparation of a disinfectant. Sodium hypochlorite chlorinates cyanuric acid in alkaline medium (NaOH) to give sodium dichloroisocyanurate, with NaCl and water as by‑products. Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Electrophilic aromatic nitration (mixed‑acid nitration). Fluorene undergoes nitration with nitric acid generated in situ from sodium nitrate and concentrated sulfuric acid, yielding 2‑nitrofluorene, sodium bisulfate and water. Performed in conc. H₂SO₄, typically 0‑5 °C to avoid over‑nitration; no additional catalyst.

Substitution reaction; converts an alcohol to an alkyl bromide. Key step involves phosphorus tribromide reacting with cyclooctanol to replace the hydroxyl group with bromine. Conditions: anhydrous, typically in an inert atmosphere. Solvent: ether or dichloromethane.

High‑temperature oxidation (combustion) of erbium nitride. ErN reacts with O₂ at ≥1000 °C in a flowing oxygen or air stream, producing erbium(III) oxide (Er₂O₃) and nitrogen gas. No solvent or catalyst; solid‑state reaction.

Thermal or catalytic decarboxylation of a hydroxycinnamic acid; converts the acrylic side chain into a vinyl group while releasing carbon dioxide; employed to produce flavor and fragrance compounds such as 4‑vinylphenol; often performed at 180–250 °C either neat or on a solid base/oxide (e.g., CaO, CuO) in a flow reactor; can also be carried out enzymatically with phenolic acid decarboxylases at mild temperature; no solvent is required for the high‑temperature route, while aqueous buffers are used for the enzymatic method.

Acid‑base neutralization. Trifluoroacetic acid reacts with ammonium hydroxide in water to form ammonium trifluoroacetate and water. Carried out at room temperature in aqueous solution; no catalyst needed.

Hydrolysis of diethyl selenate in water (or dilute acid) to regenerate selenic acid and ethanol. Conducted by heating the ester in aqueous medium, optionally with 1 M HCl to accelerate cleavage of the Se–O‑ethyl bonds. Typical reflux for 1‑2 h yields selenic acid in solution and liberates ethanol.

Base‑catalyzed transesterification (alkoxy exchange) of ethyl 3‑bromopropionate with sodium methoxide; purpose is to replace the ethoxy group with a methoxy group, producing methyl 3‑bromopropionate; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of methoxide on the carbonyl carbon and departure of ethoxide; carried out in methanol (or ethanol) under reflux; catalytic or stoichiometric NaOMe is used; sodium ethoxide formed remains in solution.

Reduction; selective reduction of an aromatic aldehyde to the corresponding primary alcohol using sodium borohydride. The aldehyde carbonyl is converted to a benzylic –CH₂OH group. Typically performed in methanol, ethanol, or a methanol‑THF mixture at 0 °C to ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Swern oxidation of a benzylic primary alcohol to an aldehyde; purpose is to generate homovanillin without over‑oxidation. Key transformation: R‑CH₂OH → R‑CHO, producing dimethyl sulfide and triethylammonium chloride. Conducted in anhydrous dichloromethane at –78 °C: oxalyl chloride added to DMSO, then the alcohol, followed by dropwise addition of triethylamine at low temperature, then warm to 0 °C.

Base‑catalyzed saponification of phenyl butanoate; purpose is to generate the phenoxide and carboxylate salts. Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl, ejecting phenoxide which remains as its sodium salt; the acid fragment becomes sodium butanoate. Conditions: aqueous NaOH (1–2 M) at reflux, often in a 1:1 ethanol–water solvent system, 1–2 h.

Type: Friedländer quinoline synthesis (condensation of an o‑amino‑aryl aldehyde with a ketone). Purpose: Construct a quinoline heterocycle. Key transformation: Condensation of 2‑aminobenzaldehyde with acetone, followed by cyclization and dehydration to afford 4‑methylquinoline and water. Typical conditions: Reflux in a protic or polar aprotic solvent (e.g., acetic acid, ethanol, or polyphosphoric acid) under acidic catalysis (HCl, H₂SO₄) or with ammonium acetate as a mild acid. Reaction times: 2–6 h.

Radical halogen exchange (partial fluorination) of dibromomethane with elemental fluorine; one bromine atom is replaced by fluorine to give fluorodibromomethane, with HF as by‑product. Performed under dilute F₂ (≤5 % in inert carrier) at low temperature (‑78 to 0 °C) to control the highly exothermic reaction; inert solvent such as CCl₄ or perfluorinated solvent may be used. Reaction is typically initiated by UV light or a radical initiator; no metal catalyst is required.

Redox (metal‑aqua regia) reaction; tin is oxidized to SnCl₄; nitrate component of aqua regia is reduced to NO₂, and chloride is liberated as Cl₂ and HCl gas; typically performed by adding tin to a cold mixture of concentrated HCl and HNO₃ (3:1) under stirring; the reaction occurs in the acidic aqueous medium, no additional catalyst.

Acid–base neutralization (salt formation); permanganic acid reacts with barium hydroxide to produce aqueous barium permanganate and water. The reaction proceeds in water at room temperature; simple stirring is sufficient, no additional reagents needed.

Double displacement/precipitation; ferric sulfate exchanges cations with potassium ferrocyanide to give soluble potassium sulfate and insoluble iron(III) ferrocyanide (a blue precipitate). Conducted in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; filtration isolates the solid product.

Fischer esterification; a primary alcohol (1‑butanol) reacts with a carboxylic acid (heptanoic acid) to form the corresponding ester (butyl heptanoate) and water. Requires an acid catalyst such as concentrated H₂SO₄, reflux in a non‑polar solvent (toluene or benzene) with a Dean‑Stark apparatus to remove water and drive the equilibrium to products.

Dry reforming of methane: an endothermic reforming reaction that converts methane and carbon dioxide into synthesis gas (CO and H2). Typically carried out at 800–1000 °C in the presence of a nickel‑based catalyst (e.g., Ni/Al2O3) under an inert carrier gas. No solvent; high‑temperature furnace conditions.

Phosphate ester formation (condensation of phosphoric acid with an alcohol); purpose is to synthesize a mono‑alkyl phosphate. Key transformation is nucleophilic attack of propanol on the phosphorus center, loss of water and generation of propyl dihydrogen phosphate. Typical conditions: neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (e.g., toluene) at 80–120 °C with removal of water (Dean‑Stark trap). No additional catalyst required.

Halogen exchange (formation of a metal halide from its oxide); titanium dioxide reacts with hydrogen bromide gas to generate titanium tetrabromide and water. Carried out under dry HBr atmosphere at elevated temperature (≈200–300 °C) in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no additional catalyst is needed.

Double displacement/precipitation; ammonium oxalate and lead(II) nitrate exchange ions to give insoluble lead(II) oxalate precipitate and soluble ammonium nitrate. Performed in aqueous solution at room temperature with gentle stirring; the solid is collected by filtration.

Base‑catalyzed saponification; sodium hydroxide hydrolyzes cyclohexyl methacrylate to sodium methacrylate and cyclohexanol; carried out in aqueous NaOH at room temperature or mild heating; the reaction is quantitative and the sodium salt can be precipitated or further acid‑neutralized.

Reductive amination; propionaldehyde reacts with dimethylamine to form an imine intermediate that is reduced by sodium cyanoborohydride to give N,N‑dimethylpropylamine. Conducted in a polar aprotic solvent such as methanol or dichloromethane, buffered to pH 5‑6, at 0 °C to room temperature; sodium cyanoborohydride serves as the mild reducing agent.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) of alkali metal salts; sodium azide exchanges anions with lithium bromide to afford lithium azide and sodium bromide. Executed in water or aqueous ethanol, often with gentle heating to improve solubility; no catalyst needed.

Oxidation; strong oxidizing conditions convert benzaldehyde to benzoic acid while reducing KMnO4 to manganese dioxide precipitate. Usually carried out in alkaline aqueous medium (e.g., NaOH solution) at 0–25 °C, then the mixture is acidified to precipitate MnO2 and give the acid product. Water is solvent; MnO2 and water are formed.

Selective aldehyde reduction; 2,2,2‑trifluoroacetaldehyde is reduced by sodium borohydride to 2,2,2‑trifluoroethanol, producing sodium borate as a by‑product. Reaction carried out in methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; NaBH4 is the hydride source.

N‑aryl coupling (Buchwald‑Hartwig or Cu‑catalyzed Ullmann type); piperazine acts as a nucleophile toward 2‑iodopyridine to give 1‑(2‑pyridyl)piperazine. Typical conditions: Pd catalyst (e.g., Pd₂(dba)₃) with BINAP or CuI with phenanthroline, base such as K₂CO₃, solvent DMF or dioxane, 80‑120 °C for several hours.

Isothiocyanate formation using thiophosgene; 4‑hydroxybenzylamine reacts with thiophosgene to generate 4‑hydroxybenzyl isothiocyanate, releasing two equivalents of HCl. Conducted in dry dichloromethane at 0 °C to rt, with an organic base (e.g., triethylamine) to neutralize HCl; thiophosgene acts as the electrophilic C=S source.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation. Triammonium arsenate reacts with silver nitrate, precipitating insoluble silver arsenate while forming soluble ammonium nitrate. Carried out in water, often in the dark or under low light to prevent silver photoreduction; ambient temperature, no catalyst.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation; Na₃PO₄ reacts with Sc(NO₃)₃ to form insoluble scandium phosphate precipitate and soluble NaNO₃; performed in water at ambient temperature with stirring; filtration isolates ScPO₄.

Acid‑base neutralization (salt formation) of a metal oxide; CdO reacts with acetic acid to give cadmium acetate and water; usually refluxed in aqueous or alcoholic solution to ensure complete dissolution of CdO; product can be isolated by evaporation or crystallization.

Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid using KMnO₄; 2‑(thiophen‑2‑yl)ethanol is oxidized in aqueous alkaline KMnO₄ (often with heating under reflux); after reaction the mixture is acidified to protonate the carboxylate, affording 2‑thiopheneacetic acid; MnO₂ precipitate is filtered off.

Metathesis (acid–base) reaction; Ni(CH₃COO)₂ reacts with HCl to exchange ligands, producing NiCl₂ and acetic acid; carried out in aqueous solution, usually at room temperature or with mild heating; NiCl₂ remains in solution, acetic acid can be removed by distillation.

Electrophilic chlorination (alpha‑halogenation) of ethyl chloroformate catalyzed by FeCl₃; Cl₂ in the presence of FeCl₃ adds a chlorine to the ethyl group, yielding 1‑chloroethyl chloroformate and HCl; performed in anhydrous chlorinated solvent (e.g., CH₂Cl₂) at low temperature to avoid over‑chlorination; HCl is evolved as a gas.

Acid-base deprotonation; sodium hydride abstracts the acidic proton of valproic acid to give sodium valproate and hydrogen gas; typically performed in an aprotic, dry solvent such as THF under inert atmosphere at 0 °C to room temperature, no catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed acetal hydrolysis; aqueous sulfuric acid protonates the diethyl acetal of acetaldehyde, leading to cleavage into acetaldehyde and two equivalents of ethanol; carried out in water or water/organic mixture, often refluxed, with H₂SO₄ as catalyst.

Double‑displacement precipitation; Ni²⁺ exchanges with Na⁺ to form insoluble NiCO₃ and soluble NaCl; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; water is the solvent, and the precipitated carbonate is filtered and washed.

This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction where the telluride ion (Te²⁻) from sodium telluride attacks methyl bromide, forming methanetellurol (CH3TeH). Water serves as a proton donor, and the reaction occurs under basic conditions (generating sodium hydroxide as a byproduct). Solvent is typically aqueous or mixed phase. Purpose is alkyl telluride synthesis.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrate; cyclopropyl nitrate is converted to cyclopropanol with formation of nitric acid and water; performed in aqueous concentrated H₂SO₄, typically heated to reflux; the sulfuric acid provides the catalytic medium; no other catalyst needed.

Nitrate‑ester formation (nitration) of a secondary hydroxyl; concentrated HNO₃ nitrates the remaining hydroxyl of isosorbide mononitrate to afford isosorbide dinitrate and water; usually conducted at 0 °C to 5 °C in the absence of additional solvent or in a non‑nucleophilic solvent such as acetic acid, sometimes with H₂SO₄ as a promoter.

Metathesis/acid‑base exchange; perchloric acid protonates acetate ion, producing acetic acid and the salt silver perchlorate; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature, no special catalyst needed.

Electrophilic α‑halogenation of a ketone (halogen addition to the enol form); replaces an α‑hydrogen of acetophenone with bromine to give phenacyl bromide (α‑bromoacetophenone) and HBr. Conducted with Br₂ (1 equiv) in an inert solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, usually at 0 °C to 25 °C, protected from light.

Staudinger reduction of an azide; triphenylphosphine reacts with allyl azide, forming triphenylphosphine oxide, releasing nitrogen gas, and delivering allylamine; typically carried out in anhydrous THF or dichloromethane at room temperature under inert atmosphere, no additional catalyst.

Acid‑base salt formation between calcium carbonate and fumaric acid; purpose is to synthesize calcium fumarate while releasing CO₂; the carbonate reacts with two equivalents of fumaric acid, producing calcium fumarate, water, and carbon dioxide gas; carried out in aqueous suspension or dilute acid medium, often with gentle heating and stirring to promote CO₂ evolution; water is the reaction medium.

High‑temperature solid‑state synthesis of a transition‑metal dichalcogenide. Metallic molybdenum and elemental tellurium are intimately mixed and heated in an inert atmosphere (argon or vacuum) or sealed quartz tube at 700–1000 °C. The elements combine to give molybdenum ditelluride (MoTe₂) as a layered solid. No solvent or catalyst is required.

Conversion of a carboxylic acid to an acid chloride; thionyl chloride reacts with 2‑naphthoic acid to replace the hydroxyl of the carboxyl group with chlorine, generating 2‑naphthoyl chloride with evolution of HCl and SO₂ gases; usually performed refluxing in a dry solvent such as dichloromethane or toluene, under nitrogen, with the gaseous by‑products vented.

Esterification via nucleophilic acyl substitution of phthaloyl chloride with 1‑butanol to give dibutyl phthalate; purpose is to prepare the di‑ester plasticizer; key transformation is replacement of the chloride atoms by butoxy groups, releasing HCl; typically performed in an aprotic solvent such as dichloromethane or THF at 0 °C to room temperature; a base (e.g., pyridine, triethylamine) is added to neutralize the generated HCl.

Reaction type: Radical halogenation. Purpose: Chlorination of alkanes to form alkyl halides. Key transformations: UV light initiates Cl• radicals; hydrogen abstraction forms hexyl radicals, which react with Cl2. Reaction conditions: Chlorine gas under UV light, gas-phase or non-polar solvent (e.g., CCl4).

Direct combination of elemental fluorine and chlorine to form the interhalogen chlorine monofluoride (ClF); a simple synthesis of an interhalogen compound; no chemical transformation beyond bond formation between the two halogens; usually carried out in the gas phase at low temperature (often –78 °C to 0 °C) in an inert carrier gas; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidation of sulfite ions to sulfate by molecular oxygen; used to convert ammonium sulfite into ammonium sulfate, a valuable fertilizer; key redox step is oxidation of S(II) to S(VI) with O₂ as oxidant; conducted in aqueous solution under stirring, often at ambient temperature with gentle aeration or bubbling of air/oxygen; no special catalyst is required, though basic conditions (pH ≈ 8–9) can accelerate the reaction.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of cyclopentylmethyl iodide with cyanide ion from sodium cyanide to give cyclopentylacetonitrile and sodium iodide; purpose is to install a nitrile functional group; key transformation is inversion of configuration at the carbon bearing iodine as cyanide attacks; typically run in a polar aprotic solvent such as DMF or DMSO at 50–80 °C; excess NaCN may be used; no additional catalyst required.

SN2 displacement of chloride in 1‑chlorooctane by cyanide ion from sodium cyanide to afford octanenitrile and sodium chloride; a standard method for preparing primary nitriles from alkyl halides; key step is backside attack of CN⁻ on the primary carbon; reaction is performed in polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO, or acetonitrile) at 40–80 °C; inert atmosphere may be used to avoid oxidation; no catalyst needed.

Acid–base reaction between trimethylsilanol and elemental sodium forming sodium trimethylsilanolate and hydrogen gas; purpose is to generate the silanolate anion for further organosilicon chemistry; key transformation is deprotonation of the silanol O–H bond with simultaneous H₂ evolution; carried out under inert atmosphere (argon or nitrogen) in dry THF or diethyl ether at 0 °C to room temperature; stoichiometric sodium metal is required; no catalyst is used.

Acid–base reaction with gas evolution; scandium carbonate reacts with phosphoric acid to form scandium phosphate, water, and carbon dioxide gas; performed in aqueous medium, gentle heating helps release CO₂ and drive reaction to completion; no catalyst, water as solvent.

Solid-state metathesis synthesis; prepares antimony(III) telluride (Sb2Te3) a semiconductor material. Key transformation: double replacement of SbCl3 and Na2Te forming NaCl and Sb2Te3. Typically performed by thoroughly grinding the reagents, placing them in a sealed quartz tube under inert atmosphere and heating to 600‑800 °C for several hours. No solvent; catalyst not required.

Electrophilic aromatic halogenation (Friedel‑Crafts type); used to introduce a chlorine substituent onto naphthalene to give 1‑chloronaphthalene. Chlorine gas reacts with the aromatic ring, releasing HCl. Commonly carried out in an inert, non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chloroform, at reflux, with a Lewis‑acid catalyst (FeCl3 or AlCl3) to generate the electrophilic Cl⁺ species.

Conversion of a secondary alcohol to an alkyl chloride using phosphorus oxychloride (Appel‑type halogenation). 3‑Methylbutan‑2‑ol is transformed into 2‑chloro‑3‑methylbutane with release of HCl and formation of phosphoric acid. Reaction is usually performed in pyridine (which acts as solvent and HCl scavenger) at 0 °C to room temperature. No metal catalyst required.

Suzuki‑Miyaura cross‑coupling; constructs a C–C bond between 2‑iodothiophene and phenylboronic acid to afford 2‑phenylthiophene. Base (K2CO3) deprotonates the boronic acid, Pd(PPh3)4 catalyzes transmetalation and reductive elimination. Typical conditions: reflux in a mixture of THF (or dioxane/toluene) and water, inert atmosphere (N2 or Ar), 80‑100 °C. By‑product KI forms.

Acid–base neutralization; cobalt(II) carbonate reacts with strong sulfuric acid to release CO2 and form soluble cobalt(II) sulfate in water; performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature with stirring.

Strong oxidative cleavage of a terminal alkyne; KMnO4 in aqueous alkaline medium oxidizes 1‑pentyne to butanoic acid and carbon dioxide. Reaction is carried out by refluxing the alkyne with excess hot KMnO4 (often in the presence of NaOH) in water. KMnO4 acts as both oxidant and catalyst; the process proceeds through formation of a glycolate intermediate that fragments to the carboxylic acid and CO2.

Acid dissolution of a mixed‑oxide salt; concentrated HCl converts insoluble lead chromate into soluble chromic acid (H2CrO4) and precipitates lead(II) chloride, with water as by‑product; typically conducted in aqueous HCl, often with gentle heating, no catalyst needed.

nucleophilic substitution fluorination; replaces -OH in benzoic acid with fluoride; generates benzoyl fluoride, sulfur dioxide, hydrogen fluoride; carried out using thionyl fluoride in inert solvents like dichloromethane at elevated temperatures.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation (electrophilic aromatic substitution); chlorobenzene reacts with 4‑chlorobenzoyl chloride in the presence of AlCl3, a Lewis‑acid catalyst, to install a benzoyl group yielding 4,4′‑dichlorobenzophenone while releasing HCl; performed under anhydrous conditions in non‑protic solvents such as CH2Cl2, CS2 or nitrobenzene, usually at 0–50 °C followed by reflux.

Hydroformylation (oxo process, carbonylation); propylene is carbonylated with a 1:1 mixture of CO and H2 in the presence of a transition‑metal carbonyl catalyst (typically Rh‑ or Co‑based with phosphine ligands) to give isobutyraldehyde; reaction conducted at 80–120 °C and 1–10 MPa syngas pressure in an inert hydrocarbon solvent like toluene.

Acid‑metal single‑displacement (redox) reaction; gadolinium metal reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form gadolinium(III) sulfate (Gd2(SO4)3) and hydrogen gas; carried out in aqueous solution at ambient temperature or with mild heating; water serves as solvent, no catalyst needed.

Reaction type: metathesis/precipitation (base‑induced hydrolysis). Purpose: produce holmium(III) hydroxide as a precipitate and neutralize the chloride. Key transformation: HoCl₃·6H₂O + 3 NaOH → Ho(OH)₃ (solid) + 3 NaCl + 6 H₂O. Typical conditions: dissolve holmium chloride hexahydrate in water, add aqueous NaOH solution dropwise with stirring, temperature 20–60 °C; the hydroxide precipitates immediately. Solvent: water; catalyst: none.

Catalytic hydrogenolysis of an ester; H₂ (high pressure) over a nickel catalyst (e.g., Raney Ni or Ni‑Al) cleaves the C–O bonds of propyl 2‑methylpropanoate to give 2‑methyl‑1‑propanol and 1‑propanol; typical conditions are 50–100 atm H₂, 150–200 °C, in a solvent such as ethanol or isopropanol.

Catalytic cycloaddition of carbon dioxide to propylene oxide forming propylene carbonate. General type: CO2 fixation / cyclic carbonate synthesis. Purpose: produce propylene carbonate, a valuable solvent and electrolyte component. Key transformation: the epoxide ring opens and incorporates CO2, giving a five‑membered cyclic carbonate. Typical conditions: CO2 pressure 5–30 bar, temperature 80–150 °C, catalyst such as a metal‑salen complex, quaternary ammonium salt, or Zn/Co halide. Common solvent: polar aprotic solvents (e.g., acetonitrile) or solvent‑free ionic liquids.

Halide metathesis (halogen exchange) between arsenic triiodide and potassium bromide; the iodides are displaced by bromide to afford arsenic tribromide and potassium iodide; usually performed by grinding the solids together or refluxing in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetone, no catalyst required.

Thermal pyrolysis; heating thioacetamide alone causes breakdown into acetamide and H₂S. The C=S bond is oxidatively eliminated as H₂S while the carbonyl is retained as the amide. Typical conditions are 180‑250 °C under nitrogen or argon atmosphere, often in a sealed tube or flow reactor; no solvent is required.

Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) of a benzyl chloride by water. Water acts as the nucleophile on 1-(chloromethyl)-4-nitrobenzene, yielding 4‑nitrobenzyl alcohol and HCl (often neutralized in situ). Reaction proceeds slowly; accelerated by heating (80‑100 °C) in water or a water‑ethanol mixture, sometimes with a base to trap HCl.

Precipitation (double‑replacement) reaction in aqueous solution. Adding aqueous ammonia (or ammonium hydroxide) to a solution of bismuth nitrate precipitates bismuth hydroxide as a white solid while forming soluble ammonium nitrate. The reaction occurs at ambient temperature with stirring; water is the medium and no catalyst is required.

Ester hydrolysis (acid or base‑catalyzed); O,O‑dimethyl phosphorodithioate undergoes water‑mediated cleavage of the P–OCH3 bonds, yielding methanol and the corresponding phosphorodithioic acid (or its salt); performed in aqueous acid (e.g., HCl) or base (e.g., NaOH) at reflux; solvent is water or water/organic mixture.

Condensation (nucleophilic addition‑elimination) forming a biguanide skeleton; cyanoguanidine (H₂N‑C(=NH)‑NH‑C≡N) reacts with guanidine (H₂N‑C(=NH)‑NH₂) to give biguanide (H₂N‑C(=NH)‑NH‑C(=NH)‑NH₂) and release of ammonia. Commonly performed by heating a mixture of the two reagents in water or ethanol at 80–120 °C for several hours; a base (e.g., NaOH) may be added to accelerate deprotonation, but no metal catalyst is required.

Hydration of ethylene: electrophilic addition of water across the C=C bond to form ethanol; industrially performed in the vapor phase using phosphoric acid supported on silica at about 300 °C and 60–70 atm; no solvent, solid H₃PO₄/SiO₂ catalyst.

Thermal decomposition; solid gold(III) nitrate decomposes upon strong heating to afford gold(III) oxide, nitrogen dioxide gas, and oxygen gas; conducted by heating the nitrate above ~200 °C in a dry furnace; no solvent or catalyst is required.

Direct fluorination (halogenation) of elemental ruthenium to give ruthenium pentafluoride; employed to prepare the high‑oxidation‑state RuF5 which is a volatile fluoride; performed with dry F2 gas at elevated temperatures (≈300‑500 °C) in a fluorination reactor; no solvent, inert metal container used.

Redox (carbothermic reduction); carbon reduces chromium(IV) oxide to chromium(III) oxide while being oxidized to carbon monoxide. Used in metallurgical processes to generate CO gas and obtain Cr2O3. Requires high temperatures (≈1000–1500 °C) in a dry, solid‑state furnace; no solvent or catalyst needed.

Base‑catalyzed esterification (transesterification) of phenylacetic acid with dimethyl carbonate to give methyl phenylacetate and methanol. Employed for preparing aromatic esters. Typically performed at 80–120 °C under reflux in an aprotic solvent (e.g., toluene or bulk) using a tertiary amine or metal alkoxide catalyst; removal of methanol drives the equilibrium forward.

Double‑replacement (metathesis) precipitation: neodymium chloride solution is mixed with an aqueous solution of sodium fluoride. Nd³⁺ exchanges anions with Na⁺, precipitating insoluble neodymium(III) fluoride and leaving sodium chloride in solution. Conducted at room temperature or with gentle heating; water is the solvent, and agitation promotes complete precipitation.

Knoevenagel‑type condensation followed by intramolecular cyclization between 4‑bromobenzaldehyde and cyclopentane‑1,3‑dione, yielding a brominated indenone and water. Utilized to construct fused indanone frameworks. Conducted in ethanol or methanol with a weak base (piperidine, ammonium acetate) at reflux; water is eliminated during the condensation step.

Fischer esterification of 2‑chloro­benzoic acid with methanol to afford methyl 2‑chloro­benzoate and water. Standard method for preparing methyl aryl esters. Performed by refluxing methanol with catalytic sulfuric or p‑toluenesulfonic acid (≈60–80 °C); methanol serves as both reactant and solvent, and removal of water shifts the equilibrium.

Partial reduction of 2‑methoxybenzonitrile to 2‑methoxybenzaldehyde using diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H). Provides selective conversion of nitriles to aldehydes. Reaction carried out at –78 °C to 0 °C under inert atmosphere (dry THF or toluene) with 1.0–1.2 equiv DIBAL‑H; quench with methanol/water after completion.

Type: oxidative combustion/thermal oxidation. Purpose: conversion of MoSe2 to recover MoO3 and volatilize Se as SeO2; used in ore processing or material recycling. Key transformation: MoSe2 is oxidized, yielding MoO3 (solid) and SeO2 (volatile). Conditions: heating in air or O2 at 500–800 °C; flow of oxygen ensures complete oxidation. No solvent; reaction carried out in a furnace.

Synthesis of N‑(2‑chlorophenyl)thiourea via condensation of 2‑chloroaniline with carbon disulfide in basic aqueous medium, followed by acidification with HCl. Generates aryl thioureas used as ligands or building blocks. Procedure: cool aqueous NaOH solution, add CS2, then 2‑chloroaniline; stir at 0–5 °C, then acidify with HCl to precipitate the thiourea, producing water and NaCl as by‑products. No organic solvent required.

Hydrazone formation (condensation of an aldehyde with phenylhydrazine). The aldehyde function of L‑arabinose reacts with phenylhydrazine to afford L‑arabinose phenylhydrazone, eliminating water. Reaction conditions generally involve refluxing in ethanol or methanol (50–80 °C) with a catalytic amount of acetic acid or pyridine to promote nucleophilic attack and to neutralize the HCl from phenylhydrazine·HCl. The hydrazone serves as a protected form of the sugar and is useful for identification or further chemical manipulation.
Acid–base neutralization; CO2 is absorbed by aqueous NaOH to form sodium bicarbonate, a buffering solid. Typically performed in water at ambient temperature; no catalyst required.

Oxidation (N‑oxide formation); bis(trimethylsilyl) peroxide transfers an electrophilic oxygen to pyridine, yielding pyridine N‑oxide and trimethylsilanol as by‑product. Conducted in anhydrous aprotic solvents such as dichloromethane or THF, usually at 0 °C to rt, without additional catalyst.

Heterocycle‑forming condensation; thiosemicarbazide reacts with 2‑chloroacetaldehyde, cyclizing and eliminating water to give 2‑chlorothiazole. Commonly carried out by refluxing in ethanol or ethylene glycol (often with a catalytic amount of acetic acid) for several hours.

Ion‑exchange precipitation in solution; silver bromide reacts with tetraethylammonium chloride to swap halides, precipitating insoluble AgCl and forming soluble tetraethylammonium bromide; carried out in water or dry acetonitrile, protected from light, no additional catalyst.

Electrophilic addition of HCl to an alkene (Markovnikov addition); protonation of the double bond in (E)-3‑methylhept‑3‑ene followed by nucleophilic attack of chloride gives 3‑chloro‑3‑methylheptane. Usually carried out in dilute aqueous HCl or anhydrous HCl gas in a non‑polar solvent (e.g., CH2Cl2) at 0 °C to rt; no catalyst is required.

Redox reaction (oxidation of oxalic acid, reduction of permanganic acid); oxalic acid is oxidized to CO2 while Mn(VII) in permanganic acid is reduced to MnO2 precipitate, producing water as a by‑product. Conducted in strongly acidic aqueous solution (often concentrated H2SO4) with heating to accelerate the reaction; no external catalyst needed.

Electrophilic addition (hydrohalogenation) of HBr to a terminal alkene; converts the C=C of 2‑methyl‑1‑butene into a C–Br bond giving 2‑bromo‑2‑methylbutane (Markovnikov orientation). Usually carried out at 0–25 °C with aqueous or gaseous HBr in a non‑protic solvent such as dichloromethane; no catalyst required unless anti‑Markovnikov is desired.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1) of tertiary alcohol 2‑methyl‑2‑butanol using dry phosphorus pentoxide. Water is eliminated to afford the corresponding alkene 2‑methyl‑2‑butene. Typical conditions: 120–150 °C under anhydrous conditions, often neat or in a high‑boiling inert solvent (toluene); P₂O₅ acts as the dehydrating agent.

Partial reduction of an ethyl ester (ethyl pyridine‑4‑carboxylate) to the aldehyde (pyridine‑4‑carbaldehyde) using one equivalent of diisobutylaluminum hydride (DIBAL‑H). The reaction proceeds at –78 °C in anhydrous ether (THF or toluene) under nitrogen; after completion the mixture is quenched with methanol/water, releasing ethanol as the by‑product.

Oxidation of a tertiary am (N,N‑dimethyldodecylamine) its N‑oxide with dimethyldioxirane (DMDO). DMDO is generated in situ from acetone and Oxone and reacts at 0 °C to room temperature in acetone (often with a small amount of water) to give the N‑oxide; no additional catalyst is required.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction: fulminic acid reacts with aqueous AgNO₃, exchanging anions to give insoluble silver fulminate precipitate and nitric acid; carried out in cold dilute aqueous solution; no catalyst needed.

High‑temperature hydrogenation reduction of germanium dioxide to germanium monoxide with water as the by‑product. Conducted under H₂ pressure (10–50 bar) at 400–600 °C, typically over a metal catalyst such as Cu or Ni; the process occurs in the gas phase or in a sealed tube.

N‑alkylation of a primary amine (SN2) to afford a secondary amine; purpose is to form N‑ethyl‑butan‑2‑amine; key transformation is nucleophilic attack of ethylamine on the carbon bearing bromine of 2‑bromobutane, displacing Br⁻ and generating HBr; commonly carried out in anhydrous ethanol or THF at reflux using excess amine (which acts as base) or with a mild inorganic base such as Na₂CO₃ or K₂CO₃ to neutralize the produced HBr.

Acid‑base reaction of aqueous hydrofluoric acid with potassium silicate to form potassium fluoride, water, and fluorosilicic acid (H₂SiF₆). Performed in aqueous solution at ambient temperature; no catalyst is required, water serves as the solvent.

Selective ketone reduction of a β‑keto‑ester. Ethyl 3‑oxopentanoate (a β‑keto‑ester) is reduced by sodium borohydride to the corresponding β‑hydroxy ester (ethyl 3‑hydroxypentanoate). The ester carbonyl remains untouched. Reaction is carried out in a protic solvent such as methanol or ethanol at 0 °C to ambient temperature. After consumption of the ketone, the mixture is quenched with water and the inorganic by‑product (sodium metaborate) is removed by filtration.

Hydrolysis of an isocyanate; water attacks the N=C=O group of 4‑isocyanatobenzonitrile yielding 4‑aminobenzonitrile and carbon dioxide. Typically performed in aqueous solution at ambient or slightly elevated temperature; acid or base catalysts (e.g., HCl, NaOH) can accelerate the reaction.

Double‑displacement/precipitation reaction; aqueous potassium chromate reacts with zinc oxide and water to precipitate zinc chromate and generate soluble potassium hydroxide. Conducted in water at room temperature with stirring; no special catalyst required.

Peptide condensation (dehydration synthesis) of two glycine molecules forming glycylglycine and water; a peptide bond is formed between the carboxyl of one glycine and the amino group of the other. Usually carried out under dehydrating conditions or with coupling reagents such as DCC or EDC in aprotic solvents (DMF, DCM) and mild heating to drive off water.

Acid‑base hydrolysis of a metal nitride; three equivalents of hydrochloric acid protonate yttrium nitride, releasing ammonia gas and forming yttrium(III) chloride. Carried out in aqueous HCl at room temperature or with mild heating; gas is collected, solution contains YCl₃.

Acid–base ion exchange (metathesis); aqueous lead(II) acetate is treated with nitric acid, forming soluble lead(II) nitrate and acetic acid; conducted at room temperature in water, no catalyst required.

Acid‑base metathesis (salt exchange) – Sulfuric acid protonates the iodide salt MgI₂, producing soluble magnesium sulfate and liberating hydroiodic acid. Usually carried out in aqueous solution, often with gentle heating to drive off HI gas; no special catalyst required.

Salt formation (acid‑base neutralization) of pyridoxine with pyrrolidine dithiocarbamate to give the therapeutic salt metadoxine; typically carried out by mixing equimolar amounts in aqueous or alcoholic solution, gentle heating if needed, followed by removal of solvent to isolate the solid; no catalyst required; purpose is to combine a vitamin B6 analogue with a dithiocarbamate moiety for hepatoprotective activity.

Double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction between soluble potassium carbonate and sparingly soluble barium oxalate in water, producing insoluble barium carbonate precipitate and soluble potassium oxalate; generally performed at ambient temperature with stirring; no catalyst; used to exchange the anions and isolate barium carbonate.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of chloromethane by hydrogen sulfide (or its conjugate base HS⁻); forms methanethiol (CH₃SH) and HCl. Usually performed in aqueous or alcoholic solution with NaHS or Na₂S as a source of HS⁻, refluxed to drive the reaction; no additional catalyst.

Esterification via nucleophilic acyl substitution; an ethoxide ion attacks propionyl chloride to give ethyl propionate and NaCl. Typically carried out in anhydrous ethanol (or THF) at 0 °C to room temperature under inert atmosphere; no additional catalyst required.

General type: Base‑catalyzed ester saponification. Purpose: produce the water‑soluble sodium salt of p‑hydroxybenzoate, employed in formulation of soaps or as a precursor for further derivatization. Key transformation: hydroxide attacks the carbonyl of methylparaben, forming a carboxylate anion and liberating methanol. Typical conditions: aqueous NaOH (0.5–2 M) at ambient temperature or gentle heating (40–60 °C) for 30 min to 2 h. No organic solvent is required, though a small amount of ethanol or methanol can improve solubility. Catalyst: the hydroxide ion itself; reaction is usually quantitative.

Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis (cleavage) of methyl vinyl ether; purpose: convert a vinyl ether into carbonyl compounds; key transformation: proton‑assisted cleavage of the C–O bond of the vinyl ether giving acetaldehyde and methanol; typical conditions: aqueous strong acid (e.g., H₂SO₄) at 0–50 °C; common solvent: water or water/organic mixture.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of 3‑methyl‑2‑butanone to 3‑methyl‑2‑butanol; hydrogen gas is passed over palladium on carbon (5–10 % Pd/C) in a solvent such as ethanol, methanol or THF at 1–5 atm H₂ and 20–50 °C; purpose is the conversion of a ketone to the corresponding secondary alcohol.

Palladium‑catalyzed carbonylative amidation (Buchwald‑Hartwig type) of 1‑bromo‑4‑fluorobenzene with ammonia and carbon monoxide to afford 4‑fluorobenzamide with HBr as a by‑product; typical conditions: CO pressure 10–30 bar, Pd precursor (e.g., Pd₂(dba)₃) with tri‑tert‑butylphosphine ligand, base (e.g., Na₂CO₃), solvent such as toluene or dioxane, temperature 80–120 °C; purpose is formation of an aryl amide via insertion of CO.

Multicomponent condensation (Debus–Radziszewski imidazole synthesis); purpose: construction of the imidazole heterocycle from simple carbonyl and amine components; key transformation: condensation of two carbonyl groups (glyoxal, formaldehyde) with ammonia to form the imidazole ring with loss of water; typical conditions: reflux in alcoholic or aqueous medium, often in presence of a mild acid or ammonium acetate as catalyst; common solvents/catalysts: ethanol or methanol, sometimes acetic acid or ammonium acetate.

Redox/acid‑base reaction of zinc metal with ammonium chloride in water, generating ammonia gas, hydrogen gas and soluble zinc chloride; carried out by adding zinc to an aqueous NH₄Cl solution and heating (reflux) to accelerate gas evolution; no catalyst; used to liberate NH₃ and H₂ while converting Zn to Zn²⁺.

Halogen‑hydride exchange reaction of chlorine gas with lithium hydride producing hydrogen chloride gas and lithium chloride salt; performed in a dry inert solvent (e.g., THF or diethyl ether) at low temperature under an inert atmosphere to control exotherm; no catalyst; serves as a method to generate HCl and LiCl from solid reagents.

Ullmann-type copper‑catalyzed nucleophilic aromatic substitution (C–O bond formation). Aryl bromide (3,5‑dichlorobromobenzene) is hydrolyzed in aqueous NaOH with Cu₂O as catalyst to replace bromine by hydroxide, yielding 3,5‑dichlorophenol and NaBr. Typical conditions: reflux in water/ethanol mixture, Cu₂O (5–10 mol %) under aerobic atmosphere; solid product isolated by filtration.

Double displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction; aqueous barium selenite reacts with dilute sulfuric acid, exchanging anions to give insoluble barium sulfate precipitate and soluble selenous acid; performed in water at ambient temperature, no catalyst required.

Aqueous double‑displacement (metathesis) acid–base reaction. Phosphoric acid protonates samarium(III) nitrate, precipitating samarium(III) phosphate while generating nitric acid in solution. Usually performed at ambient temperature in water; the insoluble SmPO₄ is filtered off, and the filtrate contains HNO₃.

Thionation (halogen‑sulfur exchange) – Phosphorus tribromide reacts with elemental sulfur to give phosphorothioic tribromide (PSBr₃), inserting a sulfur atom into the P–Br bond to form a P=S functionality. Conducted under anhydrous, inert atmosphere (N₂ or Ar) at reflux in a non‑polar solvent such as carbon tetrachloride or chlorobenzene; no catalyst needed.

SN2 nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis); converts 2‑chloroethanamine to ethanolamine by replacing the chlorine with a hydroxyl group; purpose is to obtain the primary amino alcohol; typically carried out with aqueous NaOH (1–2 equiv) at reflux temperature; reaction medium is water or a water‑ethanol mixture, no additional catalyst required.

Hydrolysis of phenyl isocyanate to aniline with evolution of carbon dioxide; a nucleophilic addition of water across the N=C=O functionality followed by decarboxylation. The overall transformation converts PhNCO + H₂O → PhNH₂ + CO₂. Usually performed in aqueous media (or a water‑organic mixture) at ambient temperature or gentle heating; can be catalyzed by a weak acid or base to increase the rate. No organic solvent is strictly required.

Friedel‑Crafts acylation of benzene with ketene using aluminum chloride as Lewis acid catalyst. The electrophilic ketene (CH₂=C=O) forms an acylium ion complex with AlCl₃, which attacks benzene to give acetophenone after work‑up. Conditions: anhydrous AlCl₃ (1–2 equiv), dry solvent (CH₂Cl₂, CS₂, or nitrobenzene), temperature 0 °C to reflux, exclusion of moisture; quench with ice‑water to decompose the AlCl₃ complex.

Aqueous precipitation double‑displacement (metathesis) reaction. Lead(II) nitrate and rubidium hydroxide exchange ions, forming insoluble lead(II) hydroxide precipitate and soluble rubidium nitrate. Conducted in water at room temperature; the Pb(OH)₂ solid is isolated by filtration, while the filtrate contains RbNO₃.

Conversion of hexadecan‑1‑ol to 1‑bromohexadecane using phosphorus tribromide; a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) that replaces the hydroxyl group with bromide. The alcohol is treated with PBr₃ (1 equiv) in anhydrous dichloromethane or carbon tetrachloride at 0 °C to room temperature under nitrogen; the reaction mixture is then quenched with ice water and the organic layer washed to afford the alkyl bromide.

Acid‑base neutralization yielding a volatile acid. Sodium cyanide reacts with difluoroacetic acid to give hydrogen cyanide gas and sodium difluoroacetate. Performed in aqueous solution, often at low temperature (0–5 °C) to minimize HCN loss; the gas is captured or scrubbed, and the sodium salt remains dissolved. No catalyst required.

Acid‑metal reaction; furnishes praseodymium(III) fluoride and hydrogen gas. Pr(0) is oxidized to Pr³⁺ and HF provides F⁻, while protons are reduced to H₂. Conducted in aqueous hydrofluoric acid (often 5‑20 % HF) at ambient or mildly elevated temperature (0‑50 °C). Reaction vessels must be compatible with HF. No catalyst; water is the reaction medium.

This is a dehydration‑cyclization (condensation) of 4,5‑dimethyl‑o‑phenylenediamine with formamide to form 5,6‑dimethylbenzimidazole, releasing water. It is a common method for constructing benzimidazole heterocycles. Typical conditions: heating neat formamide or a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., DMF, DMSO) at 150‑200 °C, often in the presence of an acid catalyst such as polyphosphoric acid or HCl, under an inert atmosphere.

Decarboxylative de‑alkylation (thermal/metal‑mediated decarboxylation) of 4‑bromo‑phenylacetic acid to give 4‑bromotoluene and CO₂. Commonly achieved by heating the acid salt (e.g., potassium or copper salt) at 300–350 °C, or by treating the acid with copper powder or CuO as a catalyst under reflux in a high‑boiling solvent (e.g., quinoline). The reaction removes the carboxyl group as carbon dioxide.

This reaction is the complete combustion (oxidative degradation) of tetraethyllead in excess oxygen, producing carbon dioxide, water vapor, and lead(II) oxide. It is a high‑temperature oxidation used in analytical combustion or waste destruction. Conditions: flame or furnace, temperature > 800 °C, with a large excess of O₂; no solvent or catalyst required.

Oxidation; converts the aldehyde group of cyclopropanecarbaldehyde to a carboxylic acid, yielding cyclopropanecarboxylic acid. Typically performed with chromic acid (Jones reagent, CrO3/H2SO4) in aqueous acidic medium, often using acetone as co‑solvent, at 0 °C to room temperature.

Alkene isomerization (double‑bond migration); 1‑nonene is converted to the more substituted 2‑nonene by a catalytic process, commonly using solid acid catalysts (e.g., silica‑alumina) or transition‑metal catalysts (Pd, Rh) at 150–200 °C; reaction typically run in an inert hydrocarbon solvent or solvent‑free.

An acid‑base neutralization in which hydroiodic acid protonates yttrium hydroxide, yielding yttrium(III) iodide and water. The reaction proceeds readily in aqueous solution at ambient or mildly heated temperatures. No special catalyst is needed; the medium is typically water or a water‑methanol mixture.

Catalytic hydrogenation (reduction) of methyl hydroperoxide; converts to methanol and water; CH3OOH + H2 → CH3OH + H2O; performed with transition‑metal catalysts (Pd/C, Pt, Raney Ni) under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 50–150 °C; solvent typically alcohol or water.

A double‑displacement (metathesis) precipitation reaction where sodium hydroxide dissolves cadmium oxalate, forming soluble sodium oxalate and insoluble cadmium hydroxide, which precipitates. Conducted in aqueous solution at room temperature with stirring; the solid Cd(OH)₂ is filtered off. No catalyst required.

Menshutkin alkylation (SN2) of a quaternary ammonium precursor. Dimethylammonium acetate acts as nucleophile; methyl iodide alkylates the nitrogen to give tetramethylammonium iodide and acetic acid (from proton transfer to acetate). Performed in a polar aprotic solvent such as acetonitrile or acetone, often at 0 °C to room temperature and sometimes under reflux for complete conversion. No additional catalyst needed.

Nucleophilic substitution (SN2) of benzyl chloride by the trimethylsilyl anion (Na+ [Me₃Si]−) to give benzyltrimethylsilane and sodium chloride. Performed in an aprotic polar solvent such as THF or DMF under an inert atmosphere (nitrogen or argon), typically at 0 °C to room temperature. The reaction benefits from dry conditions but does not require additional catalyst.

Electrophilic halogenation/ether formation: hydrogen bromide reacts with formaldehyde and methanol to generate bromomethyl methyl ether (CH₃OCH₂Br) and water. The process is carried out by bubbling HBr gas into a cold methanol solution containing formaldehyde, usually at 0‑5 °C, often in an ether or dichloromethane solvent to control temperature and suppress side reactions. No catalyst is needed.

Acid‑catalyzed ether formation (condensation). Methanol and tert‑butanol are dehydratively coupled in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid, producing methyl tert‑butyl ether (MTBE) and water. Typical conditions: 60–80 °C, catalytic H₂SO₄, excess tert‑butanol as solvent; water is removed by azeotropic distillation.

Ester aminolysis (hydrazinolysis) to give a carboxylic‑acid hydrazide. Hydrazine attacks the carbonyl of ethyl furan‑2‑carboxylate, displacing ethanol and forming furan‑2‑carboxylic‑acid hydrazide. Conducted under reflux in ethanol or methanol (or neat hydrazine) for several hours; no added catalyst required.

Selective reduction of an aldehyde to a primary alcohol with sodium borohydride. 4‑Bromobenzaldehyde is reduced to 4‑bromobenzyl alcohol. The reaction is performed in a protic solvent such as methanol, ethanol, or a THF‑water mixture at 0 °C to room temperature, usually under inert atmosphere; the work‑up involves aqueous quench and extraction.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification; converts a phenol into its acetate ester, releasing water. Typically performed by heating 2,6‑dimethyl phenol with excess acetic acid in the presence of a strong acid catalyst (e.g., H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH) under reflux; common solvents are glacial acetic acid or toluene (for azeotropic water removal).

Acid‑base neutralisation (salt hydrolysis). Sodium 2,6‑dihydroxybenzoate is treated with aqueous hydrochloric acid, protonating the carboxylate to give free 2,6‑dihydroxybenzoic acid and forming sodium chloride in solution. Typically carried out at room temperature with dilute HCl; the product precipitates on cooling and is filtered.

High‑temperature halogenation (oxidative fluorination) of a metal silicide; fluorine gas attacks thorium silicide, converting thorium to ThF₄ and silicon to volatile SiF₄; conducted in a dry stream of F₂ at 400–600 °C in an inert carrier gas, no solvent.

Acid‑catalyzed Fischer esterification of a benzoic acid derivative. 4‑Mercaptobenzoic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of catalytic H₂SO₄, forming the ethyl ester (ethyl 4‑sulfanylbenzoate) and water. Typical conditions: reflux ethanol with 0.5–1 equiv H₂SO₄, removal of water (e.g., Dean–Stark) to drive equilibrium. Purpose: conversion of the carboxylic acid to its ethyl ester while retaining the thiol substituent.

Acidic precipitation of silica from a silicate salt. Potassium silicate solution is acidified with concentrated hydrochloric acid, converting silicate ions to silicic acid which polymerises and deposits as solid SiO₂, while potassium ions form KCl and water is generated. Reaction is performed in aqueous medium, often with gentle heating to aid silica gel formation; the solid is filtered and washed.

Catalytic hydrogenation of 4‑hydroxybutanal to 1,4‑butanediol; purpose is complete reduction of the aldehyde to an alcohol; key transformation is addition of H2 across the C=O bond; typically performed with a heterogeneous catalyst (Pd/C, Raney Ni, PtO2) in a solvent like ethanol, methanol or water under H2 pressure (1–5 atm) at 50‑100 °C; the metal catalyst facilitates the hydrogen transfer.

Complete combustion of a saturated hydrocarbon. Propylcyclohexane reacts with excess molecular oxygen under ignition temperature, yielding carbon dioxide and water as the only gaseous products. The process requires an open flame or spark, sufficient O₂ supply, and proceeds at high temperature (≥800 °C) with rapid oxidation of all carbon and hydrogen atoms.

Direct combination (oxidation) reaction forming sodium peroxide; oxygen inserts into sodium oxide lattice to give Na2O2. Typically carried out by heating solid Na2O in a stream of dry O2 at 300‑400 °C; no solvent or catalyst required.

Acid‑catalyzed dehydration (E1) of 3‑methylheptan‑2‑ol. Typically performed with strong acid such as H₂SO₄ or p‑TsOH, heated to 120–150 °C, often neat or in a non‑polar solvent like toluene. Eliminates water to afford the more substituted alkene 3‑methyl‑2‑heptene.
